title: Michigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweaters
excerpt:
Jane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with Canada

The CEO of a Michigan credit union is no longer employed the...
body_text:
Jane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with Canada

The CEO of a Michigan credit union is no longer employed there, according to the organization, after she posted on social media what appeared to be an AI-generated image of her and her family wearing sweaters emblazoned with the Donald Trump-associated words “Lake America”.

In the statement recently announcing that Jane Smith would no longer be its CEO, Family First Credit Union also apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused”.

Smith had been the chief executive officer of the Family First Credit Union when she posed for a family photo at the Detroit airport en route to Halifax, Canada. She reportedly used ChatGPT to edit the family’s sweaters to say Lake America, which since late August has been the name that Trump ordered the US’s federal government agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid the president’s trade war with Canada.

Smith then shared the image on Facebook on 11 September – the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the US – along with the caption: “Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will.”

The post ended with “Lol lol”. It went viral and then provoked backlash from people in Canada – where a portion of the lake is.

Those online users found it disrespectful, and the post has since been deleted according to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) News.

Many in the comments highlighted that the post was particularly insensitive, given Halifax’s role in hosting thousands of stranded airplane passengers who were diverted there when US airspace closed on the day of the 9/11 attacks.

As the controversy intensified, Family First Credit Union – based in Saginaw, Michigan – said it was reviewing the situation. Smith, meanwhile, apologized, expressing regret, maintaining that the post was the result of poor judgment and saying that she understood why it would be offensive.

“We weren’t trying to make a political statement,” Smith told the Detroit television news station WJRT. “However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun” at the changing of the name of one of the Great Lakes.

“I understand if I was someone in Halifax and I thought a poor group of people walked in wearing those sweatshirts, it is highly offensive and I would understand why they would be so angry,” she continued in her remarks to WJRT. “I am not a person that would ever want to offend or hurt anybody.

“I do regret having any post that would make someone feel like we don’t value them as human beings.”

Despite her apology, the credit union made it clear that it had parted ways with Smith.

“Jane Smith is no longer employed by Family First Credit Union, effective immediately,” said a statement from the organization shared on social media.

After saying Smith’s interim successor would be Jason Acosta, the statement continued, “We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.

“We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first.”

Family First Credit Union’s statement about Smith came after broader repudiation in Canada and beyond of Trump’s executive order changing Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America.

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, explained in a post on social media that the body of water’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people – and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US’s declaration of independence from the UK.

“Canadians … know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he wrote on X.

Several US governors in the US’s Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change. Michigan borders the Canadian province of Ontario along with four of the five Great Lakes.

The only one of the Great Lakes that Michigan does not border is Lake Ontario. New York is the only US state that Lake Ontario borders.

Trump’s order has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake. It also has no power to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.

title: Ex-American Idol contestant told lover he dreamed of killing wife, murder trial hears
excerpt:
Alleigha Botner tells court Caleb Flynn, charged with murder of wife Ashley Flynn, sent her AI love songs

The Ohio former pastor and American Idol contestant accused of fatally shooting his wife fant...
body_text:
Alleigha Botner tells court Caleb Flynn, charged with murder of wife Ashley Flynn, sent her AI love songs

The Ohio former pastor and American Idol contestant accused of fatally shooting his wife fantasized to his then lover about killing his spouse and sent her AI-generated love songs, according to evidence presented at trial this week.

Caleb Flynn, 40, is on trial for aggravated murder in connection with the 16 February shooting death of Ashley Flynn. He also is charged with two counts of felonious assault and three counts of tampering with evidence, according to a March indictment. Flynn has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Prosecutors say Flynn – motivated by a desire to be with his girlfriend, Alleigha Botner – shot his sleeping wife twice in the back of the head. He allegedly altered the crime scene to look like a deadly home invasion.

Flynn’s defense team has acknowledged the affair, but said at trial it does not make him a murderer. “A man can make selfish decisions without committing a crime,” defense attorney Emily Smith said.

Investigators recovered songs from Flynn’s phone, where he reflected on his friendship with Botner evolving into a romantic relationship.

“That first time I saw you the room disappeared, love at first sight even though I was scared,” a voice sang in a style reminiscent of Christian rock, according to video broadcast by Court TV. “Life is now empty, since the moment I lost you,” the song ended.

A second version with similar lyrics but delivered in a somber tone was also played to the court.

Botner was 20 when she met Flynn at their church, Botner testified. Flynn was 36 or 37 at the time.

“At first it was: I want her dead. I wish she was gone. And then it was: if I could kill her and not go to jail, I would. And one night, he was up really late – he told me he was thinking about ways to kill her,” Botner, now 24, said.

Flynn also repeatedly said he hated his wife in several texts to Botner.

During an August 2025 cruise to celebrate the married couple’s 15th wedding anniversary, Ashley Flynn found texts her husband had sent to Botner. She tried to arrange a coffee meet-up with Botner. Botner avoided the conversation, saying she was busy.

In January, Botner gave Caleb Flynn an ultimatum: leave your wife or it’s over.

At about this time, Flynn sent her the AI-generated songs.

On 14 February, two days before Ashley was shot, Botner testified that Flynn said he was getting a divorce and would finally be free of his wife, to which Botner said she did not believe him. “I told him that I don’t trust him and that I’m moving on with my life,” she said on the stand.

When Ashley Flynn was found dead, her sister Kayla Keyt did not have knowledge of the affair. She told police when Caleb was arrested that they had the wrong guy. “I trusted Caleb with everything I had in me … He was completely innocent. I really believed that with all of my heart,” Keyt said.

The FBI subsequently informed her of the affair.

Keyt said news of the affair made the couple’s two daughters “mostly broken-hearted for mommy”.

“They said she loved daddy more than anyone else in life. So why did daddy not love her as much?” she testified.

Flynn appeared briefly on American Idol’s 12th season in 2013, describing music as his passion and saying his wife nudged him to go on the show.

The trial, which is expected to wrap by the end of next week, will resume on Monday.

title: Trump and Chinese president Xi end summit without major agreement on AI
excerpt:
Xi’s state visit to the US emphasized personal rapport with the US president, rather than substantial agreements to pause their respective countries’ AI arms race

Donald Trump and Chinese president X...
body_text:
Xi’s state visit to the US emphasized personal rapport with the US president, rather than substantial agreements to pause their respective countries’ AI arms race

Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping wrapped up their Washington summit on Friday, facing criticism that they had squandered an opportunity to pause their countries’ artificial intelligence (AI) arms race.

The three-day state visit emphasised pageantry and personal rapport rather than substantial agreements. The US president and Xi discussed the wars in Iran and Ukraine and the status of Taiwan. Their biggest policy announcement was a modest two-month extension of a trade truce.

But despite the presence of top tech executives at a White House state dinner on Thursday night, Trump and Xi failed to deliver the AI breakthrough that some experts and foreign governments had hoped for amid warnings that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity.

“It was such a layup,” said Ro Khanna, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives’ select committee on China. “If [Trump] had just said, look, we have established technical working groups and we’ve agreed to a framework that has called for DeepSeek and Moonshot and Alibaba to sit down with Anthropic and OpenAI and Gemini and with technical experts and they’re going to commit to at least a pause on any self-improving AI, he could have looked like he was a statesman taking the lead.

“I believe Xi Jinping would have agreed to some of at least the technical working groups. But he [Trump] didn’t want to; he has no interest in doing that.”

It was the first visit to the White House by a Chinese president in more than a decade and Xi’s second state visit to the US. Three days of pomp and circumstance culminated on Friday with Trump and Xi drinking tea. Trump said ⁠the summit ⁠had produced great strides and that “our ​farmers are going to be happy,” but did not provide details.

The pair then went to the National Archives, where Trump and Xi looked at the original Declaration of Independence, the constitution and Bill of Rights. Trump told reporters they were comparing China’s documents to America’s founding documents. “Ours goes 250 years, which is great, and we’re proud of. Theirs goes 6,000 years. So there’s a little difference between 6,000 and 250. But we’re very proud of our 250.”

On Thursday, Xi acknowledged that the US and China have the “responsibility to develop and manage AI for good” and “ensure that the development of AI is always ​under human control”. China aims to have next-generation smart terminals and AI agents reach more than 90% penetration by 2030.

But Trump – who has repeatedly said the US must forge ahead to maintain its lead over China – appeared more focused on his push to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence”, later claiming on social media that Xi “seems to like” the term without divulging the substance of their discussions.

Later Trump hosted a black-tie state dinner attended by titans of the tech industry. Bernie Sanders, an independent senator of Vermont, used social media to label a photo of Trump and Xi’s table with guests’ net worth: Elon Musk of SpaceX and Tesla ($928bn), Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ($3.5bn), Jensen Huang of Nvidia ($186bn) and Tim Cook of Apple ($3.1bn). Sanders commented: “A government of, by and for the billionaire class.”

But their counterparts in the Chinese tech industry were not present and there was little sign of either country making even a symbolic gesture to apply the brakes.

Khanna commented: “Trump didn’t have to have some groundbreaking treaty like Reagan and Gorbachev did [on nuclear weapons]. He could have at least said, look, we’re going to have a working group of Chinese and American technologists working together to make recommendations and enforcement and verification of the labs.”

Jonathan Czin, a fellow in the China Center at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, agrees that an opportunity was missed. “We are in this potentially transformative moment for both countries and for the world and for technology and, instead of having a meeting that would meet the moment, you got theatre of the absurd in lieu of that,” he said.

“Even going into this meeting, you’re dealing with a septuagenarian and octogenarian who may or may not have ever had first-hand contact with actually using AI and what happens with this technology rests on their two shoulders. The only thing they seemed to agree about is that neither of them wants to slow down with this technology, regardless of their actual understanding of it.”

The state visit underlined the contrast between Trump’s treatment of democratic allies such as Canada and authoritarian rivals such as China. He broke from tradition to give Xi a red carpet welcome when he landed at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.

He also found time to show Xi around the White House, including a gallery wall of presidents where Joe Biden is mockingly depicted as an autopen, a construction site for his White House ballroom and a new helicopter landing pad. “He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite,” Trump said.

But the summit was somewhat overshadowed by Trump’s decision last week to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, sparking a legal fight. On Thursday, Chinese state media were welcomed into the White House grounds even as members of America’s free press were frozen out, though later they gained entry. As in May, when Trump visited Beijing, the leaders did not hold a press conference.

Czin of the Brookings Institution added: “I had very low expectations going into this meeting for anything of substance and the meeting managed to underwhelm even those low expectations. We went from the mezzanine down into the basement. In terms of the substance, it’s not clear to me what the US got out of this.”

Senate Democrats also criticised the summit, arguing that Trump failed to secure meaningful concessions from Beijing on trade, security, human rights or AI.

Chuck Schumer, the minority leader in the Senate, said: “As usual, Trump acts based solely on who flatters him at the moment, where the nearest photo op is, and what headline he covets. If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll greet you plane-side.”

Trump and Xi are on track to meet twice more this year. In November, Xi will host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, and in December the Group of 20 summit will be held at the Trump National Doral Miami golf club in Florida.

Ted Nugent is something of a modern-day Renaissance Man.

The one they call Uncle Ted is a rock god, a conservationist, an unabashed conservative voice and a hell of a hunter to boot.

And nowhere was that more evident than the latest picture Nugent posted to his social media page from one of his most recent hunts earlier this month.

Full disclosure, I trust the man who gifted us "Stranglehold," so when he said this buck was "100% real," I was inclined to believe him, but I ran this picture through some AI detectors just in case and he ain't lying.

Nugent is pushing 80 years old, but you wouldn't be able to tell based on this picture, as the man looks as full of life as ever and has an absolute trophy of a deer to show for it.

I guess that's what no drinking, no drugs and living off the land will do for you.

A portrait of musician Ted Nugent. (Getty Images)

He certainly lives up to his Motor City Madman moniker, that's for sure.

Clearly, hunting is something that is near and dear to Nugent's heart, so it's nice to see him going out and using his platform to bring some of these issues to a more mainstream audience.

title: Brandi Glanville emptied her 401(k) after spending ‘hundreds of thousands’ on medical bills

Brandi...
body_text:
Reality star Brandi Glanville explains why her recent financial strain made turning down opportunities more difficult and pushed her to prove she could perform again on FOX's "Special Forces."

Brandi Glanville needed a comeback — personally and financially.

After years of costly health struggles turned her life upside down, the former "Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" star told Fox News Digital she needed to get back to work.

"I had the leisure of saying no in the past, but then I had all these medical bills and whatnot," she admitted. "So I had to say yes. And it was kind of like at a time where I needed to prove to myself that I could do it again."

BRANDI GLANVILLE ENDS UP IN URGENT CARE AFTER TRYING VIRAL TIKTOK TREND

Brandi Glanville revealed that she emptied her 401(k) and spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on medical bills while searching for answers to her debilitating health problems.  (FOX via Getty Images)

But for Glanville, the financial fallout from her health battle has been just as daunting as the physical toll.

"The medical system here is broken," Glanville explained. "So I have, like, from 8 a.m. on, I have creditors from, like, medical things calling me, like from Cedars-Sinai. It's out of control. Like I spent hundreds of thousands of dollars that I had saved. I emptied my 401(k). And it's all for medical bills. And I had insurance, and they told me nothing was wrong. I'm so angry. You know, going into my mid-fifties I had a cushion and that's gone. So it's very scary right now."

After years of suffering, Glanville revealed in September that she had been diagnosed with highly resistant ESBL Klebsiella and Enterobacter with biofilm, coccidioidomycosis, also known as Valley fever, Demodex dermatitis and mononucleosis.

Glanville has said her daily IV treatment was expected to cost between $3,300 and $6,000 per month.

WATCH: BRANDI GLANVILLE SAYS HEALTH BATTLE FORCED HER TO SPEND ‘HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS'

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Brandi Glanville said her ongoing treatment for multiple infections and illnesses is expected to cost between $3,300 and $6,000 per month. (Getty Images/Brandi Glanville/TikTok)

Glanville previously shared that she believed she picked up a parasite after visiting Morocco in 2023. She suffered from facial paralysis and was initially diagnosed with stress-induced angioedema. She told Fox News Digital at the time that she spent more than $70,000 in an attempt to find an answer to the medical mystery that consumed her daily life and disfigured her face.

After everything her body had already endured, Glanville was determined to test her limits on "Special Forces: World's Toughest Test." One challenge pushed those limits further than she expected.

While filming the show, Glanville said contestants were trained on how to fall from a helicopter into the water. But moments before her jump, an instructor told her to keep her head up — a last-second direction she said left her little time to react.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Brandi Glanville also detailed suffering a perforated eardrum, concussion, bruised sternum and cracked rib after hitting the water during a helicopter challenge on "Special Forces." The show airs Thursdays at 9:00 p.m. ET on FOX. (Pete Dadds/FOX)

"My head hit the water. It was like a Mack truck – it, like, ran over my head. I thought that was it," she recalled. "And then a few seconds later, my body hits the water so hard. It was paralyzing almost. I was like, 'Oh my God.' But it was in slow motion."

The former "Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" star said she suffered a perforated eardrum, a concussion, a bruised sternum and a cracked rib — injuries that forced her to travel by boat to the hospital because doctors didn't want her flying. Glanville recalled battling an intense headache on top of the excruciating pain from her rib injury, which made it difficult to breathe or cough.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Brandi Glanville said the painful experience ultimately made her feel proud for pushing herself and completing the challenge. (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images for Rachel Strauss)

Once at the hospital, Glanville said doctors warned her she couldn't fly and told her she could be stuck there for at least two weeks and potentially need surgery. But after spending several days recovering and returning to the hospital for another evaluation, the reality star said she was determined to leave — even if doctors still weren't thrilled about her getting on a plane.

Battered but undeterred, Glanville said she still considered the experience a personal victory.

"Honestly, I'm so proud of myself. I feel like a badass, even though I didn't last long," she told Fox News Digital. "I went in, I conquered, I got hurt, and then I left and that was enough for me. "

"Special Forces: Worlds Toughest Test" airs Thursdays at 9:00 p.m. ET on FOX.

Fox News Digital's Tracy Wright contributed to this report.

title: Turning Point USA knew of security concerns yet insisted Charlie Kirk speak outdoors, report says
excerpt:
According to report, school staff recommended event move to a more secure location weeks before Kirk was fatally shot

A new report says that Turning Point USA insisted the conservative political grou...
body_text:
According to report, school staff recommended event move to a more secure location weeks before Kirk was fatally shot

A new report says that Turning Point USA insisted the conservative political group’s leader Charlie Kirk speak outdoors at Utah Valley University – where he was ultimately assassinated – despite security concerns raised with his team by the school’s leaders and its police chief.

The independent report with those findings was commissioned by UVU and released on Friday. The report examined security procedures leading up to the 31-year-old’s fatal shooting on 10 September 2025 during a talk at the university’s campus in Orem, Utah.

According to the 158-page report, school staff recommended Turning Point USA (TPUSA) move its event to a more secure location weeks before Kirk’s slaying. However, TPUSA “insisted upon” an outdoor location which “created significant protective operations considerations”, the report said.

It added that a face-to-face, pre-event briefing and walkthrough with UVU police chief Jeff Long and the TPUSA protection detail – including the organization’s security supervisor Dan Flood – “should also have occurred” on UVU’s campus hours prior to the event.

“Chief Long texted Dan Flood to meet on the Hall of Flags outdoor pedestrian walkway at 11[am], however, this face-to-face meeting did not occur,” the report said.

Kirk was shot and killed by a sniper that day in the early afternoon.

According to the report, the university also asked TPUSA for an estimated attendance figure. But the organization never provided one, despite saying it would control ticketing for the event, Utah’s Salt Lake Tribune newspaper reported.

“Based on our review of all available information, that at no time during the events leading up to the assassination of Charlie Kirk, or in its aftermath, did any employee or agent of UVU act in bad faith or in willful and wanton disregard for the safety of others,” the report said.

However, it also noted UVU’s having deferred to TPUSA on various event logistics. “Several key event security decisions were deferred to the TPUSA field representative even though UVU staff members raised concerns, including concerns related to holding the event in the outdoor fountain courtyard area and using TPUSA’s ticketing process,” the university’s report said.

“Those decisions placed the event in an area that was more difficult to control and limited UVU’s ability to obtain reliable, real-time information regarding anticipated attendance and crowd size.”

The report added: “UVU should have retained decision-making authority over key security-related issues, including venue selection, ticketing, access control and other conditions necessary to support campus safety.”

In response to the report, Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said: “UVU hosted this event, and in doing so, assumed responsibility for the safety of all in attendance, including Charlie. The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement.

“Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU’s fatal shortcomings that day.”

Meanwhile, a statement from Jon Anderson, UVU’s president, said the university had a responsibility to “learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations”.

“This requires humility, an honest examination of our policies and practices, and a commitment to act on what we learn,” Anderson’s statement also said.

Anderson, who became the university’s president in August, also said in his statement that UVU had made “meaningful progress in strengthening campus safety over the past year”.

Kirk’s family is planning to sue the university. His family alleged in a 16 September legal notice presaging wrongful death litigation that UVU had placed “a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event … surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms” – and that the setup was like “walking him into a fishbowl”.

UVU said it was aware of the notice and said it “addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes”, according to the Tribune.

Utah resident Tyler Robinson has been charged with aggravated murder in connection with Kirk’s killing. He has pleaded not guilty, and no trial date had been set for him as of Friday.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

excerpt: Kylian Mbappe scored the only goal of the game before having to come off grimacing with a knee injury, as France won 1-0 in Turkiye in the UEFA Nations League in new coach Zinedine Zidane’s first game...
body_text:
Kylian Mbappe scored the only goal of the game before having to come off grimacing with a knee injury, as France won 1-0 in Turkiye in the UEFA Nations League in new coach Zinedine Zidane’s first game in charge on Friday.

The Real Madrid star was moved out to the left wing by his new coach after being used through the middle of the France attack under former coach Didier Deschamps at the recent World Cup, which he ended as the top scorer with 10 goals.

It was from the left that Mbappe, France’s all-time top scorer, notched his 67th international goal, controlling and firing into the net low at the near post after being set up by Michael Olise.

He winced in pain as his teammates came across to celebrate the goal at the Kocaeli Stadium in Izmit, about 100km outside Istanbul.

Mbappe tried to carry on after receiving treatment, but eventually slumped to the ground and looked concerned as he prodded the outside of his left knee, before walking off to be replaced by Desire Doue.

France and Real will now nervously wait to discover the extent of the injury, with Les Bleus playing three more games over the next 10 days before the club season resumes.

The sight of his star player and skipper coming off overshadowed Zidane’s first match since being appointed coach in late July on a deal to 2030.

The France legend and 1998 World Cup winner is making his return to elite coaching for the first time since his second stint in charge of Madrid ended in 2021.

France, beaten in the semifinals at the World Cup by eventual winners Spain, are in Group A1 of this edition of the Nations League and will now go to Brussels to face Belgium on Monday. Belgium won 2-0 away to Italy on Friday.

Zidane, whose last match as a player came for France against Italy in the 2006 World Cup final, will then make his home debut as coach against the Italians at the Stade de France next Friday.

His first team selection was not dramatically different from the side that regularly played at the World Cup, although Bournemouth’s Adrien Truffert was in at left-back while Manchester City’s Rayan Cherki came into the starting XI.

Olise, the Bayern Munich star who lit up the World Cup, was unlucky not to open the scoring late in the first half when his superb strike was tipped over by home goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir.

France goalkeeper Mike Maignan responded at the start of the second half as he tipped over an attempt by Abdulkerim Bardakci for Turkiye, who finished bottom of their group at the World Cup, despite a 3-2 win over cohosts the United States.

Mbappe’s goal came shortly after, and the visitors later saw Jules Kounde hit the post before Turkiye were reduced to 10 men late on.

Cakir came flying out of his area to halt Bradley Barcola as the France substitute raced through on goal. German referee Felix Zwayer initially waved play on before undertaking a VAR review, after which he decided the goalkeeper had handled the ball, which meant a red card.

Turkiye, coached by former Italian international Vincenzo Montella, will host Italy next on Monday.

title: UK Prime Minister says football fans 'singled out' by alcohol ban not imposed on rugby matches
excerpt: Premier Lacrosse League co-founders Paul Rabil and Mike Rabil join award winners CJ Kirst and Mike Manley to discuss honoring 9/11 hero Welles Crowther. The group also teaches the 'Fox & Friends Weeke...
body_text:
Premier Lacrosse League co-founders Paul Rabil and Mike Rabil join award winners CJ Kirst and Mike Manley to discuss honoring 9/11 hero Welles Crowther. The group also teaches the 'Fox & Friends Weekend' hosts some basic lacrosse skills.

United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham is pushing back against England’s restrictions on alcohol at men’s soccer matches, calling the ban "discrimination" and suggesting the rules could be tested on a trial basis.

Burnham told reporters, "I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out," as he argued that they should not face restrictions that do not apply to spectators at other sporting events.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Under current laws, fans are prohibited from drinking alcohol in view of the pitch at stadiums hosting clubs in England’s top five tiers of men’s football. Those restrictions do not apply to other sports.

ANDY BURNHAM TAKES OVER AS UK PRIME MINISTER, CALLS FOR 'NEW POLITICAL MODEL'

Andy Burnham delivers his inaugural speech as UK's new Prime Minister on on July 20, 2026 in London, England. The Member of Parliament for Makerfield becomes the UK's 59th Prime Minister, succeeding Sir Keir Starmer, who resigned as leader of the Labour Party and Prime Minister in June. (Photo by Dan Kitwood/Getty Images) (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)

The Football Supporters’ Association, which advocates for football fans in England and Wales, has called for the "outdated" legislation to be reviewed. Police chiefs, however, have warned against relaxing the law and want to meet with Burnham to "explain the challenges."

The legislation dates to 1985, when it was introduced by Margaret Thatcher’s government for football grounds in England and Wales. Then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behavior" at stadiums.

Burnham’s connection to the sport is personal. He is a proud football fan and a season-ticket holder at Everton, the Premier League club.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham stand together before the English League Cup match between Everton and Wolverhampton Wanderers at Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool, England, on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Anthony Devlin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Prior to becoming the head of government of the U.K., Burnham spoke out against restrictions on football fans while attending a rugby league match at Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium. Unlike during men’s football games, spectators were allowed to consume alcohol in the stands.

While in New York City for the United Nations General Assembly, Burnham was asked whether his position had changed now that he was in Downing Street. "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different," the prime minister replied.

"And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis. But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."

Cardiff City fans attend the Premier League match against Newcastle United at Cardiff City Stadium in Cardiff, Wales, on Aug. 18, 2018. (Cardiff City FC/Getty Images)

Government sources told the BBC that Burnham was restating a long-held personal view rather than announcing a new government policy. Within government, however, the comments are not being interpreted as a sign that Burnham intends to change the law, according to the outlet.

A spokesman for the U.K. Football Policing Unit warned that changing the law could create new challenges for police and raise concerns about the "safety of staff and fans at football games."

The spokesman said: "Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behavior from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behavior."

FSA chairman Tom Greatrex pushed back against that argument, saying it was "unfair to criminalize football fans for having a pint while watching the match, especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol (while) watching an Oasis gig or rugby league."

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

England has already taken a different approach in the Women’s Super League, where all clubs can serve alcohol in the stands this season after two successful trial campaigns.

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

title: What would a US diesel export ban mean for global fuel prices?
excerpt:
Diesel prices have hit record highs as the tensions between the United States and Iran, along with the war between Russia and Ukraine, disrupt key oil and fuel trade routes.

On Friday, the average pr...
body_text:
Diesel prices have hit record highs as the tensions between the United States and Iran, along with the war between Russia and Ukraine, disrupt key oil and fuel trade routes.

On Friday, the average price for a gallon (3.79 litres) of diesel was $6.50, up from $5.61 a month earlier, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks fuel prices daily.

The spike has prompted the administration of US President Donald Trump and Republican lawmakers to consider restricting US diesel exports ahead of upcoming midterm elections.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in August found that 47 percent of voters said the cost of living was the single most important factor in deciding how they would vote in the midterms — more than twice the share who cited the next-most important issue, “democratic values and norms”.

A new Marist poll also found that Americans have more confidence in Democrats than Republicans to handle the economy, with 42 percent choosing Democrats compared with 34 percent for Republicans.

Amid that voter sentiment, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Thursday that he was in touch with major oil refiners to gauge interest in a potential voluntary restriction on diesel exports, according to the Reuters news agency.

That followed remarks by Trump on Tuesday that he supported restricting diesel exports from the US, the world’s largest diesel exporter.

Energy analysts and industry groups have warned that an export ban could have unintended consequences, potentially pushing up fuel prices in the US and abroad.

Even though the US is the world’s largest diesel exporter, diesel is traded on a global market.

Disruptions to refineries in Russia and the Middle East have reduced the amount of fuel available worldwide, putting more pressure on US producers to fill the gap. In Russia, for example, drone attacks have damaged major refineries, forcing a cutback or halt in production.

“While US refineries are running at full tilt and higher than normal, the global gaps remain,” Rachel Ziemba, senior adjunct fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.

It comes as US diesel supplies are also shrinking. As of September 11, inventories had fallen to 107.9 million barrels, the lowest in more than four decades, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

With global supplies tightening, diesel prices have risen around the world — including in the US. Because American producers can sell their fuel into the global market, they are drawn to the soaring global prices rather than simply setting a lower price for domestic consumers.

In Washington, DC, leaders have flirted with the idea of pushing US companies to stop or slow exporting diesel.

Republicans have been pushing for a slowdown or outright ban of exports in an effort to lower costs for consumers ahead of the pivotal midterm elections, where cost of living is becoming a critical issue.

Such a move, they hope, would reduce local diesel prices, which is significant as diesel is used in trucks to haul food and most products, Ziemba said, adding that US diesel exports are equivalent to about 40 percent of domestic consumption.

On Tuesday, Chuck Grassley, a Republican from Iowa, called on the president to put in place a temporary halt on exports.

“I encourage President Trump to put a temporary embargo on diesel exports through executive action,” Grassley said.

Republican Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska made a similar call: “The cost of diesel is just too damn high. I’m calling for a temporary pause of American diesel exports so that we can rebuild our reserves ahead of winter,” Sullivan said in a statement on Tuesday.

In the House of Representatives, Congressman Tim Burchett of Tennessee introduced two bills that would restrict US diesel exports: One would impose a ban through January 2027, while the other would restrict exports if the national average price reaches $5 a gallon.

The administration has not made any official policy announcements, and the White House told Al Jazeera that the president is evaluating all options.

Oil and gas industry experts say that a ban could drive up prices rather than bringing them down.

“Diesel trades on a world market, just like corn. farmers don’t sell cheaper to Americans, and refiners can’t either since they buy crude at global prices. force a lower price and they’ll make less diesel. less supply means higher prices, not lower,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X.

A ban would prevent or restrict US refiners from selling diesel to buyers overseas, theoretically leaving more fuel available in the domestic market.

Analysts at Wood Mackenzie, a research and consulting firm, say that keeping more diesel stateside would ultimately fill up US storage tanks but also force refineries to cut production. That could affect other markets that rely heavily on US fuel, including Latin America and Europe, forcing them to compete with other global buyers for supplies and driving up prices for the global market.

Wood Mackenzie says China is the only major producer with enough spare refining capacity to potentially make up much of the shortfall.

“China is currently the only country with material spare refining capacity that could cover the loss of US refinery throughputs. However, China may well decide it is not in its interest to intercede,” analysts said.

Wood Mackenzie has warned that a ban could quickly fill US diesel inventories, forcing refiners to cut crude runs and potentially increasing US petrol imports.

That was also the view of an S&P Global analysis, which found that a complete ban could also mean that production would be reduced as storage capacity is filled up with unsold diesel. According to the analysis, that could lead to production cuts of as much as 750,000 barrels a day, which could put the US into being a net importer of petrol in the fourth quarter of this year.

An export ban would affect US refiners and consumers, as well as countries that rely on US diesel.

“They [export bans] may provide temporary relief, but diesel is a global commodity. Treat one part of the system, and the effects travel elsewhere. Trade-offs are inevitable. Refiners are unlikely to cheer a blanket ban. Voluntary, controlled export reductions would generally be less disruptive in the short term,” Maksim Sonin, visiting scholar at Stanford University’s Precourt Institute for Energy, told Al Jazeera.

Disruptions to US exports could reduce the amount of fuel available on the global market. Wood Mackenzie analysts say countries in Europe and Latin America that rely heavily on US fuel could be forced to compete with other producers for supplies.

“If implemented, it would lead to European and Asian product prices increasing as the buyers of US fuel, mostly in Latin America, scramble to find new supplies, bidding up supplies. European crack spreads could widen, and overall we might see more disruptions,” Ziemba added.

“Given these issues, the US may opt for a mixture of carrots and sticks aiming to incentivise refineries to keep producing, perhaps including penalties if they cut production. There may be voluntary export quotas rather than a formal ban, and there may be exemptions for countries that provide crude oil to the US, like Mexico,” Ziemba said.

That could put pressure on consumers not only at the petrol pump but in the skies as well.

Airlines for America, an airline industry trade group, has also warned that an export ban could lead to higher prices for airlines and travellers, according to the Reuters news agency. The trade group did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

The broader concern from analysts is that restricting exports could reduce US refinery production rather than simply redirecting diesel to US consumers, potentially putting upward pressure on fuel prices both domestically and internationally.

“It’s unlikely to help US consumers much given how it fails to solve underlying problems and could backfire if refineries hold on to production. The best way to address this is to end the conflicts prompting the shortages,” Ziemba said.

title: Florida GOP nominee blasts 20-year Dem incumbent as a 'socialist' rubber-stamp with 'precious little to show'
excerpt:
The FL-14 GOP hopeful takes aim at the 10-term incumbent's record, accusing her of empowering radical policies and refusing to debate ahead of November.

Calling out federal waste and foreign aid subs...
body_text:
The FL-14 GOP hopeful takes aim at the 10-term incumbent's record, accusing her of empowering radical policies and refusing to debate ahead of November.

Calling out federal waste and foreign aid subsidies while pointing to his own record of bucking party leadership in Tallahassee, GOP 14th congressional district nominee Mike Beltran promises to bring a sharp litigator’s cross-examination to Washington’s budget crisis.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital detailing his bid to unseat 20-year Democratic incumbent Kathy Castor, the former Florida state representative laid out a case rooted in strict fiscal accountability, pledged to challenge even Republican leadership on bloated federal budgets, and warned of the Democrats' embrace of socialism.

(Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

HOUSE CONSERVATIVES UNLEASH MULTIMILLION-DOLLAR MIDTERM BLITZ AGAINST DEM 'SOCIALIST' INSURGENCY

Beltran argues that despite her lengthy tenure on Capitol Hill, the people of Tampa Bay have not been served well by Kathy Castor.

"People in Tampa Bay have precious little to show for Kathy Castor's two decades of incumbency. She's had no major legislative initiatives. All she's really done is rename post offices. And all that's likely to happen if we reelect her is for her to rename every post office from Tampa to Timbuktu.

"She votes with her party over 90% of the time, including radical socialists. She voted in lockstep with Nancy Pelosi and she's poised to elect the Speaker Hakeem Jeffries. And Speaker Hakeem Jeffries would appoint a Chair Raskin, a Chair Omar, a Chair Cortez, and those folks would push radical policies in Congress that are completely out of line with what Tampa families need."

Beltran argues that in the Florida Legislature he served as an independent conservative voice, not automatically beholden to party leadership, and pledges to continue that approach in Washington.

"I've had the courage to vote against special interests even when my own party had lost its way. I've voted against insurance companies, home builders, trial lawyers, I voted against various special interests…whenever somebody was doing something that wasn't good for Tampa families.

"And I had that bipartisan record throughout my time, starting in 2019 and continuing through to 2024, unlike my opponent who discovered bipartisanship merely weeks ago. So I'm always going to do what's best for the communities that I represent, regardless of party, regardless of special interests, regardless of pressure. And that's what I'm proud of, having that independent voting record."

Rep. Kathy Castor, D-Fla., takes her seat for the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party hearing in the Cannnon House Office Building on Tuesday, January 30, 2024.

Beltran argues that the United States needs to reexamine its military and geopolitical relationships, with an eye to fiscal prudence:

"It cannot be a one-sided exchange. You cannot have a wealthy country like Germany spend under 2% of GDP on their military when we're spending over 5% of our GDP on our military budgets, about a trillion dollars. And a lot of that is spent overseas protecting other wealthy countries.

"You see Ukraine and Israel, they're defending themselves from their adversaries. They're doing a good job of that. But we are borrowing $2 trillion a year from countries like China. And that's causing inflation. And what that says is that we don't have money to be sending, particularly to wealthy allies like Germany and Spain.

"These are countries where we have bases, where we've had trouble getting basing privileges or overflight rights for the conflicts that we do need to engage in. And we shouldn't be subsidizing them anymore.

"You see Israel spends over 10% of GDP on defense, as does South Korea. Those countries are carrying the weight of their own defense, but we don't see that from all of our NATO allies. And they're a lot closer to these rogue states, to these conflict regions than we are. They should be doing more, and they're doing less, and that's unacceptable."

As an attorney, Beltran makes the case that he will bring a strong skill-set to Capitol Hill, to do away with business as usual and to fight for the citizens of Hillsborough County:

The US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Sunday, May 18, 2025. (Alex Wroblewski/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"My legal skills are quite good. I'm a good cross examiner. I'll be good at scrutinizing witnesses who come before committees that I serve on. I've litigated in the federal courts, so I know the federal statutes. I know issues that need to be redressed. I know how to write statutes so that they can be easily applied by judges, so that attorneys can counsel their clients on what the law is and what they need to do to comply with that.

"I'm proud to be a practicing attorney. I've helped a lot of businesses and individuals throughout Tampa Bay for almost 20 years.

FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY

"And my opponent is also an attorney, but she hasn't practiced in a very long time. She was, I think, a land use attorney, she says, before she was a county commissioner. But I don't think she brings that same skill-set. I've never seen her cross-examine a witness to any effect. And I haven't seen her apply her legal skills to any legislative initiative. In fact, it's kind of difficult to identify anything that she's enacted that's of any particular value to Tampa or otherwise."

Kathy Castor has repeatedly voted against the interests of ordinary Americans in Florida's 14th district, Beltran argues:

"Well, she opposed tax cuts for the middle class and working class and retirees. She opposed removing taxes on tips, removing taxes on Social Security, removing taxes on overtime.

"And she wanted to pay, through taxpayer funds, for trans surgeries for children. And that was a very recent vote. That wasn't something that we have to reach into ancient history to find. And I opposed that.

"I see no reason why a single mother here in Hillsborough County should be paying taxes to pay for trans surgeries for minors while she actually is being taxed on her overtime or her tips."

Beltran pledges to confront the leadership of his own party if he disagrees with their policies, but also notes he will work with Democrats:

AOC claimed Charlie Kirk's "rhetoric and beliefs were ignorant, uneducated and sought to disenfranchise millions of Americans." (Fox News)

"Obviously, we've had Republicans who have also spent too much money. And so I'm going to go to Washington. I'm going to work with my party, and I'll work across the aisle, and I'll work with any administration that's in power to identify waste, fraud, and abuse, identify unnecessary government programs, identify savings, and identify cost controls, and make sure that we are the fiscal conservatives that we say we are.

"That's what's necessary to save this country because we need to balance the budget and we need pay down the debt and we need to live within our means, because if we don't balance our budget, then the budget will be balanced for us and it will be done when somebody cuts off our credit and people stop lending to us."

Finally, as democratic socialist candidates have won Democratic primaries across the nation and in Florida, Beltran notes that Castor has consistently refused to condemn socialist ideology, or candidates with such views in her own party.

"We see Kathy Castor, who's embraced Angie Nixon, who is one of those avowed socialist candidates. She said that her party was a big tent party, and that needs to be a very big tent to accommodate Angie Nixon…I'm not sure I'd like to be in a tent of any size with her, but my opponent welcomes her with open arms.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, a Democrat from New York, during a news conference at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday, March 19, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"And she's going to vote in lockstep with these socialists, first to elect Hakeem Jeffries and then to appoint these socialists to committee chairmanships. She's done very little to distance herself from the radicals within her party. Even as she masquerades recently as a moderate, she will empower the socialists.

"And that's really what's at stake in November. It's not just me, it's not just Kathy Castor, it is the direction of the country and whether we're going to embrace these radical policies, or whether we are going to have economic growth and prosperity and safety here in the United States."

David Unsworth reports on Latin America. You can follow David Unsworth on Twitter @LatinAmerUpdate

title: Brewery that offered free beer when Trump dies faces possible closure after state revokes alcohol permits
excerpt:
A Google Map image of the Minocqua Brewing Company in Minocqua, Wisconsin, taken on an unknown date. (Google Maps)

The owner of Minocqua Brewing Co. said Monday that the Madison taproom in Wisconsin ...
body_text:
A Google Map image of the Minocqua Brewing Company in Minocqua, Wisconsin, taken on an unknown date. (Google Maps)

The owner of Minocqua Brewing Co. said Monday that the Madison taproom in Wisconsin will likely shut down by the end of the year after state officials revoked the company’s alcohol permits.

Channel 3000 reported that Minocqua Brewing Co. owner Kirk Bangstad said the Madison taproom is likely to shut down as the business continues fighting the state’s decision.

The brewery has become known for its outspoken messaging against President Donald Trump.

WISCONSIN BREWERY THAT OFFERED 'FREE BEER' WHEN TRUMP DIES SAYS ALCOHOL PERMIT REVOKED

A split image of the Minocqua Brewing Company and its owner, Kirk Bangstad. Photos taken on unknown dates. (Google Maps; Facebook/Minocqua Brewing Company)

The Wisconsin Department of Revenue (DOR) revoked brewing permits for the company’s Minocqua and Madison locations after alleging violations involving beer transported from Illinois without the required permits and tax payments. The brewery has disputed the state’s action and accused officials of targeting it because of its political views.

The department told Fox News Digital in a statement Thursday that there is a hearing on the company's appeal on Nov. 18, and that the revocation does not take effect until appeals are done, adding that the "DOR is dedicated to fair and consistent enforcement of alcohol beverage regulations in Wisconsin and takes action when the laws are not followed, as occurred here."

Bangstad’s breweries have made headlines for offering free beer if President Trump dies.

On Jan. 22, the Minocqua Brewing Company appeared to suggest it would give free beer to patrons if Trump was killed, and while not explicitly using his name, posted on Facebook, "Free beer, all day long the day he dies."

'FREE BEER' FOR TRUMP DEATH DEM ACTIVIST RUNNING FOR WISCONSIN GOV: 'I WILL WIN' IF THEY SILENCE ME

The Minocqua Brewing Company is under fire again for explosive calls for political violence against President Donald Trump. (Minocqua Brewing Company/Facebook)

"Show us this post when it happens in a few months and we’ll make good on that promise," the post continued.

The post was updated to say, "We meant the Madison Taproom because that’s open all year, if he dies in the summer, then it’s gonna be the Minocqua Taproom."

In reply to comment on the post, the company also did not refer to Trump by name but said the message referred to a high-profile figure when asked whether the timeline for the deal could be moved up earlier.

After the April shooting at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner where Trump was present, the company wrote on Facebook, "Well, we almost got #freebeerday."

KENTUCKY GOVERNOR SAYS HE RECEIVED 2 CALLS FROM AGENCIES INDICATING MCCONNELL HAD 'PASSED'

The Minocqua Brewing Company in Wisconsin has a history of pushing progressive politics. (Screenshot/Google Earth)

The brewery also offered half-price beer when Sen. Mitch McConnell dies.

"When they announce that McConnell’s Faustian dance has finally ended, we’re gonna start serving our beer at ‘half price,’ because we promised #halfpricebeerday on the day they unplug the ventilator," the brewery said in an Instagram post.

McConnell, who is 84, was absent from the Senate for months after being hospitalized for a fall in his home earlier this year. The Kentucky Republican returned to the Senate last week ahead of key votes.

Bangstad, who owns the brewery, is also the founder of the Minocqua Brewing Company SuperPAC, which "aims to remove Republican federal and state elected officials who perpetuated the election lies that caused the Insurrection of January 6, 2021, and whose downplaying of the seriousness of COVID-19 caused so many unnecessary deaths in our country," according to the brewery’s website.

Reached for comment by Fox News Digital, the brewery made disparaging remarks about Trump and again noted that it will host a "#freebeerday" when the president passes.

"Reminder, however, no red hats allowed," the brewery added.

Rachel del Guidice is a culture reporter for Fox News covering the intersection of politics, faith, family, and American culture.

title: Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial database to check voter citizenship
excerpt: The US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration to use a controversial federal database that uses citizenship information and other sensitive data to identify voters suspected...
body_text:
The US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration to use a controversial federal database that uses citizenship information and other sensitive data to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens.

Critics have questioned the reliability of the data, warning it could  result in US citizens being wrongly removed from electoral rolls.

In June, a federal judge ruled that the system was illegal and violated the privacy rights of Americans.

But the top court's conservative majority ruled that the National Voter Registration Act prohibits broad purges of voter rolls in the weeks before an election, which limits any "potential impact" of the decision ahead of the midterms.

But states can still check the citizenship of individual voters.

The three liberal-leaning justices on the Supreme Court dissented from the majority decision.

One of the dissenting Supreme Court justices, Ketanji Brown Jackson, expressed concern that this could mistakenly revoke the voting rights of eligible voters.

"The harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the non-existent harm that the government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take," she wrote.

The Department of Homeland Security programme, known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (Save), allows officials to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls.

The database was first created in 1986 to help officials verify the citizenship or immigration status of those applying for public benefits.

But the Trump administration last year expanded its search capabilities by allowing bulk searches using sensitive information from Social Security rolls.

In June, however, US District Judge Sparkle L Soonnan - a Biden-appointee - ruled that the revamped system shows that the federal government "knowingly trampled on the privacy rights" of US citizens "in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote".

A federal appeals court allowed her ruling to stand, only to be overridden by the Supreme Court on Friday.

The top court ruled that a 1996 law allows DHS to seek citizenship and immigration data from federal agencies, and has "an obligation to respond" to states seeking that information.

The use of the Save programme by individual states is voluntary.

The previous judge's order, the Supreme Court ruled, "prevents the federal government from using the programme it believes is best suited to the task".

Voting rights groups called the ruling "profoundly disappointing".

"...it puts millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration's unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections," the League of Women Voters, the lead plaintiff in the case, said in a statement.

"We will be doing everything in our power to protect Americans' voting and privacy rights by ensuring that the district court decision stands," it said.

Lawyers for the Trump administration have long argued that the system is lawful and necessary to prevent non-citizens from voting. A total of 27 states currently use the system to check voter citizenship.

Critics, however, have pointed to a number of cases of the system already having led to mistakes.

For example, officials in Travis County, Texas, found that of nearly 100 voters identified as non-citizens, at least 10% of them - and potentially more - were US citizens, according to US media reports.

Since the state began checking its voter rolls with the Save system last year, only three non-citizen voters have been charged with illegally voting in Texas.

Some states, like Georgia, have worked with the government on the Save programme.

Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican, has touted his office's work with the programme and his recommendations to improve the system.

Raffensperger told the BBC his office thoroughly vetted the government-provided data  to determine whether flagged individuals were non-citizens, even interviewsing some of the voters in question to ensure accuracy.

"There's always guardrails in place, to make sure that we never denied the right to vote," Raffensperger said.

Since returning to the White House in January last year, the Trump administration has sought to reform the US electoral system, a process that has included a bid - rejected by the Supreme Court - to reign in mail-in ballots.

In 2024, for example, Texas Governor Greg Abbott announced that 1,930 people with a "voter history" had been removed from electoral rolls out of a total of nearly 18 million registered voters.

The figures are far below the hundreds of thousands of non-citizen voters that Trump and the Department of Homeland Security have previously suggested were on voter rolls.

Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

title: New Jersey lieutenant governor resigns after sexual harassment accusation
excerpt:
Investigation determined Dale Caldwell violated state ethics rules and engaged in harassing behavior

Dale Caldwell, the lieutenant governor of New Jersey, resigned from his position on Friday, after ...
body_text:
Investigation determined Dale Caldwell violated state ethics rules and engaged in harassing behavior

Dale Caldwell, the lieutenant governor of New Jersey, resigned from his position on Friday, after the release of a report accusing him of sexually harassing a female staffer, among other ethics violations.

New Jersey’s governor, Mikie Sherrill, announced on Friday afternoon that Caldwell had submitted his resignation to her earlier in the day.

The decision by Caldwell, 66, came one day after Sherrill called on him to step down after an investigation determined he violated state ethics rules and engaged in behavior that constituted sexual harassment.

The 61-page report said it found credible evidence that Caldwell made romantic advances toward a female staffer’s friend, tried to secure a promotion for his girlfriend and gave tickets to personal guests without reimbursement.

The New Jersey Globe was the first to report on Caldwell’s resignation.

Sherrill, a Democrat, said she would appoint the state’s acting comptroller, Shirley Emehelu, as the acting lieutenant governor.

The change-up comes just weeks before midterm elections, which the lieutenant governor is responsible for overseeing.

The New Jersey governor initiated an investigation into Caldwell in May after receiving an anonymous letter that accused him of “bringing uninvited female guests to events while traveling using taxpayer funds” and “hitting on women at functions”.

Ultimately, investigators concluded that aspects of the allegations were credible.

In one instance, investigators said Caldwell made a romantic advance toward a female staffer’s friend and then made a “derogatory or demeaning reference” about women after his advances were rebuffed.

Caldwell allegedly told the staffer that women like them were ambitious and successful and needed a man in a position to help them, “but you young women are looking for young sperm”.

Investigators also found that Caldwell advocated for the promotion of his girlfriend, a state employee, to a “senior leadership position”. Caldwell acknowledged that he did not disclose the nature of his relationship with the state employee until he was confronted.

Caldwell had pushed for his girlfriend’s promotion, even after being informed he was under investigation. Ultimately, she did not get the promotion and no longer works in state government.

Credible evidence also determined Caldwell brought at least three personal guests, including his girlfriend, to ticketed events, in his capacity as lieutenant governor, without advance authorization or payment.

After Sherrill announced the report’s findings and called for Caldwell to resign, it was unclear whether or not he would step down.

A lawyer for Caldwell initially called the investigation “one-sided” and said the report’s findings were “palpably deficient and create a dangerous and challenging precedent for anyone who wishes to defend against anonymous conjecture and character assassination”.

As lieutenant governor, Caldwell was also serving as New Jersey’s secretary of state, who is the chief elections officer.

body_text:
Sports Talk takes a shocking turn when a caller informs Cal that he is the latest recipient of the Nobel Prize.

The NHL is still working through its preseason, and already we have a candidate for the worst penalty of the year, and possibly ever.

The Philadelphia Flyers hosted the Boston Bruins in their penultimate tune-up before their season-opener against their arch-rivals, the Pittsburgh Penguins.

Now, the Broad Street Bullies came out on top in this one, 2-0, but that wasn't the story. Instead, all of the talk after the game had to do with Flyers forward Trevor Zegras getting a minor for delay of game for "improperly wearing equipment."

MLB TELLS UMPIRE DOUG EDDINGS HE MADE A MISTAKE IN DEMANDING CARDINALS PITCHER STRAIGHTEN HIS HAT

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Zegras hopped over the boards to take a faceoff with the back of his jersey tucked into his pants. Most of us wouldn't think twice about it, but an official saw it and sent him to the sin bin.

That's because this season, officials have been told to crack down on players not wearing equipment properly, and technically, he was.

But that doesn't make it any less absurd.

MASSACHUSETTS YOUTH HOCKEY PLAYER SUSPENDED AFTER VICIOUS SLASHING INCIDENT GOES VIRAL

Flyers star Trevor Zegras was dealt a penalty for tucking the back of his jersey into his pants. (Photo by Len Redkoles/NHLI via Getty Images)

At the risk of sounding like a certain cartoon sports radio host, it used to be that tucking your sweater into your pants was the cool thing to do.

According to The Athletic, Zegras confirmed after the game that he had been issued a warning before he was given the penalty, which is in line with the rulebook. Had he done it again, it would've been a game misconduct.

Head coach Rick Tocchet mentioned afterward that the league had given a heads-up about this push — which focuses on everything from visors to neck guards to, of course, jerseys — a few weeks earlier.

Trevor Zegras and the Flyers defeated the Boston Bruins 2-0 on Thursday in Philadelphia. (Kyle Ross-Imagn Images)

"They told us, in all fairness, two, three weeks ago," Tocchet said. "I didn’t even think about it. … Obviously, can’t do it anymore. Regular season starts, we can’t have a penalty like that. I actually had to put (forward Matvei Michkov’s jersey) down on the bench."

Hey, rules are rules... but nothing says preseason like the league picking a rule that never gets enforced to the point that most of us forgot it existed, and then dropping the hammer.

title: Airport X-ray reveals shocking illegal stash concealed beside passenger's Xbox

TSA officers rec...

Airline industry expert Gary Leff of Texas breaks down an incident involving two passengers who acknowledged attempting to sneak a prohibited item past security at Dallas Love Field.

TSA officers recently made an unexpected find inside a passenger's checked bag after an Xbox triggered an alarm.

The unusual discovery was announced by the Transportation Security Administration (TSA).

The incident occurred this month as a passenger was moving through the TSA line at LaGuardia Airport (LGA) in New York City when an alarm went off.

TSA OFFICER SEES ALARMING SHAPES ON X-RAY BEFORE STOLEN CIVIL WAR MYSTERY UNRAVELS

"The bag alarmed on an Xbox gaming system, and TSA Officer Ashley Leo, who was manning the on-screen resolution area, diverted the bag to the checked baggage resolution area, where Supervisory Transportation Security Officer (STSO) Christopher Ramos was stationed," the TSA said in a statement.

It's what Ramos found beside the Xbox that stood out.

The incident took place at LaGuardia Airport in New York City, pictured above, where TSA officers screen passengers and baggage. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

As he searched through the bag, he discovered "a plastic bag containing several fake IDs next to the Xbox that prompted the alarm," per the TSA.

"I noticed various driver’s licenses with different dates of birth and different class types, but all with the same photograph," Ramos said in a statement.

AIRPORT X-RAY SHOWS TERRIFYING OBJECT TAPED IN CARRY-ON TO SKIP CHECKED BAGGAGE FEE

"I was focused on following our screening procedures and paying close attention to anything that appeared unusual."

He added, "When I discovered the fraudulent IDs, I knew it was important to report the situation through the proper channels."

A passenger was arrested at LaGuardia Airport after TSA officers discovered multiple fake IDs while screening a checked bag. (TSA)

After involving TSA management, airport officials and Port Authority police, authorities confirmed the IDs were fraudulent and arrested the passenger moments before he was scheduled to board his flight.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"STSO Christopher Ramos’ strict adherence to standard operating procedures, diligence and situational awareness prevented the fraudulent IDs from entering the airport’s secure area," TSA LGA Federal Security Director John Essig said in a statement.

While searching the bag, an officer (not pictured) discovered several fake IDs in a plastic bag next to the Xbox that had triggered the alarm, according to the TSA. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images; Getty Images)

"Identifying fraudulent IDs is an important part of TSA’s layered security approach. It helps ensure that people entering secure areas of the airport are who they claim to be and supports the safety of the traveling public."

Fox News Digital reached out to TSA for further comment and details.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The incident comes amid a string of unusual discoveries by TSA officers at airports across the country.

TSA officers at LaGuardia Airport, which is pictured above, discovered several fraudulent IDs after an Xbox gaming system triggered an alarm inside a passenger's checked bag. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

In Texas, TSA officers at Dallas Love Field Airport recently discovered a pocketknife concealed inside a tube of toothpaste during routine carry-on screening.

Also, recently, TSA officers at Tampa International Airport in Florida discovered a 4-inch, double-edged knife concealed inside a baseball bat-shaped flashlight.

Kelly McGreal of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.
