title: Two-year NHS waiting times reveal system’s struggle with rise in ADHD and autism awareness
excerpt:
NHS assessment bottlenecks have knock-on effects, leading to delays in medical help and lack of access to specialist support

That NHS boards have imposed minimum two-year waiting times for attention ...
body_text:
NHS assessment bottlenecks have knock-on effects, leading to delays in medical help and lack of access to specialist support

That NHS boards have imposed minimum two-year waiting times for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism assessments shows a health service struggling to deal with the consequences of huge changes in understanding of and social attitudes to these conditions.

Sharp rises in referrals for clinical assessments over the past six years mean nearly 1 million people in England are on ADHD waiting lists, with the average wait already over a year (64 weeks). About 295,000 await an autism assessment.

Formal diagnosis has grown in recent years, slowly from the early 2000s and rapidly since 2020. Between 2020 and 2022, annual incidence of autism diagnosis in three- to 25-year-old males rose from 185 to 580 per 100,000, and from 45 to 320 in females.

The lengthening waiting lists tell a tale not only of an NHS under financial strain and short of key staff, but also one of deepening distress for many patients and families for whom diagnosis is the key to clinical treatment and other forms of support.

The explosion in diagnosis reflects the role of the NHS as a crucial gateway for a range of social support. If assessment bottlenecks mean it cannot deliver timely clinical assessments, this has serious knock-on effects; delays not just in medical help but in access to specialist support in schools or financial support through disability benefits.

This trend has caught public services by surprise, causing alarm at the Treasury and triggering a bitter culture war that on one side derides this trend as the product of faddish and woke overdiagnosis, and on the other is hailed as the belated recognition of genuine conditions with real-life challenges for individuals.

The interim report of a government-commissioned review into these trends by Peter Fonagy, published earlier this year, did not take sides. “Unmet needs, misdiagnosis and concerns about over-medicalisation can coexist in the same system,” he wrote, with a nod to the raging culture war debates.

What was not in doubt was that more people were experiencing distress, especially younger people, he concluded, and more people were seeking help as a result. Thresholds for referral had lowered, driving more referrals into an NHS poorly equipped to deal with the rise in demand.

That increase in part reflected improved clinical understanding and greater recognition of unmet needs, especially in previously underdiagnosed groups such as girls and young women. “Some groups that were historically under-identified are now entering the services in greater numbers,” the report said.

Diagnosis was also driven by institutional demand, whether in schools or the benefit system. It operates as what Fonagy describes as the “practical mechanism through which individuals obtain access to support, adjustments or formal recognition” – or what culture warriors disdain as the “golden ticket”.

The bigger picture driving increases in referrals for diagnosis includes a variety of other factors: the impact of the pandemic, economic insecurity, greater public awareness and a decline in stigma surrounding ADHD and autism.

Fonagy is expected to deliver his final report in the next few weeks. He has shown why the NHS is under huge strain coping with the rise in referrals for autism and ADHD. His next task is harder: to recommend ways of fixing the system.

title: ‘Devastating’: council rejects Frome residents’ bid for regeneration project
excerpt:
Locals raised £1m for Mayday Saxonvale scheme involving homes and park but Somerset officials agreed deal with London-based real estate company

A bold bid by residents of a progressive town in the En...
body_text:
Locals raised £1m for Mayday Saxonvale scheme involving homes and park but Somerset officials agreed deal with London-based real estate company

A bold bid by residents of a progressive town in the English West Country who raised almost £1m to create what could have been the UK’s largest community-led regeneration project is in tatters.

More than 1,000 residents of Frome in Somerset had clubbed together with the aim of building homes, workspaces, a riverside park and a lido on a brownfield area in their town centre.

But rather than selling the 5-hectare (12-acre) site to the community-led Mayday Saxonvale project, Somerset council has agreed a deal with a real estate investment company based in Soho, central London.

The announcement of the preferred bidder’s identity at a packed meeting in Frome town hall was greeted with shouts of “who?”, “shame on you” and “stitch-up”. Some of those who had worked on the Mayday project for more than five years were in tears.

The Liberal Democrat-led council said it hoped the prospective owners would work with Frome residents but admitted the sale was unconditional.

Some local people fear that rather than providing the sort of mixed development with a generous proportion of affordable homes they envisaged, the prospective owners will be free to build expensive riverside houses and lucrative accommodation for elderly people.

“It’s devastating news,” said Sara Butler, a Frome town councillor. “So many people have worked so hard on trying to ensure this site is developed with the best interests of Frome. It’s been a town-wide mission and this is a slap in the face.”

Frome is famed for its independent, renegade spirit and the leader of the town council, Fiona Barrows, said the idea of the Mayday plan had been to create homes that local people could afford and places where they could work.

She said the town council would work with the prospective owners but criticised the transparency of the process. “Saxonvale is simply too important to Frome to be treated as an ordinary land disposal,” she said.

Susie Jenkins Temple, who had got together with friends to put money up for the Mayday project, said it had been an extraordinary effort. “Across Frome, people reached into their own pockets because they believe this place matters,” she said.

Many local people suspect Somerset council’s executive had decided who to sell the site to before it met at Frome town hall on Wednesday to hear last-minute appeals from the townsfolk.

The way the identity of the successful bidder was revealed added to residents’ suspicions that the meeting was little more than a PR exercise.

Within two minutes of Somerset council announcing the identity of the preferred bidder – Newcore Capital – at the end of an impassioned meeting, it had issued a full press release on the deal. Less than 15 minutes later, Newcore released its own press release.

Paul Oster, an executive director of Mayday Saxonvale community benefit society, said the chance to create the UK’s largest community-led regeneration project had been lost.

The council argued it could not be sure Mayday had the full funds for the project. However, as well as the money invested by local people, Mayday had secured £1.2m from the social impact fund Resonance – the largest investment it had offered. Mayday said it had other investors interested. It is thought the agreed sale price for land was about £3m.

Jon Rolls, the head of developing communities at Resonance, said that without local ownership there was a “real danger” that Saxonvale would become another regeneration scheme done to a community, rather than by and with that community.

He said: “The people of Frome haven’t simply expressed an opinion. They organised behind this vision and invested their own money.”

Other Newcore projects include a 3.2-hectare (8-acre) site in east London, where the plan is to build a new supermarket, community health centre and childcare facilities alongside 1,047 new homes, and a care home and retirement living apartments on a brownfield site in Cambridge.

In its statement, Newcore said it was committed to working closely with the people of Frome “to understand local aspirations, discuss the opportunities and constraints and work collaboratively to develop the plans in partnership with the community”.

It added: “Emerging proposals are likely to include a range of new homes, intergenerational accommodation, community facilities including space for local artists, open space and new car parking.”

title: NSW cop asked friend ‘what would you do if I told you I killed somebody’ before alleged murders, court told
excerpt:
Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington terrace in early 2024

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking n...
body_text:
Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington terrace in early 2024

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beau Lamarre-Condon asked a friend, “What would you do if I told you I killed somebody?” nine months before allegedly murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, a Sydney court has heard.

The New South Wales police officer then assured the friend he hadn’t killed anyone, before admitting he had entered Baird’s house while he was away, before stealing a Polaroid camera and eating an Easter egg.

Lamarre-Condon has been accused of fatally shooting Baird, 26, and his partner, Davies, 29, with a police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

The 31-year-old has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Georgia Cook, a close friend of Lamarre-Condon, told the NSW supreme court on Friday that the policeman had become “infatuated” with Baird during their brief relationship.

When the relationship ended in April 2023, Cook said Lamarre-Condon continued to speak about Baird.

He asked her a concerning question when they went to dinner a month later, Cook told the jury.

“One of the first things he said was, ‘What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?’” she told the jury.

Cook told Lamarre-Condon she wouldn’t help as she didn’t want a ghost haunting her, the court was told.

Lamarre-Condon laughed it off and said: “Don’t worry I didn’t do that, but I did do something crazy.”

Cook told the court the policeman said he had been watching Baird from outside his home, including on one occasion when he had friends over.

Lamarre-Condon saw Baird and his friends take photos using a Polaroid camera the officer had given him as a gift, Cook said.

When the group left Baird’s home, Lamarre-Condon had seen where the house key had been placed, Cook said.

“He had got the key, unlocked the door, stole the Polaroid camera and ate Jesse’s Easter egg,” she said on Friday.

Lamarre-Condon would travel to Baird’s home in his mother’s car and wear a black hoodie so he wouldn’t be recognised, the court was told.

The policeman and Baird began seeing each other again briefly a few months later.

But Baird ended the relationship in November 2023 after the accused went through his phone and deleted messages from other men. Lamarre-Condon was “really upset”, according to another one of the officer’s friends, Shae Davison.

Lamarre-Condon asked to stay at her house because he did not want to be alone, Davison told the jury.

The police officer arrived at her home with a backpack the next day and asked to send a message from her Instagram to Baird as “one last try to win Jesse back”, she told the court.

But Lamarre-Condon did not want her to read the message, claiming there were medical details he did not want her to know.

She didn’t want to do it initially but said: “He put a lot of pressure on me, he said he never asked anything of me, he’s so upset, can I help.”

“He wore me down,” Davison said on Friday. “It felt like guilt-tripping to me and using my friendship to get what he wanted.”

She agreed, on the condition Lamarre-Condon read out the text to her, while leaving out the medical details.

When he read out the message, she asked him to delete parts that weren’t true, and it looked like he was typing and actioning her edits, she told the court.

He then sent the note in a series of messages, and told her she was allowed to read it after 4 December 2023, when he told her he was set to undergo surgery. He left her home about an hour after he arrived.

The 1,600-word Instagram note claimed Davison had gone to Westmead hospital with Lamarre-Condon.

“He was told he had a cancerous tumour growing in his left shoulder joint/ligament area,” the text read out in court stated.

“Worst-case scenario, it could result in … possibly having his arm amputated.

“He was then immediately subscribed [sic] numerous medications … everyone knows these medications are some of the strongest you can be subscribed, which throw off your hormones massively, which throws off how a person can act in their day to day life.”

The friend told the jury she had not attended the hospital with Lamarre-Condon, nor did he clear this part of the text with her.

The messages tried to justify the officer going through Baird’s phone and stated “this is very out of character for him”.

“There is real love there, trust can be built back on that,” the note purportedly from Davison stated. “Even if you guys never hang out again, I know Beau wants to make things right.”

The friend was unsure if Baird read the messages but said it was possible he had seen them through Instagram’s preview function. Lamarre-Condon later asked her to unsend the messages.

She obliged and tried to ask him about the content of the messages but he did not want to talk about them.

“He was quite annoyed, I could tell in his voice he was frustrated that I had [read them],” she said.

It’s alleged Lamarre-Condon began planning to murder Baird in early 2024.

The defence team has claimed the police officer was acting in self-defence after he disguised himself as an Uber Eats driver and entered Baird’s home on the day of the shootings.

The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

title: Pakistani forces kill Afghan Taliban fighters in border escalation
excerpt:
Pakistan has foiled an “attempted Afghan aggression” on the Pakistan-Afghan border.

Pakistani security sources said several Afghan members of the Taliban were killed in an intermittent exchange of fi...
body_text:
Pakistan has foiled an “attempted Afghan aggression” on the Pakistan-Afghan border.

Pakistani security sources said several Afghan members of the Taliban were killed in an intermittent exchange of fire in the Gulistan area of the border on Friday and that fighting was ongoing.

There has been no official confirmation from either country involved.

The Afghan government said on Thursday that it would deliver an “appropriate response” to Pakistani air attacks on 10 locations in Afghanistan earlier in the day.

The strikes were in response to a “deliberate and unlawful incursion into Pakistan by drones” on Wednesday, Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said on Thursday.

Tarar said in a post on his X account that Pakistan’s aerial and drone attacks hit “terrorist hideouts and support infrastructure including drone launching and storage sites”.

He also posted a video said to show the military strikes on the Afghan sites.

Afghanistan’s government spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid said the air strikes targeted Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces.

Taliban officials denied that their government launched drones against Pakistan on Wednesday.

The air raids on Thursday were carried out amid growing tensions between the former allies over attacks by armed groups in Pakistan, which triggered their worst fighting in years in February.

Islamabad accuses Kabul of harbouring fighters who stage cross-border attacks, but Afghanistan’s government denies harbouring anti-Pakistani armed groups and says the attacks are Pakistan’s internal problem.

The escalation threatens mediation efforts by China, Turkiye, Qatar and Saudi Arabia to broker a lasting peace between the two neighbours.

title: UMass Dartmouth football murder suspect overstayed tourist visa, received deferred action: federal sources
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Nigerian national accused of killing a UMass Dartmouth football player entered the U.S. on a tourist visa and overst...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Nigerian national accused of killing a UMass Dartmouth football player entered the U.S. on a tourist visa and overstayed it before receiving deferred action under both the Biden and Trump administrations, multiple federal law enforcement sources told Fox News.

Chukwunonso Uzoma David Uzoma Eze is charged with murder in connection with the stabbing death of UMass Dartmouth football player Marvins Antoine, 19, during an altercation in Providence, Rhode Island, over the weekend.

A second player, Kensley Macean, 19, suffered stab wounds to his head and neck and was taken to Rhode Island Hospital, according to the Providence Police Department.

Sources told Fox News that Eze first entered the U.S. on a B-2 tourist visa in 2015.

INDIAN NATIONAL ACCUSED OF ARIZONA GIRLFRIEND'S MURDER ENTERED US ON STUDENT VISA: FEDERAL SOURCES

Chukwunonso Uzoma David Uzoma Eze entered the U.S. on a tourist visa in 2015 and later remained in the country after his authorized stay expired, multiple federal law enforcement sources told Fox News. (Providence Police Department; kickstand)

Eze received two extensions on his visa under the Obama administration before remaining in the country after his authorized stay expired, according to the sources.

Sources said the Biden administration approved Eze's request for deferred action in September 2022.

He applied for deferred action again in February 2025 and October 2025, with the latter request approved under the Trump administration on Oct. 8, 2025, according to the sources.

Deferred action is a discretionary decision by the federal government to temporarily delay an individual's removal from the United States. It does not provide lawful immigration status.

DHS said Eze applied for employment authorization in August 2023, but the request was rejected the following month.

‘CRIMINAL ALIEN’ DUO CHARGED IN DEADLY CONNECTICUT HOME INVASION AS DHS MOVES TO YANK GREEN CARDS

Nigerian national Chukwunonso Uzoma David Uzoma Eze is charged with murder in the fatal stabbing of UMass Dartmouth football player Marvins Antoine, 19, in Providence, Rhode Island. (Providence Police Department)

He applied again for employment authorization in February 2025 based on deferred action, and DHS said that application remains pending.

If convicted of murder, Eze will lose his deferred action, according to DHS.

According to Providence police, the stabbing took place at about 12:30 a.m. Saturday in the parking lot outside Mezzo Lounge.

Police said the incident stemmed from an altercation involving people who had been inside the lounge before the stabbing.

Antoine was killed after a stab to the chest, while Macean suffered stab wounds to his head and neck.

Two UMass Dartmouth football players were stabbed during an altercation in Providence, Rhode Island, leaving one dead and another hospitalized, police said. (kickstand)

Eze was later located and taken into custody by the UMass Dartmouth Police Department, police said.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: Xi got Trump's red carpet welcome - but not everything he wanted
excerpt:
Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go?

President Xi Jinping's summits with Donald Trump have one clear aim.

China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise ...
body_text:
Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go?

President Xi Jinping's summits with Donald Trump have one clear aim.

China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan.

On this visit, however, despite Trump rolling out the red carpet for him, the Chinese leader didn't get everything he wanted.

The trade truce that saw both countries pause a tit-for-tat tariff war and prevent a further escalation, was extended by only a few months - from November to January.

Beijing had hoped for at least a year as Xi looks to ride out the remainder of Trump's presidency.

This means key disputes on tariffs, China's dominance on rare earth supplies and access to advanced US chips are being kicked forward into yet another round of negotiations.

This suggests the US wants China to do more to fulfil its side of the bargain before offering longer-term concessions.

Trump and Xi attend a dinner at the White House

The uncomfortable truth for Xi is that his domestic economy is in trouble. While the country sells a record number of goods around the world, consumers at home are holding back. Youth unemployment remains stubbornly high and property prices have slumped in a country where 80% of people own their own homes.

Trade is helping to prop up growth, making access to overseas markets more important than ever. Xi needs to protect those exports from the kind of debilitating tariffs the US imposed last year.

On Taiwan, Xi once again made clear that US arms sales to Taiwan are a red line for China.

The US is bound by law to provide the self-governing island with the means to defend itself.

In May, Xi warned Trump that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict".

Trump then delayed the approval of a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, describing it as a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing.

Xi may have seized on that opening during the talks and likely argued that restraining support for Taiwan reduces the risk of conflict.

On Thursday he reiterated his hope that the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence.

However,  Trump - who is coming under some bipartisan pressure to continue US support to Taiwan - is yet to make any public response to the Chinese leader's comments.

The two leaders did at least discuss artificial intelligence (AI) although it's unclear whether they agreed to any safeguards.

All eyes were on whether they would make any concrete decisions on AI - such as an agreement to hold a summit - in the wake of an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for the slowing down of AI development to make it safer. That followed a warning by a top safety researcher from the company that there was a "greater than 10% chance" that AI could cause the extinction of humans.

But besides Xi talking about the importance of ensuring AI "is always under human control" we didn't get much else. Trump has most recently dismissed fears of human extinction from the technology as a "hoax".

And, of course, let's not forget the pandas. The gift of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to Atlanta was first heralded in April, but Xi has now announced they will arrive in just a few days as China's panda diplomacy resumes.

There may be more announcements to come as the two prepare to have tea and visit the national archives on Friday.

Pandas have played an important role in Chinese diplomatic measures

But for now, one of the summit's biggest victories for Beijing may have been the optics.

The lavish welcome, a personal greeting at the airport and a state banquet featuring sesame crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy have been welcomed by those watching from China. It will have helped cement Xi's image at home as Trump's equal.

Memes contrasting the two leaders have spread widely on Chinese social media. One popular image shows Trump grimacing as bomber jets fly overhead, while Xi remained impassive.

Xi has found a way to manage one of the world's most unpredictable leaders. But while Trump talks of a "truly great friendship", China's leader is focussed on something bigger: securing China's place alongside the United States as a superpower.

The pandas, the pageantry and the warm words may help smooth this relationship. But beneath the spectacle, the competition between the world's two most powerful countries remains as fierce as ever.

title: Packers' shocking blowout loss to Falcons should put coach Matt LaFleur on the hot seat
excerpt: Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, Kevin Wildes and Greg Jennings discuss whether it is too early to panic over the Green Bay Packers' collapse, then break down the Philadelphia Eagles' first win under a n...
body_text:
Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, Kevin Wildes and Greg Jennings discuss whether it is too early to panic over the Green Bay Packers' collapse, then break down the Philadelphia Eagles' first win under a new offense. They then break down whether they are buying stock in the Cincinnati Bengals and react to Myles Garrett going on IR. (00:00) Intro
(00:30) Packers Collapse
(04:40) Eagles' First Game with New Offense
(10:28) Buying Stock in Bengals?
(14:36) Myles Garrett to IR
(19:43) MNF Prediction

The Green Bay Packers finally opened Lambeau Field for the first time this regular season, where they hoped to make it 14 straight home openers where they’ve come away with a victory on Thursday night against a struggling Atlanta Falcons team.

Instead, the Packers were blown out by an 0-2 team on their home turf, and now a big question arises.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Should head coach Matt LaFleur be on the hot seat?

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur takes the field before a game against the Atlanta Falcons at Lambeau Field on Sept. 24, 2026, in Green Bay, Wis. (Getty Images)

LaFleur signed a multi-year contract extension at the beginning of this year, which wasn’t considered a "prove-it deal," per ESPN. But what happened in this 35-14 loss certainly warms his seat as the Packers fall to 1-2 to start the year.

It wasn’t just this performance, either. In Week 1, a second-half collapse resulted in a Vikings victory to open the season. Then, the Packers were close to falling to the New York Jets on the road in a game they were heavily favored. It took overtime in rainy conditions to escape New Jersey with a 20-17 win.

As for Thursday night’s performance, it was more of the same that was seen in the first two weeks: a lack of diversity between the run and pass games, poor offensive line play and quarterback Jordan Love not being able to handle the pressure in his pocket.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The sold-out Lambeau Field crowd was raining down boos and jeers from the stands throughout this contest, as Love and his receivers couldn’t get on the same page, drives stalled and the Falcons started to find their offensive spark now that Michael Penix Jr. was finally healthy enough to play.

Oh, and Bijan Robinson once again proved why he is one of those rare NFL talents with his ability to totally take over a game when he has the ball in his hands.

Before we get to the Falcons’ positives in this game, back to LaFleur’s situation in Green Bay. Since last year, including the Wild Card Round, the Packers are just 1-7 in their last eight contests. As the fan base collectively shakes their heads at the start of this season, and audibly shows their frustration at the first home game of the season, could the thought of keeping sustainability at the head coach position change in Green Bay?

LaFleur entered his eighth season with the Packers this year, and he is the only active head coach that has been with his team that long and not reached the Super Bowl. Yes, it’s still early in the season, but just food for thought.

On the other sideline, there were tons of smiles, and none more infectious than that of Robinson, who finished the game with 194 rushing yards and two touchdowns. All week long, the Packers preached stopping Robinson, understanding that’s exactly what happened in Weeks 1 and 2, when the Falcons struggled to get anything going on offense.

Bijan Robinson of the Atlanta Falcons celebrates with Olamide Zaccheaus after scoring a touchdown against the Green Bay Packers during the first quarter at Lambeau Field on Sept. 24, 2026, in Green Bay, Wis. (Getty Images)

Well, Robinson torched this Packers defense with chunk runs, including a 55-yarder, and that also made life easier for Penix’s return under center.

The Falcons’ signal caller, whom they wished could’ve been healthy to start the year but hadn’t been fully recovered from his torn ACL in 2025, found his rhythm after opening the game with an interception on Atlanta’s first drive. The Falcons drew up quick passing plays for Penix to get going, and once the Packers had to respect Robinson’s running ability, play-action passes were Penix’s bread and butter.

Most of them went to Drake London, who also had his breakout game of the season. Like Robinson, he also had 194 yards, though through nine receptions, including a 68-yard catch-and-run that sealed the deal in the fourth quarter for the Falcons. He may not have had a touchdown, but this was the performance Penix needed after not finding anything with Cooper Rush in the first two games of the year.

Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur runs onto the field before a game against the Atlanta Falcons at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wis., on Sept. 24, 2026. (Getty Images)

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

For the Falcons, perhaps they simply needed competent quarterback play all along, and new head coach Kevin Stefanski can put together wins now that he has one in place, especially if the defense continues to play the way they did in an incredible performance.

But for the Packers, tough questions need to be asked already this year because it seems to be picking up where it left off in the worst ways possible.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Young men flee Tigray amid fears of forced recruitment
excerpt: Tigray, Ethiopia – Gebru, 27, says he was taken from his neighbourhood to a local administration office with other young men. His parents feared he would be sent to fight and searched for a way to get...
body_text:
Tigray, Ethiopia – Gebru, 27, says he was taken from his neighbourhood to a local administration office with other young men. His parents feared he would be sent to fight and searched for a way to get him out. They eventually paid to secure his release, he says.

“I was taken to the office with other young men. My parents found a way to get me released by paying 20,000 [Ethiopian] birr ($123) in cash.”

After he was released, Gebru left Tigray for Addis Ababa.

“My parents were afraid that if I stayed, I would be taken again. They told me to leave Tigray and save myself.”

Gebru is among young men who say they are leaving Tigray because they fear being forcibly recruited to fight as political and military tensions rise in the northern Ethiopian region.

Nearly four years after the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement ended the war between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), reports of forced recruitment and military mobilisation have raised fears among young conflict survivors that they could once again be drawn into fighting.

The African Union-brokered agreement ended two years of war in Tigray, but key issues – including contested territory, the return of displaced people and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces – remain unresolved.

Human Rights Watch reported in July that Tigrayan authorities and forces had forcibly recruited civilians, including children as young as 15, since at least April. The organisation documented cases involving former combatants and other men and boys who it said were taken from streets, homes, workplaces and gold-mining areas.

The allegations come as tensions between the federal government and the TPLF have risen, with both sides accusing the other of military mobilisation. Heavy fighting was also reported near Ethiopia’s border with Sudan in August.

For some young men, the response has been to leave.

Shewit, 24, had been trying to rebuild his life after the war. He was studying at Mekelle University, running a language-class business he had started about a year earlier and helping to look after his younger siblings.

But as reports of recruitment and military mobilisation increased, he said staying in Tigray began to feel unsafe.

“I had already survived one war. I didn’t want to go through another,” he told Al Jazeera.

He eventually left for Addis Ababa, leaving behind his family, his studies and his business.

“I left behind my siblings, who depended on me, and a business I had sacrificed so much to build.”

He says he does not want to return unless he can bring his family with him.

“I don’t want to go back. In fact, if I can, I want to bring my family and my siblings here with me.”

Gebrehiwot, 28, is still in Tigray. He fought during the previous war but says he does not want to return to the battlefield.

He says the experience changed the way he viewed the war’s political and military leadership, particularly after seeing wounded fighters and families of dead soldiers struggle after the fighting ended.

“We were told that we were fighting for our people, but after the war ended, I saw wounded fighters and families of the dead being abandoned.”

He says reports that former combatants were being called back increased his fears.

“Former combatant friends were being called back to the army and I heard some had been taken away forcibly. I was afraid I would be next, so I left my hometown and moved to Mekelle, hoping I would not get identified here.”

Unlike Shewit and Gebru, he has not left Tigray. But he says his experience of the previous war makes the prospect of another mobilisation difficult to contemplate.

“I know what the battlefield looks like. I don’t want to go back there and risk not coming home.”

Human Rights Watch says the recruitment allegations extend beyond former fighters to civilians and young people.

“We found that both former fighters but also civilians – young men, sometimes boys – were being abducted, detained,” said Laetitia Bader, the organisation’s Horn of Africa director. “Sometimes in the streets, in marketplaces, also in mining areas which is an important form of livelihood in the region.”

Bader said Human Rights Watch had documented cases involving minors as young as 15.

The organisation also said a mobilisation proclamation introduced in June criminalised desertion and attempts by relatives to prevent loved ones from being conscripted.

For young people who survived the previous war, Bader said, the reported recruitment was another reason to flee.

“The forced conscription continues to have an impact. Young people continue to try to flee the region not only because of the forced conscription but also the devastating humanitarian situation in the region,” she said.

The TPLF has disputed allegations of forced recruitment, saying young people were joining voluntarily. TPLF spokesman Michael Asgedom previously described the allegations as a “mistaken narrative”.

Al Jazeera contacted Asgedom for a response to the allegations in this story, but he did not respond to calls or text messages.

Muauz Gidey Alemu, an assistant professor of political science and lead researcher at the Tigray Institute of Policy Studies, said the recruitment should be understood within a broader political and security crisis that followed the Pretoria Agreement.

“The emergence of forced conscription at this particular moment should not be understood simply as a military recruitment exercise,” he said. “It is better understood as a symptom of the deeper political and security crisis that has developed around the incomplete implementation of the Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement.”

Gidey said the agreement had stopped large-scale fighting but had not resolved all the political and security issues surrounding the post-war period.

“The present situation demonstrates that Pretoria produced an effective cessation of large-scale warfare but an incomplete peace settlement,” he said.

He said continued mobilisation could create a cycle in which insecurity fuels military recruitment, which then deepens insecurity.

“Political insecurity generates military mobilisation; military mobilisation reinforces political insecurity; political insecurity then becomes an argument for further mobilisation,” Gidey said.

For the young men interviewed by Al Jazeera, however, the question is less about the political calculations driving mobilisation than about whether they can avoid being pulled back into war.

Gebru says leaving became his way of protecting himself.

“After what happened, I knew I could not stay there and live normally. I felt that the only way to protect myself was to leave.”

Shewit is now in Addis Ababa, separated from his family and the life he had been rebuilding.

“I didn’t leave because I wanted to. I left because I wanted to have a chance to build a future.”

Gebrehiwot, who remains in Tigray, says his hopes are simpler.

“I don’t want anything extraordinary. I just want to live peacefully, stay with my family and never have to pick up a gun again.”

title: Oil prices jump after Yemen’s Houthis claim attacks on Saudi facilities
excerpt:
Oil prices have jumped following renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, including claimed strikes on facilities belonging to state-run energy giant Aramco.

Brent crude, the key yar...
body_text:
Oil prices have jumped following renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, including claimed strikes on facilities belonging to state-run energy giant Aramco.

Brent crude, the key yardstick of global prices, rose more than 3 percent on Thursday as the attacks stoked fears of additional disruption to energy supplies already facing constraints due to the US-Israel war on Iran.

Brent futures for November ended the day above $106.50 a barrel on Thursday, after earlier exceeding $108.

Prices eased slightly on Friday morning in Asia, with the benchmark standing at $105.77 a barrel as of 02:00 GMT.

The Houthis on Thursday said they had launched missile and drone attacks on a “sensitive target” in Riyadh and Aramco facilities in the Red Sea city of Yanbu.

The rebel group said both operations “achieved their objectives successfully” in a statement carried by the Houthi-run Yemen News Agency.

Saudi-led coalition forces said earlier that they intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards the kingdom.

Saudi authorities have not confirmed whether the attacks caused any damage or casualties.

Aramco, which supplies roughly 10 percent of global oil demand, did not respond to inquiries outside of regular business hours.

The latest flare-up in violence in the Middle East comes as the US and Iran are engaged in renewed diplomatic efforts to find a resolution to their seven-month conflict on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Thursday that he hoped Washington would return to their Memorandum of Understanding on ending the war, which lapsed in mid-August without a peace deal, before the US midterm elections in November.

“Relative to the post-war trend, these levels remain elevated and reflect the reality that critical supply routes and facilities are still vulnerable,” Tim Waterer, chief market ‌analyst at KCM Trade in Sydney, Australia, told Al Jazeera.

“Diplomatic efforts on the sidelines of the UN are providing some counterweight, but until there is clearer evidence of a durable de-escalation, the upside bias remains in place,” Waterer said.

June Goh, a senior oil market analyst at Sparta Commodities in Singapore, said oil would likely stay above $100 a barrel as long as the war on Iran continued.

“With no clear resolution in sight, the gap in oil inventories globally is getting wider,” Goh told Al Jazeera.

title: NSW police officer killed ‘instantly’ after car she was travelling in crashed into tree in Redfern
excerpt:
The marked police car was travelling with its sirens on when it hit a tree in inner-city Sydney about 1.30am on Friday

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news em...
body_text:
The marked police car was travelling with its sirens on when it hit a tree in inner-city Sydney about 1.30am on Friday

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A New South Wales police officer who was killed on duty when the car she was travelling in crashed into a tree in Sydney has been named as 20-year-old Mia Lay.

NSW police said the marked police car was travelling under lights and sirens along Gibbons Street in Redfern when it crashed at about 1.30am on Friday.

The officers were responding to a reported vehicle theft at Glebe.

Lay, a constable who had been with the force for 16 months, died instantly in the crash.

The 20-year-old police officer showed exceptional promise, the NSW Police Commissioner, Mal Lanyon, said.

“There is nothing I can easily say that takes the pain away but please know that Mia was a loved police officer,” he said.

Lanyon said it was too early to provide any specific details about the speed the police vehicle was travelling until the crash investigation was completed.

Paramedics treated the 24-year-old male constable who was driving before he was taken to hospital in a stable condition.

A crime scene has been established, and police have declared a critical incident.

The NSW police watchdog said it would monitor the force’s investigation into the crash to “ensure public confidence”.

The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission said it could not independently investigate the incident until NSW police finished its probe, and any coronial or criminal proceedings were over.

The premier, Chris Minns, and the police minister, Yasmin Catley, said their thoughts were with Lay’s loved ones.

“Today is a dark day, a very sad day. We’ve lost a beautiful, young, enthusiastic and … wonderful police officer,” she told reporters after meeting with her parents.

“Our police officers dedicate themselves to looking after others, and today the NSW Police family is mourning one of its own.”

Minns said he was also thinking of the officer injured in the crash and those who responded at the scene.

The NSW opposition leader, Kelly Sloane, said she was “heartbroken” by the news.

“(Lay) was out working while most of us were asleep, protecting the community,” she said.

Lay’s partner is also reportedly a serving police officer and has been offered support.

The police union paid tribute to their fallen colleague saying they were shocked by her death, days out from National Police Remembrance Day on 29 September.

“The death of this officer is sad evidence of the dangers they face,” the Police Association of NSW president, Kevin Morton, said.

“In the coming days, as the community learn more about this officer, it will become apparent what a special young person they were. We grieve with our members and commit to supporting their family into the future.”

Nearby Regent Street was closed in both directions on Friday morning between Lawson and Cleveland streets.

title: Saudi, Turkish, Pakistani chiefs plan urgent talks amid Yemen fighting
excerpt:
Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan have announced they are planning an urgent meeting of their chiefs of staff to discuss ways to support the kingdom under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.

The anno...
body_text:
Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan have announced they are planning an urgent meeting of their chiefs of staff to discuss ways to support the kingdom under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.

The announcement followed a meeting on Thursday in New York between Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, according to the Saudi Press Agency.

The statement did not say when the military chiefs would meet or what form of support could be considered.

Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7 to strengthen collective deterrence and expand defence cooperation.

The pact stipulates that an attack on one of the three countries is considered an attack on them all.

The three countries have since begun setting up mechanisms under the pact. Their foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs met in Istanbul on August 31 for the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee, agreeing to establish a secretariat in Saudi Arabia and to deepen military cooperation.

Thursday’s foreign ministers’ meeting also condemned attacks targeting Mecca as well as civilian and economic facilities in Saudi Arabia, and it affirmed the kingdom’s right to defend itself under Article 51 of the UN Charter.

The diplomatic moves came as Saudi Arabia reported a fresh wave of attacks from Yemen.

Saudi Arabia said its air defences shot down six ballistic missiles launched towards Taif and Yanbu on Thursday.

Major-General Turki al-Malki, the coalition spokesman, said further Houthi escalation would be “dealt with firmly”. Saudi Civil Defence authorities had issued alerts in several areas before later saying the danger had passed.

The Houthis separately claimed missile and drone attacks on a “sensitive target” in Riyadh and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu.

France has also offered to provide defensive support to Saudi Arabia. President Emmanuel Macron said Paris would send military assets to help protect Yanbu.

“We are going to send military assets, meaning soldiers, radars and defence systems to protect this site,” Macron said in an interview with TF1 on Thursday.

The cross-border attacks have coincided with some of the heaviest fighting inside Yemen since hostilities escalated again.

Fighting across several fronts in Yemen killed at least 150 Houthi fighters and members of government-aligned forces in the 24 hours leading into Friday, according to an AFP news agency tally.

The toll compiled by AFP included 98 fighters on the government side and 52 from the Houthis, with clashes reported around the Kahboub Mountains and areas between Lahj and Taiz overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

The Houthis have also expanded their presence along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including by taking the port city of Mocha and strategic islands. The gains have strengthened the group’s position around Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s busiest shipping corridors. About 12 percent of global trade normally passes through the waterway, according to AP.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government has urged greater international involvement, warning at the UN General Assembly that Houthi control around the strait poses a wider economic risk.

Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader Al Alimi-Bawzer accused the Houthis of using freedom of navigation as leverage, saying their actions were “taking hostage the entire global economy”.

The renewed fighting has forced more than 230,000 people from their homes since the beginning of September, according to UNHCR, as clashes spread across multiple front lines. The agency said the latest displacement has added to about 5.2 million people already internally displaced across Yemen.

UNHCR said families have been uprooted across governorates, including Hodeidah, Taiz, Lahj, Aden, Abyan, Marib, al-Dhalea and Shabwah, with many fleeing at short notice and leaving with few belongings.

Shelter, food, clean water, healthcare and protection services are among the most urgent needs, while host communities and displacement sites are becoming increasingly overstretched.

title: Meet 'the devil': Actor who plays Satan, Judas Iscariot shares power of comedy in uncertain political times
excerpt: Actor and Babylon Bee producer Jarret LeMaster, the voice of Bumblebee in "Optimus Prime: Awakening," tells Fox News Digital why his Christian faith makes playing villains like Satan an unexpectedly g...
body_text:
Actor and Babylon Bee producer Jarret LeMaster, the voice of Bumblebee in "Optimus Prime: Awakening," tells Fox News Digital why his Christian faith makes playing villains like Satan an unexpectedly good fit.

Jarret LeMaster has played some sinister roles as Satan, Adolf Hitler and Judas Iscariot — but now he's stepping into one of pop culture's most beloved franchises as Bumblebee.

The Christian actor, writer and former worship leader voices the Autobots in "Optimus Prime: Awakening," the new animated short accompanying the 40th anniversary theatrical re-release of "The Transformers: The Movie."

But LeMaster told Fox News Digital there is one thing he would rather not do on camera: kiss another woman.

"I don't wanna kiss anybody, and so playing bad guys makes a lot of sense for me," LeMaster said. "They never kiss anybody, you know, they just murder them."

BILLY BALDWIN ADMITS HE REFUSED TO KISS CO-STAR AFTER WEEKS OF TENSION ON SET

Jarret LeMaster, dressed as the devil as part of a comedic portrayal for The Babylon Bee, poses with his wife, Christina, at an event. LeMaster told Fox News Digital that Christina runs a large homeschool program in California. (Courtesy of Jarret LeMaster)

"When you're murdering somebody, you're always pretending," he continued. "When you're kissing someone, you are always actually kissing them. And so, you know, that's my line. I don't wanna cross that line.

"Playing bad guys really works for my family," he joked. "And then my kids can look up to me as a great villain."

It's an unusual résumé for someone who spent years working in church ministry.

LeMaster said he still volunteers and leads worship at his local church, although he tends to keep some of his acting work "on the DL."

SKILLET’S JOHN COOPER SAYS CHRISTIANS WHO CALL ROCK MUSIC ‘DEMONIC’ ARE ‘GETTING THE GOSPEL WRONG’

Jarret LeMaster appears in a scene from Angel Studios’ "Homestead." (Courtesy of Jarret LeMaster)

"Sometimes people are upset that I play 'Woke Jesus.' Sometimes people think that it's weird that I played the devil. Sometimes people were offended that I would, you know, play Adolf Hitler," he said. "The one that is not offensive is Bumblebee. People are very excited about that for some reason."

LeMaster's path from church ministry to professional villain began when he got a call one day asking him to play a Russian murderer in a sketch for Christian satire outlet The Babylon Bee.

"We need a Russian murderer. You kind of look like that," LeMaster recalled being told.

At the time, he was working full time at his church and with the Bee. He initially assumed the company must be based somewhere like "Idaho or Narnia," only to discover it was in California.

'THE PASSION OF THE CHRIST' RETURNS TO THEATERS IN 4K WITH A 'RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST' SNEAK PEEK

Jarret LeMaster poses in costume as the devil while filming a sketch for The Babylon Bee. (Courtesy of Jarret LeMaster)

"I don't know why I always get cast as bad characters," LeMaster said. "I think it's probably just because I'm bald... I blame the media. I blame [actor] Jason Statham."

His latest role puts LeMaster firmly on the other side of the good-versus-evil divide.

"Optimus Prime: Awakening" features LeMaster as Bumblebee alongside Frank Welker as Megatron and Soundwave and the late Peter Cullen as Optimus Prime. The short accompanies a 40th anniversary rerelease that exceeded initial box-office projections, prompting additional theatrical dates through Oct. 7.

LeMaster said he initially underestimated the significance of the project because director Josh Wassung was a friend.

FROM DISNEY MAGIC TO ANCIENT FAITH: DAVID HENRIE ON WHY GEN Z IS FLOCKING TO CHURCH

Jarret LeMaster and his family attend the "Homestead" premiere on Dec. 10, 2024, in Los Angeles. (Getty Images for Angel Studios)

"I thought this was my friend's little movie, this little Transformers movie that he was making for Hasbro," he said.

Then he learned Cullen was involved. LeMaster praised the longtime Optimus Prime actor for embodying "strength and gentleness and kindness" and "protecting the weak."

"Who am I? Why do I get to play Bumblebee?" LeMaster recalled wondering.

For LeMaster, even the Transformers role connects back to his faith.

"It's an opportunity to sort of spread good news in the kingdom through, you know, robots," he said.

Jarret LeMaster portrays the devil during a sketch for The Babylon Bee, while wearing a 'Harris-Walz' sweatshirt. (Courtesy of Jarret LeMaster)

And despite joining the Autobots, LeMaster admitted Satan remains particularly fun to play.

"I love playing the devil because he is so much like me," he said. "I know that sounds really weird."

His Babylon Bee version of Satan is less fire-and-brimstone than frustrated corporate middle management.

"What if the devil was an HR director?" LeMaster said.

"You know, guys, it's been a rough quarter," he said in character. "Make sure that you put cover letters on all the things you turn in, please."

Jarret LeMaster attends the "Homestead" premiere on Dec. 10, 2024, in Los Angeles. (Getty Images for Angel Studios)

Beneath the joke is a serious approach to portraying villains. LeMaster said he looks for something good in a character's motivations and then considers how it became distorted.

"There's nothing that the devil can create in and of himself. He can only take what's good and he can twist it," he said.

"You always start with a good guy and then you can twist it to something evil," LeMaster added. "That's kind of what I think the best villains end up being like."

Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Turning Point USA fires back at ICE shooting lawyer over deleted Charlie Kirk post
excerpt:
Fox News correspondent Brooke Taylor reports on protests in Austin, Texas, after an I.C.E. agent shot a Venezuelan illegal immigrant on ‘Special Report.’

Turning Point USA (TPUSA) spokesman Andrew Ko...
body_text:
Fox News correspondent Brooke Taylor reports on protests in Austin, Texas, after an I.C.E. agent shot a Venezuelan illegal immigrant on ‘Special Report.’

Turning Point USA (TPUSA) spokesman Andrew Kolvet fired back Thursday at the attorney representing a Venezuelan man shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Austin, Texas, calling the two a "perfect match" after the lawyer drew criticism over a deleted social media post referencing the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.

Kolvet, a spokesman for TPUSA and executive producer of "The Charlie Kirk Show," told Fox News Digital that the organization backed the federal immigration officers involved while criticizing attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch and her client, 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez.

"We stand with our brave men and women of ICE who are defending American sovereignty and keeping American citizens safe," Kolvet said. "While everyone is entitled to their defense, it's not surprising the quality of lawyer an illegal alien from Venezuela attracts who had a final notice of deportation before leading law enforcement on a dangerous high speed chase."

REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR

Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet blasted the attorney representing Wilber Garces Perez after her deleted social media post referencing Charlie Kirk resurfaced. (Getty Images)

Lincoln-Goldfinch drew criticism this week after a since-deleted social media post referencing Kirk resurfaced. In the post, she questioned how someone could resist being shot while invoking Kirk.

"How do you resist getting shot in the neck? Does Charlie Kirk have any advice on that?" Lincoln-Goldfinch said in the post.

She previously addressed the controversy in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying her office determined the post could be interpreted differently than intended and removed it.

"A post referencing the death of Charlie Kirk was removed from our account. We recognized the post could be misconstrued and that's why it came down. We have also addressed this issue internally," Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

HOW CHARLIE KIRK’S ASSASSINATION CHANGED THE WAY CONSERVATIVES APPROACH HOSTILE OPPONENTS

Attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch faced criticism after a deleted post asked whether Charlie Kirk had "any advice" on resisting being shot in the neck. (Onaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images; Michael S. Schwartz/Getty Images)

The dispute came as new evidence emerged about the ICE operation that ended with Graces Perez being shot. Surveillance footage published Wednesday showed at least two federal law enforcement vehicles pursuing Graces Perez's vehicle with emergency lights flashing and sirens sounding before the shooting. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed the video's authenticity to Fox News Digital.

Lincoln-Goldfinch has disputed the federal government’s account, saying Garces Perez was working as a DoorDash driver when an unmarked vehicle struck his car and that he did not initially know federal agents were pursuing him. She has also challenged DHS’s characterization of his immigration status.

DHS said Garces Perez is a Venezuelan national who had a final order of removal and was the subject of a targeted vehicle stop. The department also said his work authorization had expired in 2025 and disputed claims about his treatment following the shooting.

"No amount of smears and false narratives will slow down ICE from doing its job to arrest illegal aliens from our communities," DHS said.

AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARKS FIGHT OVER VENEZUELAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT'S DEPORTATION

Surveillance footage showed federal vehicles pursuing Garces Perez with lights and sirens before the Austin encounter that ended with an ICE officer shooting him. (Austin Police Department)

Austin police released body-camera footage Tuesday showing officers arriving immediately after the shooting and helping Graces Perez from his vehicle. The video contradicted an earlier claim that federal agents pulled him from the car, although the videos did not capture the shooting itself.

The shooting has also moved into federal court. Lincoln-Goldfinch’s firm filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent Garces Perez’s immediate removal, and a federal judge ordered that he remain in the country so he can appear at a Sept. 30 hearing.

The circumstances surrounding the shooting remain under investigation. Homeland Security Investigations, with assistance from the FBI, is leading the federal investigation, while Austin authorities have also reviewed evidence surrounding the encounter.

Fox News' Louis Casiano and Brooke Taylor contributed to this report.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

You can send news tips to cj.womack@fox.com and follow CJ on Twitter.

title: Trump-Xi summit: Four key takeaways from the Washington, DC, meeting
excerpt: US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping seemed to put sources of tension between their countries to the side during the second day of Xi’s three-day visit to the United States...
body_text:
US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping seemed to put sources of tension between their countries to the side during the second day of Xi’s three-day visit to the United States, where he met with Trump and toured the White House.

Trump touted what he described as a “great meeting” with Xi on Thursday, as the two superpowers seek greater dialogue despite differences over issues such as Iran, Taiwan, AI and trade.

“From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people,” Trump said.

Here are a few key takeaways from Xi’s second day in the US.

When Trump first returned to the White House, he announced severe tariffs on Chinese goods that quickly set off a trade war between the world’s two largest economies and warnings of wider fallout around the globe.

Despite such a rocky start, Trump and Xi have sought to dial back tensions and improve their personal ties, even if there is an understanding that core areas of disagreement aren’t likely to change.

The US president has sometimes talked about China’s status as a rising power as a source of admiration, even as those changes bring it into competition with the US.

“We had a great meeting,” Trump told reporters on Thursday, without offering further details.

For his part, Xi stated on Thursday that the US and China should take steps to avoid the “Thucydides Trap”, a term used by international relations scholars regarding the risk of conflict between a rising power and an existing power.

“It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses,” Xi said, adding that both countries were deeply interconnected and should engage in “healthy” competition that is “kept within bounds”.

While Xi’s visit is focused on improving ties with Trump and the US, several issues have also been at the centre of discussions between the two leaders. One is the US war on Iran, which was launched by the US and Israel in February and has led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and surging global energy prices.

Trump has called on China to support US efforts to isolate Tehran economically and reopen the strait, which was open before the war. Beijing, Iran’s largest trading partner, has been hesitant to get involved.

No breakthroughs on the issue were reported during talks between Trump and Xi on Thursday, with the Chinese president stating that he supported the US and Iran returning to an interim agreement that was supposed to pave the way for a larger peace deal.

That truce broke down shortly after it was announced in June.

While Xi’s visit to the US has been marked by pomp and ceremony, some Democratic and Republican lawmakers have complained that the spectacle amounts to a celebration of a US rival.

“Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party,” said Republican Senator Roger Wicker.

That line of criticism was shared by Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, who said that Trump “always deludes himself into thinking that, by ingratiating himself with authoritarians, he’s somehow going to get his way”.

Others said that diplomacy between the US and China is a positive thing that will help the two powers avoid potentially disastrous conflict.

“I’m glad this meeting is happening; diplomacy is key,” Republican Senator Rand Paul said in a social media post. “Talk more, war less.”

US ties with Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, remain a core flashpoint in relations between Washington and Beijing.

During their meeting on Thursday, the Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported that Xi urged Trump to oppose Taiwanese independence and handle the issue “prudently”. The White House has yet to release its own summary of the talks and remarks on Taiwan.

The Chinese leader is likely to continue pressing Trump to avoid acts that Beijing views as provocative.

Trump stated after a meeting with Xi in May that he would postpone final approval of a $14bn arms package for Taipei, and has called arms sales a “very good negotiating chip” with China.

That transactional approach has angered some in Washington, who see US promises of military aid to Taiwan as a core commitment.

But the US has long taken an expedient approach to relations with Beijing and Taipei, seeking stronger ties with China as it emerged as an economic powerhouse and maintaining an official policy of encouraging a peaceful resolution of the dispute without taking either side.

Taiwan has expressed concern that China could use coercion, both economic and military, to bring the island under its control.

A May Economist/YouGov poll found that people in the US are much more likely to view Taiwan as an ally of the country than China. Asked whether the US should prioritise good relations with Beijing or preventing China from seizing control of Taiwan, respondents were split 36 percent to 35 percent.

Less than 40 percent of those polled said the US should be prepared to use military force to stop China from controlling Taiwan.

title: From Nagaland to a path to the Oscars: Indian film brings a rarely seen world to global cinema
excerpt:
Watch: Indian film brings a rarely seen world to global cinema

There is something pleasingly improbable about Angh.

The film comes from Nagaland, a mountainous state of fewer than two million people...
body_text:
Watch: Indian film brings a rarely seen world to global cinema

There is something pleasingly improbable about Angh.

The film comes from Nagaland, a mountainous state of fewer than two million people on India's northeastern frontier, and is in Konyak, a tribal language unfamiliar to most Indians, never mind audiences abroad. It was director Theja Rio's first feature and most of its cast faced a camera for the first time.

And yet, at the Toronto International Film Festival this month, this quiet film won the Platform Prize, a major juried award.

The award is intended to recognise films with a particularly distinctive directorial voice. The jury praised Rio's "refreshing perspective" and the film's portrait of a world rarely encountered on the international screen.

The win also gives Angh an unusual route towards the 2027 Academy Awards. Under new rules, winners of designated prizes at six international festivals can qualify for consideration in the International Feature Film category without relying solely on their country's official submission.

This does not make Angh an Oscar nominee. But it does place a Konyak-language film from one of India's smallest states inside a global conversation from which such stories have been almost entirely absent.

Rio still sounds slightly startled by it. When we speak in Delhi, roughly 72 hours after the win, he has barely had a moment to breathe - Toronto, flights, interviews, more interviews.

"There were a lot of good films in the competition", he says, including films by far more seasoned directors. His producers were confident.

"They thought we were going to win. I wasn't."

He is also less solemn than Angh might suggest. Before cinema, he wanted to be a rapper - "a kid from Compton instead of a kid from Nagaland", as he puts it. His tastes still range happily from Black Thought, the lead rapper of American hip-hop group The Roots, to his favourite filmmaker, the Iranian director Abbas Kiarostami.

But for his first feature, he turned close to home.

Set in the early 1960s, Angh follows Anghba, the ageing hereditary chief of a Konyak village, and his young son, as the world around them changes. The Konyaks are one of Nagaland's 17 major tribes, concentrated in the eastern district of Mon, where such chiefs are known as Anghs. Even today, some older men bear facial tattoos associated with the Konyaks' historical practice of headhunting.

Anghba is the ageing hereditary chief of a Konyak village in Nagaland in the film

Anghba and his son are among the last in their region to hold to an ancestral faith as Christianity spreads.

Then an American missionary, played by Scottish actor Douglas Henshall, arrives. The father resists but the son is now curious.

Rio says the idea for the film came a few years ago, when he was visiting Mon for another project. What struck him was how closely different generations seemed to live alongside one another there.

Within a single family, he says, a grandfather might be a former headhunter, his face still tattooed; two generations later, his grandson might play guitar in a rock band.

"It feels like you've jumped on a time machine," Rio says. "The past and the present sort of coexist together."

The year also matters. Nagaland, which was earlier part of Assam state, formally became an Indian state in December 1963, during a period of profound political and social change.

By then, Christianity had been spreading among Naga communities for decades, bringing changes extending beyond religious belief into customs, rituals and everyday life.

From right: Theja Rio poses with Nancy Nisa Beso, the film's producer, and actors Anglong Konyak (who plays the village chief, Anghba) and Sobino Rengma (who plays the son, Amao)

Dr B Amo Konyak, a scholar of Konyak society, says the changes during this period were almost like a disappearance.

Some practices were lost; others "survived in fragments" - in the memories of elders, in family heirlooms. What had once been part of everyday life became heritage.

But Dr Konyak says culture did not simply stop. People carried parts of it into new religious and social worlds. Traditions survived, but changed meaning as they changed form.

It's this moment of transition that Rio wanted to capture.

"The past 50 or 60 years have brought extraordinary churn," he says, widening the distance between generations.

In Angh, he explores this through the relationship between the father and son who "intimately love and care about each other very deeply", even as their worlds begin to pull apart.

Critic Siddhant Adlakha was struck by the ambiguity the film captures. "Progress and tradition can be nonlinear, even entwined," he says, "rather than strictly opposing forces."

Angh traces the relationship between a father and son as they reconcile with larger changes

The film is yet to reach a wider audience, but its brief trailer offers a glimpse of how Rio constructed this world. Mist hangs over steep green hills; figures move through forests and village paths; fire and lamplight pick faces out of the darkness.

The landscape is beautiful but not merely picturesque - a small world held together by ritual, family and geography, while something larger presses in from beyond its edges.

Adlakha singles out the quiet close-ups of Anghlong Konyak, the first-time actor who plays the chief, and the "gentleness" with which Rio captures his "subdued rage".

What the camera saw mattered almost as much as where it was looking from.

Konyak people have long been viewed from the outside.

Dr Konyak points to explorers, colonial officials, missionaries and photographers drawn to tattooed faces, ornaments, weapons and headhunting, while the lives behind them often receded from view.

The forest plays a central part in the storytelling of the film

Rio was conscious of inheriting that history. "There have been several films and documentaries made about Nagaland," he says, "but these sort of films tend to follow the gaze of the explorer rather than the subject."

With Angh, he wanted to reverse that gaze, asking viewers to "step inside the shoes of these characters".

The change is subtle but consequential. The Konyaks are no longer an exotic remnant of the past, but people living through what Dr Konyak describes as "love, grief, conflict, faith, uncertainty and generational change".

Konyak advisers worked on dialogue, costume and production design, and much of the cast was drawn from first-time Konyak performers. The forest, too, belongs to the people moving through it. Adlakha says Rio treats it "not just as a setting, but as a home with a history", much as an urban filmmaker might treat Mumbai or New York.

Rio and cinematographer Adam Pietkiewicz shot Angh on 16mm film, drawing on photographs and footage of missionaries and Naga communities from the 1950s and 60s.

They wanted to recreate the grain, texture and atmosphere of those archival images, while shifting the point of view from outsider to subject.

It was an evocative choice - and a logistical headache.

Unlike digital footage, the exposed film could not simply be reviewed on set. Every four or five days, the cans had to be sent to Mumbai for processing, while the crew carried on shooting without knowing exactly what they had captured.

The film also stars Sottish actor Douglas Henshall, who plays a Christian missionary

During a night shoot with Henshall, an old Second World War Jeep was supposed to be driven into frame. It behaved perfectly through rehearsals. But when the cameras began rolling, the engine refused to start. After repeated attempts, the crew managed to capture just one take of the Jeep entering the frame.

"It was a very difficult night," Rio says.

Angh may be Rio's first feature, but its journey places it within a widening map of Indian cinema, especially in the northeast.

Adlakha points to filmmakers such as Assam's Rima Das and Meghalaya's Dominic Sangma whose work, he says, reveals "how complex and multifaceted the idea of Indian cinema happens to be".

Rio thinks Nagaland still remains at the edge of that scene. Its film industry is, as he puts it, "at a very nascent stage", with little of the reach enjoyed by India's established filmmaking centres.

But he hopes some of the attention around Angh travels back with it.

There are, he says, "so many talented filmmakers with so many beautiful stories that are yet to be told".

For now, though, Rio is looking forward to something more ordinary - getting back to Nagaland.

"I want to play football with my friends."

Sydney Sweeney has balanced her Hollywood career with a growing business portfolio and an increasingly public romance with Scooter Braun. (Brianna Bryson/WireImage)

SYDNEY SWEENEY SIZZLES IN WONDER WOMAN CORSET COSTUME AS SHE SOAKS UP SUMMER ROMANCE WITH SCOOTER BRAUN
