title: America's best national parks for fall revealed — plus the NPS director's personal picks
excerpt:
Acting National Park Service Director Jessica Bowron joins OutKick OutDoors to discuss why protecting America’s national parks and historic sites matters and why there is

Year after year, the Great S...
body_text:
Acting National Park Service Director Jessica Bowron joins OutKick OutDoors to discuss why protecting America’s national parks and historic sites matters and why there is

Year after year, the Great Smoky Mountains are America’s most-visited national park. Turns out, fall might be its most impressive season.

A new study ranking the best national parks for an autumn getaway put the Smokies at No. 1, ahead of Acadia, Shenandoah, Rocky Mountain and Grand Teton.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

The research, conducted by Sudoku Bliss, analyzed National Park Service visitation data from September through November between 2021 and 2025, along with Google ratings and reviews. Great Smoky Mountains earned the top overall score after welcoming nearly 19 million fall visitors over that five-year span.

Best for: Sweeping mountain views, colorful fall foliage and beginner-friendly campground options (Getty Images)

And if you're looking for a second opinion, the acting director of the National Park Service happens to agree.

During a recent interview with OutKick OutDoors, Jessica Bowron named the Smokies and the Blue Ridge Parkway when asked where she'd send someone chasing fall colors.

6 OF THE BEST FALL CAMPING DESTINATIONS IN AMERICA, PLUS GEAR BEGINNERS SHOULD PACK

"I would send them to the Blue Ridge Parkway, with a close partner being the Great Smoky Mountains National Park," Bowron said. "Two really incredible parks to see the fall colors."

The Smokies finished well ahead of the rest of the field in the study, with a fall score of 94.7.

Acadia National Park in Maine ranked second at 86.6, followed by Virginia's Shenandoah National Park at 76.0, Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado at 74.1 and Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming at 72.9.

The rest of the top 10 included Yosemite, Zion, Yellowstone, Cuyahoga Valley and New River Gorge.

HERE'S HOW TO DO THE SMOKY MOUNTAINS WITHOUT TRAFFIC AND CROWDS

And the rankings weren't based on visitor totals alone.

The study weighted total fall visits, total visitor hours, Google ratings and the number of reviews containing autumn-related language. Shenandoah, for example, had fewer visitors than several parks ranked below it, but 18.4% of its Google reviews mentioned fall — the highest share among the top 10.

An overlook at Shenandoah National Park. (Douglas Rissing / Getty Images)

So while the Smokies won on sheer popularity and overall score, the list includes everything from classic East Coast leaf-peeping destinations to red rocks and wildlife-heavy Western parks.

Bowron also shared some good news for travelers planning a trip along the Blue Ridge Parkway this fall.

"Just within the next few weeks, we should be reopening additional sections of the parkway that were hit by Hurricane Helene just two years ago," Bowron told OutKick OutDoors. "We're really excited to get that work wrapped up and see visitors back on that parkway."

Linn Cove Viaduct on the Blue Ridge Parkway in the fall. The road winds through the mountains under a blue morning sky. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

For anyone planning a fall road trip through the region, that's certainly worth keeping an eye on.

If your idea of a relaxing fall weekend does not involve joining everybody else in America at the Smokies, Bowron also offered a more under-the-radar option.

Her pick: Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park.

And this wasn't just an answer pulled from a list.

"I was there just yesterday, actually, we went for a hike on the C&O Canal with my husband and my daughter," Bowron said.

She highlighted the more than 100-mile towpath running from the Washington, D.C., area into Western Maryland, with opportunities to hike, bike and branch off onto other trails along the way.

"I don't know that folks recognize what an incredible resource that is," she said.

That might be the better play for travelers who want fall scenery without traffic and crowds.

Fall gets most of the attention this time of year, but Bowron said winter opens up a completely different set of possibilities.

For warmer-weather trips, she pointed to places like Death Valley, Mojave, Everglades and Saguaro — parks that can be far more comfortable once summer temperatures disappear.

A saguaro cactus forest in Saguaro National Park, Ariz., during sunset. (Getty Images)

And for travelers who actually want the snow, there are plenty of options for that, too. The Rockies offer snowshoeing and cross-country skiing, while Utah's Bryce Canyon National Park is a great place for winter hiking, snowshoeing and skiing among its snow-covered red rock formations.

Bowron warned, though, to check park websites for road closures, weather conditions and available facilities before you go.

"Days are going to be shorter. Conditions are going to change," Bowron said. "They're going to be very different from what you might expect in the summer."

A woman poses in Bryce Canyon National Park. (Getty Images)

So don’t be sad your summer vacation has come to an end. Because for the national parks, now is when things start getting really good.

Love all things parks and outdoors? Follow OutKick OutDoors on Instagram and TikTok!

title: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn plan to begin Gaza's reconstruction
excerpt:
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45 billion (£1.85 billion) during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

The funding will be spr...
body_text:
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45 billion (£1.85 billion) during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

The funding will be spread across 66 programmes over six months, and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal, among other needs.

But the board admitted substantial donations were still needed, with $18bn pledged but only $280 million handed over so far. The board estimates full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4bn over the next decade.

Jared Kushner, Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded the project faced "different delays on different things, for whatever reason".

"The goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed to doing it," he told the meeting of board members and stakeholders.

He was joined in New York by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who said the group had made "real progress" over the past year.

"All of the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results, with billions of dollars donated and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," Witkoff added.

In addition to fundraising, the plan faces significant challenges including how to ensure security for those operating in Gaza, overhaul internal governance and find consensus between Israeli and Palestinians officials.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a separate press conference on Wednesday that "a number of countries have stepped forward and pledged financial assistance" and the board was "looking for more that will participate in that".

Former UK prime minister and board member Sir Tony Blair told the meeting: "The responsibility on us is huge"

In August, a senior official on the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the Palestinian armed group Hamas.

In August, Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.

At least 1,381 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".

The Board of Peace was created as part of Donald Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which he unveiled alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September last year.

Hamas agreed to return all 48 remaining hostages being held in Gaza in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Gaza detainees, and to the idea of handing over the governance of Gaza to Palestinian technocrats.

In July, Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which will see it lay down its arms, provided Israel ends "all forms of aggression" and withdraws its forces from Gaza.

But that was later rejected by Netanyahu, who said the military would stay in Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.

The Board of Peace was originally thought to be an international organisation intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide.

US launches phase two of Gaza peace plan with new technocratic government

If Hamas disarmament plan holds, it could mark first credible step to ending Gaza war

Netanyahu's rejection of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word

Board of Peace's Gaza envoy criticises Israeli strikes and Hamas actions

title: Massachusetts restaurant owner assaults teen dine-and-dashers, pulls gun during scuffle, police say
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Massachusetts restaurant owner allegedly beat two teenage dine-and-dashers and pointed a gun at a larger group that ...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Massachusetts restaurant owner allegedly beat two teenage dine-and-dashers and pointed a gun at a larger group that gathered after he chased the pair down when they skipped out on their bill last week, authorities said.

Nadim Kashouh, 62, chased the teens – a 17-year-old girl and Javonnie Lee, 18 – after the pair darted out of Nadim’s Downtown Mediterranean Grill on Friday evening without paying their $92.40 bill, the Boston Globe reported.

Kashouh reportedly chased the teens and caught them at a convenience store.

JIMMY JOHN'S EMPLOYEE ACCUSED OF OPENING FIRE ON CAR, SHOOTING 14-YEAR-OLD GIRL IN LEG: POLICE

Nadim Kashouh, 62, chased the teens – a 17-year-old girl and Javonnie Lee, 18 – after the pair darted out of Nadim’s Downtown Mediterranean Grill in Springfield, Massachusetts, police said. (Google Maps)

The teens reportedly told the police that they tried to pay their tab twice but bolted after their card was declined both times, according to the newspaper.

Kashouh, an immigrant from Lebanon who came to the United States in 1990, allegedly grabbed the girl's phone and demanded they pay. He then elbowed the girl and punched Lee in the face, the Springfield Police Department said.

"As a larger group gathered, Kashouh is alleged to have pointed his firearm in the direction of the group. Kashouh stated he did so in self-defense," police spokesperson Ryan Walsh said, according to WMTV.

NYC ALLEGED DINE-AND-DASH INFLUENCER PEI CHUNG EVICTED FROM LUXURY APARTMENT AS SHE SIT SIN JAIL

Walsh said Kashouh's firearm and his license to carry permit were seized. He is charged with two counts of assault with a dangerous weapon, armed robbery with a firearm, and assault and battery.

Meanwhile, the two teens will be issued criminal complaints for defrauding a restaurant.

Kashouh appeared in court earlier this week, according to his restaurant's Facebook page.

"He maintains his innocence and says he acted in self-defense. As this matter moves through the legal process, Mr. Kashouh looks forward to the opportunity to fully address the facts and circumstances surrounding the incident," the post states.

"Having just celebrated over 25 years serving the Springfield community, Mr. Kashouh is incredibly grateful for the many clients, guests, friends, and community members who have reached out and continued to support him and Nadim’s," it continued. "He sincerely thanks them for their kindness and support during this time."

Kashouh was born in Monrovia, Liberia, before moving to Lebanon as a child in 1974 where he worked in the family business during the summer, the New York Post reported.

Despite the allegations against him, some came to his defense.

"I have known Nadim to be respectful, fair, calm, and incredibly hardworking," Maureen Pinette, who worked for him between 2012 and 2014, wrote on Facebook. "I've watched him deal with difficult situations and difficult people, and I have never known him to be someone who simply loses his cool."

"I see so much of Nadim in both of his children—the love, the loyalty, the work ethic, and the way they show up for the people around them," she added. "I’ve also watched Nadim give to people and to his community without needing recognition for it. He has done things for people simply because they needed help."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the restaurant and the Springfield Police Department.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Sri Lanka court convicts 15 men over deadly Easter Sunday bombings
excerpt:
Dozens of police and commandos were deployed to the courtroom before the verdicts were announced

Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday ...
body_text:
Dozens of police and commandos were deployed to the courtroom before the verdicts were announced

Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500.

Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted.

The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead.

All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the bombings on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody.

The court session was adjourned before sentencing.

The accused, who had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, were handcuffed in pairs and brought to the High Court in the capital Colombo in two prison buses.

Most of those killed were Sri Lankans, many of whom were children.

They included celebrity chef Shantha Mayadunne and her daughter, an entire young family of five, at least eight members of staff from the hotels targeted and five members of the same family from the western Sri Lankan city of Negombo.

The foreigners who died included 11 Indians, eight Britons and five Americans.

Among the dead there were also citizens of Australia, Bangladesh, China, Denmark, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.

Three of Danish billionaire Anders Holch Povlsen's children died in the attack on the Shangri-La hotel, while the family had been holidaying there.

In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities.

In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks.

Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions.

For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks.

The verdict comes as a separate investigation into former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists.

The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics.

Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations.

Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations.

Sri Lankan court to deliver verdict on deadly Easter bombings

Sri Lanka Easter bombings victims named 'heroes of faith' by Vatican

title: Chicago's half-empty schools reveal a crisis city leaders refuse to confront
excerpt:
Pastor and Project H.O.O.D. founder Corey Brooks says Black women and families need to be empowered in America.

On the West Side of Chicago, Frederick Douglass Academy had a grand total of 27 student...
body_text:
Pastor and Project H.O.O.D. founder Corey Brooks says Black women and families need to be empowered in America.

On the West Side of Chicago, Frederick Douglass Academy had a grand total of 27 students inside a building that was built for 1,000 students. That is only 2 percent of the building's capacity. The school was one of 13 Chicago schools that had fewer than 100 students. Across the city, 35 percent of schools are less than half full. The Chicago Public Schools system has lost more than 77,000 students since 2010.

So where are all the students disappearing to? The answer is an indictment of the city and its public school sector.

It is true that many families have left the city because of its rising cost of living. I know many Black families who have moved out, and their numbers are in the tens of thousands. It is also true that the birth rate in Chicago has dropped by nearly 50 percent in less than 20 years. It is not surprising that many graduates choose to leave the city instead of staying and starting families here.

NEW YORK CITY'S DECLINING PUBLIC SCHOOL ENROLLMENT PROJECTED TO LOSE OVER 150K MORE AS POPULATION DECLINES

But these are not the only reasons why so many public schools are suffering from abysmal enrollment numbers.

The children who live on the West Side and South Side did not all disappear. They chose not to go to their neighborhood public high schools. I cannot blame them. Students stuck in these schools tell me they can't learn because the teachers cannot control the rowdier kids. There's a lack of discipline, and rules are hardly enforced. Some students even tell me that some teachers don't even try and just pass the kids. So kids know that if they challenge the teachers and make trouble, they will often give up and award them a passing grade.

An empty Chicago Public Schools classroom is seen on Dec. 15, 2025. (Antonio Perez/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

JONATHAN TURLEY: CHICAGO SCHOOLS REWARD PROTEST WHILE STUDENTS CAN'T READ

The students and parents hear all of these stories, and that plays a major role in why they are choosing to enroll in magnet schools, charter schools, parochial schools, and even private schools. CPS still enrolls most of the city's remaining kids, but its share slipped from about 75 percent to 71 percent. That is roughly 18,000 children who live in Chicago and chose something else. Parents in Kids First workshops said school quality is one of the reasons families stay or go.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TOUTS ‘HARD RESET’ FOR AMERICAN SCHOOLS, VOWS TO PUT PARENTS ‘BACK IN CHARGE’

If we look more closely at the statistics, it is easy to see why so many families have opted out of public schools, especially Black families. In the same district, Black students in selective enrollment high schools are three times more likely to read at grade level than Black students in traditional public schools. When it comes to math, the numbers are even starker. Black students are five times more likely to be proficient in math in selective enrollment schools than their peers in public schools. Parents are seeing the data, and they're voting with their feet.

It doesn't help that the Chicago Teachers Union has made a mockery of itself. The head of the union doesn't even send her own children to the public schools that she oversees. The CTU has continued to choose politics over its teachers and schools time after time. In 2025, CTU spent a record $4.2 million on politics and lobbying while spending less than 18 percent of its total spending on representing teachers. It poured millions into electing Mayor Brandon Johnson, a former CTU organizer. It then used that alliance to freeze school closings and to fight school-choice initiatives that have been a boon to many poor parents.

STEVE MOORE, ED POZZUOLI: STOP FUNDING SCHOOL SYSTEMS. LET THE MONEY FOLLOW THE CHILD

If it couldn't get worse than that, CTU also helped kill Illinois' Invest in Kids scholarships because they allowed kids to escape the public schools. Not only that, CTU has made the national news several times for using "days of action" to turn kids into activists for whatever left-wing cause is in vogue at the moment. So why would CTU be shocked when families see all of this political activity and instead choose to get the best education for their children?

POWERFUL TEACHERS' UNIONS SHARE STRIKING LINK WITH STATES STRUGGLING TO TEACH KIDS TO READ

I want to be clear that I'm not here to slander teachers. Many of them are excellent, but they will tell you, as they have told me, that they are trapped in a system that does not allow them to teach to the fullest of their abilities. One told me, "I want to teach algebra, and I want to experience that joy when I see a child struggling at the beginning of the year only to become masterful by the end of the year — I don't want to teach activism."

That is why the buildings are empty. The people who run these buildings are largely the problem.

They have created schools that hold little appeal to families. This is America, a capitalist society, where people will always choose what is best for them. No parent wants to drive that extra hour or pay extra fees or tuition, but they will do so for their child's education. If the public schools want to bring these students back, then they have to buck the existing leadership.

They have to return to the original purpose of the public schools: to develop young minds into educated, upstanding citizens. The empty buildings are a symbol of how far we have strayed from that original purpose.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM PASTOR COREY BROOKS

Pastor Corey Brooks, known as the "Rooftop Pastor," is the founder and Senior Pastor of New Beginnings Church of Chicago and the CEO of Project H.O.O.D. (Helping Others Obtain Destiny), the church's local mission. He gained national attention for his 94-day and 343-day rooftop vigils to transform the notorious "O-Block," once known as Chicago's most dangerous block, into #OpportunityBlock. Learn more at ProjectHOOD.org.

title: Dem reactions within moments of Austin ICE shooting spark viral outrage locally, online: 'Disqualifying'
excerpt:
Fox News Digital spoke to retired Austin police officer Dennis Farris about the left’s reaction and rhetoric following an ICE shooting that made nationwide headlines.

Democrats in Austin, Texas are f...
body_text:
Fox News Digital spoke to retired Austin police officer Dennis Farris about the left’s reaction and rhetoric following an ICE shooting that made nationwide headlines.

Democrats in Austin, Texas are facing criticism both online and from a retired cop who spoke to Fox News Digital after rushing to attack Immigration and Customs Enforcement moments after a suspected illegal immigrant was shot before any investigation had taken place.

An ICE officer shot a man in Austin on Sunday and almost immediately, before basic facts had been established in the case, and before the man had been identified as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, elected Democrats in Austin were speaking out against ICE, including Rep. Greg Casar, Councilman Mike Siegel, and Mayor Kirk Watson.

"It is awful that this war has come to our doorstep," Casar, a member of the progressive Squad caucus, said during a Sunday press conference in a clip that was highlighted by the White House Rapid Response account on X.

"And as the mayor said, unfortunately it is not a surprise. Just a few weeks ago as we saw the ICE surge come to Austin, especially to north central Austin, I and others said that ICE needed to leave before someone was shot like in Minneapolis or like in Corpus Christi or like in Chicago, and that day is here and so I think the message remains that for Austin to be safe, ICE should end its surge here in our community."

BRANDON GILL UNLOADS ON DEMOCRATS OVER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH RAPING TEEN: 'COLLATERAL DAMAGE'

(Sara Diggins/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images) (Sara Diggins/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

Casar and his fellow Democrats quickly sparked viral social media criticism from conservatives accusing the left of selective outrage when it comes to crime, particularly illegal immigrant crime.

"Where was the outcry from this guy last fall when an illegal alien in Texas used a machete to behead a man in front of his spouse and child?" Former Assistant Secretary of Homeland Security for Public Affairs Tricia McLaughlin posted on X. "The perpetrator reportedly kicked the head of the victim ‘around like a soccer ball.’ "

"There it is," Townhall’s Amy Curtis posted on X. "The Democrats want no immigration laws. They want to destroy this nation. Remember this in November."

"This sort of rhetoric should be disqualifying for any elected official," Texas Republican State Rep. Andy Hopper posted on X. "You cannot faithfully take the oath of office and be for open borders. "

Dennis Farris, president of the Austin Police Retired Officers Association, told Fox News Digital he expects that kind of rhetoric from Casar and Siegel but was surprised to hear Mayor Watson rush to place blame on ICE both in the press conference and on social media.

‘OUT OF CONTROL’ KILLINGS IN SPANBERGER’S VIRGINIA REACH ‘INSANE’ POINT AS MIGRANT CHARGED IN STABBING SPREE

"With Casar, it didn't surprise me, that’s Greg Casar, he's a bomb thrower, he's been a bomb thrower and he's been a reactionary known for shooting his mouth off before he has all the facts," Farris said. "He did that when he was on the city council. He did it in the Mike Ramos shooting. That’s just Greg Casar, He's known for his theatrics."

"I've known the mayor a long time, consider the mayor a friend, I was really shocked at how visceral his reaction was, he's usually a lot more measured," Farris said. "I can understand being upset but the way he reacted, I think, raised the temperature in Austin because he is the one that he is, the leader, right? He is the city leader. He's the mayor. He's the one supposed to be trying to keep things calm and I think his reaction yesterday made it worse."

Watson’s post was "ratioed" on social media, yielding far more negative comments and quote tweets than positive ones, with locals and internet users accusing him of fanning the flames before the facts were known.

"Honestly shocking Mayor @KirkPWatson would issue this sort of statement knowing full well the investigation has barely started, Hope he’s not about to make an Adler-esque 2nd term turn," prominent Austin attorney Adam Loewy posted on X, referencing former Austin Mayor Steve Adler who presided over the 2020 George Floyd rioting in the city.

Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of Casar, Watson, and Siegel for comment.

Farris rejected Democrat claims that ICE is "surging" in Austin and said that federal immigration authorities, whether ICE or INS, have been conducting deportations in Austin for decades without any fanfare.

"They've been arresting people that were in the country illegally and I think what we're seeing here is that the reaction to it is because of Trump, it's the Trump administration doing it and it's just another way to dislike the president for whatever reason you want to dislike him for," Farris said.

In the aftermath of the shooting, Austin Police said three people were arrested, several police vehicles were damaged, and two officers were injured after hundreds took to the streets throwing rocks, bottles, and piece of concrete at officers, Fox News national correspondent Brooke Taylor reported.

DHS sources confirmed to Fox News on Sunday that Garces Perez is an illegal immigrant from Venezuela with a final order of removal. DHS said Garces Perez illegally entered the United States under the Biden administration. The agency said he was shot during a law enforcement operation.

Perez’s attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, claims he was driving for DoorDash when an unmarked truck sideswiped him, chased him and struck his car again before an ICE officer shot him in the back of the neck.

Protesters confront police officers (not picured) after city officials said that a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a person earlier in the day in Austin, Texas, U.S. September 20, 2026. REUTERS/Nuri Vallbona (REUTERS/Nuri Vallbona)

"Wilber entered through CBPOne seeking asylum," Lincoln-Goldfinch posted on X on Monday. "He was inspected and entered lawfully through a port of entry. He was issued a valid work permit. The issue regarding the deportation order is that he moved and changed addresses. There was a notice for a hearing sent to the wrong address that he missed, which is VERY common. We are working on that. He will be released from detention, his immigration matter will be resolved, and the agencies will be held accountable."

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

Our colleagues on the US blog will cover him in more detail h...
body_text:
The US president made the comments as he arrives at the UN headquarters in New York

Meanwhile, Trump is arriving at the UN HQ right now.

Our colleagues on the US blog will cover him in more detail here, but I will pick up all his Europe-related comments here.

After very brief doorstep comments – almost exclusively mocking CNN - he answers a reporter’s very loud question by saying his message to Putin is: “settle the war.”

Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is speaking next, and then it will be Trump.

In other very important news, the escalators at the UN HQ appear to be functioning absolutely fine on Trump’s arrival, in sharp contrast to last year’s incident.

US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz also seems to be very happy about this fact.

Let’s hope the teleprompter is ready for Trump’s speech, too.

Meanwhile, Trump is arriving at the UN HQ right now.

Our colleagues on the US blog will cover him in more detail here, but I will pick up all his Europe-related comments here.

After very brief doorstep comments – almost exclusively mocking CNN - he answers a reporter’s very loud question by saying his message to Putin is: “settle the war.”

Guterres also talks about the importance and relevance of the UN in today’s world, as he argues that:

“The world does not need the weaker United Nations. It needs the UN strong enough to face the world as it is, and determined enough to build the world as it should be.”

He says that in his 10 years he has learned that “the greatest power is not the power to dominate; [but] the power to build a future that works for everyone.”

“Our shared future will be forged by whether humanity can govern power wisely, by upholding the law before impunity becomes normalised, by ending wars, before they consume generations. By tackling inequality, before societies fracture. By accelerating climate action, before tipping points are crossed, and by governing artificial intelligence before it governs us.

This is the challenge before this General Assembly, the United Nations and humanity itself.”

He signs off declaring his resolve to follow these principles in the last 100 days in the office, and pledging he will always keep championing them even once he left the post.

“I will continue to stand up for the values of the United Nations Charter, and I will never, ever give up,” he declares to warm applause and a standing ovation.

UN general assembly president and Bangladeshi foreign minister Khalilur Rahman is next to speak, with US president Donald Trump expected near the top of the hour.

In a paragraph that would look ridiculous in 2016 – but very much does not in 2026 – UN secretary-general António Guterres has issued a stark warning on the escalation of autonomous technology.

“Artificial intelligence must be shaped by humanity, with humanity and for all humanity. And as we confront the challenges ahead, let us not retreat from two fundamental principles. Let’s say with one voice, children must never become the test subjects for unregulated systems.

And let us resolve that life and death decisions must never be surrendered to machines. Killer robots must have no place in our future.”

Guterres also speaks at length about the prospect of AI, and risks associated with its rapid rise, just as “the very developers building these systems are now pulling the alarm.”

He says that “governments must assume their responsibilities” to scrutinise AI and work on “transparency, trust and cooperation.”

“Not despite geopolitical rivalry, but precisely because of it.

At a pivotal moment during the cold war, strategic rivals came to recognise the need to manage shared existential risks. They built mechanisms to reduce misunderstandings, manage escalation and prevent catastrophe. At that time, it was the nuclear armament. Today, artificial intelligence demands the same clarity of purpose and sense of urgency.”

UN secretary general António Guterres is now speaking in the opening debate of the UN general assembly.

He warns that “across the Middle East, conflicts are cascading,” as he urged leaders to use the week in New York “for de-escalation and dialogue.”

Continuing on the Middle East, he says “all the fighting must stop, and humanitarian aid must flow.”

He specifically picks up on “the devastating situation in the occupied Palestinian territory,” saying that in the three years following the “abhorrent terror attacks” on 7 October, “what followed was an onslaught on Palestinians and Gaza” at scale that has no comparison.

“Violence, displacement and settlement expansion by Israel in the occupied West Bank are bulldozing the path to peace and raising the spectre of ethnic cleansing. We cannot allow the two state solution to disappear before our eyes,” he warns.

He then turns to Ukraine, talking about how “Russia’s full scale invasion has subjected a sovereign country to a brutal war, in blatant violation of the charter.”

“Civilians continue to be killed far from the frontlines, mainly in Ukraine, but also more recently in parts of Russia. Homes, energy and water systems and transport have come under repeated attack, threatening food and energy supplies and supply chains globally.”

He also mentions the crises in Sudan and Myanmar, and talks about the need to reform the UN security council by adding a permanent seat for an African nation.

Swedish prosecutors are investigating possible election fraud that has raised uncertainty about the recent election there.

A preliminary investigation into potential election ⁠fraud in Borlange, a town in the largely rural county of Dalarna, central Sweden, might still affect the final ​result. Sweden’s election review board could decide on a re-run or recount of the vote, which elects 11 members of parliament, if it decides the result is suspect.

Reuters, citing local media, reports that the prosecutor’s investigation centred on the election of Mohamed Abdukardir Ali, a Left Party candidate for parliament. Ali told Swedish TV that the allegations were false.

Reuters is carrying a Kremlin read-out of a call between Russia’s president Vladimir Putin and Saudi crown prince ⁠Mohammed bin Salman. It said ‌the two ‌leaders held a detailed exchange ‌of views on the situation in the Middle East, and “the ⁠importance of ensuring the safe ​and ​unimpeded passage of vessels ​through the region’s international ​waterways was emphasised.”

Just a quick note with bit of guidance on timings today, as we are inevitably looking at events across the ocean.

Donald Trump’s speech to the UN general assembly is expected around 10am New York time. That’s 3pm UK, 4pm in most of Europe.

Our US blog colleagues will cover it in excruciating detail if you don’t want to miss a single thing, but rest assured I will pick up key bits on Europe here.

The Greenland deal signing ceremony is expected around 10.30am (3.30pm UK, 4.30pm Europe).

And Trump’s sit-down with Zelenskyy will be around 13.15am New York time, so 6.15pm UK, 7.15pm Europe.

title: Court quashes 1976 convictions over link to corrupt London police officer
excerpt:
Christopher Poulter and Kevin Biggs, who  died  in 2004, exonerated of mailbag theft after new evidence emerged

Two men have had theft convictions quashed at the court of appeal half a century after ...
body_text:
Christopher Poulter and Kevin Biggs, who  died  in 2004, exonerated of mailbag theft after new evidence emerged

Two men have had theft convictions quashed at the court of appeal half a century after they were wrongfully arrested because of a corrupt police officer, although one did not live to see his exoneration.

Christopher Poulter and Kevin Biggs were 21 and 18 respectively when they were convicted in 1976 of taking 13 mailbags from a wagon in Clapham goods yard in London.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) referred their case to the court of appeal earlier this year after new evidence emerged about the disgraced police officer DS Derek Ridgewell.

Ridgewell was jailed for seven years in 1980 after stealing more than £1m in goods, and was found to have framed innocent young black men for his own crimes, the CCRC said. He was one of three officers said to have seen Poulter and Biggs taking the mailbags and fleeing by car. The men’s defence was that they had been in a pub in Tooting, in south London, all night, before being approached by officers and arrested.

Poulter was sentenced to a year in prison and Biggs was sentenced to borstal training, at their hearing at inner London crown court 50 years ago.

The innocence of Biggs, who died in 2004, emerged through an investigation by the British Transport Police, who were searching for victims of Ridgewell. He and Poulter are the 14th and 15th people to have their convictions quashed in relation to Ridgewell’s misconduct. They were convicted alongside a third man, Stephen Simmons, whose conviction was quashed in 2018.

At a hearing on Tuesday, Lord Justice Edis, sitting with Mr Justice Lavender and Mr Justice Linden, said their appeals should have been heard together. “It had not been possible to add any relatives of Mr Biggs, who had by then died, or find Mr Poulter, so they could be joined on to the appeal by Mr Simmons. The two appeals are allowed and the convictions quashed.”

Speaking after the hearing, Jenny Wiltshire, the head of serious and general crime at Hickman &and Rose and who has represented many of Ridgewell’s victims, said it was a “disgrace” British Transport Police had taken so long to track people down.

“It is now half a century since these two men were found guilty of a crime they did not commit. The British Transport Police knew for certain that the police officer whose evidence sent them to jail was corrupt just four years after they were convicted, and probably a lot earlier.

“The British Transport Police did nothing at the time and have only relatively recently started to take this issue seriously. As a result of this inaction, Christopher Poulter has lived the majority of his life as a convicted criminal. Kevin Biggs died as one.”

The CCRC chair Dame Vera Baird KC said: “It is absolutely right that that these men have had their convictions quashed by the court today. Anyone else who believes they have been convicted through the actions of Derek Ridgewell should apply to us so we can investigate whether we can also refer your case to the courts.”

The British Transport Police have been contacted for comment.

title: Trump set to address UNGA with Middle East and Ukraine on agenda – US politics live
excerpt:
While the contents of his speech are unknown, Trump last year caused a ⁠stir with a combative address; president also due to meet with 11 world leaders

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog....
body_text:
While the contents of his speech are unknown, Trump last year caused a ⁠stir with a combative address; president also due to meet with 11 world leaders

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Donald Trump is expected to ⁠start the day with a speech to assembled delegates at the UN General Assembly, before meeting with no fewer than 11 world leaders, bilaterally or in group settings.

While the contents of his speech are unknown, Trump last year caused a ⁠stir with a combative address, telling the audience that their countries were “going to hell” for, among other things, climate policy and mass migration.

The president is then set for a whirlwind schedule of meetings with ⁠leaders from four continents on Tuesday. It comes against the backdrop of an unstable Middle East and a four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine that shows no signs of abating.

Trump will meet with British prime minister Andy Burnham, Ukrainian ‌president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Venezuela’s interim leader Delcy ‌Rodriguez, Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland prime minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and the representatives of the Gulf states of the United Arab Emirates, ‌Saudi Arabia, Oman, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar.

In the evening, he may meet dozens more leaders, albeit briefly, during a leaders’ reception. Trump met with French president Emmanuel Macron on Monday and additions to his Tuesday schedule are possible.

Here, my colleague Robert Tait provides some analysis on what may be expected from Trump’s address:

The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds. Newsrooms including the New York Times and the Washington Post also decided to hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage on Monday until midnight as part of the collective effort. More here.

The barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights. The parties are seeking a temporary restraining order that would immediately lift the ban – and return access for the journalists – while the case plays out. More here.

Trump is bracing for a loss in the lawsuit brought by the three media organizations, as he considers that the judge presiding over the case – his own appointee – previously ordered the White House to restore credentials for journalist Jim Acosta. “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote on Truth Social.

Trump said that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms. More here.

The Venezuelan man who was shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday spoke out from detention on Monday afternoon when he was able to call his lawyer, in the middle of a press conference, and plead for better medical care. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine and is in much discomfort. More here.

Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Republican subject of a House ethics complaint that she had sex with three staff members, and paid one to keep quiet, has said the allegations are untrue – and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her. More here.

Trump is arriving at the UN HQ right now.

After very brief doorstep comments – almost exclusively mocking CNN - he answers a reporter’s very loud question by saying his message to Putin is: “settle the war.”

In his address to the world leaders gathered at the UN general assembly in New York, the UN secretary-general, António Guterres, said the world must work together in “interdependence” to solve problems.

“The fault lines in our world are widening,” Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, said, citing geopolitical conflicts, the climate crisis and the rapid development of artificial intelligence.

But instead of letting the future continue to veer toward fragmentation, transactionalism and mistrust, he called for “a world built on interdependence – and sustained by a dense web of economic, political, social and technological connections.”

Senator John Curtis, a Republican from Utah, on Tuesday published a letter calling for a key Senate committee to investigate Donald Trump’s son over his personal and business dealings with foreign governments, as well as his shady ventures in cryptocurrency and predictions markets.

Curtis’ letter to the Senate Judiciary Committee follows a bombshell report from ProPublica earlier this month that found Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch with close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, had helped bankroll Trump Jr.’s lavish Bahamas wedding earlier this year.

In a post to social media that unveiled the letter, Curtis appeared to criticize his party for ignoring Trump Jr.’s conduct after having relentlessly investigated similar allegations against Joe Biden’s son, Hunter.

“A toaster is a wedding gift,” Curtis wrote in a post to social media revealing the letter. “A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else. Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden’s foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now. ‘Trust us’ was not enough then, and it is not enough now.”

Curtis’ letter represents a rare Republican break from Trump, close to a midterm election over which alleged corruption by the president and his family is one of several issues weighing on the party.

But Curtis’ concerns over Trump Jr.’s dealings stated in his letter go beyond the wedding, citing his pursuit of real estate deals abroad that have included meetings with foreign heads of state, his stake in defense contractors, and his promotion of Trump family-backed cryptocurrency ventures that have generated immense wealth for the president and his family.

He also took aim at Trump Jr.’s deep investment in the nascent and dubiously legal prediction market industry, most notably through his ties to Polymarket, that depend on a lenient hand from federal regulators his father has power over.

“These reports raise legitimate questions about foreign access to members of a sitting president’s family and whether such relationships can create actual or perceived expectations of favorable treatment,” Curtis wrote. “They also may create expectations of a returned favor that would not be in the best interests of the American people or our allies, and could even create national security vulnerabilities.”

Curtis called on the leadership of the Senate Judiciary Committee, currently headed by Republican Chuck Grassley, to subpoena both Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden as part of a sweeping inquiry into how presidents’ family members have leveraged their ties to the office for personal enrichment.

After months of mounting concerns that the campaign against Iran has critically depleted the US supply of munitions, Trump took to social media – not long before he was set to address world leaders at the United Nations – to dismiss the fears.

“The cowards and traitors would love to say the United States is low on munitions,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “It’s not true. We have more munitions than we could ever possibly think of using, and are building them up now at levels we have never seen before.”

(Several outlets, citing officials within the Trump administration, have reported that a critical shortage of key munitions, including missile interceptors, is shaping decision-making around the war. In a report published earlier this month, the Defense Department’s inspector general acknowledged the supply constraints, writing that the missile expenditure in Iran has “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.”)

The US and Iran have been at war since February, when Trump, alongside Israel, launched a series of missile strikes that killed the country’s supreme leader. Since then, the remains of Iran’s hardline leadership have dug in, blockading the vital Strait of Hormuz, a key artery of oil shipping, and launching waves of drones and missiles at US bases and ships in the region.

The US has retaliated by striking Iranian targets and oil tankers, and by imposing withering economic sanctions aimed at forcing the regime back to the bargaining table.

Those efforts, so far, have not yielded the kind of capitulation that Trump has demanded to end the war.

A series of top Republicans heading to Iowa and New Hampshire – key states in the presidential primary – have raised the possibility of a contentious 2028 field for the GOP nomination, The Washington Post reported on Tuesday.

Senator Ted Cruz, a onetime 2016 primary opponent of Trump’s, and John Kennedy, a senator from Louisiana, have both visited Iowa in recent weeks. Senator Rick Scott of Florida headlined a party event in New Hampshire.

Add to them senator Rand Paul, the longtime libertarian from Kentucky who has often clashed with Trump, and representative Thomas Massie, a congressman from the state who Trump helped oust via a primary challenge. Neither has ruled out a presidential run.

Federal immigration officials in Texas prevented US representative Veronica Escobar from fully conducting her congressional oversight duties at a controversial Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center, the lawmaker said in an interview with the Guardian.

Escobar, a Democrat who represents El Paso and surrounding areas on the US-Mexico border in west Texas, conducted an oversight visit last month at the Camp East Montana ICE tent facility housed in the Fort Bliss military base, after two separate “disturbances” had been reported there in recent weeks.

But when she arrived to scrutinize conditions at the camp, the largest ICE detention center in the country, she said she was not allowed to speak with any of the detained immigrants. She also requested surveillance footage of the reported incidents but said she has not received it.

“The administration obviously has attempted to block congressional oversight,” Escobar said in a telephone interview with the Guardian. “It’s been very challenging at times. And that has depended on, to a large extent, what the directive has been from the administration.”

The constraints placed on Escobar is one of the latest instances in which the Trump administration has limited members of Congress’s ability to conduct oversight visits into federal immigration detention centers.

Escobar and other federal lawmakers sued the Trump administration last year for blocking such access. Despite a federal judge ruling in favor of the lawmakers last December, there have been subsequent reports of ICE officials placing limits on or turning away members of congress when attempting to conduct oversight visits.

“Oversight, during the second Trump administration, has certainly been significantly more challenging than during the first Trump administration,” Escobar added.

President Donald Trump has said he is working on a “massive” deal to buy fertiliser from Belarus, pivoting away from main supplier Canada amid an escalating trade dispute, and moving instead toward an ally of Russia.

“The United States is working on a massive deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” Trump said on his Truth Social network. “The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our farmers and ranchers.”

In recent weeks Trump has stepped up his trade war with Canada, a long-term US ally and the country’s biggest supplier of potash.

The announcement on Monday shows Washington’s willingness to pursue dialogue with Minsk despite its repression of dissidents and support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

The US imports most of its potash – a chemical salt used to manufacture fertiliser – and prices soared after the Ukraine war began in 2022.

In 2024, 79% came from Canada, 11% from Russia and 4% from Belarus, according to the US Geological Survey.

Donald Trump said on Monday that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms.

At a news conference following their closed-door meeting at Gracie Mansion, Trump and Mamdani appeared friendly as they have in previous meetings. Mamdani said he and Trump held a “wide-ranging” discussion, which touched on affordable housing and immigration, but did not offer extensive details regarding any disagreements between them.

Asked whether he challenged Trump over his decision to ban CNN, MS Now, and Politico from White House grounds, Mamdani said: “I told the president that we’re going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in.”

“It’s interesting because they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn’t very worried about that,” Trump chimed in, pointing to the large assembly of press on the lawn.

The visit to Gracie Mansion, ahead of the president’s speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday, was a measure of Trump’s apparent respect for the 34-year-old mayor of his native New York. It was the first presidential visit to the historic riverside residence in 45 years, following Ronald Reagan, who met there with Ed Koch in 1981.

The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds.

The collective decision came after the barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights.

The ban was an extraordinary escalation of Trump’s battle against news outlets. After a coalition of networks including ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – which along with CNN form a press “pool” that share the responsibilities of capturing and distributing footage of the president carried by news outlets worldwide – announced they would cease coverage in solidarity with the barred outlets, the White House promoted its own feed online, branding it “Trump TV”. The channel purported to show “top past moments, announcements, and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place”.

“Get real-time updates and live events streamed DIRECTLY to your phone,” the White House posted on social media. “No noise. Just the news that matters most – straight from the Trump Administration.”

It is extremely rare for a president to travel or make public appearances without the accompaniment of a representative from the White House television pool. Network cameras have provided coverage of the president since 1950.

On Monday, the ban against CNN meant that no broadcaster was covering Trump’s midday ribbon-cutting to unveil a new White House helipad. Although the White House provided a livestream, without professional boom mics and audio setup, the president’s remarks were inaudible over the sounds of a helicopter’s engine running in the background.

The president abruptly announced his ban against outlets this weekend in a Truth Social post, saying he had enough of “purposely negative stories” about him. Journalists had their press badges confiscated by Secret Service on Saturday.
