The barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights. The parties are seeking a temporary restraining order that would immediately lift the ban – and return access for the journalists – while the case plays out. More here.

Trump is bracing for a loss in the lawsuit brought by the three media organizations, as he considers that the judge presiding over the case – his own appointee – previously ordered the White House to restore credentials for journalist Jim Acosta. “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote on Truth Social.

Trump said that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms. More here.

The Venezuelan man who was shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday spoke out from detention on Monday afternoon when he was able to call his lawyer, in the middle of a press conference, and plead for better medical care. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine and is in much discomfort. More here.

Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Republican subject of a House ethics complaint that she had sex with three staff members, and paid one to keep quiet, has said the allegations are untrue – and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her. More here.

title: British banks told not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins
excerpt:
MPs send out letter as Israeli government seeks bids for construction of large E1 settlement in West Bank

British banks and financial institutions are receiving written warnings from MPs that they sh...
body_text:
MPs send out letter as Israeli government seeks bids for construction of large E1 settlement in West Bank

British banks and financial institutions are receiving written warnings from MPs that they should not invest in Israel’s E1 settlement project even though new UK laws banning trade with illegal settlements are unlikely to be in place for months.

A letter was sent to banks on Tuesday by the all-party Britain-Palestine group of MPs saying the onus was now on banks to review their obligations not to cooperate with new settlements.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced two weeks ago plans for a complete ban on trade with illegal settlements and new sanctions on those co-operating with building the settlements. But complex secondary legislation needed for the powers to come into force may take six to nine months to pass through parliament.

The issue is urgent since the Israeli government is seeking bids for two tenders for the construction of as many as 3,400 houses, including more than 1,300 for which the tender closes on 25 October, two days before the elections.

Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, said in 2025 that the E1 settlement “practically erases the two-state delusion” by splitting up territory that would be set aside for a Palestinian state. The settlement plan has long been delayed due to its uncontested political impact on the prospect of a two-state solution, still the main peace plan backed by the west and Gulf states.

Finance, insurance and guarantees are required before construction starts. One of Miliband’s motives in acting earlier this month, before the Israeli elections, was not just to express his deep concern at the scale of settler violence in the West Bank but to deter UK finance from helping with the tenders or the construction. It has been alleged that he overrode some diplomatic advice in acting before the elections.

The all-party group said: “The immediate question is what commitments institutions were willing to make while the detailed rules are being developed, and how they would respond when restrictions take effect”. The letter, signed by two Labour MPs, Debbie Abrahams and Andy McDonald, states: “Commitments made now may be difficult to unwind when restrictions commence; the allocation of costs will depend on the contracts and applicable law. We ask boards to consider this interim risk before agreeing new or increased commitments.”

The letter adds: “We ask you to place potential E1 and settlement-related exposure on the board’s agenda and on the risk register, and to reach a reasoned decision on whether the associated sanctions, legal and reputational risk sits within the institution’s stated risk appetite.”

It is argued that postcodes provide the locality of a product’s origin, and nothing is being attempted that would stop trade in general with Israel.

Abrahams said: “We are not asking to pre-empt the law. We are asking boards a question they should be able to answer today: what exposure are you prepared to carry while the sanctions regime is written and on what evidence?”

The all-party group said it intended to publish replies to its letter by 10 October.

title: SEE IT: Top Dem operative draws line at ‘deplorable’ Hasan Piker after touting party’s ‘big tent’
excerpt: Democratic National Committee’s Chairman Ken Martin distanced the Democratic party from controversial streamer Hasan Piker and called out Republicans ahead of midterm elections. (Credit: Nicholas Ball...
body_text:
Democratic National Committee’s Chairman Ken Martin distanced the Democratic party from controversial streamer Hasan Piker and called out Republicans ahead of midterm elections. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin distanced his party from far-left streamer Hasan Piker, calling his past remarks "disgusting and deplorable" while defending Democrats as a "big tent" that encompasses a wide range of political views.

"Let me just say that I think it's absolutely disgusting and deplorable the things that Hasan Piker has said," Martin said. "But he does not represent the Democratic Party, and he certainly doesn't represent the viewpoints of almost every one of our candidates and our elected officials."

Martin made the remarks after Fox News Digital asked how the party is navigating divisions among Democrats as socialist candidates gain prominence, including Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

RASKIN CALLS PIKER’S RHETORIC 'IRRELEVANT DISTRACTION' AFTER THE STREAMER SAID HE'D VOTE FOR HAMAS OVER ISRAEL

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, speaks at the Michigan Democratic Nominating Convention in Lansing, Mich., on Aug. 29, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

"Look, no one should confuse unity with unanimity in the Democratic Party, right?" Martin said. "We are a big tent party. We have lots of different viewpoints and ideas and all sorts of issues."

Piker has been scrutinized for a slew of past comments critical of Israel — one of his most controversial comments was claiming that the U.S. "deserved 9/11."

Martin previously joined other party leaders and prominent Democrats in condemning rhetoric blaming Jewish Americans for threats and violence, calling it "dangerous, wrong, and antisemitic," but his statement did not name Piker.

"Criticizing the policies and actions of the Israeli government is one thing," Martin posted to X last month. "Blaming American Jews for the hatred, threats, and violence directed at them is something else entirely. It is dangerous, wrong, and antisemitic."

The comments come as El-Sayed, who campaigned with Piker during Michigan's Democratic primary, has sought to distance himself from the streamer as Republicans make their association a midterm attack line.

EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PIKER, ISRAEL AND SOCIALIST TIES AFTER MIKE ROGERS SKIPS SENATE DEBATE

Twitch streamer Hasan Piker appeared on the campaign trail with Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

Martin also called out Republicans for cutting the House’s September session short and leaving Capitol Hill weeks before the midterm elections, telling Fox News Digital there is crucial legislative work that will be left unfinished.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week that he was canceling votes scheduled last week and sent lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess. Johnson has defended the decision, saying the House had "done its work."

"Republicans… they're afraid to actually come to Washington for a whole host of reasons, right?" Martin said. "They've recessed saying mission accomplished six weeks early when they could actually do something to help the American people."

"What the hell are they doing? Where are they going? You know what, Democrats are here. We're ready to work. We are ready to pass legislation that actually helps get people a chance, an opportunity, a chance to get ahead. Where the hell are the Republicans?"

WHY THE HOUSE LET OUT EARLY IS A MATTER OF DEBATE AFTER JOHNSON SAYS CHAMBER HAS 'DONE ITS WORK'

Ken Martin, chairman of the Democratic National Committee, speaks during a press conference with Texas Democrats at the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades union hall on August 5, 2025, in Aurora, Illinois. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

Martin also predicted Democrats would win control of both chambers in November as the elections inch closer, with roughly six weeks until Americans vote to determine which party will control the Senate and the House.

"Mark my words right here," Martin said. "You heard it here first, right? 47 days left. The Democratic Party is going to take control of the House back, and we're going to control the Senate back, and we're not going to screw around like these Republicans have."

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Ed Davey promises £17bn income tax cut if Lib Dems are elected
excerpt:
Growth created by rejoining EU single market and customs union would fund change, Davey tells the party’s conference

Ed Davey has unveiled a plan for a £17bn income tax cut in a speech aimed at shori...
body_text:
Growth created by rejoining EU single market and customs union would fund change, Davey tells the party’s conference

Ed Davey has unveiled a plan for a £17bn income tax cut in a speech aimed at shoring up the party’s support among former Conservative voters, but which risked disappointing some Liberal Democrat MPs who want a bolder vision for the party.

Addressing the party’s annual conference in Brighton, the Lib Dem leader said the proposal, which would eventually increase the threshold for paying income tax to £15,000 and raise the level at which people pay the 40p higher rate by about £6,000, would be paid for entirely by increased growth.

This growth, the Lib Dems argue, would be created through rejoining the EU’s single market and customs union.

As making a deal with the EU would take time, the actual tax cuts would only happen in the final year of a parliament, potentially as late as 2034, costing £17bn. In the interim years, thresholds would be raised by inflation, thus keeping levels effectively stable.

There would also be a smaller increase to the 45p additional rate of tax, currently payable above £125,000.

Setting out what he described as “trusting people to spend their own money, not telling them the state knows best”, Davey took aim at what he called “the post-Brexit stealth taxes” of frozen thresholds, notably on the higher 40p rate.

“Thirty years ago, just 2 million people paid it. Now it’s 9 million,” he said. “A tax band designed for stockbrokers is now holding back teachers and nurses. That’s not fair. It’s not right.”

The plans mark a distinct shift in the party’s fiscal approach. While it is eyecatching and could appeal to the many former Conservative voters who backed the Lib Dems in 2024, helping them take 60-plus Tory seats, it is likely to cause unease among some of the party’s MPs.

A number of them have called privately for a more ambitious and comprehensive vision of what the party stands for, amid polling that shows most voters do not have much of a sense of this.

Davey’s advisers, however, argue that the cost of living is the subject that most affects many voters, and that tax cuts – even up to eight years in the future – directly address this.

Other elements of the speech included previously-trailed new policies, including a proposal for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation treaty to halt the development of super-intelligent AI.

The tax-cutting plan is predicated entirely on the EU allowing a swift deal on single market access, which could become even more difficult if rightwing populists take power in more EU states, and on this then increasing growth.

The Lib Dems insist the numbers stand up, saying they are based on a report from an independent economics consultancy, which calculated that a deal with the EU could generate 0.5% growth in the first fiscal year alone.

Reform UK has already pledged to increase the personal tax allowance to £15,000, paid for in part by significant cuts to social security.

Davey noted this in the speech, saying: “Think about that. Reform say you can have a tax cut, but only if they get to punish disabled people at the same time. We say no. We can cut taxes and support the most vulnerable people in our country.”

Opening his speech with a warning that black-shirted, and balaclava-wearing far-right protesters who gathered in Dover and Portsmouth “would tear our country apart”, Davey compared groups such as Patriot Platform to Oswald Mosley’s fascists in the 1930s, the National Front in the 70s and to Nick Griffin and the BNP.

“Each time, they tried to turn neighbour against neighbour, tried to pit community against community, tried to turn our streets into battlegrounds,” he said. “But we didn’t let them. The British people said no.”

He said this time, far-right vigilantes were not acting in isolation, but were the most visible part of a far-right threat that was “extremely well funded” and promoted by figures such as Elon Musk and given credibility by “cynical politicians like Nigel Farage”.

Davey slammed Farage as a cynical politician who was “not just willing, but eager to fan the flames of hatred and intolerance to make himself richer”.

He said: “It is the worst of Trump’s America. We must not let it become Farage’s Britain.” Pointing to the £72m donations Reform had received from two crypto billionaires, Davey added: “If there was any doubt before, there can’t be now. We are in the fight of our lives. And it is a fight we must win.”

title: High-mileage electric cars are more reliable than petrol ones, study finds
excerpt:
EVs with 90,000 to 120,000 miles on the clock are more likely to pass MOTs than petrol models of the same age

Motorists buying a secondhand car with a lot of miles on the clock are likely to find an ...
body_text:
EVs with 90,000 to 120,000 miles on the clock are more likely to pass MOTs than petrol models of the same age

Motorists buying a secondhand car with a lot of miles on the clock are likely to find an electric vehicle (EV) ultimately more reliable than a petrol vehicle, according to a study.

An analysis of 47.4m MOT tests found that after cars were driven 90,000 to 120,000 miles, EVs were about 25% less likely to fail than petrol models of the same age (based on a failure rate of 16.5% versus 22.1%).

Beyond 120,000 miles, 16% of EVs failed, compared with 23.5% of petrol cars. The study found relatively little difference between the two fuel types at lower mileages.

The study by the consultancy New AutoMotive on behalf of the industry group the British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association (BVRLA) comes as a growing number of EVs change hands. Many used to belong to company and leasing fleets so have potentially racked up a lot of miles.

Toby Poston, the BVRLA chief executive, said that mileage is “one of the first things people look at when buying a used car, and passing 60,000 or 70,000 miles can have a big impact on how a vehicle is perceived”.

He added: “What this data shows is that mileage alone should not put consumers off. A well-maintained, higher-mileage electric car can be an extremely durable used vehicle.

“That matters because the used market is where the transition to electric becomes accessible to millions more motorists. Giving buyers confidence in these cars will be critical to creating a healthy and affordable secondhand EV market.”

Ben Nelmes, the chief executive of New AutoMotive, which carried out the research, said that high mileage “isn’t a proxy for poor condition in the way buyers have traditionally assumed. The data suggests the mechanical simplicity of an electric drivetrain starts to become increasingly valuable as cars accumulate miles.”

The study also identified areas where electric cars performed worse, particularly tyres. EVs recorded nearly twice as many tyre defects as petrol cars and older, low-mileage electric cars showed increased friction-brake defects. Researchers attributed the latter to corrosion associated with the brakes being used less frequently.

MOT tests examine statutory roadworthiness, including brakes, tyres, suspension, steering and lights, but do not measure battery health, degradation or charging performance. This information would therefore need to be considered alongside mechanical roadworthiness when assessing any used EV, the researchers said.

“This isn’t an argument for buying a used EV without doing your homework,” Poston said. “Buyers should look at its history, condition, tyres and battery health just as they would scrutinise the engine, gearbox and service history of a petrol or diesel car.

“What we can now challenge is the idea that an electric car with 80,000 or 100,000 miles on the clock should automatically be regarded as worn out.”

title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror's lawyer torches 'Looney Tunes motion' to investigate him
excerpt: A mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case prompts holdout juror Michael P. Desronvil to defend his position through a statement. Criminal defense attorney Mercedes Colwin breaks down the juror's reasoning...
body_text:
A mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case prompts holdout juror Michael P. Desronvil to defend his position through a statement. Criminal defense attorney Mercedes Colwin breaks down the juror's reasoning and outlines potential next steps for prosecutors in Massachusetts, including a possible retrial or negotiated plea deal as the high-profile legal battle continues.

Lindsay Clancy's defense team is calling for an investigation into the holdout juror who sought to find her guilty of murder in the strangling of her children and using his refusal to bow to peer pressure to ask a judge to dismiss her charges — prompting a blistering response from his lawyer.

"The 'Looney Tunes' motion filed yesterday by Kevin 'Shooter McGavin' Reddington to investigate Michael is not just an attack on Michael for being the courageous lone holdout juror," attorney Edward Paltzik wrote on X Tuesday morning, referring to the holdout, Michael Desronvil.

"Reddington's motion is actually a full-frontal attack on the U.S. Constitution," Paltzik warned. "Because if the new normal is that jurors are going to face brutal reprisals for disagreeing with a defense attorney, you can kiss the Sixth Amendment goodbye."

LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS FACE DILEMMA: RETRIAL OR PLEA DEAL IN CASE INVOLVING 3 STRANGLED CHILDREN

Michael P. Desronvil, the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, which ended in a mistrial. (Fugitive TV)

He warned that if the judge grants defense demands for an investigation into his client it would undermine the American criminal justice system in the long run.

"If we follow his destructive proposal to its logical conclusion, we're going to have an endless cycle of prosecutors investigating holdouts who oppose 'guilty' and defense attorneys investigating holdouts who oppose 'not guilty,'" he wrote. "Pretty soon we'll end up with... a retrograde justice system that will look a lot like the Hatfield-McCoy Feud: a cycle of carnage so malignant that its origins will fade in importance, replaced by the hopeless death spiral of the cycle itself."

Reddington, in a motion filed Friday, called for a "limited inquiry" into the holdout, for information about his background and potential criminal history, phone records, courthouse surveillance video and more.

Lindsay Clancy looks at jurors as Judge Sullivan asks them to start deliberations for a sixth day. The Lindsay Clancy jury resumes deliberations for a sixth day on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026. ( )

Neither Paltzik nor Reddington immediately responded to requests for comment from Fox News Digital Tuesday morning.

LINDSAY CLANCY JUDGE CALLS MISTRIAL, THEN GRANTS DEFENSE ONE HOUR STAY FOR APPEAL

In a separate filing, another attorney for Clancy, Martin Weinberg, argued that Judge William Sullivan's decision to overrule a defense objection at trial should be grounds for dismissing the charges against the 36-year-old defendant on double jeopardy grounds. That motion also centered on the holdout juror and allegations that he ignored the judge's instructions and the law.

Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

"The jury twice informed the Court that one of its members was refusing to apply the Court's instructions regarding the fundamental concept of reasonable doubt," Weinberg wrote. "After the first such report, the Court asked each juror individually whether he or she was able to apply the law. Upon receiving the second report, the Court tempered its response even further, simply reminding all jurors as a group of their obligation to follow its instructions generally. The Court denied Ms. Clancy's explicit requests to go further."

LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR MAKES NEW PROMISE AS LAWYER WARNS OF PUBLIC ATTACKS

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Kevin J. Reddington addresses the media outside of Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., on Thursday, September 3, 2026. His client, Lindsay Clancy, is on trial for the murder of her three children in 2023. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

Weinberg's motion argued that Sullivan's decision to declare a mistrial before investigating the holdout is improper, alleging that the jury foreperson accused the holdout of making "statements acknowledging doubt but refus[ing] to apply it to the verdict as the law states."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Paltzik has said he began representing Desronvil last week as the holdout faced mounting public pressure from his fellow jurors, Clancy's defense and her supporters among the public.

Patrick Clancy exits Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., on Monday, July 27, 2026. His ex-wife, Lindsay Clancy, is on trial for the murder of their three children. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

JUROR ON LINDSAY CLANCY TRIAL SAYS 'WE LET DOWN LINDSAY' FOLLOWING MISTRIAL

Several other jurors have spoken publicly following Clancy's mistrial, which was declared on Sept. 4. Some, including the jury foreperson, have accused Desronvil of ignoring his own reasonable doubts about the prosecution's case, a claim he denied in his only public remarks.

"I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement last week, first made to NewsNation. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present."

Paula Devlin speaks with Fox News Digital about the Lindsay Clancy trial, Whitman, Massachusetts, Monday, September 14, 2026. Devlin was a juror in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital))

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

He said that based on the physical evidence, witness testimony and the prosecution's presentations, he "thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned."

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, admitted killing her children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — but argued she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings. Prosecutors argued she planned the murders and understood that what she was doing was wrong.

Nicole Kidman has plenty of thoughts about the season finale of "Lion...
body_text:
Jill Wagner told Fox News Digital that her typical day on the farm begins at 6:30 in the morning and includes a lot of hard work.

Nicole Kidman has plenty of thoughts about the season finale of "Lioness."

The hit CIA/military show created by Taylor Sheridan aired its season three finale on Sunday after a gritty and dark ride focused on the kidnapping of Joe (Zoe Saldaña).

'LIONESS' STAR LAYSLA DE OLIVEIRA REACTS TO THE EXPLOSIVE RESCUE EPISODE IN SEASON THREE

The rescue mission went down in episode seven, and the eighth and final episode of the latest season – titled "The Unraveling" – finally revealed who was pulling the strings the entire time.

The seemingly sweet and innocent woman from season one has become a brutally violent villain out for revenge. It was a full-circle moment for viewers. You can read my full breakdown here.

ZOE SALDAÑA SHARES BEHIND THE SCENES INSTAGRAM POSTS FROM BRUTAL 'LIONESS' TORTURE SCENE

Nicole Kidman as Kaitlyn in "Lioness," episode eight of season three. (Photo Credit: Ryan Green/Paramount+)

Kidman, who plays Kaitlyn, spoke with Entertainment Weekly about the finale and touched on one of the most shocking moments:

The murder of Oleksandra, who ultimately was completely innocent of any wrongdoing.

LIONESS STAR MICHAEL KELLY CALLS TAYLOR SHERIDAN 'ONE OF THE GREATEST STORYTELLERS' IN ENTERTAINMENT

"She absolutely has a moral code and conscience, but she always weighs it up against cost. At the same time, she’s not mired down in regret. She’s a move-forward person, in the same way that when people play sports, you don’t get stuck on a previous point. title: Iran delegation to present narrative of resilience, diplomacy at UNGA
excerpt: Tehran, Iran – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and his team are heading to New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), where they are expected to express grievances about the United S...
body_text:
Tehran, Iran – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and his team are heading to New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), where they are expected to express grievances about the United States’ war on Iran, but also look at ways of resolving it.

Pezeshkian, who departed Tehran on Tuesday morning local time, is joined by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and other officials, and is scheduled to address the 193-member assembly on Wednesday.

“The issues we will raise at the UN concern expressing the plight of the Iranian nation, the crimes that have been committed against it, and the distrust that has been created,” Pezeshkian told reporters before boarding a flight out of Tehran.

He also warned that the renewed use of force by Iran’s foes would be counterproductive.

“We will make the enemies disappointed,” he said.

Araghchi, who had arrived in New York earlier, said his main goals during meetings on the sidelines will be to “defend the rights and interest of the Iranian people”.

The war started by the US and Israel on Iran on February 28 continues, with disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz that have affected global energy prices.

In the backdrop, Araghchi slammed the UN’s lacklustre performance in establishing peace and security.

“Trust in this organisation has been lost, and this is unfortunately because of its ineffectiveness in establishing international peace and security,” he said.

He said the Minab school bombing by the US and the assassination of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on the opening day of the war would be among the issues Iran will raise at the UN.

The Iranian delegation will be in New York for five days and is scheduled to return to Tehran on Saturday.

The US has denied visas to Pezeshkian’s accompanying media team and imposed tight restrictions on their movement in the country, according to the president’s office. Iranian delegates will also be barred from buying luxury goods during their stay.

Still, Pezeshkian plans to hold discussions with Iranian expatriates, intellectuals, think tanks and media in the coming days.

The UNGA brings together representatives of nearly 130 countries at the body’s headquarters in New York.

This year’s assembly, which begins on Tuesday, comes as the US tightens economic pressure through sanctions and a naval blockade on southern Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz.

US President Donald Trump said earlier this week that he was considering a new major military assault on Iran, but wanted to hear from the Arab leaders of the region first. He is set to meet with representatives from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and Bahrain in the coming days to discuss the war on Iran.

This and a military escalation in Yemen, where Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces are fighting the Iran-aligned Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, are other concerns for the assembly.

The Houthis have expanded control over the strait of Bab al-Mandeb in recent weeks after making rapid military advances in western Yemen and the Red Sea coast.

Regional mediators – including Pakistan, Qatar, Oman and Turkiye – have pushed for a diplomatic end to the crisis amid prospects of escalated conflict.

As Iran demands a return to the memorandum of understanding signed with the US in June to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, its diplomats are expected to sit down with mediators in New York as well.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera earlier this week that Tehran has communicated seven conditions to the US to reopen the strategic waterway.

These included an end to war on all fronts, the release of Iran’s frozen assets, the lifting of the blockade on Iranian ports, an end to military attacks on Iranian territory, and noninterference in the country’s internal affairs. But he also said Iran remains prepared for escalated fighting, and could potentially abandon the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) depending on future US actions.

There are conflicting views in Iran about how to end the war with the US, with some parties open to a peaceful resolution and more hardline factions seeking to continue or intensify the war until all Tehran’s demands are met.

Hossein Mohebbi, the spokesman of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), told local media on Tuesday that Iran was prepared to use new weapons systems against the US if necessary, and pointed to its recent attacks on US warships.

But he added that the country was open to peace. “If our national interests call for it to conduct some negotiations alongside war, we must negotiate,” he said.

Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, had already said both options remain on the table, but said hardline factions have no end date for the war of attrition. Other factions underestimate Iran’s capabilities and believe it must surrender, he said.

“The first keeps the country in a state of perpetual crisis and the other offers national resources and dignity to the enemy on a platter,” Ghalibaf said. “Both approaches realise the enemy’s wish for disturbing the country’s cohesion and unity.”

Trump said on Sunday he would “probably be open” to meeting Pezeshkian in New York, although the Iranian government’s IRNA news service dismissed this as a “new propaganda game”.

The government’s daily Iran newspaper said New York could offer a “platform for the Iranian narrative”. The hardline Kayhan newspaper wanted Pezeshkian to turn the UN into “a courtroom for American crimes”.

Public expectations in Iran are sceptical that the UN meetings will produce any political breakthrough to end the war, which has deepened the average Iranian citizen’s economic woes.

“I think Pezeshkian going [to New York] is better than him not going, but there is no hope that anything comes of it,” one Iranian told Al Jazeera in western Tehran, on condition of anonymity due to security concerns.

Another resident of the capital also said she harboured no hopes of a diplomatic resolution.

“I think if [the politicians] want to, then yes, there can be an opening, but they don’t want to,” she said.

title: Four days in Oxford: Inside the chaotic return of Lane Kiffin to Ole Miss, that turned into pure cinema
excerpt:
OutKick's Trey Wallace talks to Ole Miss football fans at The Grove about their feelings on Lane Kiffin ahead of his return to campus.

The absolute gem of a weekend in Oxford has come and gone, with ...
body_text:
OutKick's Trey Wallace talks to Ole Miss football fans at The Grove about their feelings on Lane Kiffin ahead of his return to campus.

The absolute gem of a weekend in Oxford has come and gone, with a day of college football that could rival anything we’ve seen in recent memory. Ole Miss versus LSU delivered pure cinema, largely because of Lane Kiffin’s dramatic return to Oxford.

Now, all sides can move on until the two teams meet again next year in Baton Rouge. While much of the theatrics surrounding Kiffin’s return felt like an attempt to sell tickets to a show that had already sold itself, the weekend still delivered an experience that will be remembered for decades.

LANE KIFFIN WALKED BACK INTO OXFORD AS THE MAIN CHARACTER, BUT OLE MISS AND PETE GOLDING STOLE HIS SPOTLIGHT

Both Ole Miss and LSU fans will now come to grips with the fact that life goes on, especially during the 2026 season.

Next up, the Rebels will travel to Gainesville for a showdown with the Florida Gators, while LSU will host Texas A&M in Baton Rouge with both teams coming off what could turn into consequential losses as the CFP race heats up.

But to put a bow on one of the craziest ten-month stretches in college football, it might be best to give you a glimpse of what life was like inside and outside Vaught-Hemingway Stadium last week.

LANE KIFFIN’S RETURN TO OLE MISS COMES WITH BETRAYAL, LAWSUITS AND MEMORIES OF HIM TRYING TO BURN IT ALL DOWN

Ole Miss prepares for a wild weekend, as Lane Kiffin returns to Oxford as the head coach of LSU. (Trey Wallace/OutKick)

In the best way possible, the town was buzzing just as you'd expect for a top-10 showdown between two SEC teams with such a storied past.

Add on the fact that former coach Lane Kiffin was returning to Ole Miss for the first time since he abruptly left the Rebels before their College Football Playoff run, and you had a powder keg of emotions ready to explode with just one lit match.

'HE'S DUST': OLE MISS STUDENTS RIP LANE KIFFIN AS LSU COACH PREPARES FOR HATRED IN OXFORD

I first noticed it on Thursday afternoon, while enjoying an afternoon walk around the infamous "Square" that makes up downtown Oxford. As I sat down for lunch inside Ajax Diner, which encompasses all that is good with southern cuisine, I couldn’t help but overhear two gentlemen who were both wearing Ole Miss polos discussing the upcoming showdown.

"We really need to win this game," one diner attendee said about the upcoming game. "I can't imagine how that bastard will act if they [LSU] win."

Fans flock to Oxford ahead of the LSU versus Ole Miss showdown on Saturday afternoon. (Trey Wallace/OutKick)

In reality, this was one of the more interesting dynamics of the week. The "what if" dilemma that Ole Miss fans were bantering about. Whether that was in the local apparel stores that are located in the downtown area, or the plethora of restaurants within walking distance of the majestic looking government building that sits in the middle of the "Square."

I even found myself in the middle of a conversation about the upcoming game while I was filling up my gas tank.

ELLA LANGLEY, DISTRACTIONS AND LANE KIFFIN: PETE GOLDING CALLS OLE MISS-LSU ‘HIGH SCHOOL HOMECOMING’

"What ya think man? I just happened to hear you talking on the phone about the game or something you're writing," another Ole Miss asked me while standing at the pump (I guess I was talking a bit loud). We really need to send him a message, but they look damn good as well."

As I gave him my reasonings as to why I thought Ole Miss would end up winning the game on Saturday, it was as if I was also calming his nerves of what could potentially be coming.

"I like the way you think man. Be careful out here this weekend, it might get a little crazy," the Oxford local politely replied.

Inside the Chaos and Emotion of Lane Kiffin’s Unforgettable Return to Ole Miss (Trey Wallace/OutKick)

That's another thing about these college towns that feel as though gets lost on folks who haven’t truly experienced a college football weekend: the buildup with outside noise can be overblown.

Why would I assert that? Mainly because noted analyst, or however you'd like to describe his role, Stephen A. Smith made it a point to say he was not attending the game out of fear of what Oxford would turn into on Saturday.

I want to make this point very clear: I never once felt my safety was at risk during my time in Oxford.

Sure, this would be an atmosphere that most of us had never covered before, with ten months of buildup filled with hatred and verbal jabs. But, it seems as though a lot was made of potential riots or the safety of Lane Kiffin being at risk was done to sell the game for a television rating.

In reality, this was an Ole Miss fan base that was pissed beyond measure about an airport exit out of Oxford following the Egg Bowl last season. They were upset that Kiffin would essentially try to burn it down on the way out, after not getting what he wanted in coaching the Rebels during their CFP run.

I knew this was going to be a different type of experience as I started my walk to the stadium, with a Louisiana state trooper carrying a bag that contained his sniper rifle. His colleague walked up to a State of Mississippi trooper and politely asked "Hey there, I'm trying to help my guy get his weapon into the stadium. Can you direct me to the right person?"

Inside the Chaos and Emotion of Lane Kiffin’s Unforgettable Return to Ole Miss (Trey Wallace/OutKick)

Outside, where the LSU busses would arrive, stood a large walkway fence that would prevent fans from either side getting close to the team and their head coach.

Standing next to a colleague, we could hear the police radio detailing LSU's eta to the stadium.

"Thirteen minutes out, they are running a little behind. Let's get everyone on the ground prepared," a dispatcher said.

At that moment, security workers expanded the blue fence, creating the walkway for LSU's arrival.

And just like the ones I would hear on my way back to the AirBnB I was staying at in the area, you could hear the police sirens blaring in the distance. The opposing team, along with their flamboyant head coach, had arrived at 4:49 p.m. central time to a cheers and boos from fans hoping to get a glimpse of Lane Kiffin walking back into Vaught Hemingway Stadium.

Head Coach Lane Kiffin of the LSU Tigers arrives at Vaught Hemingway Stadium in Oxford, Miss., on Sept. 19, 2026. (University Images via Getty Images)

More than sixteen State Troopers from both Louisiana and Mississippi were in some capacity guarding the Tigers on this day.

They lined the walkway in the same manner as they lined the field as the Tigers head coach would make his grand entrance, waving at fans in an awkward way. It was almost as if this was a red-carpet event, with security that would rival the president's entourage.

Unfortunately for LSU, they could have used a defense like that during the first half against Ole Miss and Trinidad Chambliss, as the Rebels held a 24-7 lead at halftime.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Inside the Chaos and Emotion of Lane Kiffin’s Unforgettable Return to Ole Miss (Trey Wallace/OutKick)

Luckily for those watching at home, or the LSU fans that made the trip to Oxford, the Tigers would put together a comeback that provided more drama on the field than anything we witnessed off of it.

By now, you've all seen it. Trinidad Chambliss takes one to the house, followed by Ole Miss head coach Pete Golding making the incredible call to go for the two-point conversion that his offense secured. An eight point lead, with LSU getting one final chance to tie it up.

As police officers stood in the end-zone watching for any Ole Miss students that would throw objects onto the field, it was the Rebels defense that sent this crowd into one last frenzy as they intercepted LSU's Sam Leavitt to seal the win.

Defensive players for the Rebels would run past Lane Kiffin and the LSU staff, pointing and glaring, rightfully gloating about how this on-field show would come to an end.

Just as Trinidad Chambliss took a knee to end this magical game, I wondered aloud to a colleague about whether Ole Miss students would storm the field.

Turns out on this night, the celebrations would take place in the stands, and I can't say I was disappointed by the fact I wouldn’t have to worry about being trampled while trying to capture the scene.

Lane Kiffin of the Louisiana State Tigers reacts during the first half against the Mississippi Rebels at Vaught Hemingway Stadium on Sept. 19, 2026, in Oxford, Miss. (Getty Images)

Walking from Lane Kiffin's postgame press conference, following super-agent Jimmy Sexton into the Ole Miss athletic facility for Pete Golding's availability, the Rebels faithful basked in the glory of what they had just witnessed.

A jubilant crowd walked around outside Vaught Hemingway Stadium. But, they weren’t waiting to get one final glimpse of Lane Kiffin as he walked to the LSU busses.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

No, students and fans were making their way back to the 'Grove' or the 'Square' to celebrate, while we listened to both coaches discuss this wild showdown. It felt as though there was one big sigh of relief that incapsulated the entire area, knowing Kiffin wouldn’t be leaving Oxford with the win, while also understanding that Pete Golding would be just fine moving forward.

Finally, after being on-campus for 14 hours, I finished my story and headed for the parking garage. What was waiting for me back at the AirBnB was on my mind. I had booked this rental not actually investigating its actual location.

Inside the Chaos and Emotion of Lane Kiffin’s Unforgettable Return to Ole Miss (Trey Wallace/OutKick)

Turns out, I was staying in what was essentially a college neighborhood filled with condos and townhouses.

Just as the day I arrived in Oxford, the southern hospitality was waiting for me at the upstairs guesthouse I rented, with seven Ole Miss students watching highlights on the couch.

"Hey dude, that was f—–g awesome. You want a beer man? Come on, have a beer with us!"

While I appreciated the gesture, and probably could’ve used one or two, I politely passed on the drink

The week, which had been building for ten months, had come to an end. And with that, the circus that was the "Lane Kiffin return" could be closed, at least for a year.

Once again, the cinema around college football delivered.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

title: Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate
excerpt:
Richard Newby to chair inquiry commissioned in response to discrimination case brought by David Campanale, who is seeking £790,000 in damages

The Liberal Democrats have quietly commissioned a review ...
body_text:
Richard Newby to chair inquiry commissioned in response to discrimination case brought by David Campanale, who is seeking £790,000 in damages

The Liberal Democrats have quietly commissioned a review into the treatment of figures within their ranks who hold religious views, weeks after the Guardian revealed a religious discrimination claim against the party by the former candidate David Campanale.

Campanale, a former BBC journalist, was selected in 2021 as the party’s candidate for Sutton and Cheam but was removed in August 2023. He has argued in a civil case against the party that discrimination against his Christianity cost him his political career.

Richard Newby, the former Lib Dem leader in the House of Lords, has been appointed to chair the party’s inclusion and faith review, which will examine how the party treats candidates and members of different faith and those without.

The inquiry, which has not been publicly announced, was set up in direct response to Campanale’s case, the Guardian understands, with figures at the top of the party understood to be keen to show they take the issue seriously.

The Guardian revealed last month that Campanale was seeking almost £790,000 in damages after the party admitted direct and indirect discrimination on the grounds of religion or belief, and failures in dealing with complaints about his treatment.

The case prompted the former Lib Dem leader Tim Farron and former deputy leader Simon Hughes to call for an independent inquiry into Campanale’s treatment by the party, as well as an apology.

The party cannot comment on court proceedings and will instead use Lord Newby’s review to seek to answer the general question of whether people of faith are being discriminated against, and to what extent any evidence shows this.

Hughes told the Guardian he would pursue a separate investigation once Campanale’s case was resolved.

“The Newby review is explicitly not about any past or present legal case and cannot be about David’s case, which is still before the courts and with one remaining possible internal party appeal,” he said. “The review however is greatly to be welcomed and I believe it will allow the party to meet one of the two big objectives which David, [the] Lib Dem Christian Forum, I and others were seeking.”

The Newby review was announced last week to party members via an email from the Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, and president, Josh Babarinde, days before the start of the party’s conference in Brighton.

It will examine whether candidate approval, selection and deselection processes are inclusive of different faiths, whether candidates receive adequate support, the operation of complaints and disciplinary processes, and training for local party officers.

A Lib Dem source said: “This review offers no remorse, no apologies to members misled so badly nor contrition towards the victims of breaches including Campanale and other Christians who once formed a bedrock of activists among our party’s nonconformist tradition. All should have had an apology by now.

“As it stands, the review looks like a ploy to impress a court judge as the review of Campanale’s case is meant to be published right before damages are considered.”

Another source said: “The review doesn’t recognise the pain [Campanale’s case] brought on members, and it has to be asked why key individuals refused to act when they received complaints or requests to investigate complaints around Campanale’s deselection.”

Campanale submitted a schedule of loss that puts his claim at £788,740.75, including interest. It seeks compensation for injury to feelings, aggravated damages, past and future earnings, the loss of an MP’s pension, counselling costs and the “loss of a chance” or “loss of political capital”.

In his claim, Campanale said that at a meeting in January 2022 he was questioned about his Christianity by about 30 people and asked whether he was enjoying his “martyrdom just like Jesus did”.

Questions have emerged within the party about the remit of the review. A number of Lib Dem figures and activists have also privately criticised its lack of formal announcement. One figure questioned whether Newby would have access to complaints and candidate selection material, and whether the review would extend beyond religious faith to other protected beliefs.

There is a particular concern among some members about whether the review will examine the party’s treatment of people with gender-critical beliefs. In a motion passed at party conference on Monday, members rejected official guidance by the equalities watchdog on how organisations should implement the supreme court ruling on transgender people, calling it “discriminatory and unworkable”.

The party’s conference fringe programme over the weekend included discussions about Christian nationalism and political use of religion.

The Lib Dems previously said the party was “home to people of all faiths and none, including many Christians”, but have declined to comment.

title: AI could be a bubble and is not yet making Australia more productive, Michele Bullock says
excerpt:
RBA governor says AI is ‘great white hope’ but its adoption is so far adding to inflation, rather than economic growth

The Reserve Bank governor said AI could be a bubble and there was no evidence it...
body_text:
RBA governor says AI is ‘great white hope’ but its adoption is so far adding to inflation, rather than economic growth

The Reserve Bank governor said AI could be a bubble and there was no evidence it is making the economy more efficient, as the Albanese government claims the technology will solve Australia’s economic malaise.

Ahead of an expected interest rate rise next week, Michele Bullock also said the slump in house prices was deeper than others in Australia’s recent history.

Resurgent oil prices and inflation are weighing on markets but US tech stocks surged on Monday after Facebook owner Meta debuted its new Muse AI agent and saw its shares rise 11%.

Bullock said a messy slump in tech values could hurt economic activity, speaking at a CEDA event in Sydney.

“All central banks are a little bit worried about that,” Bullock said.

“Some people think it’s a bubble, some people don’t. I don’t have a particular view one way or the other, but it’s a risk that I think we’re watching.”

Bullock said the RBA and its overseas colleagues believed AI was “the great white hope” to make economies more productive but had seen little sign of any effect yet, with rapid adoption and investment in datacentres adding to inflation instead.

She cited research from the RBA’s South Korean counterpart that found employees adopting AI tended to produce the same output but work 1.5 hours less each week.

“[While] people fiddle around and try and figure out what to do with this new technology, productivity actually can decline,” Bullock said. “But once we reimagine our business processes… then you might see productivity take off.”

The Australian government’s intergenerational report, released on Tuesday, relied on the potential “profound” boost from AI in its projection that Australians’ inflation-adjusted per-person economic activity would rise from $99,200 today to $157,300 by 2066.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, told The Guardian’s Australian Politics podcast: “It’s the most transformative thing that will happen in our lifetime.”

The report assumed productivity would return to its long run level of improving by 1.2% a year, which economists have said appears unlikely. If productivity only rose by 0.8%, per-person activity would only hit $136,600 by 2066.

Bullock said on Tuesday: “Many have put it, ‘well, it’s an unrealistic assumption, we’re not going to get that.’ I guess the way I’m trying to think about it is, ‘okay, that’s what we’ve got to aim at.”

As the government defends Australia’s easing rate of immigration, Bullock said immigration was almost entirely responsible for Australia’s economic growth in the last year.

Bullock said new arrivals did not add to inflation as they typically worked as well as spending money. She said the exception was the housing market, as new immigrants did not immediately generate new housing supply.

“Where it bites is the housing market, because the housing market can’t respond,” she said.

One Nation has called for more migrants to leave Australia than arrive over three years, including reducing the number of temporary migrants by more than 750,000.

Labor has instead planned to tighten the existing immigration intake, which home affairs minister Tony Burke said would be “part of the solution for the housing crisis” – but Burke warned more severe cuts could “trash the economy”.

House prices have fallen 3.1% over the past three months after the RBA lifted interest rates three times and the government reformed property investor tax breaks. Bullock said home loan approvals had slumped, in her most explicit public comments on the budget to date.

“They’ve dropped for everyone but they’ve really dropped a long way for investors, so it has changed the dynamic for investors, whether it’s worth investing in housing or not,” she said.

Bullock said housing had become “pretty unaffordable” before the decline, which she described as “a slight dip down after a very long run up”.

“The downturn is sort of in the lower range … but it’s certainly not out of the ballpark of the sorts of downturns we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

She declined to say whether she would recommend an interest rate increase next Tuesday. Traders are betting on more than a 90% chance rates will rise from 4.35% to 4.6%, which would be a 14-year high.

title: Jacinda Ardern and husband Clarke Gayford buy $5.3m home in Sydney’s northern beaches
excerpt:
Former New Zealand prime minister’s purchase biggest recorded in suburb of Dee Why this year

Jacinda Ardern and her husband, Clarke Gayford, have bought a $5.3m house in Sydney’s northern beaches, ac...
body_text:
Former New Zealand prime minister’s purchase biggest recorded in suburb of Dee Why this year

Jacinda Ardern and her husband, Clarke Gayford, have bought a $5.3m house in Sydney’s northern beaches, according to a source with knowledge of the sale.

The former New Zealand prime minister settled on a house in Dee Why after looking at properties in the area including in nearby Curl Curl.

The sale – handled by Raine & Horne Northern Beaches and first reported by the Sydney Morning Herald – is the biggest the suburb has recorded this year, according to the source familiar with the transaction.

The Guardian has contacted Gayford and a representative for Ardern for comment.

In February, Ardern’s office confirmed she was living in Australia, following media reports that she, her husband and their daughter, Neve, had attended open home viewings in Sydney’s northern beaches.

“The family has been travelling for a few years now,” a spokesperson from her office told the Guardian at the time.

“For the moment they’re basing themselves out of Australia – they have work there, and it brings the added bonus of more time back home in New Zealand.”

The spokesperson did not elaborate on when the family arrived in Australia nor what kind of work they were doing, but noted it was not unusual for former leaders to spend time overseas after leaving office.

Ardern announced her retirement from politics in January 2023, after five years as New Zealand’s prime minister and the leader of the country’s Labour party.

When she was elected to the top job in October 2027, Ardern became the world’s youngest-serving female leader, aged 37, and later became the second woman to give birth while holding elected office.

Since leaving office, Ardern has taken up dual fellowship roles at Harvard University, continued her work on the Christchurch Call – a project she established to combat online extremism, after the Christchurch mosque shootings – and joined the board of trustees of Prince William’s Earthshot prize.

New Zealand has been grappling with a surge in the number of citizens leaving the country because of a weak economy, high living costs and high unemployment. Many of these people have moved to Australia.

title: Middle East crisis live: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warns it will ‘change geography of war’ if US escalates conflict
excerpt:
The US president said in an interview ahead of the United Nations meeting that he was considering ‘wiping Iran out’

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps warned it would “change the geography of the war” ...
body_text:
The US president said in an interview ahead of the United Nations meeting that he was considering ‘wiping Iran out’

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps warned it would “change the geography of the war” if the US escalates the conflict, after Donald Trump issued fresh threats against the Islamic Republic.

In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Trump said “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future”, adding that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.

A spokesperson for the IRGC, Hossein Mohebbi, responded with a warning that if the US were to launch fresh attacks against Iran, Tehran would use “new weapons with capabilities into the battle”. “If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Mohebbi was quoted as having said.

“Our targets will no longer necessarily be the same as before,” he said, according to the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting, adding that Iran has targets that have not yet been struck.

The comments come as the US and Iran remain locked in an impasse over the strait of Hormuz and after attacks on the Saudi capital, Riyadh, by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels.

The Houthis, who operate independently of Iran’s instructions, have seized territory along the country’s Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping route that links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Saudi Arabia has used it as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis have also attacked oil facilities and other types of infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, in response for Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. The attacks have further disrupted energy markets, pushing up global fuel prices, including in the US, where consumers have been hit hard.

Iran hugely benefits from the Houthis fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on the US to relent over Iran, which has insisted it will not allow the reopening of the strait of Hormuz until all its conditions have been met.

With diplomatic negotiations stalled, traffic in the strait continues to be severely disrupted, with Iran firing on commercial ships and demanding it first approve passage along its authorised route.

In response, the US, which started the war on Iran alongside Israel in February, is maintaining a counter-blockade of Iranian ports while intensifying economic pressure. The US has also fired on commercial shipping in the region and has killed Iranian civilians in its strikes.

In a joint statement, the Group of Seven (G7) foreign ministers called on Iran to end military support to Houthi forces in Yemen.

The ministers representing Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK and the US said “we call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions”.

“All threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith,” it added.

They also called on Iran “to end its arming of and support for the Houthis,” alleging Tehran is in violation of past UN security council resolutions.

Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would violate a UN embargo, and has said it only supports the group politically.

However, smuggled Iranian weapons have been seized from shipments bound for Yemen, and a report by UN experts in 2024 documented extensive military ties between the Houthis, Iran and its other allies.

According to a report in the New York Times, the US president, Donald Trump, has wavered for weeks over whether to act on appeals from Saudi Arabia for military help in fighting the Houthis.

On Wednesday, the president had reportedly met with advisers and said he did not favour strikes.

But the following day, his close ally, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, called Trump again to ask for his help to halt the Houthi’s rapid advance, the outlet reported, citing administration officials.

After this phone call, Trump reserved his position and told the Pentagon to prepare for airstrikes against the Houthis, according to the report. But by Sunday, Trump had changed his mind again and said there would be no US airstrikes against the Iranian-backed rebel group, at least for now.

The US bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group, as it agreed to stop targeting shipping in the Red Sea. The US has directly kept out of the conflict ever since.

Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and government forces supported by Saudi Arabia has killed 154 people in the past two days, military sources told the AFP news agency, and has sparked a refugee crisis.

“The death toll from Saudi airstrikes, clashes and artillery fire in the governorates of Taiz, Al-Jawf, Marib and Saada stands at 118,” Houthi military sources said, while government sources reported 36 killed in their “ranks”, according to AFP.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that started in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally recognised government from Sanaa, the country’s capital, driving it south towards Aden.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states subsequently intervened on behalf of the ousted government, with a mostly aerial campaign that was condemned for its deadly impact on the civilians of Yemen.

Neither side was able to gain much ground in Yemen’s mountainous terrain, and the Houthis remained in control over the northwest, where most of the population lives.

The two sides agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022, which, despite some skirmishes, largely held until July, when a Saudi airstrike hit the runway of the airport in Sanaa, preventing the landing of an Iranian flight carrying a high-ranking Houthi delegation.

The already shaky UN-brokered ceasefire has since completely collapsed, with the two sides exchanging missiles, drones and air strikes.

title: Mother charged after allegedly fatally stabbing one child and seriously injuring two others in Blue Mountains
excerpt:
A woman has been accused of murder and two counts of grievous bodily harm with intent to cause murder

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A mother has been charged after alle...
body_text:
A woman has been accused of murder and two counts of grievous bodily harm with intent to cause murder

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A mother has been charged after allegedly fatally stabbing one child and seriously injuring two others in the Blue Mountains.

Emergency services responded to reports on Sunday that three children and a woman had been found in a vehicle in Valley Heights with stab wounds. New South Wales police said bystanders who were first on the scene attempted to perform first aid while contacting triple zero.

A five-year-old child died at the scene, and two other children, aged one and three, were taken to Westmead Children’s hospital. They are in a critical but stable condition.

The woman, 42, was transported to Westmead hospital.

The woman was charged on Tuesday with murder (DV) and two counts of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to murder. She was refused bail and will remain in custody until her next court appearance next month.

Police said the woman had not previously come to the attention of police and that investigators were not looking for anyone else in relation to the incident.

The alleged domestic violence incident came at the end of a horror weekend across New South Wales, after three women were allegedly murdered inside their homes within a 12-hour period on Saturday.

The police deputy commissioner Peter McKenna described the weekend as devastating.

“It’s a horrific and tragic weekend and it’s like one that I don’t remember in my career,” he told Nine’s Today on Monday.

“Those three … plus the no-more-tragic situation that we had in the Blue Mountains. Put them all together and it’s unfathomable.”

title: UK not ‘on the slide’, Burnham to tell UN as he gears up for first meeting with Trump – UK politics live
excerpt:
Burnham is heading to New York for the United Nations general assembly

Andy Burnham has opened the door to fighting the next election on the UK rejoining the EU, but said his immediate priority was c...
body_text:
Burnham is heading to New York for the United Nations general assembly

Andy Burnham has opened the door to fighting the next election on the UK rejoining the EU, but said his immediate priority was continuing to rebuild bridges with European allies. Pippa Crerar has the story, which is based on what Burnham told journalists as he spoke to them in what reporters call a “huddle” on his flight to New York.

Good morning. Andy Burnham is at the United Nations general assembly today and in a speech to the world (or, technically, to people in the hall and anyone watching on TV at around 2am UK time), he will say that Britain is not “on the slide”.

Speaking to reporters on the plane to New York, Burnham said:

double quotation markThe plan for Britain is about ‘what is our direction over the next 10 years and how do we make life more affordable for people’. That is my main priority, that’s what people are looking for.

I hear people saying the country is on the slide – we’re the fastest growing in the G7, there’s lots to be proud of, there’s a lot right with the country and I’m going to give a really upbeat message when I speak.

But the story of the day will instead focus on Burnham’s meeting with someone who does think the UK is “on the slide”, or at least claims to think that. “Your country’s in trouble. You’re on the edge of disaster,” Donald Trump told a GB News reporter recently.

In her overnight story ahead of the meeting, Pippa Crerar, who is on the trip with Burnham, says Burnham is going to adopt a middle-of-the-road approach to the US president when they meet. She says:

double quotation markGovernment sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as [Keir] Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality.

This is a reference to Starmer offering Trump an unprecedented second state visit when they first met at the White House. Theresa May also found herself pimping the monarch at her first meeting with Trump. There were good reasons for both offers at the time, and they bought both newbie PMs some goodwill from the White House monster, but it did not last and both those encounters are now recalled as moments of national embarrassment. As long as today’s meeting is cordial, Burnham will probably be happy with something more low-key.

It is hard to know what can be achieved in any meeting with Trump because he is so unpredicable. Later Burnham has another meeting with a president which will get far less coverage, but may turn out to be more consequential. The PM is meeting Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, for the first time and, with the prospects of the EU-UK reset in jeopardy, there is a lot to discuss.

9am: The final day of the Lib Dem conference in Brighton starts. The debates this morning will include one on the Lib Dems’ water policy.

2.30pm: Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, gives his keynote speech at the conference.

Around 4.45pm (UK time): Andy Burnham is due to meet Donald Trump at the UN in New York.

Late afternoon/early evening (UK time): Burnham has bilateral meetings with Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, and others.

Late evening (UK time): Burnham co-chairs a meeting on the Middle East with other leaders including Emmanuel Macron, the French president, and Mark Carney, the Canadian PM.

Around 1.50am (UK time): Burnham gives his speech to the UN before flying back to the UK.
