title: Popular honeymoon destination declares national emergency over massive HIV surge
excerpt: A couple was exploring underwater near Fiji’s Salamanda shipwreck when William Paterson signaled for a photo, then pulled out a ring beneath the surface — catching his girlfriend, Kim, completely off ...
body_text:
A couple was exploring underwater near Fiji’s Salamanda shipwreck when William Paterson signaled for a photo, then pulled out a ring beneath the surface — catching his girlfriend, Kim, completely off guard. (SWNS)

Fiji has officially declared a national HIV emergency on its shores after alarming data revealed that one in 60 adults in the South Pacific island nation is currently living with the virus.

The Fijian government is urgently expanding testing and treatment to combat a massive surge in new infections, which the United Nations program UNAIDS notes has increased 12-fold over the past 15 years, according to The Associated Press (AP).

Highlighting the rapid acceleration of the crisis, Fiji recorded more than 2,000 new cases in 2025 alone, representing a staggering 16-fold increase compared to 2019, The New York Times reported.

HIV EPIDEMIC EXPLODES IN POPULAR HONEYMOON DESTINATION AS CRYSTAL METH USE SURGES

The scope of the epidemic is vast for a nation of fewer than one million people.

UNAIDS estimates that some 9,000 people were living with HIV in Fiji as of 2025. Just five years ago, the infection rate was one in 167 adults, but it has since climbed to one in 60, with one in 50 pregnant women now infected, the AP said.

A popular honeymoon destination for Americans, Fiji has declared a national HIV emergency after data revealed that one in 60 adults in the South Pacific island nation is living with the virus. (iStock)

The human toll is already mounting. Fifty-nine infants were born in 2025 with the virus, as the AP and Reuters reported — and 18 died before their first birthday.

Health officials have pointed to a growing epidemic of injected drug use as the primary catalyst.

As island nations increasingly serve as transit hubs for illicit drugs moving toward Australia and New Zealand, local markets for substances like methamphetamine have flourished.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

The emergency stems from a sharp rise in high-risk methamphetamine use, with widespread needle sharing among drug users acting as a primary driver for the surging infection rates, the AP reported.

Antonio Lalabalavu, Fiji's health minister, announced that the situation, previously labeled an outbreak in January 2025, now requires a comprehensive, whole-of-government response.

Coral reefs and beaches at Fiji Paradise Islands are popular among Americans on their honeymoons. (iStock)

Lalabalavu emphasized that the approach is focused on protecting people rather than judging, watching or shaming them.

The government is expanding free testing, providing clean needles for drug users, and offering free antiretroviral treatments, addressing a critical gap given that currently only 39% of patients know their status and a mere 22% are receiving care.

The international community is raising alarms over the speed of the transmission.

Winnie Byanyima, UNAIDS executive director, said the situation in Fiji is one of the sharpest increases in new HIV infections globally — serving as a stark reminder that the AIDS epidemic is not over, AP and Reuters reported.

Health officials warned that because Fiji operates as a major transport and tourism hub, the crisis could easily spread to other South Pacific nations. (iStock)

Regional health directors also warned that because Fiji operates as a major transport and tourism hub, the crisis could easily spread to other South Pacific nations if swift, stigma-reducing action is not taken by government, community and religious leaders.

In December, the World Health Organization (WHO) released a rapid assessment detecting unsafe injecting practices.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

These practices can put people who inject drugs in Fiji at an increased risk of HIV transmission.

The "Bluetooth trend" has impacted the spread — with individuals injecting the blood of an already intoxicated person to achieve a high when they cannot afford their own drugs.

There were 1,583 new HIV cases reported in 2024, while 1,226 cases were indicated in the first six months of 2025, according to the assessment.

American divers and snorkelers are drawn to the region for its vibrant coral systems like the Beqa Lagoon and the Taveuni reefs. (iStock)

The most popular drug was crystal methamphetamine, with the assessment finding that 50% of interview participants injected themselves with a potentially contaminated syringe.

At the time, Munkhtuya Altangerel, U.N. Development Program representative, said the findings of the assessments were a wake-up call.

"Fiji’s HIV epidemic is not just a health issue — it is a development and human rights challenge that threatens lives, communities and progress," said Altangerel in a release.

"We must act decisively and urgently to scale up harm reduction, expand access to HIV testing and treatment, and ensure that no one is left behind."

Ashley J. DiMella of Fox News Digital, as well as The Associated Press and Reuters, contributed reporting.

Jessica Mekles is an editor on the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Ed Davey takes aim at Reform and Elon Musk as Lib Dem conference begins
excerpt:
Leader says party ‘won’t give up the fight’ to defeat ‘nasty populism’ in first-day speech to delegates in Brighton

The Liberal Democrats’ leader, Sir Ed Davey, took aim at Nigel Farage and Elon Musk...
body_text:
Leader says party ‘won’t give up the fight’ to defeat ‘nasty populism’ in first-day speech to delegates in Brighton

The Liberal Democrats’ leader, Sir Ed Davey, took aim at Nigel Farage and Elon Musk on the first day of his party’s annual conference, saying Lib Dems would not give up the fight to defeat “nasty populism” and Reform UK’s “£72m arsenal of hate and lies”.

On stage at Brighton Centre, Davey called on the assembled delegates not to be deterred in the face of Reform’s hope “that the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down until eventually we just give up”.

He also praised earlier speakers for showing “why we care and why we fight” and contrasted this with Reform, which, he said, “care about their own bank balance and they fight because two crypto billionaires gave them 72 million quid”.

Davey, who entered conference season having to address frustrations over his leadership expressed by some Lib Dem MPs, also used the speech to recall his early political life as a student campaigning successfully for his university college to boycott Barclays, due to its investments in apartheid-era South Africa.

He spoke of his “visceral shock [and] overwhelming anger at seeing human beings treating other human beings with total contempt” and drew parallels between that experience and the need to not look away “when we see human dignity under attack”.

Davey said: “Today – we are back. Fighting again the fight that fired me up at university. The fight to end injustices. In our country and around the world. The fight to defeat the nasty populism of Trump, Le Pen, the AfD and the rest.

“The fight to stop the world’s richest man who learned racism in apartheid South Africa from funding racism around the world.”

He also referred to the “fight to defend the Royal National Lifeboat Institution after volunteers for the coastal rescue charity were recently targeted online amid anti-migrant protests”.

He said “Reform know they don’t speak for the real United Kingdom” – and what Farage was “counting on to get him to No 10” was that people would get “tired, depressed, fed up with seeing Zia Yusuf on BBC Question Time week after week”.

But Davey said he hoped Reform were watching and would see “a party that won’t be ground down. That won’t be deterred. That won’t give up the fight.”

Also during the first day of the conference, Lib Dem health spokesperson Helen Morgan set out a £600m plan to improve maternity care, including proposals to bring in one-to-one midwifery for every woman in labour backed by a round-the-clock senior consultant.

The party said the measures will pay for themselves by reducing how much the NHS has to spend on compensation for maternity negligence claims every year – totalling £1.3bn in 2024-25.

Munira Wilson, the Lib Dem education spokesperson, said the party would introduce a guarantee to provide 100 hours of work experience for students from GCSE age to 18 to tackle the crisis of young people not in education, employment or training.

body_text:
Caleb Williams and the Chicago Bears face off with the Minnesota Vikings following an explosive Week 1 win. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, Kevin Wildes, and Danny Parkins ask if the Bears will "embarrass" the Vikings, and if Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills made a statement with their win over the Detroit Lions. Plus, Parkins makes his picks for Week 2, including the Arizona Cardinals, Philadelphia Eagles, and New York Giants.

Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay is a football mastermind, Coach of the Year award winner, and a Super Bowl Champion. He's reached the mountain top in the NFL, but his comments on a recent "60 Minutes" episode revealed how those accolades and finding his identity in the pursuit of winning, ultimately left him empty.

While sitting down with L. Jon Wertheim, McVay opened up about insecurities and a lack of fulfillment, which almost led to him walking away from coaching to pursue a career in broadcasting. "The lies I told myself were ‘Once we win a Super Bowl, I’ll be happy’," McVay said. "My identity was so tied up into winning or losing games, and that’s where I felt my self worth lied."

Hearing this I couldn't help but think about Tom Brady's "60 Minutes" interview, which echoed these same sentiments by McVay about a lack of fulfillment in winning awards, Super Bowls and other accolades.

Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay speaks during a news conference after the NFC Championship NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks, Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026, in Seattle. (AP Photo/John Froschauer)

BILL BELICHICK CONFIRMS FEUD WITH TOM BRADY WAS FICTION, PRAISES HIS QUARTERBACK'S LEADERSHIP FROM DAY ONE

Even after winning three Super Bowls by the age of 27, Tom Brady admitted that the championships didn’t provide the lasting fulfillment he expected. In a 2005 interview with "60 Minutes," Brady was asked what he still wanted after accomplishing so much at such a young age. His response was sobering: "There’s got to be more than this." Brady explained that despite reaching the pinnacle of professional football success, he was still searching for something deeper. Twenty years later in a newsletter, Brady reflected on that statement saying that there is "more to life than playing football and winning championships."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

McVay later explained, "I was ready to run away from coaching and hide behind a convenient narrative of some media opportunities." But then his wife told him: "That never sounded like the kind of leader you wanted to be."

Sean McVay and Veronika Khomyn attend the 15th Annual NFL Honors at Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco, Calif., on Feb. 5, 2026. (Getty Images)

When I hear stories like this, I'm reminded of all the times I've found my worth in what I do, as if that is who I am. My job is not my identity, neither is it for McVay. Our successes are not what define us. For those of a competitive nature, success is never enough. There's always something bigger and better. There's always another championship to win, more money to make, and more followers to gain. If that's what you think will provide you the hope, peace, value, and fulfillment we're all searching for, it will leave you feeling empty. It's fleeting, ultimately.

Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay talks to quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) during the first half of the NFC Championship NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks, Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026, in Seattle. (AP Photo/Stephen Brashear)

Pursuing excellence in your job is not a bad thing, as long as it is not made into an idol because you consider it the source of your worth and happiness. It will fail you every time. This is why I personally believe that putting your identity in anything other than Jesus Christ may provide satisfaction for the short term, but it will not satisfy you eternally.

title: Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar
excerpt:
US President Donald Trump has announced that he will form an "AI Force" and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar amid warnings about the emergent technology.

In a social media post on Saturday, he...
body_text:
US President Donald Trump has announced that he will form an "AI Force" and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar amid warnings about the emergent technology.

In a social media post on Saturday, he said his administration "will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth" of the industry, and pushed back against calls to slow down the development of AI until better safeguards are put in place.

His post came as a slew of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have spurred calls for coordinated action on the technology's development.

Trump offered no details or a timeline for his plan.

Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings

"AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country's GDP," he said on social media, adding that he wants the US to continue leading China in AI.

AI now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech, and it is expected to be discussed when Trump meets President Xi Jinping next week.

Meanwhile, Trump said his administration would use the existing criminal and civil justice system to target any bad actors using the AI.

He also repeated comments that criticism  and concerns around the potential dangers of AI are a "hoax".

Watch: Cyber Correspondent Joe Tidy considers if could AI wipe out humanity, and how it might do it

Claims by current and former researchers that the tech will endanger humanity - with one suggesting there is a greater than 10% chance of it "killing all humans" - have raised alarm bells in recent weeks.

Major AI companies have been racing to develop better systems, including creating what they call super intelligence - theoretical tech which is smarter than humans.

AI titans Anthropic, OpenAI and Google - the tech companies behind Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, respectively - have also disclosed  instances of security breaches or incidents in which their chatbots were used for "malicious activity".

Anthropic head Dario Amodei recently called for AI development to slow down and proposed industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.

Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI have both said they agree with his recommendations.

Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, told BBC that a "kill switch" that can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry.

The warnings have prompted US lawmakers to propose legislation around the technology but Altman suggested this week that Washington has struggled to keep pace with the new tech and how to regulate it. He said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep it safe.

"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman told a conference in San Francisco.

In the UK, MPs across parties and peers have identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence and have argued that existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth.

The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) has published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats.

Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons

title: NORAD F-16 intercepts aircraft that violated restricted airspace over Camp David with Trump present: officials
excerpt: An F-16 fighter jet was caught on camera closing in on a small airplane near Jefferson Township, New Jersey, outside Trump's Bedminster golf club, where temporary flight restrictions were in place. (C...
body_text:
An F-16 fighter jet was caught on camera closing in on a small airplane near Jefferson Township, New Jersey, outside Trump's Bedminster golf club, where temporary flight restrictions were in place. (Credit: X / Joe Afflerbach)

A NORAD F-16 fighter jet intercepted an aircraft that violated restricted airspace over the area of Camp David Saturday morning while President Donald Trump is spending the weekend there, according to officials.

There is a permanent no-fly zone over Camp David in Maryland, with additional restrictions when the president is there.

NORAD dispensed flares during the intercept to get the pilot’s attention, and were able to safely escort them out of the area, the Defense Visual Information Distribution Service (DVIDS) said in a release.

NORAD F-16S INTERCEPT MULTIPLE AIRCRAFT VIOLATING TEMPORARY FLIGHT RESTRICTIONS OVER NEW JERSEY

A U.S. Air Force F-16 fighter jet seen flying in 2016. (SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Should NORAD aircraft intercept a general aviation aircraft, the pilot should immediately come up on frequency 121.5 or 243.0 and turn around to reverse course until receiving additional instructions on one of those frequencies," the release said.

NORAD F-16S INTERCEPT MULTIPLE AIRCRAFT VIOLATING FLIGHT RESTRICTIONS OVER NEW JERSEY

President Donald Trump leaving the White House on Marine One on Friday evening. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)

Turmp left for Camp David on Friday evening.

"Pilots! @NORADCommand fighter aircraft intercepted an aircraft violating restricted airspace over Thurmont, MD, resulting in flares being deployed," the First Air Force, part of NORAD, wrote on X on Saturday. "Make sure to check NOTAMs before takeoff to ensure you have current information about TFRs in your area. Stay Safe, Fly Informed!"

A view of the main lodge at Camp David. (Whitehouse.gov)

A plane was last intercepted over Camp David in June when Trump was staying there. That pilot was also safely escorted away.

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

One month into the new ‌Premier League season, excuses about bedding-in processes and newly assembled squads needing time to gel are wearing thin and for Manchester United ⁠there is an acute sense ⁠of urgency as the international break looms.

United are by no means the only ‘big club’ enduring a faltering start to the campaign but after so much pre-season optimism, the spotlight has fallen very much on manager Michael Carrick ahead of ⁠Sunday’s trip to Fulham.

Al Jazeera takes a closer look at the game:

United have ⁠lost three of their six matches in all competitions and suffered a damaging League Cup exit on Wednesday, surrendering a 2-0 ⁠lead to Brighton & Hove Albion.

Their only win in four league games came at home to promoted Ipswich Town.

United started the better in the VAR-dominated Manchester derby last Sunday, but played second fiddle to the away team after City were reduced to ten men.

The London club have made a slow start under new manager Alvaro Arbeloa and are yet to win in the league.

A draw at Liverpool last week and a League Cup win at West Ham United in midweek offered glimpses of better things to come.

Carrick accepted responsibility for the team’s poor start but said the focus must remain on finding ⁠solutions rather than assigning blame.

“It’s my responsibility and I’m fine with that. It’s not a blame ⁠game. Blame me, no problem, but it’s ⁠not about blaming people,” said the 45-year-old boss.

“It’s about finding solutions. It’s a whole collective thing. It’s about what you focus on. I know where we want to get to ‌and we want to get there fast.”

United won 3-2 in their last meeting which came in the Premier League at Old Trafford on February 1.

Casemiro and Matheus Cunha put United two up before a chaotic finale that saw Raul Jiminez net an 85th minute penalty for the Londoners before Benjamin Sesko and Kevin traded injury time strikes.

The teams shared a 1-1 draw in the Premier League match. Emile Smith Rowe’s 73rd minute goal levelled matters after Rodrigo Muniz put through his own net in the 58th minute.

Fulham won 2-1 at Old Trafford in the Premier League on February 24, 2024. Harry Maguire appeared to have sealed a point for United in the 90th minute when he cancelled out Calvin Bassey’s 65th minute goal, but Alex Iwobi got Fulham’s winner in injury time.

United have won three of the five meetings since then.

Fulham have not recorded a home win against United since December 2009. Danny Murphy, Bobby Zamora and Damien Duff sealing a 3-0 home win.

Of the 10 matches since then, United have won nine, scoring 21 and conceding six.

Opta’s supercomputer has given Manchester United a 47.4 percent chance of winning, while offering Fulham only a 28.3 percent chance of victory.

This will be their 94th meeting, with Manchester United winning 59 of the encounters and Fulham 14.

Kenny Tete misses out due to concussion at Anfield last week.

Tom Cairney is also absent with a knee injury, but Ryan Sessegnon will have a late fitness test as he returns from a groin problem.

title: Israel’s president pardons soldier who killed wounded Palestinian in 2016
excerpt:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has expunged the criminal record of a former soldier convicted of manslaughter for killing a wounded Palestinian in Hebron a decade ago.

Herzog announced on Saturday th...
body_text:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has expunged the criminal record of a former soldier convicted of manslaughter for killing a wounded Palestinian in Hebron a decade ago.

Herzog announced on Saturday that he had shortened the remaining erasure period on Elor Azaria’s record, effectively clearing it despite opposition from Israeli army Chief of Staff Lieutenant-General Eyal Zamir.

In a letter to the defence minister, Zamir and other senior officers said Azaria “has refrained from expressing remorse and taking responsibility for his actions, even a decade after his conviction”.

The president’s office said it had taken the military’s position into account but decided the circumstances justified allowing Azaria to “open a new chapter in his life”.

Azaria, an army medic at the time, was filmed shooting Abdel Fattah al-Sharif in the head in March 2016.

Al-Sharif had stabbed and wounded a soldier but had already been shot by Israeli troops and had lain on the ground for about 11 minutes before Azaria killed him.

Azaria was convicted by a military court in 2017 and sentenced to 18 months in prison, later reduced to 14 months. He was released in May 2018 after serving nine months.

Herzog’s office said the decision followed a request from Defence Minister Israel Katz in July and was based on “the passage of time, the completion of his sentence, and the remorse he has expressed”.

The statement added that the pardon was issued “in the spirit” of Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, and did not challenge the original legal proceedings.

Katz welcomed the pardon, writing on X that it “sends an important message to [Israeli army] soldiers and their families: We do not abandon our fighters”.

Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, called the decision “deeply moving” and urged Herzog to grant a similar pardon to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is on trial for corruption.

The 2016 shooting generated intense debate in Israel and drew international condemnation at the time.

The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs had condemned the shooting as an “extrajudicial execution” and a “war crime”, saying the video footage “demolished all the slogans chanted by the occupation leaders about the ethics of the Israeli army”.

The family of al-Sharif had dismissed the legal proceedings as a “farce” aimed at improving Israel’s international image rather than delivering justice.

The United Nations human rights office described the original sentence as “excessively lenient” and said it risked “reinforcing the culture of impunity”.
In 2024, the Joe Biden administration barred Azaria and his immediate family from entering the United States, citing an “extrajudicial killing”.

title: Israeli president pardons combat medic who shot dead wounded Palestinian attacker
excerpt:
Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter of man who stabbed soldier continues to divide country

Israel’s president has pardoned a combat medic who shot dead a badly wounded Palestinian attac...
body_text:
Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter of man who stabbed soldier continues to divide country

Israel’s president has pardoned a combat medic who shot dead a badly wounded Palestinian attacker who had stabbed a soldier in the occupied West Bank, in a case that divided the country a decade ago.

Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter and his release after serving two-thirds of his 18-month sentence drew enormous attention in Israel, where military service is compulsory for most Jewish men.

In his first interview after his release, Azaria said he would “act exactly the same, because that’s how I needed to act”.

Azaria had approached Abdel Fattah al-Sharif as he lay on the ground, unarmed and badly hurt, after stabbing a soldier in the city of Hebron. A mobile phone video captured Azaria shooting al-Sharif in the head.

The office of president Isaac Herzog said in a statement on Saturday that he acted on the recommendation of defence minister Israel Katz. The statement cited the time that had passed, and the spirit of the approaching Yom Kippur, or Day of Atonement, holiday as among the factors in the decision.

Herzog’s office also said that Azaria, who was 20 when he was sentenced, had “expressed his sorrow” in his request. The statement noted that in an earlier request, he called his gunshot an “operational error”.

In a separate statement, Katz called it a “right, humane and fitting decision” and said Azaria had been in a “complex operational mission”.

But the military’s chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, had said in a letter to the defence minister that the pardon should not be granted, Israeli media reported.

The conviction was a rare case of a military court ruling against a soldier for deadly action taken in the field. Top generals had pressed for his prosecution, while many in the Israeli public supported Azaria at a time when there had been a series of stabbings and car-ramming attacks by Palestinians or Israeli Arabs. Some supporters protested outside his trial.

On Saturday, Israel’s hard-line national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said in a statement that “cancelling the criminal record of someone who killed a terrorist makes me emotional and very happy”.

Some Palestinians and human rights groups had described Azaria’s sentence as far too lenient. Prosecutors had sought a sentence of three to five years.

The statement by Herzog’s office on Saturday said that his decision “does not constitute a reassessment of the case”.

The divisions over Azaria’s case led to public polling and political pressure that led the defence minister at the time, Moshe Ya’alon, to resign.

After the verdict, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for Azaria to be pardoned.

After the sentencing, the Palestinian government minister in charge of prisoner affairs, Issa Karaka, called it a “joke”.

title: Trump says he is banning CNN and Politico from White House
excerpt:
Trump has taken an aggressive approach to the White House press corps since returning to office last year.

US President Donald Trump has announced that he is "immediately" banning CNN, MS NOW and Pol...
body_text:
Trump has taken an aggressive approach to the White House press corps since returning to office last year.

US President Donald Trump has announced that he is "immediately" banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, the latest twist in his fraught relationship with media outlets.

In a post on Truth Social on Friday, Trump said that the outlets "constantly write or report fiction or lies" about his administration, although he provided no examples.

Trump later called it a "very simple ban", but did not explain how it would work. It is unclear whether employees of those outlets would be prevented from entering the White House grounds.

CNN swiftly slammed the move as an "illegal assault" on American press freedoms. The move by Trump is likely to be met with legal challenges.

Reporters from both Politico and CNN were still on the White House grounds shortly after the announcement was made.

A crew from CNN was also travelling with Vice-President JD Vance to and from an event in Iowa.

In a statement, the network called a potential ban illegal and said it "stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting."

"We have a right under the US Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government," the CNN statement said. "Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right."

The BBC has contacted Politico and MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, which have not released statements.

In his post Trump said: "Media outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report fiction and lies when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration or the United States of America. Other news outlets to follow."

The post did not mention specific stories or reporting that led to the move.

Asked about the ban in the Oval Office, Trump said that there was "no reason" for the announcement being made on Friday afternoon.

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years," he said. "You get sick of it."

Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but did not name any specific news outlets.

He also acknowledged that legal challenges may follow his announcement.

"I think it's good to point it out, whether it survives or doesn't," he added. "To be honest with you, I don't think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day."

Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump and administration officials have repeatedly clashed with members of the White House press corps.

In February, the White House announced that it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondent's Association.

The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America".

The Associated Press swiftly filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

The president often clashes with reporters in the Oval Office on Air Force One and during White House events, often referring to them as "fake news" and "rude".

In his first term, Trump also banned CNN correspondent Jim Acosta from the White House, although they restored his credentials after CNN sued.

The announcement was immediately criticised by leading advocacy organisations for freedom of the press.

In a statement on Friday afternoon, the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University said that "with so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you'd think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now".

"If President Trump means to expel these news organizations from the White House press pool, his action is doubly unconstitutional because the press pool is a 'public forum' under the First Amendment, which means the president can't exclude journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints," the institute's executive director, Jameel Jaffer, said.

A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expects Trump's ban to be quickly struck down by the courts because it is "flatly unconstitutional".

"The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said the group's president Bruce Brown, calling the potential ban "textbook viewpoint discrimination."

The Freedom of the Press Foundation also said it was illegal, adding: "It's also hard to imagine a dumber move."

Trump "has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn't helped him," it said, saying "these outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public".

Trump has pursued legal action against a number of US and international news outlets, including the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and the BBC.

Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

title: 'Pro-life' vs 'socialism': GOP lawmakers divided over controversial guaranteed income programs
excerpt:
Founder and Director of Mothers & Infant Cash Coalition Tegan Lecheler told Fox News Digital that their support for cash assistance has been praised by the right.

Although guaranteed income programs ...
body_text:
Founder and Director of Mothers & Infant Cash Coalition Tegan Lecheler told Fox News Digital that their support for cash assistance has been praised by the right.

Although guaranteed income programs have faced partisan pushback nationwide since gaining national traction in 2018, a growing faction of conservatives is finding common ground with direct cash initiatives centered on mothers and newborns.

According to Tegan Lecheler, national program director for the Mother and Infant Cash Coalition (MICC), the "common-sense" nature of early childhood cash transfers has prompted conservative lawmakers and advocates to reach out to her organization in support.

"I think we're in a really polarized time politically right now," Lecheler told Fox News Digital. "We are not a political organization and want to work to improve families' outcomes. We believe an effective strategy for doing that is to build a big tent – a wide tent with a lot of people underneath it."

EXCLUSIVE: PENCE GROUP KNOCKS VANCE PLAN TO PAY STAY-AT-HOME PARENTS UP TO $9K PER CHILD

Rx Kids is a cash assistance program that’s intended to issue $1,500 cash to new and expectant mothers in the Motor City as well as $500 per month after a child’s birth for at least six months. The program is considered the largest cash aid program for prenatal and infant care in the country. (iStock)

Lecheler noted that early childhood support aligns with pro-family conservative principles.

"Some of the solutions that we're putting forward really resonate with have been folks who agree that people should be able to have families that look the way they want," Lecheler said. "There are certain factions that are excited by the idea of cash transfers specifically within the period surrounding the birth of a child because it enables families to have the number of kids that they want to have."

Founded in 2023, the Mother and Infant Cash Coalition grew out of a broader movement toward direct financial support for young families. Lecheler, who previously managed operations with The Bridge Project — an unrestricted cash transfer initiative launched in 2021 that operates across 14 red, blue, and purple states — noted that momentum for direct cash assistance built rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Advocates and researchers increasingly argue that flexible cash benefits offer a more cost-effective way to improve family stability than traditional, highly restricted in-kind welfare programs.

As direct cash initiatives expanded, organizations focused specifically on the perinatal period — from pregnancy through early infancy — began coordinating nationwide. That collaboration formed the Mother and Infant Cash Coalition, which aims to leverage early-childhood cash transfers to strengthen family stability and drive better maternal and child health outcomes. Member organizations include the Magnolia Mother’s Trust (MMT), launched in 2018, which provides selected mothers with $1,000 per month in unconditional cash for a full year.

Mayors for a Guaranteed Income, a coalition of over 150 mayors, bids to solve the affordability crisis with cash handouts. The coalition is responsible for over 100 pilot programs launched since 2018 and the establishment of the program in Cook County, Illinois, which was the first municipality to expand a guaranteed income program permanently.

Despite fierce national pushback against guaranteed basic income (GBI) programs — which opponents often criticize as "lottery socialism" — Lecheler stresses that conservative interest often stems from fiscal pragmatic arguments.

"There are other folks who are excited about it from sort of an efficiency angle, and think about this work because it is a lower administrative burden," Lecheler told Fox News Digital. "It is also more cost-effective to prevent poor birth outcomes like low birth weight or preterm birth than it is to respond to them after the fact."

MAYORS WANT TO KEEP HANDING OUT FREE CASH AFTER FEDERAL FUNDS DRIED UP

Founded in 2023, the Mother and Infant Cash Coalition grew out of a broader movement toward direct financial support for young families, according to Tegan Lecheler, the coalition's director. (Getty Images )

The debate over early cash aid reached a flashpoint in Michigan over "Rx Kids," a citywide initiative providing expectant mothers with a lump-sum payment of $1,500 during pregnancy, followed by $500 per month for up to 12 months post-birth. While Rx Kids is not a member of the Mother and Infant Cash Coalition, it operates on a similar direct-cash model.

Michigan House Republicans launched a formal inquiry into the initiative, which has absorbed more than $300 million in combined public and private funding. House Oversight Committee Chairman Rep. Jay DeBoyer, R-Clay Township, criticized the program's lack of oversight, arguing it functions as a "redistribution of wealth" that fails to solve systemic poverty without spending guardrails.

However, other Michigan Republicans view the policy through a pro-life lens. State Sen. John Damoose, R-Harbor Springs, publicly broke with critics to endorse the initiative.

"Helping moms and babies truly fits into the call of Jesus," Damoose wrote in an op-ed for the Detroit Free Press. "I believe in the sanctity of life. I believe we need to be champions for the unborn. That means more than just calling ourselves ‘pro-life’ — it means doing everything we can to make it easier for expectant moms to choose life. It means being there for families from the very beginning — and offering them the resources they need to thrive."

MICHIGAN REPUBLICAN LAWMAKER WARNS GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAMS DO NOT WORK, VOICES OPPOSITION TO STATE POLICY

Similar policy rifts are playing out nationwide as conservative lawmakers evaluate direct cash policies alongside conservative economic priorities.

"We have people from the right that have organically reached out to us to voice support," Lecheler noted, pointing to conservative support for policies like the Federal Child Tax Credit (CTC) and proposals to expand Child Care and Development Fund assistance.

"Cash assistance is widely supported across party lines, and we see that with the proliferation of cash proposals at the federal level, continued support for different versions of the CTC, as well as promising pilots like Rx Kids and the ASCEND program in New Mexico," Shafeka Hashash, Director of Cash Initiatives at Economic Security Project (ESP), told Fox News Digital. "Growing concerns about the cost-of-living crisis and how AI will impact the workforce are also driving bipartisan support for cash."

IOWA SUPERVISOR SLAMS BAN ON GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAMS AS STATE ‘WAGING IDEOLOGICAL WARS’

The Supreme Court of Texas issued a ruling that prohibited Harris County from launching a guaranteed income program which was disputed by Attorney General Ken Paxton. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Nevertheless, major state-level legal and legislative efforts to restrict or eliminate cash transfer programs continue in red states:

As of 2026, four red states — Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, and South Dakota — have enacted laws banning or restricting local guaranteed income and unconditional cash-aid programs. In addition, Kansas passed similar restrictive legislation when a bill became law without the governor's signature.

To date, Cook County remains the primary local municipality to enact a permanent guaranteed basic income program. For advocates like Lecheler, the policy push comes down to basic economic survival for young families.

"In the richest country in the world, I feel strongly that families shouldn't have to work three or four jobs just to keep food on the table," Lecheler said.

Joshua Q. Nelson is a reporter for Fox News Digital.

Joshua focuses on cultural trends, education, and public policy. He extensively covered reparations developments across the U.S., the Department of Education, and immigration issues.

Joining Fox News Digital in 2019, he previously graduated from Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and received the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton Public Policy Certificate.

title: Olympic swimmer Réka György calls out Virginia Governor Spanberger for withdrawing female sports regulation
excerpt:
Olympic swimmer and former Lia Thomas opponent Réka György says Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger 'hurt' female athletes by pulling Virginia women's sports regulation

Hungarian Olympian Réka Györg...
body_text:
Olympic swimmer and former Lia Thomas opponent Réka György says Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger 'hurt' female athletes by pulling Virginia women's sports regulation

Hungarian Olympian Réka György, who lost a place in an NCAA swimming final after competing against transgender swimmer Lia Thomas, criticized Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration for abandoning a proposed regulation intended to protect female sports and private spaces.

György was one of three female swimmers who petitioned the Virginia Board of Health to enact the regulation last year. The board unanimously approved the petition under former Gov. Glenn Youngkin, but the regulatory action was withdrawn in July after Spanberger took office.

"It’s really sad for me because I had the petition filed a year ago, and Youngkin approved it and wanted to take the next step and protect female athletes and female spaces in Virginia," György told OutKick.

VIRGINIA GOVERNOR ABIGAIL SPANBERGER QUIETLY ROLLS BACK YOUNGKIN'S PLANS TO PROTECT GIRLS' SPORTS

Virginia Tech swimmer Reka Gyorgy swims in the 400 IM consolation finals during the NCAA Swimming and Diving Championships on March 18, 2022, at the McAuley Aquatic Center in Atlanta, Ga. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

"I don’t like to see that people are using their power, especially political power, to make decisions and hurt other people. And also, it’s coming from a female."

György added that she was "really disappointed" by the decision.

György filed the petition in April 2025 alongside former Roanoke College swimmers Lily Mullens and Carter Satterfield. It asked the Board of Health to adopt regulations preventing biological males from participating on female-only athletic teams or entering female-designated spaces where women and girls could be undressing.

After receiving more than 2,300 public comments, the board voted 14–0 in August 2025 to begin the regulatory process. The Youngkin administration subsequently approved a Notice of Intended Regulatory Action, which was published that November.

SUPREME COURT MAKES RULING ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS

Abigail Spanberger, governor-elect of Virginia, during an inauguration ceremony at Capitol Square in Richmond, Virginia, US, on Saturday, Jan. 17, 2026. Democrat Abigail Spanberger was sworn in as governor of the Commonwealth of Virginia on Saturday, becoming the state's first female leader. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

However, the Spanberger administration withdrew the action on July 30, after an additional public-comment period had concluded. The withdrawal was not accompanied by an announcement from the governor’s office and was later published in the Virginia Register of Regulations.

The official notice said the State Board of Health would not proceed "upon review of statutory authority."

György questioned why the administration did not call greater public attention to the decision.

"I have a feeling that she’s afraid of the backlash of people, what they’re going to say or think," György said. "Other than that, I don’t know what her motivation is."

György’s advocacy stems from her experience at the 2022 NCAA Division I Women’s Swimming and Diving Championships. The Virginia Tech swimmer finished 17th in the preliminary round of the 500-yard freestyle, one place short of advancing to the consolation final.

Thomas, a biological male who identifies as a transgender woman, qualified for the championship final and went on to win the national title.

"Because the rule-makers let him compete in the women’s category, I got bumped out from the final," György said. "I got 17th, and I wasn’t allowed to swim in the finals. It ended up being me who got knocked out of the finals at night."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

György represented Hungary at the 2016 Rio Olympics and was a two-time ACC champion and two-time NCAA All-American during her career at Virginia Tech. She said she had devoted approximately 18 years to swimming before her final collegiate championship appearance.

"I put everything into swimming that I had," she said. "The 2022 NCAA Championships was my senior year in college, so I was ready to retire from swimming, but before I did that, give my best. I had everything that I was capable of putting into practices to prepare myself to give my best at that competition.

"And the chance to actually swim in the final was taken away."

György also recalled sharing a women’s locker room with Thomas during the championship meet.

"You were in just constant fear," she said. "You had no idea when he was going to enter the locker room."

György explained that putting on a high-level racing suit can take between 15 and 25 minutes, preventing swimmers from simply changing quickly and leaving.

"I was always looking behind my shoulder because I had no idea when my privacy was going to be robbed away," she said. "You try to cover yourself, which usually you don’t do because you are surrounded by other females and you don’t have that issue. But that competition was different."

The experience ultimately prompted György to become an outspoken advocate for sex-separated athletic competition and private spaces.

"I just had this feeling that I had to speak up because, obviously, the people who were in charge of that competition didn’t do anything to protect us females," she said. "One day, maybe I will have a daughter, and I don’t want my daughter to be in a situation where I had to share the locker room and compete against a male."

György, who continues to live in Virginia, joined the petition effort after being contacted about the controversy involving Mullens, Satterfield and the Roanoke College women’s swimming team.

In 2023, members of the team objected when a transgender student sought to join the women’s roster. Roanoke College later said the student had chosen not to compete.

University of Pennsylvania swimmer Lia Thomas accepts the winning trophy for the 500 Freestyle finals during the NCAA Swimming and Diving Championships on March 17th, 2022, at the McAuley Aquatic Center in Atlanta, Georgia. (Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

György said she has not yet contacted Spanberger because she only recently learned the regulatory action had been withdrawn, but she plans to seek a conversation with the governor.

"I want to tell her that I hope she sees where I’m coming from," György said. "I hope she sees where other people are coming from when we are trying to protect little girls and females in sports and women-only spaces."

"Title IX was created for a reason," she added. "I really do hope that she is going to follow this rule, and she is going to stand up for women in Virginia."

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

title: UK court clears woman of voicing support for Hamas in university speech
excerpt:
A London court has cleared a British woman of supporting Palestinian group Hamas in a speech she gave outside her university in 2023.

The jury at the Central Criminal Court, more commonly known as th...
body_text:
A London court has cleared a British woman of supporting Palestinian group Hamas in a speech she gave outside her university in 2023.

The jury at the Central Criminal Court, more commonly known as the Old Bailey, on Friday found Sarah Cotte, 22, not guilty of expressing support for the group that’s designated a “terrorist” organisation under UK law.

Public prosecutors had alleged that Cotte voiced support for Hamas two days after the group led the deadly attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023.

During a speech she gave outside the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) in London at the time, she expressed “unconditional solidarity” with the Palestinian resistance, the court was told. Prosecutors claimed this was a “thinly veiled reference” to Hamas.

Cotte repeatedly rejected attempts to equate the two, telling the court: “I don’t support Hamas and I have never supported Hamas. I was supporting the right to resist.”

Speaking to Al Jazeera after the verdict on Friday, Cotte said the court’s decision was a “testament to how people are feeling about British support for Zionism”.

“I never condemned the right to armed struggle in Palestine,” Cotte said. “I didn’t let them corner me and make this a conversation about what Zionists want to talk about.”

Instead, she said, “I used it as a platform to talk about what I thought was important, which was the Palestinian struggle, British support for Zionism and our rights as people of conscience.”

Hamas was officially proscribed in its entirety by the UK government in late 2021, when its political wing was also banned. Its military wing, the Qassam Brigades, has been proscribed since 2001. Those found guilty of supporting such groups can face up to 14 years in prison.

On the final day of the week-long trial on Friday, Cotte again denied expressing support for Hamas during her speech at SOAS while she was a student there and argued that she had only expressed support for Palestinians’ “right to resist”.

“I think that the killing of civilians is always a tragedy. At the same time, I don’t think it is a surprise,” she told jurors about her comments regarding Hamas’s October 7 attack.

“I think saying it is understandable and agreeing with it is two different things, so I think it is understandable and could be justified,” she explained.

“I don’t think it’s my role to impose conditions on the Palestinian people and their struggle,” Cotte added.

In comments to Al Jazeera after the verdict, she said: “This victory will re-energise the whole of the solidarity movement … We stand with the Palestinian people and their right to be agents in their struggle for freedom.”

Responding to the not guilty verdict, Anas Mustapha, head of Public Advocacy at CAGE International, said the ruling showed that “ordinary people will not accept the criminalisation of speech in support of the Palestinian right to resist occupation.”

“Sarah Cotte has been found not guilty, and we are delighted for her, her family, and everyone who stood alongside her through more than two and a half years of investigation and court proceedings,” Mustapha said.

Cotte gave the speech on October 9, 2023. She was arrested over it on January 31, 2024. An earlier trial found her not guilty of a second charge of expressing support for Hamas in a WhatsApp group chat.

title: Kyler Murray out with concussion so door opens for Carson Wentz as Vikings' new starter – perhaps for a while
excerpt: The Minnesota Vikings named Kyler Murray their starting QB over J.J. McCarthy. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if this is the right decision. Plus, they discuss Jerry Jones potentia...
body_text:
The Minnesota Vikings named Kyler Murray their starting QB over J.J. McCarthy. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if this is the right decision. Plus, they discuss Jerry Jones potentially taking shots at former Dallas Cowboy Micah Parsons.

The Minnesota Vikings and their quarterback hijinks are at it again, as Carson Wentz will start Sunday's game against the Chicago Bears because Kyler Murray remains in the concussion protocol and J.J. McCarthy remains at the back of the depth chart.

Coach Kevin O'Connell told reporters that Murray, who suffered a concussion in the regular-season opener against the Green Bay Packers, is still working his way back to health.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Minnesota Vikings quarterback Carson Wentz answers questions after an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Chargers Thursday, Oct. 23, 2025, in Inglewood, California. (AP Photo/Jessie Alcheh)

2026 NFL SEASON PREDICTIONS: DIVISION WINNERS, PLAYOFF TEAMS AND SUPER BOWL PICK REVEALED

We say again because the Vikings had Wentz starting last season in Weeks 3 through 8 when then-starter McCarthy was out with an ankle injury.

Wentz went down in Week 8 and that, as much as McCarthy's recovery, thrust the Vikings 2024 first-round back into the starting lineup.

And here we are again. With Wentz surprisingly being promoted from the No. 3 quarterback during training camp, to No. 2 ahead of McCarthy prior to last week's opener, then to the starter on Sunday at Chicago.

And all the while, McCarthy remains on the bench despite having been involved in a competition for the starting job against Murray.

Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy of the Minnesota Vikings look on during an OTA workout at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center in Eagan, Minn., on May 27, 2026. (David Berding/Getty Images)

It shows the Vikings promoted Wentz because they thought he was more experienced than McCarthy, yes, but also better.

That becomes clear because, again, it is Wentz starting ahead of a healthy McCarthy this weekend.

It also suggests Wentz has an opportunity going forward.

WHY THE MINNESOTA VIKINGS OVER 9.5 WINS LOOKS LIKE A STRONG BET EVEN WITH KYLER MURRAY UNDER CENTER

Wentz took over in the opener when Murray got knocked out of the game on the Vikings' third possession of the game. Murray was down for a time but eventually walked into the team's locker room for a concussion examination which came back positive.

The Vikings were trailing, 9-0, when Murray left and faced a 22-10 deficit with 2:08 left in the third quarter when Wentz threw a TD pass.

And then he threw another TD pass in the fourth quarter.

And the Vikings scored two other times as Wentz completed 12 of 19 passes for 133 yards with 3 TD passes and without a turnover.

So, Minny beat the rival Packers in dramatic comeback fashion.

Minnesota Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell reacts during the second half at Soldier Field on Sept. 8, 2025. (Matt Marton/Imagn Images)

O'Connell this week wasn't going to reward Wentz's role in that comeback win by benching him in favor of McCarthy.

But what if Wentz keeps playing well? What if he beats the Bears?

Would the coach bench the quarterback who helped his team get to 2-0 if Murray is ready to play in Week 3?

As ESPN noted, the starter change this week marks the 11th time the Vikings have flipped quarterbacks during a season in O'Connell's five-year tenure.

A majority of those moves came in situations similar to what the team is facing now: An injury to a starter.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Minnesota Viking head coach Kevin O'Connell interacts with Carson Wentz (11) on the sideline during the first half of a game against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on Oct. 23, 2025 in Inglewood, California. (Brooke Sutton/Getty Images)

Last year, J.J. McCarthy started the first two games but injured his ankle and missed the next five games while Wentz played.

Wentz was then injured in Week 8 and that's when McCarthy took his job back the following week. The Vikings had a 2-3 record with Wentz in the lineup.

If Wentz plays well and stays healthy and keeps winning, the question will loom: Does Murray get his job back even when he's healthy?

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

title: Trump is 'unfettered' and more comfortable with power in his second term, journalists say
excerpt:
Senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy provides details ahead of President Donald Trump's planned meeting with Gulf leaders.

NEW YORK, NY - President Donald Trump is more comfortable on the job...
body_text:
Senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy provides details ahead of President Donald Trump's planned meeting with Gulf leaders.

NEW YORK, NY - President Donald Trump is more comfortable on the job in his second term, according to a panel of journalists tasked with covering his every move.

Atlantic reporters Jonathan Lemire, Ashley Parker, Missy Ryan and Michael Scherer discussed what it’s like to cover the White House and other powerful institutions Thursday on stage during the magazine’s annual festival at Perelman Performing Arts Center in New York City.

"We’re seeing someone who completed, arguably, the greatest comeback in American political history, he trusts his instincts and very few others, and is sort of an unfettered version of himself," Lemire said.

Lemire said that Trump’s second administration is filled with "true believers" and "loyalists," while remnants of the "old Republican establishment" are long gone.

TRUMP SAYS IRAN WAR 'HOPEFULLY' NEARING END AS HOUSE SPEAKER VOWS TEHRAN WON'T GET NUCLEAR WEAPON

President Donald Trump spoke during a news conference in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on April 6, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"He also is just more comfortable with the job and how to use the levers of power," Lemire said. "That also includes the relationship with the press and how he dictated change in terms of that relationship."

Parker said the presence of Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has helped, while Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller spent the four years out of power "plotting and planning" how to run a "bigger, stronger, faster, better, more ruthless" White House the second time around.

Scherer agreed, noting that Trump came back with a much clearer idea about what he can accomplish and how it would impact his legacy.

"I was in Dallas last week when he did the midterm convention. His message was, ‘Vote for me one more time,’" Scherer said.

"There's sort of a different, almost nostalgic approach he's taking to things," he continued. "But it is really about like, ‘This is my last chance to do what I can to get to make my mark.’"

JASMINE CROCKETT DISPARAGES MAGA VOTERS, TRUMP AS 'MOST UNPATRIOTIC PEOPLE'

Atlantic journalists Vivian Salama, Michael Scherer, Missy Ryan, Ashley Parker and Jonathan Lemire. (FOX News Media)

Ryan, who covers national security and foreign policy, isn’t thrilled that the Pentagon hasn’t held a formal press briefing for months, and staff writer Vivian Salama, who moderated the conversation, said it's harder for journalists to get scoops this time.

Scherer said the lack of leaks from inside the White House showed how it "operates as a unified body" under Wiles.

"The people under her are loyal to her. They're loyal to the president also, but it operates as a functioning organization," Scherer said.

"The first Trump term, there were three or four camps in that same space. They were often warring with each other and stabbing each other in the back and competing for the president," Scherer continued. "It's harder now. It's harder to get inside the room details than it was in the first term, but it can still be done."

NEBRASKA SENATE CANDIDATE SEEMS TO CONFIRM AUDIO CLAIMING TRUMP SUPPORTERS' LIVES 'SUCK SO F---ING BAD'

Michael Scherer at The Atlantic Festival on Sept. 17, 2026.

While the second Trump administration has been tighter-lipped than the first administration, Scherer said that the Obama and Biden administrations operated like bureaucratic law firms.

"We still have more access here, I think, than we had in recent Democratic administrations, just because they had so much discipline. They had a different ethos about them," Scherer said.

title: Lane Kiffin's visit to Oxford isn't the first time a coach made an unwelcome return to his former school
excerpt: On this episode of Don’t @ Me with Dan Dakich, Dan breaks down the high-stakes, hostile homecoming as LSU prepares to walk into a wall of noise against Ole Miss. From Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry ca...
body_text:
On this episode of Don’t @ Me with Dan Dakich, Dan breaks down the high-stakes, hostile homecoming as LSU prepares to walk into a wall of noise against Ole Miss. From Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry calling for military backup to Kiffin admitting there are legitimate "safety issues" awaiting him on the sideline, SEC football culture is on full display. Dan dives into why Kiffin insists his players have nothing to worry about, how he's shifting all the game pressure onto the Rebels, and why this is easily the most anticipated narrative of the college football season.

By now, most of you are painfully aware of the game taking place in Oxford, Mississippi, this weekend between LSU and Ole Miss.

It's less of a game and more a national event, given the added stakes of Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin making his return to Vaught Hemingway Stadium for the first time since leaving the Rebels in the lurch to make his way to Baton Rouge.

There will be plenty of bad blood to go around for all parties involved, but this kind of "reunion" isn't entirely unprecedented.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Prominent head coaches will, occasionally, leave their teams on less than ideal terms, and when they make the return trip to the place they used to call home, it can get a little toxic.

With that in mind, I decided to take a look at a few other times head coaches made their way back to the schools that used to employ them and how those trips compared to Kiffin's welcome committee in Oxford.

MOUNTED POLICE, EXTRA PATROLS AND KIFFIN HATE: OXFORD PREPARES FOR OLE MISS-LSU GAME WITH EXTRA SECURITY

Some of these went a little more amicably than others, but all were fairly noteworthy, so let's dive in.

Head coach Nick Saban of the Alabama Crimson Tide is congratulated by head coach Les Miles of the Louisiana State University Tigers after Alabama defeated LSU 27-21 in overtime on Nov. 11, 2008, at Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge, La. (Getty Images)

Before he became the unquestioned GOAT in the annals of college football, Nick Saban was a wildly successful coach at LSU in the early to mid-2000s.

After a pair of SEC Championships and a national title during his five-year tenure with the Tigers, Saban departed for the NFL, leaving many folks on the bayou feeling embittered and betrayed.

Following an unremarkable pair of seasons with the Miami Dolphins, Saban decided it was time to return to the college ranks, opting to don the headset at LSU's biggest rival, Alabama, in 2007.

OLE MISS AND LSU WILL DELIVER CINEMA, BUT THE NEXT WEEK FOR EACH TEAM COULD BE THEIR MOST PIVOTAL TESTS

Tiger fans would only have to wait one year before their former head coach made his way back to Death Valley, as the top-ranked Crimson Tide made their way to Baton Rouge to play 15th-ranked LSU.

The atmosphere around the game was tense and filled with anger and resentment toward Saban, and it didn't help that the Tide escaped with a 27-21 overtime win to effectively knock the Bayou Bengals out of the SEC Championship hunt.

Saban was given a police escort out of the stadium, and years later, the six-time national champion would call leaving LSU the biggest mistake of his career.

South Carolina head coach Steve Spurrier looks back over his shoulder at a replay in the second quarter against his former team, Florida, at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium in Gainesville, Fla., on Nov. 11, 2006. Spurrier was coaching at Florida for the first time since leaving in 2001. (Getty Images)

Throughout the entirety of the 90s and into the early 2000s, Steve Spurrier and Florida football were synonymous with one another.

The Head Ball Coach won a Heisman Trophy in 1966 while quarterbacking the Gators, and when he returned to roam the sidelines in 1990, he fulfilled the prophecy of "awakening the sleeping giant" once uttered by Alabama legend Paul "Bear" Bryant.

Six SEC Championships and one national title later, and Spurrier figured he had accomplished all he needed to, leaving the friendly confines of The Swamp - the name he gave to Ben Hill Griffin Stadium - for an NFL coaching gig with the Washington Redskins in 2002.

Much like Nick Saban, Spurrier wasn't long for the pros, returning to the SEC in 2005 as the head coach of the South Carolina Gamecocks.

This didn't sit well with a majority of Gator fans, seeing their visor-clad Messiah coaching an SEC East rival, and it made it even worse that he beat his old school in his first year on the job.

When Spurrier and the Gamecocks made their first trip to The Swamp together in 2006, a game with national championship implications for the home team had new stakes attached to it.

While the fans weren't openly hostile towards their former coach (most were even downright warm), it felt almost like watching a weird alternate reality simulation for those in attendance.

The game was an instant classic, with Gators defensive end Jarvis Moss blocking a potential game-winning field goal to preserve the 17-16 win for Florida, and keep their BCS title game hopes alive in the process.

Spurrier once said "only Gators get out alive" when referring to The Swamp, and that very phrase came back to bite him on that day in November 2006.

A view of Lane Kiffin on the sideline for the Ole Miss Rebels during an SEC football game. (Getty Images)

Yes, Lane Kiffin is no stranger to making his way back to old stomping grounds, as he had to do something similar just a few years ago.

When Tennessee hired Kiffin in 2009, the then-33-year-old was fresh off of a failed stint as the Oakland Raiders' head coach, and was looking to make a splash in the SEC.

A "splash" is putting it mildly, as Kiffin immediately went into prison survival mode and tried to pick a fight with the biggest guy in the pen, that being Florida and head coach Urban Meyer.

Kiffin ruffled feathers, accusing Meyer of recruiting violations and promising to "sing Rocky Top all night long" after beating the Gators in The Swamp, but after a year of empty promises and a 7-6 campaign, the brash offensive genius left for sunny Southern California to coach the USC Trojans.

Vols fans revolted, burning couches and rioting on campus, while Kiffin left under cover of darkness.

Flash forward to 2021, and Tennessee fans finally got their chance to let their old head coach know how they really felt in person, as the Rebels made their way to Neyland Stadium.

Kiffin had bounced around as an offensive coordinator and head coach at a few different stops before settling into Oxford to coach the Ole Miss football team, and a night game in Knoxville presented an opportunity for some madness.

The game was crazy enough on its own, as the two teams combined for nearly 1,000 yards of total offense and the Vols even had the ball trailing by only five with only a minute left in the fourth quarter.

A controversial review then led to a nearly 20 minute delay, as Volunteer fans chucked mustard bottles and golf balls onto the field, the latter of which allegedly hit Kiffin.

As he was being interviewed on the field following the win, Kiffin did his best George Costanza impression, presenting the very golf ball that struck him to a shocked ESPN audience watching at home.

The fact that this game took place nearly a dozen years after his departure did nothing to snuff out the anger Vols fans held toward their former head coach.

Head Coach Bobby Petrino of the Missouri State Bears stands on the sidelines during a game against the Arkansas Razorbacks at Donald W. Reynolds Razorback Stadium in Fayetteville, Ark., on Sept. 17, 2022. The Razorbacks defeated the Bears 38-27. (Getty Images)

Here's one that a lot of people may have forgotten about, but it deserves mention all the same.

The first three instances on this list are comprised of coaches who decided to stay in conference and take jobs with rival SEC programs, but what happens when a coach who made an unceremonious exit just happens to be on the schedule by way of a cupcake matchup scheduled years before he even agreed to take the job?

For those who need a history lesson, Bobby Petrino coached the Arkansas Razorbacks in the late 2000s and early 2010s, even leading the team to a Sugar Bowl berth in 2010 and a top-five finish in 2011.

He was incredibly successful in the short time he called Fayetteville home until 2012, when he crashed his motorcycle with a former Arkansas volleyball player riding on the back.

This led to an investigation and, eventually, his termination from the university, ending a promising rise for the Razorbacks under Petrino.

A decade later, Petrino found his way back to Frank Broyles Field by way of coaching the Missouri State Bears, a lower-end FCS school.

Arkansas, conversely, was ranked in the top 10 and looked to improve upon their nine-win season in 2021 with third-year head coach Sam Pittman.

It appeared as though the Hogs were going to exact some revenge on their motorcycle-obsessed outcast, but, in a game that may have been a precursor to how the rest of the Pittman era would go, the Razorbacks needed to score 21 unanswered points in the fourth quarter to eke out a 38-27 victory.

Petrino would actually go on to be the offensive coordinator for Pittman just one year later, and would even be the interim head coach in 2025 when Pittman was given the axe.

They truly can't quit the one that got away in Fayetteville.

title: Hasan Piker calls Bin Laden a ‘spoiled brat,’ labels 9/11 ‘blowback’ in Axios interview
excerpt: Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin reports on backlash facing Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed after far-left streamer Hasan Piker claimed that America is worse th...
body_text:
Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin reports on backlash facing Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed after far-left streamer Hasan Piker claimed that America is worse than al Qaeda on ‘America Reports.’

Hasan Piker, the internet streamer and YouTube personality known for his progressive commentary, called Osama bin Laden a "spoiled brat" for his reasoning in orchestrating the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, which he called "blowback" for U.S. actions in the Middle East in the preceding years.

Speaking with Axios, Piker discussed bin Laden's remarks about why he targeted the United States: U.S. support of Israel, American oil policies and U.S. bases in the Middle East. He noted that bin Laden was once a U.S. ally when the U.S. trained, funded, and armed the mujahideen in Afghanistan during the Soviet-Afghan War.

"The action was so heinous and so violent that — and also … given his position as formerly an American ally … I think that he came across a little bit more as a spoiled brat that wasn't getting his way. With many backers in the Saudi kingdom as well, and the royal family," Piker said.

CLINTON, BUSH RECEIVED MULTIPLE WARNINGS ON BIN LADEN HIJACK PLOTS BEFORE 9/11, DECLASSIFIED FILES SHOW

Twitch streamer Hasan Piker is facing renewed scrutiny for his remarks during an Axios interview. He said Osama bin Laden was a "spoiled brat" and remarked on the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks. (Sam Barnes/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images)

The left-wing streamer said he wants fewer actors like bin Laden to "exist in general."

"The other path of least resistance is to not interfere in these affairs in general and not continue to dominate and create an environment where people are going to seek out revenge and put us in a position of danger," he said.

RADICAL EL-SAYED ALLY DOUBLES DOWN ON ANTI-AMERICAN RHETORIC WITH STUNNING TERRORIST COMPARISON

The World Trade Center in New York City, shown after being attacked by hijacked planes on Sept. 11, 2001. (Newspix via Getty Images)

Piker called the Sept. 11 attacks a "horrifying tragedy" and called them blowback for U.S. actions in the Middle East.

"Blowback is not a justification. Blowback is just what it is," he said. "A justification offers either a moral condemnation or a moral acceptance of the act. I do not accept the act of 9/11 morally".

HASAN PIKER INSISTS MIDDLE EAST WOULD BE 'MORE STABLE' IF IRAN HAD NUCLEAR WEAPONS DURING AXIOS INTERVIEW

Piker has faced backlash for remarks in the same interview where he compared the United States to al-Qaeda "pound for pound".

"Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes," Piker said. "We have caused tremendous terror all around the world".

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.
