"It’s been great to hear the feedback, and all my friends literally went the day they saw it."

Robinson and Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield were featured in the "My Greatest 7" campaign, which will be seen throughout the football season.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Amid claims of ‘mass migration’, Labor hopes a measured approach will take the hot air out of the debate
excerpt:
The country’s migration settings have become a source of discontent – but will Tony Burke’s approach be seen as the right mix?

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Tony Burke ...
body_text:
The country’s migration settings have become a source of discontent – but will Tony Burke’s approach be seen as the right mix?

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Tony Burke has promised to make Labor’s existing migration policy work better rather than announcing a dramatic cut in numbers, arguing that populist promises to slash net overseas migration will “trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy”.

The home affairs minister’s message was immediately endorsed by employer groups, who over recent days have made it clear that steps to arbitrarily slash migrant numbers would compound already severe skills shortages and hurt businesses, especially those in the regions.

“We need immigration. We just need to make sure that it is targeted for the needs of Australia in numbers and across the different categories that work for our economy,” Burke said in his long-awaited address to the National Press Club on Thursday.

“We talk about the need for extra housing. It’s pretty hard to get a house built without having a plasterer involved. In both Sydney and Melbourne, close to two-thirds of the plasterers we have were born overseas.”

Bran Black, the chief executive of the Business Council in Australia, welcomed the government’s efforts to “restore integrity to the migration system”, even as he argued against new rules that would limit the length of stay for most backpackers.

“The starting point for migration policy should not be a number to cut to, but what our economy genuinely needs,” Black said.

“Almost one in three occupations in this country are short of workers right now. That translates to not enough workers building homes, caring for us in hospitals and aged care homes, delivering infrastructure and powering the energy transition. That is the challenge that any migration policy should be looking to solve.”

Labor has taken a long time to come up with its policy prescription to fix the country’s migration settings which, after the post-pandemic surge in new arrivals, have become a source of growing popular discontent.

Spurious claims of “mass migration” have fanned the flames of this discontent, but few would argue that our system is working well and in the best interests of the country – or in the best interests of a ballooning number of people trapped in a kind of temporary visa limbo that has strained public infrastructure and patience.

Alan Gamlen, the director of the ANU’s migration hub, said Burke appeared to have announced the right mix of measures that would give the government the capacity to regulate an out-of-control temporary visa system without damaging the economy.

“They don’t seem to have fallen into the trap of chasing a net migration number,” Gamlen said.

“Burke made it pretty clear, and in a convincing way, that this is the result of a well-considered process that has been going on for a while and which addresses long-term structural issues, rather than just a kneejerk response to One Nation.”

One Nation has committed to lowering net overseas migration to 130,000 a year, and the Coalition somewhere between 150,000 and 170,000.

In comparison, Burke stuck to the government’s forecast of 225,000 people by 2027-28.

He did, however, acknowledge that there was now a public expectation that the government would pull the levers necessary to get there.

“Net overseas migration has been viewed as a budget forecast. Last couple of years, people have talked about it as a budget target,” he said.

“That is a very different way of looking at it. But given that we have the challenges we have with housing in Australia at the moment, I do think we need to be able to have these additional tools to make sure that what is published and forecast is reached.”

With business groups already suffering from skills shortages even at a time of high immigration, the home affairs minister articulated why he believed the government can win the political argument against those competing to announce the lowest targeted Nom.

“The lower [Nom] levels will trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy,” he said.

Burke pointed out that denying skilled foreign workers the opportunity to bring in family members – as proposed by One Nation – would not free up more visas for more workers.

Instead, that approach would slash the number of foreign doctors, tradies, nurses and aged care workers willing to come to our country.

“The proportion of doctors who come to Australia with family attached to their application? 50%. How many construction workers come with family attached to their application? 50%. How many nurses and aged care workers come with family attached to their application? Two-thirds.”

Whether Burke and the Albanese government can convince the public its measured approach is enough is an open question.

“Let’s see if this lets out some of the hot air in the migration debate,” Gamlen said.

title: Tony Burke rejects farmers’ claims that immigration changes will increase food prices
excerpt:
Farming lobby says shoppers will see emptier shelves and higher prices because of restrictions on backpackers

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The farming lobby’s claim th...
body_text:
Farming lobby says shoppers will see emptier shelves and higher prices because of restrictions on backpackers

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The farming lobby’s claim that immigration rule changes will increase food prices for households is wrong, Tony Burke has said, describing moves to speed up processing of backpacker visas as a positive step for agriculture.

Burke unveiled Labor’s long-awaited reforms at the National Press Club on Thursday, flagging that the plan was more limited than the government would like, due to a lack of support for wider legislation from the Coalition.

But the package has received mixed reviews, with business groups and the Coalition saying it did not do enough to lower net overseas migration levels, while refugee advocates said it showed migrants remained “political punching bags”.

The National Farmers Federation’s chief executive, Mike Guerin, said farmers would see an immediate economic impact from restrictions on working holidaymakers and other temporary migrants. He warned producers were already struggling to get workers for the harvesting season.

Backpackers seeking to stay in Australia for more than a year will be subject to a new ballot, with places severely restricted for years two and three.

“We will see a lift in the price of food,” Guerin said. 
 “We will see emptier supermarkets ... And while it’s yet to play out directly for consumers, for people in the cities, it’s very close. We will not be able to finish the harvest this year, before Christmas.”

But Burke told Guardian Australia the plan was carefully formulated, reducing demand driven settings and giving the government great control, while not damaging the economy.

He said healthcare, construction and aged care all relied on overseas workers, and broader cuts would hurt essential services.

“The economic contribution matters in terms of services that people rely on.

“The announcement we made today is about getting the processing moving again for those backpacker visas that have an obligation, if you want the extra years, to work in the regions. That’s a significant advantage … the department getting moving on the processing of those again at a faster pace.”

Burke said the agriculture sector could utilise workers from the Pacific Australia labour mobility scheme, and producers had legal responsibilities to pay staff adequately.

“I don’t think consumers believe their pathway to paying less should rely on worker exploitation.”

The government’s changes include new compliance measures to deal with people overstaying their visa, but Burke said enforcement would be measured and sensible.

About 100 new additional compliance officers will be added, along with 250 additional beds in immigration detention.

Burke said the changes were not like hardline immigration enforcement in countries overseas, such as the approach used by Donald Trump’s administration.

But the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre said the planned increase in enforcement would leave Australia “smaller, meaner and more divided”.
  “How much of its soul is the Labor party prepared to sacrifice chasing people who will never be satisfied,” founder Kon Karapanagiotidis said.
  The Greens deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi, criticised the increased immigration detention and bar on foreign students bringing family members to Australia.
  “Labor’s move to force people to choose between their family and a chance to study in Australia is soulless mimicry of One Nation tactics,” Faruqi said.

“Pauline Hanson and her billionaire backers might as well be ghostwriting Labor’s immigration policy.”
 Major employers welcomed the reforms, with the Minerals Council of Australia praising the government’s prioritisation of mining workers.
 Big business lobby group the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry said the government had avoided a damaging overcorrection and the plan would help rebuild public confidence. But its chief executive, Andrew McKellar, warned its execution via ministerial directives meant policy was being held together by “the stroke of a pen”.
 The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, accused the government of using farmers and regional industries as “whipping boys for their failure to bring down migration”. 
 Cuts to the working holidaymaker program would lead to staff shortages, the Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association chief, Wes Lambert, warned.
 “A chef, cook or hospitality manager filling a genuine shortage is valuable too,” Lambert said.

“Australia absolutely needs a sustainable migration system. But migration policy cannot simply be a numbers exercise. It must recognise where the workers are actually needed.”

title: Federal judge ties ICE agents' hands with ruling on warrantless Southern California arrests
excerpt: Fox News senior national correspondent William La Jeunesse reports from Los Angeles on Assembly Bill 1896, legislation that restricts police departments and local governments from hiring individuals w...
body_text:
Fox News senior national correspondent William La Jeunesse reports from Los Angeles on Assembly Bill 1896, legislation that restricts police departments and local governments from hiring individuals who conducted federal immigration enforcement under President Donald Trump.

A federal judge with the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California issued a preliminary injunction to block the U.S. government from conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests in the district unless the arrestee is deemed likely to escape before a warrant can be procured.

"Defendants are enjoined from enforcing their policy and practice of making warrantless civil immigration arrests in this District without a prearrest individualized determination by the arresting agent or officer of probable cause that the person being arrested is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained, as required by 8 U.S.C. 1357(a)(2) and 8 C.F.R. § 287.8(c)(2)," the order signed by U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong reads, in part.

Frimpong was nominated by former President Joe Biden during his White House tenure.

EXCLUSIVE: 25 YEARS AFTER 9/11, ICE SAYS MORE THAN 2K KNOWN OR SUSPECTED TERRORISTS HAVE BEEN DEPORTED

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents walk a detainee out of the Ventura County Government Center in Ventura, Calif., on July 27, 2026. (Blake Fagan / AFP via Getty Images)

"Mere presence within the United States in violation of United States immigration law is not, by itself, sufficient to conclude that a person is likely to escape before a warrant for arrest can be obtained," the judge's order notes.

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California encompasses the following counties: Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, San Bernardino, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties.

ANGEL DAD REBUKES DEMOCRATIC LAWMAKERS OVER SANCTUARY POLICIES AFTER DAUGHTER KILLED BY TWICE-DEPORTED FELON

The badge of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent is seen as they patrol the halls of immigration court at the Jacob K. Javits Federal Building on June 9, 2025, in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

"This ruling is one of the most important decisions to date in the community’s effort to end the federal government’s cruel and illegal practice of abducting people and separating them from their families," ACLU Foundation of Southern California senior staff attorney Mayra Joachin declared in a statement.

"By requiring immigration agents to follow the law’s requirement to make escape risk determinations before they can arrest someone without a warrant, this court order should put an end to hundreds–if not more–of unlawful arrests that continue throughout Southern California. We will closely monitor compliance with this court order, and expect the federal government to abide by it," Joachin added.

MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS

The Department of Homeland Security provided Fox News Digital with the following statement on Thursday: "ICE has authority for lawful arrests where authorized under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use 'reasonable suspicion' to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the statute and the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The Supreme Court has already vindicated us on these practices."

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Los Angeles NBC helicopter seen plummeting toward ground in dashcam video
excerpt:
Newly released dashcam video captures the final moments before an NBC news helicopter crashed, killing three people in Los Angeles. (Credit; Victoria Yera Valencia via Storyful)

Dashcam video from a ...
body_text:
Newly released dashcam video captures the final moments before an NBC news helicopter crashed, killing three people in Los Angeles. (Credit; Victoria Yera Valencia via Storyful)

Dashcam video from a Los Angeles driver captured an NBC and Telemundo news helicopter rapidly descending toward the ground moments before a fiery crash that killed three people.

The video, captured by driver Year Valencia, shows the helicopter dropping from the sky Tuesday while its crew was covering a separate deadly collision involving an SUV and a city bus.

"I downloaded the video of my dashcam. It’s a little dot on the video. It’s a crisp video and it just goes down," Valencia told KTLA, which first obtained the footage. "God, it’s so close, it could have happened to anyone. My parents walk down the street."

NBC REPORTER, PILOT AMONG THE VICTIMS IDENTIFIED IN DEADLY LOS ANGELES HELICOPTER CRASH

Eliana Moreno seen in a news helicopter. (Facebook/Eliana Moreno)

The helicopter crashed in the Chatsworth neighborhood of the San Fernando Valley, killing NBC4 and Telemundo 52 reporter Eliana Moreno, pilot George Marciniw and 29-year-old Edy Gutierrez Mejia, who was on the ground.

The aircraft went down near a storage facility and caught fire, with the blaze spreading to at least four vehicles and two storage containers.

A man takes photographs of the scene on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, where three people were killed when an NBC4 Los Angeles helicopter crashed and exploded in flames near the site of a triple-fatal SUV-Metro bus collision in Chatsworth on Tuesday evening. (Dean Musgrove/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images)

The crash came roughly two hours after the SUV slammed into the city bus in a separate collision that killed two people and injured six others, according to authorities. Police said the SUV had been traveling the wrong way, ran a red light and struck another vehicle before hitting the bus.

VICTIMS IDENTIFIED IN FATAL AMAZON CARGO JET CRASH AT MIAMI AIRPORT

Police arrested the SUV's driver, 36-year-old Bailee Lynn Rios, on murder charges Tuesday night. The Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office was reviewing the case to determine what charges, if any, would be filed in court.

The cause of the helicopter crash remained under investigation Wednesday. Video broadcast from the helicopter before it went down captured an alarm sounding inside the aircraft as it began losing altitude.

The scene on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, where three people were killed when an NBC4 Los Angeles helicopter crashed and exploded in flames near the site of a triple-fatal SUV-Metro bus collision in Chatsworth on Tuesday evening. (Dean Musgrove/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images)

National Transportation Safety Board investigator Fabian Salazar said Wednesday that the helicopter's final video could provide investigators with critical evidence as they work to determine what caused the crash. The sounds captured on the recording appeared consistent with changes in engine speed and likely cockpit advisory tones, he said.

The helicopter, a Eurocopter AS350 operated by Angel City Air, was used by NBC4 and Telemundo 52 for aerial news coverage. The NTSB is investigating the helicopter crash as well as the earlier bus collision.

Bradford Betz is a Fox News Digital breaking reporter covering crime, political issues, and much more.

title: GOP congressman presses WNBA to define ‘women’ after Enes Kanter Freedom, Royce White ruled ineligible
excerpt: Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White will reportedly be denied from entering the upcoming 2027 WNBA draft league. 'Outnumbered' reacts and debates Charles Barkley's viral comments de...
body_text:
Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White will reportedly be denied from entering the upcoming 2027 WNBA draft league. 'Outnumbered' reacts and debates Charles Barkley's viral comments defending women's sports.

Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., is pressing WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert for answers about the league’s eligibility rules, including one very basic question: How does the WNBA define "women"?

In a follow-up letter to Engelbert obtained by OutKick, the Indiana Republican and other members of Congress question the league’s handling of player safety, fan confrontations and, now, who is actually eligible to play in the WNBA.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The letter comes as Engelbert prepares to leave the league. She announced Sept. 4 that she will retire at the end of 2026 after more than seven years as commissioner, and the WNBA has already begun the process of searching for her successor.

WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert speaks before the WNBA basketball draft in New York on April 13, 2026. (Pamela Smith/AP)

That timing adds another layer to Stutzman’s request, which asks Engelbert to answer several questions about league policy before Oct. 16.

The WNBA’s collective bargaining agreement says that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." But it does not go any further in defining what that means.

That became a bigger issue this summer after Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said female athletes should not have to compete against biological men.

Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White later announced that they identified as women and planned to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft, seemingly forcing the league to address the issue directly. League sources later told media outlets that neither man was eligible for the draft.

WNBA COMMISSIONER CATHY ENGELBERT SENDS TRANS INCLUSION MEMO AFTER ENES FREEDOM, ROYCE WHITE ANNOUNCEMENTS

"How does the WNBA define ‘women’ for purposes of Article XIII, Section 1(a) of its collective bargaining agreement?" the lawmakers ask in the letter.

They then follow with: "If the WNBA has no definition of ‘women,’ why were Freedom and White deemed ineligible to join the 2027 WNBA draft?"

The letter argues that by ruling Freedom and White ineligible, the league has already shown that it recognizes a distinction when deciding who can play.

"As a women’s sports league, the WNBA must ensure the League remains exclusively for biological women," the lawmakers wrote. They also cited Cunningham’s comments and raised concerns about fairness and player safety.

But the eligibility question is only part of the letter.

Stutzman and other Republican lawmakers previously wrote to Engelbert over concerns about player safety and the treatment of Caitlin Clark. Engelbert responded by outlining the league’s review process and its efforts to create a safe environment for players.

Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., attends a House Financial Services Committee hearing on "The Annual Testimony of the Secretary of the Treasury on the State of the International Financial System" on Wednesday, May 7, 2025. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The lawmakers now argue that the league’s actions since then have not matched those assurances.

They point to Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington’s Aug. 8 Flagrant 2 foul on Sophie Cunningham and another incident involving Golden State’s Tiffany Hayes just four days later.

The letter also compares the WNBA’s handling of Carrington to the NBA’s past discipline of Draymond Green, who received suspensions after repeated physical incidents.

Stutzman also raises concerns about how the league handles confrontations between players and fans.

The letter cites Chicago Sky guard Natasha Cloud’s confrontation with Freedom during an Aug. 23 game at Wintrust Arena. It compares the lack of discipline for Cloud with the five-game suspension given to Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton after a separate confrontation with fans.

Former basketball player Enes Kanter Freedom and Natasha Cloud #9 of the Chicago Sky yell at one another during the second half between the Chicago Sky and the Indiana Fever at Wintrust Arena on August 23, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois.  (Michael Reaves/Getty Images)

The lawmakers are asking whether the WNBA has a consistent policy for players, coaches and team officials who get into verbal confrontations with spectators.

Altogether, the letter asks Engelbert to answer four questions by Oct. 16: what the league has done to address repeated physical play, how it handles confrontations with fans, how it defines "women," and why Freedom and White were ruled ineligible for the draft.

"The WNBA has an extraordinary platform and influence," the lawmakers wrote. "We urge the League to use that platform responsibly by ensuring that rules are enforced equally to protect the safety of women playing the game and fans in the stands."

title: China faces oil challenge as prices soar and supply options narrow
excerpt: Oil prices in China have surged to record highs amid mounting disruptions to exports from the Middle East, as Beijing faces an increasingly difficult balancing act between securing its own energy supp...
body_text:
Oil prices in China have surged to record highs amid mounting disruptions to exports from the Middle East, as Beijing faces an increasingly difficult balancing act between securing its own energy supplies and preventing global oil prices from climbing even higher.

Saudi Arabia has been forced to shut a key pipeline that had become an important route for getting oil to China and other Asian markets while disruption in the Strait of Hormuz restricted exports through the Gulf. The pipeline, which carries crude across the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea, was shut following attacks by an Iran-backed group in Iraq.

Its closure leaves two vital routes for Middle Eastern oil to China both disrupted in the midst of the US-Israel war on Iran and conflicts in the wider region. With access to Russian and Iranian crude also complicated by United States sanctions and other restrictions, Chinese refiners are being forced to search further afield for supplies. That scramble for available barrels is adding to pressure on oil prices, both in China and globally.

With China increasingly forced to compete for replacement supplies – risking pushing prices still higher – restoring oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has effectively blocked, has become a pressing economic and diplomatic priority for Beijing ahead of talks between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, say analysts. The meeting follows talks in Beijing on Wednesday between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi.

“What is happening in the Middle East is not good for China,” energy analyst Marc Ayoub told Al Jazeera. “China is in a critical situation,” he said, with refiners increasingly “looking into the market for players outside of Hormuz”.

Before the war, China was importing roughly 12 million barrels of crude a day and producing another 4.4 million barrels domestically, Reuters reported. It was buying more oil than its refineries needed, allowing Beijing to funnel some of the surplus into vast stockpiles that had grown to an estimated 1.4 billion barrels by the end of last year.

That helped cushion the impact on the wider oil market. As the world’s largest crude importer, China’s decision to buy fewer barrels removed demand at precisely the moment global supplies were being squeezed.

Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, told Al Jazeera, “It lies in their interests that this conflict the United States started does not lead to a global recession.”

“But that [China importing less oil] was not done to undermine the Iranians or help the Americans. The Chinese are pursuing their own interest, and their interest is that the rest of the world should not suffer economically, because if that happens it will backfire on China.”

Crude imports averaged just 8.1 million barrels per day in the second quarter – almost 4 million barrels per day, or 32 percent, lower than in the first three months of the year, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).

But those buffers are now being eroded, and Ayoub said the turnaround was being driven in part by Beijing’s decision to ease restrictions on refined-fuel exports, which had helped keep refinery activity low earlier in the war. “Independent refiners have started looking again for imports from elsewhere,” he said.

As refiners process more crude and stockpiles are drawn down, China is being pushed back into the market for more barrels. “First, they want to increase production from the refineries, and second, they want to build back their inventories,” Ayoub said.

“So the Chinese are trying to find whatever supplies they can get from the market.”

Russia is already China’s largest crude supplier, with much of its oil reaching China without passing through the maritime chokepoints disrupting Middle Eastern exports. Reuters reported that Russia supplied approximately 20 percent of China’s crude imports in 2025.

Russian ESPO crude shipped from the country’s Pacific coast can reach Chinese ports in less than a week, while oil also flows overland through pipelines. Chinese refiners have consequently scrambled for available Russian barrels, snapping up September and October ESPO cargoes unusually quickly, experts say.

US sanctions have complicated those purchases, but not stopped them. China’s seaborne imports from Russia reached 1.68 million barrels per day in August, up from 1.4 million in July and the highest since March, according to Kpler data. China also receives about one million barrels per day of Russian crude through pipelines.

Iran had also provided China with a major source of discounted, sanctioned oil before the war. China bought an estimated 1.4 million barrels per day from Iran last year, but those supplies have been sharply curtailed by the conflict and US efforts to block Iranian exports.

China can also look to producers in Latin America and Africa. Brazil was already among China’s five largest crude suppliers last year, and offered China 1.6 million barrels per day in March 2026. Meanwhile, countries including Venezuela, Angola and the Republic of the Congo have historically supplied Chinese refiners.

But there are limits to how easily those barrels can replace lost Middle Eastern supplies. Crude oil is not completely interchangeable, with Chinese refineries configured to process different grades, while substitutes can differ in density. Venezuelan crude, for example, is generally much heavier than the Russian ESPO crude Chinese refiners have been scrambling to secure.

Distance presents another constraint, with Russian ESPO reaching China in less than a week, while barrels brought across the Atlantic from Brazil, West Africa or elsewhere in the Americas face longer journeys and higher freight costs. And alternative producers have only finite amounts available to sell.

Kpler estimates that additional Russian and Iranian supplies can therefore only partially bridge China’s feedstock gap if disruption to Middle Eastern supplies persists.

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, is trying to keep China supplied, with Saudi Aramco selling at least four million barrels to China in August. But this is only the equivalent of about 129,000 barrels per day when averaged across August.

China’s biggest vulnerability is the sheer size of the gap between the crude it produces and the amount its refineries process.

China produced about 4.34 million barrels per day in August, while its refineries processed 13.91 million, according to Chinese data cited by Reuters. That left a gap of roughly 9.6 million barrels per day that had to be filled by imports or inventories.

However, China is better placed to curb oil consumption than many other major economies. The rapid expansion of electric vehicles has weakened demand for petrol, while electrification has reduced oil use in other parts of the economy. Domestic crude production has also continued to edge higher.

But there are limits to this, with aviation, heavy transport and China’s vast petrochemical industry remaining heavily dependent on oil. So as China raises refinery output and seeks to replenish the stockpiles that helped shield it from the initial shock, it will still have to compete with other buyers for constrained supplies, adding further pressure to prices.

“For crude in particular, they are looking to get any supply that is available in the market out there,” Ayoub said. “That will add pressure, and that will increase prices more.”

The growing pressure on China’s oil supplies has also increased the stakes for Beijing diplomatically, with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi meeting his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, in Beijing on Wednesday, calling on Iran and the United States to return to negotiations and urging all parties to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to safeguard international energy supplies.

The talks came a week before an expected meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Washington. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the leaders would continue discussions on Iran and China’s financial ties with Tehran, with Beijing expected to press Washington to return to negotiations and help end the disruption to shipping and stabilise global oil markets.

title: As Charles refutes Earl Spencer’s claim about Diana, how royal statements give a glimpse behind palace doors
excerpt:
From ‘there were three of us in this marriage’ to ‘recollections may vary’, a lot can be conveyed with a carefully worded phrase

As denials go, King Charles’s response to Earl Spencer’s allegations t...
body_text:
From ‘there were three of us in this marriage’ to ‘recollections may vary’, a lot can be conveyed with a carefully worded phrase

As denials go, King Charles’s response to Earl Spencer’s allegations that Charles said after Diana’s death, “We’ll forget her soon enough”, was a masterclass in the diplomatic royal rebuke.

Rarely has Buckingham Palace responded to claims in countless books on royalty. But it was straight out of the block on this one.

Little over an hour after the Daily Mail, which is serialising Spencer’s memoir Swan Song about his sister, the late Diana, Princess of Wales, had published its first extract online, a statement was issued.

Charles, the headline claimed, had told Spencer days after Diana’s death and during a heated row over funeral arrangements: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.”

The king’s swift countering, that “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”, will enter the canon of carefully constructed regal pushbacks.

As rebukes go, it is up there with the late Queen Elizabeth II’s “some recollections may vary” in response to a torrent of allegations from the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in their Oprah Winfrey interview.

Senior courtiers are often drawn from the diplomatic service and thus highly-skilled in couching the passive-aggressive denial. Deploying delicate language to devastating effect is a stock in trade at the Foreign Office.

But it is a weapon to be used sparingly. The royal mantra is, usually, “never complain, never explain”.

However, Charles’s former communications secretary Julian Payne said: “This is a much more personal situation, given its author, and therefore has a greater ability to do harm.”

That is why the palace “felt the need to set the record straight and deny these remarks have been made”, Payne told the BBC’s Today programme. Given the amount of things the palace don’t comment on, “you can imagine the strength of feeling”, he added.

Payne remains close to the king and was due to be sitting alongside him at Thursday’s AI summit just hours later, so the fact he felt able to speak so freely suggests his robust defence of Charles came with official sanction.

What is said behind palace doors usually remains private. The language may be less sensitive. But a carefully chosen phrase in public pulls back the privacy screen.

When Diana, in her highly controversial Panorama interview, said “there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded”, she reaped public revenge on her then husband and Camilla.

In return, Diana found herself on the sharp end of Elizabeth’s ire weeks later. After Diana failed to respond to the queen’s request that the couple divorce, a palace spokesperson issued a statement: “After considering the present situation, the queen wrote to both the prince and princess earlier this week and gave them her view, supported by the Duke of Edinburgh, that an early divorce is desirable.” The matter was now, officially, out of Diana’s hands.

White fury was behind the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s statement in February 2021: “We can all live a life of service. Service is universal.” It was read as a succinct and direct challenge to the late queen’s insistence they could not keep their public service roles after stepping down as working royals.

Meghan was less direct in a 2019 interview with ITV’s Tom Bradby in which he asked her if she was OK juggling life as a royal with a newborn, Prince Archie. “Thank you for asking, because not many people have asked if I’m OK,” she replied. Was it directed at the palace and the institution? A huge number of the claims the Sussexes later made, in TV interviews and in Harry’s memoir Spare, were that the duchess had been unsupported throughout her time as a working royal.

One royal famously deficient in the art of the diplomatic royal rebuke, however, was the late Duke of Edinburgh. Philip was renowned for his gaffes. When a BBC journalist politely asked the queen at a banquet at the Élysée Palace if she was enjoying her stay in Paris in 2006, Philip dispensed with tact to snap: “Damn fool question!”

title: Trump arch could have ‘adverse effects’ on nearby DC monuments, US park service says
excerpt:
National Park Service lays out concerns that planned 250ft arch could interfere with historic sites in US capital

Donald Trump’s desired triumphal arch in downtown Washington DC will likely contribut...
body_text:
National Park Service lays out concerns that planned 250ft arch could interfere with historic sites in US capital

Donald Trump’s desired triumphal arch in downtown Washington DC will likely contribute “to adverse effects to historic properties”, according to the National Park Service’s planning document, but the construction is still planned to go forward.

The president’s 250ft arch could interfere with some of the most well-known views in the nation’s capital, including the symbolic relationship between Arlington House, the Arlington National Cemetery, the Arlington Memorial Bridge and the Lincoln Memorial, which face each other to represent the reunification of the United States after the civil war.

As a result, the arch’s construction could require supplemental planning and programming to preserve history, a document and emails obtained by the Washington Post on Wednesday outlined.

“Such adverse effects cannot be fully avoided while retaining the location-dependent purpose of the undertaking,” the National Park Service wrote in the document.

Despite concerns that the arch could interfere with historic sites and would require substantial construction management control, the Trump administration wants to move forward. The document was circulated among preservationists and other groups to review and sign by noon on Monday, according to an email obtained by the Washington Post.

The Guardian has asked the National Park Service for comment.

Historic preservationists, veterans and lawmakers have consistently raised concerns about the Trump administration building the massive triumphal arch in downtown DC.

Veterans filed a lawsuit in September, seeking to halt construction of the arch, believing it would harm the symbolic relationship of historic sites representing the reconciliation of war or disrupt burials at the Arlington National Cemetery.

Some lawmakers shared fears that the arch could further complicate DC’s airspace. But Trump has been emphatic about the arch, insisting it should be 250ft high to mark the US’s 250th anniversary.

Should construction of the arch move forward, the National Park Service outlined several ways it would mitigate disruptions and potential damage to nearby monuments.

That includes installing vibration plates near the Arlington Memorial Bridge and other sensitive sites to ensure construction remains within prescribed limits, enforcing limits on noise-generating activities, prohibiting unnecessary lighting, limiting work hours and more.

The National Park Service’s document outlined roughly 37 nearby historic sites that could be affected, including the Lincoln Memorial, the National Mall, the Washington Monument, the Pentagon, the US Capitol and more.

But the National Park Service also outlined methods it could implement to preserve the history of the area, such as developing digital programs to explain the commemorative relationship between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, to show before-and-after scenes of the skyline over the Potomac River, and to describe the significance of triumphal arches.

Local preservation officers could refuse to sign the agreement, which could trigger another process that involves the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, a federal agency.

However, the Trump administration does not need the preservationists’ consent to move forward because it already received approval from the US Commission on Fine Arts, a federal advisory council made up of Trump appointees, and preliminary approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.

title: Meta ordered to remove deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguards
excerpt:
Facebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakes

Meta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to take down de...
body_text:
Facebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakes

Meta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to take down deepfake videos of a UK politician and a young Muslim woman from Facebook and do more to tackle AI-generated fake imagery.

A fake video showing a Labour party councillor in Scotland making inflammatory comments about refugees should not have been left up by Facebook, the board said. It also ruled that an AI-generated video of a Muslim campaign volunteer should have been removed after it falsely depicted her offering health advice while carrying out absurd exercises or eating junk food.

The board said Meta’s safeguards are “consistently and fundamentally inadequate” to address the rapid rise of AI deepfakes.

“From politicians to private citizens, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly being used to harass and silence women from engaging in public discourse,” said Pamela San Martin, an oversight board co-chair.

“These cases demonstrate a broader, troubling pattern in which women who engage publicly on issues are disproportionately subjected to harassment and misinformation. Meta and other social media platforms need more robust policies to address the proliferation of deepfakes.”

In the Scotland clip, the councillor is falsely represented as saying: “Refugees are welcome here, even if they rape our women, because white people do that too.”

The oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, said the video of the councillor appeared to be AI-generated, as indicated by the audio not being fully synchronised to the unnamed councillor’s facial movements.

Even when raised directly with the company by the board, Meta decided the video did not violate its content policies and did not merit an AI label.

In a blogpost published on Thursday, the board said the post should have been removed because it violated Meta’s rules on hateful conduct by alleging criminal and predatory sexual behaviour by refugees as an entire group and not as individuals. The video should also have received a “high risk AI” label, said the board, as it called for tougher measures on deepfakes.

“The majority [of the board] finds that Meta needs more robust policies on deepfakes, including expanding the situations when ‘high risk’ labels can be applied, more measures to reduce the spread of deceptive AI content, increasing the penalties for accounts that repeatedly share it, and more transparency on data around when AI labels are applied,” it said.

The board recommended nine policy changes at Meta, including ensuring algorithms demote content labelled “high risk”, making such posts less likely to appear in users’ feeds. It also recommended that Meta makes it more difficult for users to view AI-generated content by, for instance, introducing a warning screen that requires a click-through before viewing the content.

In a separate ruling, the board also ordered Meta to take down from Facebook an AI-generated video mocking a young Muslim woman in Europe taking part in a campaign to improve menstrual health education and reduce stigma around health conditions for women and girls from ethnic minority backgrounds. AI-manipulated videos and images mocking the woman had tens of millions of views online, including on Meta platforms.

The board singled out one of the videos – showing the woman exercising absurdly and eating junk food – as a breach of the company’s bullying and harassment policy. It recommended the post be removed and made three policy recommendations, including changing its definition of “unwanted manipulated imagery” to cover deepfakes of a private individual saying or doing things they did not say or do.

The board was set up by Meta in 2020 to serve as a referee for content on its platforms. Meta has been approached for comment.

title: Political insider turns anti-incumbent table on 8-year Dem in key Senate race: 'Hasn't delivered'
excerpt:
Former Sen. John E. Sununu, the 2026 Republican Senate nominee in New Hampshire, takes aim at Democratic rival Rep. Chris Pappas in a Fox News Digital interview in Concord, N.H. on Sept. 14, 2026.

CO...
body_text:
Former Sen. John E. Sununu, the 2026 Republican Senate nominee in New Hampshire, takes aim at Democratic rival Rep. Chris Pappas in a Fox News Digital interview in Concord, N.H. on Sept. 14, 2026.

CONCORD, N.H. - A Republican running to flip a blue Senate seat in a crucial battleground state is flipping the script on the Democrats' anti-incumbent argument.

Former Sen. John E. Sununu, the GOP Senate nominee who's running to return to Capitol Hill after 18 years away, charges that his Democratic rival, Rep. Chris Pappas, has "been in Washington for 8 years and hasn't delivered for New Hampshire."

Sununu and Pappas are facing off in the midterm election in the battle to succeed retiring longtime Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen in a race that's one of roughly a dozen that will determine if Republicans hold their control of the Senate.

"He has attempted very little in Congress. He's accomplished even less," Sununu said in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview this week, as he blasted Pappas, a four-term congressman.

THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DETERMINE IF REPUBLICANS HOLD THE SENATE

Former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire celebrates his Republican Senate nomination victory, in Manchester, N.H., on Sept. 8, 2026. (Jessica Sonkin/Fox News)

Sununu was interviewed ahead of a move by the Cook Political Report, a top nonpartisan campaign handicapper, to shift the race in New Hampshire from lean Democrat to toss-up. Earlier this month, another leading nonpartisan handicapper, Inside Elections, also changed their rating to a toss-up.

It was a rare move in favor of the Republicans amid a political cycle where the GOP is facing traditional political headwinds for the party in power in D.C.. Republicans are also confronting an extremely rough political climate fueled by persistent inflation, soaring fuel prices due to the ongoing war with Iran, and President Donald Trump's underwater approval ratings.

Part of it is his last name, which is a political brand in New Hampshire. Sununu's father, John E. Sununu, served six years as governor before heading to Washington, D.C., as then-President George H.W. Bush's White House chief of staff. And one of his younger brothers, Chris Sununu, recently served eight years as governor before taking a break from politics.

But also boosting Sununu, his strategy to blast Pappas as a do-nothing member of Congress during another anti-incumbent election cycle, which is a turn of the tables on the Democrats' playbook.

CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE BATTLE FOR THE SENATE

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, a U.S. Senate candidate, is joined by Sen. Elizabeth Warren of neighboring Massachusetts, at a campaign stop in Dover, N.H. on Sept. 5, 2026. (Jessica Sonkin/Fox News)

"He's been on the Transportation Committee for eight years, and New Hampshire is dead last in highway funding in New England. That hurts New Hampshire. His ineffectiveness is doing damage to the state because we're not getting the support we need from Washington," Sununu claimed.

While it doesn't rank dead last in every single metric or category, New Hampshire receives some of the lowest total and per-capita levels of federal funding for roads, highways and bridges of any state in the country, according to federal and state figures.

Pappas, earlier this year, introduced the Highway Fair Share Act, a bill to increase federal funding for infrastructure and transportation projects for New Hampshire by requiring that each state receive at least 0.5% of the total federal-aid highway formula funding.

Pappas and the rest of the all-Democratic congressional delegation in June highlighted $9 million in federal funding for New Hampshire projects.

"Chris Pappas has led efforts to expand healthcare benefits for 3.5 million veterans, bring high-speed internet to towns across New Hampshire, put more money back in the pockets of working parents, and secure millions of dollars to improve and repair roads, bridges, and buildings," Pappas Campaign Manager Rachel Petri told Fox News Digital, as she shared a long list of funding accomplishments by the congressman.

Petri said, "Chris is rated among the most effective and bipartisan lawmakers and his record stands in stark contrast to John Sununu’s record of voting to cut Medicare, leading efforts to privatize Social Security, and backing Donald Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran."

Sununu's anti-incumbent argument is a bit ironic, considering he spent six years in the House and a term in the Senate before losing a rematch with then-former Gov. Shaheen in the 2008 election.

Looking back at his years on Capitol Hill, Sununu touted his record "of writing and passing legislation under Democrat presidents, Republican presidents, a Democrat Congress, Republican Congress."

But he also emphasized, "I've been in the private sector for the last 16 years. That's a good thing, working for tech firms and small businesses, the Waterville Valley ski area [the Sununu family has had a controlling interest in the resort since 2010], teaching college. It's... a perspective that I think is missing from Washington."

WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLLS IN KEY MIDTERM RACES SHOW

Pappas, in a recent Fox News Digital interview, highlighted that New Hampshire is "a state of voters who are pragmatic, who want their lives to be better and want problems to be solved, and I can demonstrate the ways that I've been working on those issues."

"It's expanding access to health care, building more affordable housing in New Hampshire, and ensuring that we're standing up to an administration that's ignoring the day-to-day concerns of Granite Staters," he added.

But Sununu wasn't the only one taking aim at Pappas as a do-nothing incumbent. Even his long-shot socialist rival in last week's primary took a shot.

First-time candidate and scientist Karishma Manzur, in a recent Fox News Digital interview, charged that "all [Pappas] wants to do is just get his little cushy job and go to D.C., go to all these parties and these restaurants and just do whatever the bare minimum is."

Pappas ended up crushing Manzur in the primary by a two-to-one margin, and Sununu defeated former Sen. Scott Brown in a landslide to capture the GOP nomination.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Democratic congressional candidate Karishma Manzur speaks to voters at a campaign stop in Dover, New Hampshire, on Sept. 3, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

With the general election sprint underway, Republican-aligned outside groups are now pouring millions into the state to target Pappas. And Pappas is using this week's Cook Political Report race rating to ring an alarm.

"MAGA super PACs are pouring millions of dollars a week into New Hampshire to try to flip this seat. And this race is officially a Toss Up," he warned on social media.

And Pappas told Fox News Digital recently that Sununu is "backed up by out-of-state special interests and dark money in this campaign. They're outspending us 3 to 1 on TV."

Firing back, this week a Democrat-aligned super PAC started running ads charging that, after he left the Senate, Sununu cashed in by working for lobbying firms.

Sununu was endorsed earlier this year by Trump, and since then Democrats have repeatedly tied the president, whose approval ratings are well into negative territory in New Hampshire, to Sununu.

Pappas called Sununu Trump's "hand-picked candidate."

Asked about the full-court press by Pappas and Democrats to anchor him to Trump, Sununu told Fox News Digital, "I've never even met the president."

But contrasting himself with Pappas, Sununu added that "there's no question I'll be a much more effective voice with this administration."

title: Carney calls for closer ‘strategic autonomy’ and trade as Trump threatens EU over associate member offer – Europe live
excerpt:
In an address to European parliamentarians, the Canadian prime minister speaks about his hopes for what a new relationship with the EU could look like

Carney now speaks in more detail about what he t...
body_text:
In an address to European parliamentarians, the Canadian prime minister speaks about his hopes for what a new relationship with the EU could look like

Carney now speaks in more detail about what he thinks should come from Canada’s new, strong relationship with the EU.

He says Canada and Europe “should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defence, industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy, security, space and payments.”

He wants the two sides to “move towards seamless digital trade and non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services.”

He also says he wants to see deeper people to people ties, “allowing our youth to work, study and live where they want.”

He specifically suggests Canada joining Erasmus+ student exchange scheme and Horizon research scheme.

Canadian prime minister Mark Carney has called for closer ties between Canada and the EU on trade, energy, “pooled” sovereignty, mobility in a warmly received speech at the European parliament in Strasbourg.

Using the comparison of a resilient forest able to withstand crises, he proposed to “deepen those roots, widen this canopy, and grow a transatlantic forest under which our citizens can flourish as free people on free ground every single day” (12:10).

He said he was not “proposing a third bloc” to challenge “great power rivals, only with better manners,” but an alliance of resilient nations “principled enough that our strength reinforces international law rather than seeks to replace it” (12:09).

He said the strengthened partnership was needed amid a “ferocious storm” in the world caused by increasing weaponisation of trade and financial markets, technology, and ever-more assertive Big Tech platforms challenging the existing world order. “A single tree will come down in it; a forest will not,” he said (11:56).

He set out possible areas of cooperation on strategic autonomy, critical resources, digital trade and services, student mobility, academic research cooperation (11:58, 12:00, 12:04, 12:07).

He welcomed the EU’s proposals of “an associate membership” of the bloc for Canada (12:02).

Carney ends with a call to “deepen those roots, widen this canopy, and grow a transatlantic forest under which our citizens can flourish as free people on free ground every single day.”

Carney says he “wants to be precise about what I am not proposing. I’m not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power rival, only with better manners.”

“We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience. So no one, no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

He says “a Canada EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies, an alliance not defined by what we oppose, but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability.”

“An alliance that builds resilience for what it allows us to do; for our citizens and our citizens to do for themselves; an alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices, and alliance open enough that others can join an alliance principled enough that our strength reinforces international law rather than seeks to replace it.”

He says that on critical materials, Canada could help with access as it’s “among the top producers of the ten most essential for the energy transition”.

He also talks about how Canada could help the EU with its energy security, including LNH and hydrogen “at large scale to support Europe’s energy security, including by developing and leveraging new port infrastructure in our High North and on our East coast.”

He also talks about “pooling sovereignty” on compute capacity, AI and transparency, and calls for closer integration for financial services.

Carney now speaks in more detail about what he thinks should come from Canada’s new, strong relationship with the EU.

He says Canada and Europe “should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defence, industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy, security, space and payments.”

He wants the two sides to “move towards seamless digital trade and non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services.”

He also says he wants to see deeper people to people ties, “allowing our youth to work, study and live where they want.”

He specifically suggests Canada joining Erasmus+ student exchange scheme and Horizon research scheme.

Carney says”the ecosystem we’ve built is not yet equal to the ferocity of the changing climate, and nor is it moving fast enough to match the speed of the upheaval.”

He says he welcomes von der Leyen’s suggestion that Canada could become the EU’s first associate member.

He says “polling shows that an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties with Europe.”

Carney says in their relationship, Europe “brings so many things market power, research depth, advanced manufacturing, the ability and the will to set standards that the world frequently adopts a defence industrial base that’s being rebuilt at speed,” as “Canada brings energy at huge scale and in every form that the transition requires.”

“We have one of the world’s largest endowments of critical minerals, deep capabilities in space, AI and quantum. Amongst the strongest banking systems and the most expert pension capital. We have unique Arctic geography and privileged access to both Atlantic and Pacific networks.

Where our strengths differ, they complement where they overlap. They create scale. We should build on each other’s strengths deliberately, systematically and rapidly.”

He hails the success of CETA trade deal – even though 10 EU countries are yet to ratify it.

Carney says countries should be “bold and deliberate” about forming its alliances, and “not be cowed by the perceived scale of the task.”

“Just as dominance is the arrogance of the hegemon, perfection is the enemy of the good. The economics of this are clear: the leverage of the powerful and an exploitative relationship collapses well before complete independence is achieved.

Because diversity confers advantage. The objective is not self-sufficiency, it’s collective resilience.”

Carney says “Canada and the European Union can anchor our ground to hold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive.”

“This is about sovereignty, our ability to live as we wish. It’s about the freedoms we must fight for every day, because sovereignty requires resilience, the ability to withstand shocks.”

“Sovereignty today goes beyond being able to feed, fuel and defend ourselves. It now requires secure access to AI, semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems, clean energy technologies, vaccines, space based communications and we all have important gaps in these strategic capabilities, and we each must rely on individual nations or individual companies to fill them.

And that creates vulnerabilities, particularly when supposedly global companies prove national in the breach.

Closing these gaps is not possible alone, but it’s very achievable.

Collectively, Canada and Europe are each strong. Europe and Canada are stronger together.”

“Canada and Europe are not bound by geography. Even though our Danish friends know that we share a 3000 kilometre border in the Arctic. We are bound by an affinity elective, chosen, renewed and stronger for being so.”

He warns that “our societies are battered by new storms.”

“The disruption caused by climate change, the erosion of democratic norms, the weaponization of trade, the multilateral organisations we used to count on have been weakened …

Today, it is hard to reconcile sovereignty and openness. Economic integration is now being weaponized. Tariffs being used to exert pressure. Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited. Technology is transforming the nature of warfare, the structure of our economies and states ability to govern. Tech platforms aspire to sovereignty. They want to set access rules. They want to dictate the rules for regulation and even circumvent them. They want to control our data, spread disinformation, and steal our children’s childhoods.

This combination is a ferocious storm. A single tree will come down in it. A forest will not.

And that’s because beneath the forest floor, the roots of an oak intertwine with those of its neighbours, exchanging nutrients, adding strength to strength, creating a resilient, self-sustaining ecosystem.”

Carney begins by talking about historical deep ties between Europe and Canada, and recalls a Goethe quote saying “freedom and life must be earned every single day.”

“Not once in 1945, or 1956, or 1989. Every day, including this one,” he says.

He recalls a story of Canadian Lt Leslie Miller, who gathered “a handful of acorns from the shattered European landscape” during the first world war in 1917, carried them home, planted in Ontario and they grew into a majestic forest – with some of them laster repatriated to France and replanted in the same place where they were born.”

He says “seeds, values, ideas, trade, people and progress carried back and forth across the Atlantic for centuries.”

“We are not fairweather allies. We do not pursue zero sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication.

We hold common values for which we have always fought, and in whose defence we must always remain vigilant. We believe that a strong economy is not an end in itself, but a means to a just society. We are committed stewards of our natural heritage.”

As Carney walks to the podium, someone starts chanting “USA, USA.”

After a brief introduction by European parliament president Metsola stressing the links between Europe and Canada, Carney is finally about to start.

Carney is in, talking to various EU lawmakers.

Greens’ co-leader Terry Reintke is even dressed for the occassion, wearing a jersey of the Canadian hockey team.

He should be starting his speech shortly.

Canadian PM Mark Carney is about to speak at the European parliament after European Commission Ursula von der Leyen suggested yesterday the country could become an “associate member” of the EU.

And I will obviously bring you all the key lines here.

European Parliament president Roberta Metsola spoke about the commission’s proposal of an “associate membership” for Canada on Euronews earlier this morning.

She said the new third status – different to a member state or a candidate state – could open the door for closer relations with other countries, such as Australia or New Zealand.

She said it was encouraging to see “huge” interest in Canada given the close links.

Metsola insisted the emerging partnership was not just in response to US president Donald Trump’s ever-more assertive positions on trade, and that “it has always been a real friendship.”

“We are not talking about this as against anyone or any country in particular, but when friends come to us and say, let’s do more, then we will be the first open to open the door,” she said.

The EP president also insisted there was no reason for retaliation from the US.
