title: ‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journey
excerpt:
As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own territory

It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all bro...
body_text:
As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own territory

It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah.

But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own.

From point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record.

The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famous wildebeest and zebra migration across the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012.

Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published their findings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become.

“Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.”

The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings.

Two months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. Related dogs do not form new family packs, and typically have to travel long distances through the landscape to find prospective mates.

Only 6,600 or so adults remain of 39 distinct populations of African wild dogs, and the species is classified as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. Habitat loss, declining numbers of natural prey, bushmeat hunters’ snares and human conflict are among the biggest threats to their survival.

But researchers say the three brothers’ epic journey shows the wild dogs can still survive in a human-dominated landscape despite the enormous challenges they face. Alongside African savannah elephants, whose ancient migration routes are increasingly being blocked by human development, African wild dogs need to be able to make long journeys to find new homes.

“These long-term studies provide key evidence that connectivity between large landscapes is still there,” says Dr Nyambe Nyambe, director of the Kavango-Zambezi transfrontier area secretariat, a key conservation region that spans five countries, including Zambia, where governments are trying to keep space for wildlife to move through the landscape.

“If we conserve and continue to improve these connections – spanning the range of national parks, community areas, nations and regions – a lot of species like wild dogs can make the rest happen,” Nyambe says.

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

title: English Heritage trains new generation of scythers to maintain meadows and craft
excerpt:
Initiative aims to keep alive age-old skill, and at Muchelney Abbey in Somerset improve habitat for rare shrill carder bee

It sounds like something out of a Thomas Hardy novel: a merry band of men an...
body_text:
Initiative aims to keep alive age-old skill, and at Muchelney Abbey in Somerset improve habitat for rare shrill carder bee

It sounds like something out of a Thomas Hardy novel: a merry band of men and women roaming the West Country cutting meadows by hand in exchange for hunks of bread and cheese.

But the conservation charity English Heritage is recruiting a team of volunteer scythers to maintain 21st-century meadowland in the old-fashioned way.

The first scythers have been trained and will use their new skills in the meadows around an abbey in Somerset, where it is hoped that as well as helping to keep the age-old practice alive, they will protect a rare type of bumblebee.

Ginny Slade, who has completed the training, said she found there was something therapeutic about scything.

“You need a level of physical fitness but it’s also about enthusiasm and the passion to learn heritage skills,” she said. “It’s a repetitive movement. You find your rhythm and zone into it. You can really connect with the meadow, the landscape.”

The first volunteers have also found that using the scythe is something of a sensual treat – the sound of the blade cutting, the scent of the meadow.

Slade said: “Scything is a wonderful example of how traditional skills can still have a role in addressing modern challenges. We hope to help create the diverse, flower-rich habitats that pollinators need while also preserving knowledge and skills that have shaped our landscapes.”

Slade, a volunteer and community engagement manager with English Heritage, is one of the first to be trained by professionals at the Exmoor National Park Authority in the art of using and maintaining a scythe. “You want a really good scythe,” said Slade. “If you look after them, they can last generations.”

English Heritage rewards volunteers with bread and cheese (it also thought about providing West Country cider but thought this was not a good idea on health and safety grounds).

The first group of scythers will help care for the meadow at Muchelney Abbey, in Somerset, which was once a wealthy and important monastery with features including a thatched two-storey monks’ lavatory, which is unique in Britain.

They will work on a three-year project with the Bumblebee Conservation Trust to improve habitat for the shrill carder bee, a species that has declined significantly because of the loss of flower-rich grasslands.

As part of the project, English Heritage volunteers have been trained by the bumblebee trust to carry out wildlife surveys.

Rather than simply recording numbers, volunteers will monitor the relationship between bees and the meadow ecosystem, including which flowers are in bloom, which plants they are using, how far bees travel from their nests and how the habitat changes over time.

Hardy wrote about scything in prose and poetry: in Far From the Madding Crowd, Bathsheba Everdene watches haymaking, and the farm hand Mark Clark is described as “humming a tune to the strokes of his scythe”.

In his poem Four in the Morning, Hardy wrote about the “to-and-fro/Wheezed whettings of a scythe apace”.

The meadow at Muchelney is one of 100 that English Heritage pledged to create and enhance to mark the coronation of King Charles in 2023.

Slade said Muchelney was the pilot site but the idea was for the volunteers to travel to other English Heritage sites to use their skills. “We’re really at the beginning of this journey, but we’re very excited about it.”

title: Turkey detains dozens in crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists and journalists
excerpt:
Protesters teargassed as minister claims widespread raids and arrests under obscenity laws were to ‘protect families’

Turkish authorities have used accusations of obscenity to justify a wave of raids...
body_text:
Protesters teargassed as minister claims widespread raids and arrests under obscenity laws were to ‘protect families’

Turkish authorities have used accusations of obscenity to justify a wave of raids and arrests targeting the LGBTQ+ community, which has grown to include journalists as well as more than 150 arrested during protests against the raids.

Starting in the early hours of Sunday, Turkish police carried out simultaneous raids on the offices of LGBTQ+ rights organisations and HIV-advocacy groups in the cities of Istanbul, the capital, Ankara, and the coastal city of İzmir, as well as the cities of Aydın and Mersin.

“This is the widest crackdown on LGBTQ+ people in recent years,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, of Human Rights Watch.

Video released by the Turkish interior ministry showed police rummaging through filing cabinets, grabbing rainbow flags and leading people away in handcuffs, as well as raiding nightclubs and the homes of activists.

Prosecutors in Istanbul said officials seized digital equipment, drugs and a firearm, as well as arresting dozens of people in the raids.

Rights groups tracking the arrests believe that 62 people have been held on remand, but more than 100 were detained. Sinclair-Webb, who accused authorities of attempting to smear and criminalise LGBTQ+ advocacy, said: “We believe this includes others not associated with LGBTQ+ groups [detained] for drug and prostitution offences.”

While homosexuality is not illegal in Turkey, prosecutors in Ankara have accused LGBTQ+ rights groups of violating laws prohibiting “obscenity”, and those governing NGOs, although formal charges remain opaque.

Turkey’s justice minister, Akın Gürlek, said the raids and arrests across the country were part of an operation entitled “My Family is Safe” and claimed the sweep was intended to “protect our children, the institution of the family and the social order”.

As a result, Gürlek said, authorities targeted venues they claimed were associated with prostitution, distribution of obscene material “and activities exposing children to such content”.

A Turkish press freedom group, the Media and Law Studies Association, said this included seven members of the executive board of Kaos GL, one of Turkey’s oldest LGBTQ+ advocacy groups that also operates a news site.

Tuğba Tekerek, a journalist, was arrested at her home in Istanbul and taken to Ankara for questioning by prosecutors, after publishing a piece with Kaos GL on the LGBTQ+ community in the neighbouring country of Georgia.

As the initial raids sparked protests, the wave of arrests grew this week. Turkish authorities teargassed hundreds of protesters in İzmir, and detained at least 150 demonstrators in Istanbul on Tuesday as well as dozens more in Ankara.

The French news agency AFP reported that several of the arrests outside a courthouse in Istanbul took place after demonstrators unfurled a banner that read “Being LGBTQ+ is not a crime” and chanted “Long live the struggle for freedom.”

A draft amendment to Turkey’s penal code that proposed prosecuting all LGBTQ+ people in Turkey for promoting behaviour “contrary to biological sex and general morality” was withdrawn last year.

Instead, the Turkish authorities have increasingly targeted LGBTQ+ individuals and groups using broad “obscenity” charges. Eleven leaders of the Genç LGBTI+ [Youth LGBTI+] organisation went on trial last month, accused of violating constitutional provisions on “family values” and publishing images showing same-sex couples kissing, charges that carry up to three years’ imprisonment.

The justice minister linked the launch of the “My Family is Safe” campaign to a directive launched by the president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, declaring what he called “a decade of the family and population” and aiming to boost birthrates.

“Our family ties are weakening, the average age of marriage is rising, divorce rates are increasing and as a result, our fertility rate is declining. To be honest, the statistics are alarming for all of us,” Gürlek said.

But rights groups have questioned how arresting LGBTQ+ activists and demonstrators protects Turkish families. Sinclair-Webb said: “Obviously, protecting children and the family is important – no one is debating that – but in a country with a large and concerning record of domestic violence, many cases of child abuse and murders of women, the protection of the family cannot be focused on LGBT people.”

title: Prominent athlete tells Alan Jones trial he sent shirtless photo before unwanted kiss he wished ‘never happened’
excerpt:
Former 2GB and 2UE broadcaster has pleaded not guilty to 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app ...
body_text:
Former 2GB and 2UE broadcaster has pleaded not guilty to 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An alleged victim of Alan Jones has told a Sydney court that an unwanted kiss from the former shock jock more than a decade ago is seared in his memory and he wished it never happened.

The ex-sportsman, known as complainant M, agreed during cross-examination by the defence that he sent Jones a shirtless photo of him in Paris some months before the alleged kiss.

M explained the photo was sent in response to a question from Jones about how he was faring while he was overseas.

M replied “this good, haha”, accompanied by the photo which had just been taken of him, and which he thought was a good photo, the court heard on Thursday.

Jones replied: “I love the photo. I love you. I want to kiss you for hours. That is beautiful. We must catch up xxxxxx.”

Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir suggested to M that the subsequent alleged kiss at an awards night in 2015 never happened. She showed him text messages where he was affectionate to the defendant despite testifying he was shocked and embarrassed.

“I know the kiss happened because I can’t get it out of my memory,” M replied on his third day in the witness box at Downing Centre local court.

“I wanted the kiss that happened to have never have happened. In some ways I feel as though I am deflecting [in the text messages].”

Jones has been charged with 20 counts of indecent assault an two charges of sexual touching against six men. He has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges.

Bashir on Thursday suggested that a text from Jones after the event which included the words “I hope you can feel my kisses darling” did not imply any kiss happened because Jones often spoke to him like that.

Jones had said: “Great to see you. Sorry I didn’t catch up after … You looked great. I love you, I hope you can feel my kisses darling xxxx.”

M replied with a message: “Nice to see you too. I had a very long day today and I am pleased to be in bed now. Thanks mate xoxo.”

M pushed back on repeated suggestions by Bashir that he has given conflicting statements to police and in court about the awards night when the alleged kiss took place. The defence barrister asked M dozens of questions about seating arrangements, the guest list, the timing of meals and awards and which direction Jones was facing when the alleged offence occurred.

“What I may not be able to give is who was sitting at my table ... at which direction something may have happened. Those things I may not recall,” the complainant said.

Bashir said in court: “I suggest the kiss allegation could not have happened in any location. You have never said in any police statement that this happened at the [location] have you?”

The trial is in its seventh week. The former athlete is the first complainant to choose to give evidence in a closed court and come face to face with Jones. The media were given permission to cover the case from a separate location.

The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

title: US extends visa ban on Palestinian officials before UN General Assembly
excerpt: The United States Department of State has announced it will extend visa sanctions on officials of the Palestinian Authority (PA) and members of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), preventing ...
body_text:
The United States Department of State has announced it will extend visa sanctions on officials of the Palestinian Authority (PA) and members of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), preventing Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas from travelling to New York ahead of his address to the United Nations General Assembly next week for the second year in a row.

“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the State Department said in a statement.

The State Department accused the PA of violating US law by pursuing international recognition of Palestinian statehood outside direct negotiations, taking its dispute with Israel to international courts and providing payments to people the US and Israel label as convicted attackers and their families.

It added that the PA mission to the UN would keep a waiver under the UN Headquarters Agreement, which allows its regular staff to continue working even as individual officials are barred from entering the US.

Abbas’s speech this year had been expected to press for international recognition of Palestinian statehood and renewed momentum behind a two-state solution, following a wave of recognitions this month by the United Kingdom, France, Canada and other Western governments, as well as to draw attention to the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza and the rapid expansion of illegal Israeli settlements and settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank.

No Israeli officials face equivalent US travel restrictions, despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant issued against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over alleged war crimes in Gaza.

Last year’s ban drew criticism from Palestinian officials and UN human rights experts, who said the visa bans breach the US’s obligation to allow individuals invited by the UN to travel to its New York headquarters, and have argued that singling out Palestinian representatives while shielding Israeli leaders undermines Washington’s stated commitment to a negotiated peace.

title: Yemeni forces target Houthis as US rules out direct role
excerpt:
US may be 'forced to intervene' in the Red Sea

The United States reiterated its support for Yemen’s internationally recognised government on Wednesday as fighting intensified between the Saudi-led co...
body_text:
US may be 'forced to intervene' in the Red Sea

The United States reiterated its support for Yemen’s internationally recognised government on Wednesday as fighting intensified between the Saudi-led coalition and Houthi forces. US officials also held direct talks with Houthi representatives in Oman last weekend, according to sources cited by Reuters.

Yemeni government forces said that the coalition had struck Houthi positions around Mocha and that government forces had launched drone attacks in Marib. The Houthis claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Marib.

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked regional and Western allies for help, according to two officials who spoke to The Associated Press news agency. The Saudis asked France, Pakistan, Egypt and the United Kingdom to deploy air-defence support to help defend against attacks by the Houthis. One official said Saudi Arabia’s main ally and arms supplier, the US, has seen its own stock of interceptors dwindle over the course of the war with Iran.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesman Tim Hawkins told Al Jazeera that the US is “closely monitoring” the situation between Houthis and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen, adding that the US military has a longstanding “military relationship with our Saudi partners, and you see that manifesting today”.

Even as Washington assists the Saudi campaign, American officials held direct talks with Houthi representatives in Oman last weekend, according to three sources who spoke to the Reuters news agency on condition of anonymity. The meeting took place at the US embassy in Muscat with the assistance of the Omani government, two of the sources said.

At the Muscat meeting, the Houthis told US officials they had no intention of attacking US vessels and were committed to the 2025 ceasefire with the US, according to the sources cited by Reuters.

Meanwhile, the top US diplomat for Yemen, Neil Hop, told Yemen’s Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba that the US maintained its “strong support” for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, according to the US embassy in Yemen.

“The United States of America stands in solidarity with the Yemen government and its people against Iran-backed Houthi aggression,” the embassy said, citing Hop in a post on X.

The Yemeni government’s army said the Saudi-led coalition targeted Houthi outposts and equipment around the southwestern port city of Mocha. In a separate social media post, the government’s army also said they conducted drone attacks on Houthi forces in northern Marib governorate.

On Wednesday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said that “Saudi warplanes launched 40 air strikes targeting the provinces of Taiz, Marib and Hodeidah over the past 24 hours”. In response, the Houthis targeted the Khamis Mushait airbase and an oil facility in the Saudi Red Sea port city of Yanbu, the group said in a statement.

The Houthis also claimed to have shot down a Saudi fighter jet using a “locally made surface-to-air missile” over the central province of Marib. Al Jazeera’s Yemen correspondent Yousef Mawry said the downing of Saudi fighter jets “could very well mean a change in the balance of power” as “Saudi Arabia depends heavily on its ability to carry out air strikes against Houthi positions in various provinces”.

title: Three dead after flooding inundates Navajo Nation in New Mexico
excerpt:
Indigenous authorities in the United States have said that three people have been killed in flooding in the southwestern state of New Mexico, where heavy rains left roadways blocked by water.

Navajo ...
body_text:
Indigenous authorities in the United States have said that three people have been killed in flooding in the southwestern state of New Mexico, where heavy rains left roadways blocked by water.

Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren said on Wednesday that police had responded to reports of people being swept away by floodwater at 12:30am (06:30 GMT) near the community of Newcomb in northwestern New Mexico.

Nygren said that two adults and a child were killed in the incident and offered condolences to the community, while advising residents to exercise caution in areas impacted by rainfall.

“There are no words that can ease the pain of losing a loved one so suddenly, and our hearts are especially heavy knowing that three lives were lost,” Nygren said. “To the family, relatives, and loved ones who are grieving today, we offer our deepest condolences. We pray that you are surrounded by strength, comfort, and the love of your family and community in the difficult days ahead.”

The National Weather Service (NWS) in Albuquerque, New Mexico, issued a special briefing on Tuesday warning of the possibility of widespread thunderstorms in the coming days. The service repeated those warnings on Wednesday, noting that moisture levels are expected to be at record levels for mid-September.

“A Flash Flood Watch is in effect for the western third of New Mexico and the South Central Mountains today,” NWS Albuquerque said in a social media post on Wednesday. “However, flash flooding could occur anywhere in central and northern New Mexico today.”

Heavy rainfall is predicted across parts of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah through Thursday. Flash flood warnings were issued for parts of northwestern New Mexico, along with flash flood watches for large areas of central and northern Arizona.

The deaths on Wednesday come several weeks after three hikers were swept away and dozens were rescued after heavy rainfall caused flooding at the Grand Canyon, a popular destination for tourists and outdoor recreation in Arizona.

title: Snapchat 'willing to implement' daily time limits for teens, boss tells BBC
excerpt:
Watch: CEO Evan Spiegel tells the BBC he would consider a time limit on Snapchat

The boss of Snapchat says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta f...
body_text:
Watch: CEO Evan Spiegel tells the BBC he would consider a time limit on Snapchat

The boss of Snapchat says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take action.

Evan Spiegel told the BBC in an interview at the company's California headquarters that he believed setting a maximum amount of time that young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry."

His comments came as the firm revealed a slew of new features for its upcoming Specs glasses, which it said could connect to Apple iPhone and Mac devices.

Meta has been pressuring other social media companies to join it in making platform changes it agreed to as part of a recent multi-billion dollar legal settlement with US states.

Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta was facing allegations from Attorneys General for most US states who said the firm deliberately designed its apps to be addictive to young users.

It agreed to pay $12.7bn and implement a two-hour daily limit for teen users across its platforms by default, in addition to muted notifications during school hours, blocks at night and other measures.

"I think it is an important step forward in the industry in terms of really identifying industry norms, and I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms."

As part of Meta's August settlement, the company said it would implement even more stringent time limits and pay an additional $5.3bn if YouTube and TikTok follow suit. It has denied any wrongdoing as part of the deal, which will be paid over a 10-year period.

Last month, a Meta spokesperson said it was hopeful that Snap would make similar platform changes as well.

Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap have all faced a barrage of litigation alleging their apps have helped spawn a youth mental health crisis. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales.

When asked about the idea of a default time limit, Spiegel said: "I think that's a really good example of something that that we'd be willing to implement."

But Spiegel did not commit to a timeline on when Snap might take action.

"That's something we've talked about internally," he said. "I don't have more to share today."

He noted that Snap offers tools through its Family Center feature, which currently enables parents to track aspects of how their teens are using Snapchat.

"We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," Spiegel added.

YouTube-parent Google said it had no comment when asked if it planned to implement the measures in Meta's settlement. TikTok did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Evan Spiegel wearing the glasses at an event in June

Spiegel was talking to the BBC as Snapchat's parent Snap Inc announced new features for its upcoming Specs glasses.

He said the smart eyewear would use AI to suggest things for people to do based on what the tech learns about their goals, relationships and routines.

"Rather than the way that people use chatbots today where you constantly have to ask for stuff, Specs can understand what's important to you, and then offer recommendations or offer next steps," he said.

Like other smart glasses, Specs will use AI to let people see digital elements overlaid onto the world.

But the tech won't come cheap - retailing at $2,195 in the US and £1,995 in the UK.

"The target audience right now is early adopters of tech and developers as well as enterprise," Spiegel said.

The firm wants people to use the glasses for various tasks, such as streaming video, and says it can offer live translation across 60 languages.

With the device, Snap aims to offer a middle ground between VR headsets like Meta's Quest 3 and lightweight AI smart glasses offered by rivals which look more like conventional glasses.

"We're creating a totally new category here," said Spiegel.

"You have a really powerful computer that brings a lot of the immersive capability you see with VR, but they're also lightweight at just about 130 grams, so they're very wearable and they have these see-through lenses, so you can use them out in the world."

Specs is Snap's most recent foray into the wearable tech, coming a decade after its short-lived Spectacles cost the company tens of millions of dollars.

The device is also arriving as Meta is facing a significant backlash over its own smart glasses, which are estimated to be the most popular of the market.

Some online derisively call them "pervert glasses" over how they have been used to secretly film women, with one person telling the BBC they were filmed leaving the beach, while another said they were told to pay to remove a video of them from the internet.

Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. With seven million pairs having been sold according to Meta.

Snap said it has built into the design of Specs, which do not use facial recognition to identify people.

A white light flashes at the top of the glasses above the users nose when it is recording video and taking a photo.

The company says that will let people nearby see that recording is happening.

Users of Meta glasses have figured out ways to obscure components meant to indicate that a photo or video is being captured, including by tampering with the electronics in the device.

Meta says it has remotely disabled the cameras on thousands of its devices on which tampering or destruction of the indicator light was detected.

Smart glasses are 'an invasion of privacy' - Meta's are selling better than ever

The Meta glasses revolution - is it okay to film people in public?

title: Israel and Morocco agree to open embassies, upgrading diplomatic ties
excerpt:
Israel and Morocco have agreed to upgrade their diplomatic ties, including elevating their respective missions to embassies and appointing ambassadors to both countries.

A meeting between the two cou...
body_text:
Israel and Morocco have agreed to upgrade their diplomatic ties, including elevating their respective missions to embassies and appointing ambassadors to both countries.

A meeting between the two countries’ foreign ministers was hosted by the United States ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, in New York on Wednesday.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita also agreed to advance economic and trade relations, including completing two agreements by the end of this year on investment protection and preventing double taxation.

“[The] establishment of full diplomatic, peaceful and friendly relations between Morocco and Israel is in the common interest of both countries and will advance the cause of peace,” the US mission to the UN said in a joint statement on behalf of all three countries.

The two sides also agreed to expand air travel, including by reinstating direct flights operated by carriers from both nations, and confirmed plans for high-level bilateral visits in the coming months.

The announcement comes just a day after the sixth anniversary of the Abraham Accords, an initiative spearheaded by US President Donald Trump during his first term in office. The United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco, Sudan and Kazakhstan have all joined the accords, which are aimed at normalising ties between Arab and Muslim-majority countries and Israel.

title: Young newlyweds killed after boat collides with water taxi and sinks in Venice lagoon
excerpt:
The State Department renewed its Level 2 travel advisory for The Bahamas, warning Americans about violent crime, unsafe boating conditions and other safety concerns.

A pair of young newlyweds were ki...
body_text:
The State Department renewed its Level 2 travel advisory for The Bahamas, warning Americans about violent crime, unsafe boating conditions and other safety concerns.

A pair of young newlyweds were killed in a tragic accident involving a water taxi in Venice – just three months after they were married.

Gabriella Querino, 26, and Sean Michieli, 25, were killed Saturday morning in a collision involving a five-ton water taxi, Jam Press reported.

The couple was in a boat that had departed from Burano, an island in the Venetian Lagoon, about six miles northeast of central Venice.

BELOVED CRUISE SPOT WILL BE OFF LIMITS THROUGH 2027 AS SAFETY CONCERNS LINGER

They had set out to collect bait for Michieli's work as a clam fisherman.

Shortly afterward, the couple's boat collided with the water taxi — and sank.

Gabriella Querino, 26, and her husband, Sean Michieli, 25, were killed in a collision involving a water taxi in Venice. (Jam Press)

Querino was reported missing in the immediate aftermath of the crash as search efforts were hampered by strong currents and poor visibility.

Her body was eventually recovered from the lagoon.

Michieli was rushed to Venice-Mestre Hospital with severe head and facial injuries and other injuries across his body. He was pronounced brain-dead the next day.

CRUISES THROWN INTO CHAOS AS DROUGHT STRANDS SHIPS, LEAVES PASSENGERS SCRAMBLING

Querino, originally from Ribeirão Preto, Brazil, moved to Italy about two years ago.

She developed a passion for fishing alongside her husband, who was from Cavallino-Treporti, Italy, according to Jam Press.

A five-ton water taxi collided with the couple's boat, which later sank in the Venetian Lagoon, according to reports. A stock image of a Venetian water taxi is seen above. (Alessandro Levati/Getty Images)

She was working to obtain the necessary license to join her husband in the fishing industry, according to the outlet.

The couple was expecting their first child, Italian newspaper Il Resto del Carlino reported.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Querino's mother, Gisele Elorriaga, told Brazilian media her daughter "was building a life for herself over there, and she was happy," Jam Press reported.

The young newlyweds, who were expecting their first child, were killed just three months after getting married when their boat collided with a water taxi. (Jam Press)

The exact cause of the collision remains unknown.

The water taxi driver is under investigation for nautical homicide as authorities work to determine the circumstances surrounding the collision, Italian news outlet Notizie.it reported.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Venice Public Prosecutor's Office for additional information about the investigation.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The tragedy comes amid a series of deadly boating incidents around the world in recent weeks.

Venice's waterways serve as transportation routes through the Italian city, where a water taxi was involved in a deadly collision. (Andrea Merola/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Last week, a passenger ferry carrying 47 people sank while traveling between two islands in Vanuatu, leaving at least one person dead and more than 30 others missing.

Just a few weeks earlier, a ferry carrying 267 passengers and crew capsized off northern Cyprus, killing multiple people.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

title: US military claims Strait of Hormuz remains open amid ongoing blockade
excerpt: Despite an ongoing blockade on Iranian maritime trade and attacks by Iran’s military on commercial ships, the United States military has said US forces have kept the Strait of Hormuz open to commercia...
body_text:
Despite an ongoing blockade on Iranian maritime trade and attacks by Iran’s military on commercial ships, the United States military has said US forces have kept the Strait of Hormuz open to commercial shipping, including the facilitation of hundreds of millions of barrels of oil through the strategic waterway.

On Wednesday, US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for US Central Command (CENTCOM), said traffic through the strait “continues to flow” while rejecting the suggestion that Iran controls the waterway.

The US and Iran have continued to make competing claims about who has greater control of the critical Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

“Since early May, we have assisted commercial vessels moving more than 900 million barrels of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz to the global energy market,” Hawkins told Al Jazeera English’s Tom McRae.

The CENTCOM spokesperson said US forces were carrying out two simultaneous missions: facilitating commercial traffic while enforcing what he described as a highly effective blockade.

“We have redirected more than 100 ships that were trying to violate the blockade,” Hawkins said.

Hawkins added that US forces had completed clearing mines from internationally recognised primary shipping lanes in the strait several weeks ago.

“We remain vigilant. We remain present and watchful to ensure those lanes stay clear,” he said.

“The strait is open. Those lanes are open. And that is why commercial vessels continue to flow through them.”

CENTCOM’s comments come amid continued tensions over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global energy supplies.

Hawkins also defended US military operations in the region after being asked about civilian casualties and damage to civilian infrastructure.

The city of Kuhestak, located in southern Iran’s Sirik County in Hormozgan province, close to the Strait of Hormuz, was the target of multiple attacks by the US military earlier this month, with local sources and authorities saying a wedding ceremony was struck with several people killed and dozens wounded.

Hawkins said the US military “strictly adheres to the laws of armed conflict” and that its targets had been military sites, including facilities belonging to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

“We have never targeted civilians during our operations,” he said.

On damage to US military facilities caused by Iranian attacks, Hawkins said it had not affected the US military’s operational effectiveness, claiming that American forces had significantly degraded Iran’s missile capabilities and “essentially eliminated Iran’s navy”.

title: ‘People don’t have money’: Syrian fuel hikes deepen economic pain
excerpt:
Damascus, Syria – The fuel price hike hit at midnight on Sunday. By Monday morning, frustration had poured into the streets, sparking open defiance across Syria.

A sudden government decree drove dies...
body_text:
Damascus, Syria – The fuel price hike hit at midnight on Sunday. By Monday morning, frustration had poured into the streets, sparking open defiance across Syria.

A sudden government decree drove diesel prices up by 40 percent overnight and petrol by 28 percent. For millions of Syrians, the price increase is a direct threat to their survival.

Demonstrators quickly gathered in public squares from Aleppo and Idlib in the north to Hama in central Syria and Deraa in the south, burning tyres and blocking key roads – including the main highway between Damascus and Aleppo.

The initial wave of demonstrations has since eased in some areas, but the anger has not disappeared. On Wednesday, protesters in northeastern Syria blocked the M4 highway near Tal Tamr, stranding hundreds of oil tankers. Demonstrators said they would not reopen the route unless the price increases were reversed.

Beyond the protests, a black market for diesel is booming. Syrian security units have started intercepting tankers caught heading to unlicensed refineries to fill up on illegal fuel.

The anger stems from the immediate fallout from the government’s decision, which comes on the back of the high international price of oil, largely a result of the consequences of the United States-Israel war on Iran.

The United Nations estimates that nearly 90 percent of Syrians live below the poverty line; any jump in fuel costs instantly drives up the price of transport and basic food.

And Sunday’s hike came on top of repeated increases. Since February, the price of 95-octane petrol has risen by about 86 percent, while diesel has more than doubled. Over the same period, benchmark Brent crude rose by about 44 percent.

It all comes as Syria continues its recovery from a devastating, more than decade-long war, which only ended with the fall of the regime of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. The new government has been attempting to improve the country’s economy, including by successfully working to remove most of the international sanctions that had been placed on the country for years.

But for many Syrians, economic improvements are not coming fast enough.

In Damascus, minibuses – a lifeline for the working class – raised fares immediately from 30 to 45 cents. Drivers say their margins are practically gone. One US dollar is equivalent to about 130 new Syrian pounds.

Adel Ali Meree, a bus driver, worked an eight-hour shift only to see his earnings swallowed by the fuel tank.

“I spent all my money on diesel. I only have four and a half dollars left,” he explained. “At the end of the day, I might earn only $10. I could make this money doing any other kind of work. It’s just not worth it.”

Larger operators face the same grim maths. Bashar Sleiman operates a tour bus that needs 90 litres of diesel daily. With the price hikes, the cost to fill his tank jumped from the equivalent of $84 to $120.

His company hasn’t yet finalised a new pricing structure, but he expects to increase his usual $110-$125 daily rate by at least $15 to cover the increased costs.

“If a tourist comes thinking they will spend $1,500, they will need more,” Sleiman said. “The hotels, food, transportation, and a tour guide will all get more expensive. Traffic has been a bit lighter the last couple of days, but this won’t last. Nobody can afford not to generate an income.”

Cross-border routes are also taking a hit. Ahmed Sweid drives a 25-passenger bus for the Shaheen transport company, running between Idlib and Beirut.

A round trip now requires $280 in diesel alone. So far, the company has kept its ticket price at $40, relying on fully booked buses to absorb the financial blow, but operators remain anxious.

At local markets, the crisis is just as obvious. In the Mezzeh neighbourhood of Damascus, produce seller Ahmed Obeid said his delivery freight charges had tripled overnight, jumping from $4 to $12 a load.

“When fuel prices go up, transport costs go up,” Obeid said. “That extra cost is passed on to the consumer. But people don’t have money.”

Damascus officials blame the high cost of securing fuel internationally. The Ministry of Energy says Syria currently produces about 100,000 barrels of crude oil a day, while the domestic market needs roughly 300,000 to 325,000 barrels of oil and petroleum products, leaving the country heavily reliant on imports. It says about 60 percent of Syria’s diesel supply is currently imported.

Syria’s People’s Assembly was set to question Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir over the price increases on Thursday, but on Wednesday said that the session had been postponed until September 20 as the ministry needed more time to prepare.

The government does insist the price hikes are temporary.

But for Syrians dealing with ruined infrastructure and massive inflation, waiting for global markets to stabilise isn’t an option.

For a population just trying to buy groceries, a “temporary” shock is simply too long to survive.

title: Gavin Newsom blames Trump for housing costs using chart showing massive increase under Biden
excerpt: Heritage Foundation economist Peter St. Onge argued Gov. Newsom is embracing housing reforms long championed by free-market economists, but questions whether California can overcome its regulatory bar...
body_text:
Heritage Foundation economist Peter St. Onge argued Gov. Newsom is embracing housing reforms long championed by free-market economists, but questions whether California can overcome its regulatory barriers.

Gov. Gavin Newsom, D-Calif., faced backlash on Tuesday after taking a swipe at President Donald Trump for high housing costs using a chart showing a massive cost spike during the Biden administration.

On his X account, Newsom, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, shared a post reporting that U.S. homes are "now the most unaffordable in history," along with a graph showing the income needed to qualify for a median-priced home from 2005 to 2026.

"Great work, @realDonaldTrump!" Newsom wrote.

CALIFORNIA DEM, FORMER LA MAYOR VILLARAIGOSA ADMITS TRUMP'S NOT TO BLAME FOR STATE’S HOMELESSNESS, COST CRISES

California Gov. Gavin Newsom has taken several steps to address housing affordability in his state. (Marijan Murat/picture alliance via Getty Images)

However, several X users pointed out that although the chart reached its highest level during Trump's second administration, it shows a substantial increase between 2021 and 2024, when former President Joe Biden was in office.

"Hey @GavinNewsom, who was president during the biggest uptick in home unaffordability?" the Libs of TikTok account asked.

Meteorologist Chris Martz wrote, "Evidently, @GavinNewsom doesn't know how to read graphs. Housing prices skyrocketed under Joe Biden's presidency."

"California is the most unaffordable state in the country to buy a house, and it’s only gotten worse since Gavin Newsom took over. And no one in the media will call him out for saying this," Outkick writer Ian Miller commented.

California Post opinion editor Joel Pollak wrote, "You would be ashamed if they broke it down by state."

"Gavin, I guess you can’t read a graph. The biggest spike was before DJT took office," actor Doug Davidson commented.

Author Jens Heycke joked, "Aspiring presidential candidate Gavin Newsom demonstrates that he is unable to read a simple graph. This level of numeric and economic illiteracy is disqualifying."

THE SURPRISING HIDDEN COST QUIETLY ADDING NEARLY $132K TO NEW HOME PRICES REVEALED

California Gov. Gavin Newsom took a swipe at President Donald Trump over rising housing costs. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images; Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)

Other users compared Newsom's post to a since-deleted X post from the official Democratic Party’s account featuring a graph claiming that "U.S. Grocery Prices Reached Record Highs in 2025" with prices "higher today than they were on July 2024" in categories such as dairy, produce and meat.

At the time, users pointed out that the graph, in fact, showed prices skyrocketing in 2021 when Biden was president and only leveling off at the end of 2024 when Trump was re-elected.

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Newsom's post came as the California governor has been working to tackle housing affordability in his state. In 2025, he signed into law a housing package to exempt certain projects from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and streamline environmental review for qualifying housing and infrastructure development.

In July, he signed into law more housing affordability reforms focused on streamlining affordable-housing financing and project reviews.

TRUMP-BACKED HOUSING OVERHAUL TARGETING WALL STREET INVESTORS CLEARS SENATE

X users compared Gov. Gavin Newsom's post to a deleted post from the Democratic Party about grocery prices. (Bill Pugliano/Getty Images)

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital that Trump is more "laser-focused" on affordability than the "incompetent" Newsom.

"Unlike incompetent Governor Gavin Newscum, President Trump has been laser-focused on making housing more affordable. The President signed an Executive Order prohibiting large Wall Street firms from purchasing single-family homes, directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to purchase $200 billion in mortgage bonds that helped drive rates to four-year lows, and cut unnecessary red tape at a historic pace to boost supply, speed construction, and lower costs," Ingle said.

"The President will not stop fighting until the American Dream of homeownership is within reach for every American, which is why he continues to sign bold new executive orders and calls on Congress to pass further legislation," he added.

Fox News' Ashley J. DiMella contributed to this report.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

title: Lawmakers say they are standing at the gates against 'Trojan horses' promoting malign foreign interests
excerpt: Before being removed by Capitol Police, Benjamin photographs the House Foreign Affairs Committee’s official video feed, capturing herself and a fellow CodePink activist strategically seated behind wit...
body_text:
Before being removed by Capitol Police, Benjamin photographs the House Foreign Affairs Committee’s official video feed, capturing herself and a fellow CodePink activist strategically seated behind witnesses in pro-Iran and pro-Cuba T-shirts.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — In a series of exclusive interviews with Fox News Digital, lawmakers on the House Foreign Affairs Committee sounded the alarm on a sprawling network of "Trojan horse" activists, nonprofits and social media influencers allegedly amplifying the hostile messages of foreign adversaries straight through the open gates of American democracy.

The warning came into sharp focus Tuesday when CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin and two fellow activists walked into House Rayburn 2172 for a hearing on covert foreign influence operations, then strategically positioned themselves behind witnesses in T-shirts supporting the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Communist Party of Cuba.

About 30 minutes into the hearing, South and Central Asia Subcommittee Chairman Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., stopped the hearing and had Capitol Police escort them out.

"They're coming in, trying to look like one thing, but we know that once they're inside the gates that those doors are going to spring open and there's a whole other motivation for what they're trying to do," Huizenga told Fox News Digital.

At the center of the controversy is communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, who married CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans in a tropical wedding in Jamaica in 2017, soon after funneling $285 million to six pro-China, pro-communist, anti-American nonprofits in the U.S., including CodePink, according to a Fox News Digital investigation.

Lawmakers say the answer is transparency: following the money and exposing who finances the alleged "Trojan horse."

In their series of interviews, Huizenga and other committee members explained how the modern "Trojan horse" isn't made of wood but rather a network of activists, nonprofits, social-media influencers and other ostensibly American voices that foreign governments and foreign-linked actors can allegedly fund, amplify or exploit to carry their messages through the open gates of American democracy.

"They're coming in, trying to look like one thing, but we know that once they're inside the gates that those doors are going to spring open and there's a whole other motivation for what they're trying to do," Huizenga told Fox News Digital.

LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION

At the hearing, devoted to "Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America," lawmakers expressed concern about how the Communist Party of China, Russia, the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Communist Party of Cuba spread their propaganda and influence in the U.S.

The phrase "Trojan horse" comes from the ancient Greek story of soldiers concealed inside a wooden horse presented to the city of Troy. Once the horse was brought behind the city's fortified walls, the soldiers emerged and opened the gates, destroying Troy.

Huizenga stressed that Americans can hold sincere beliefs while also having those messages funded or amplified by foreign actors without necessarily knowing it. He argued that the answer to foreign influence is exposing the origins of the messaging through transparency and robust debate.

Inside the hearing room, as Fox News Digital reported, Benjamin and her fellow CodePink activists offered a vivid illustration of the debate over how political messages are created and amplified.

They sat directly behind the witnesses, placing their T-shirts in the sightline of the official committee cameras.

Benjamin then turned toward a television monitor on the side of the hearing room displaying the official video feed. She pulled out her phone, zoomed in on the image of herself and a fellow activist appearing behind the witnesses and took photo after photo of the screen.

HOUSE PANEL PROBES FOREIGN ‘TROJAN HORSES’ AS SINGHAM SCRUTINY WIDENS

Huizenga said he viewed the episode as political theater designed for an audience beyond the committee room.

"This isn't about discourse. This is about disruption," Huizenga told Fox News Digital. "It's all planned out. You see people in the crowd filming with their phones, getting ready. You knew something was going to happen because all of a sudden the phones would come out."

"It's really about theatrics," he added, arguing that confrontations can subsequently be circulated on social media to attract attention, donations and volunteers.

The episode captured the central tension running through the hearing: how does the United States expose genuine covert foreign influence without treating protected American political speech as foreign subversion?

"Transparency, transparency is the watchword," he told Fox News Digital. "We really need to make sure that people know not only the why, but the who is behind all this."

Rep. Michael Baumgartner, R-Wash., told Fox News Digital that America's open political system creates opportunities for foreign governments to try to influence legitimate domestic debates through social media, universities and other institutions.

"The American people need transparency and need to understand what is going on in this public policy discussions and whether it's podcast hosts, certain actors on social media, or things going on our college campuses," Baumgartner said. "We need to know who's behind it and what their motivations are."

Baumgartner pointed to "clear transparency on this issue" as a solution, adding that if evidence showed organizations were acting on behalf of foreign governments without complying with applicable disclosure laws, the matter could potentially be referred to the Justice Department, which oversees the Foreign Agent Registration Act, or FARA. The law requires that people and organizations acting on behalf of foreign interests register with the Justice Department.

Other lawmakers said the modern Trojan horse doesn't necessarily have to walk physically through the doors of Congress, but rather arrive via social media.

Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., described social media, influencers and protests as potential channels through which foreign governments influence American political debate. He said that "it's a real issue, whether it's on social media, influencers, protests, these things are all designed to destabilize our country."

Fine characterized what experts call "cognitive warfare" as "using our information platforms to try to poison people's minds and to create division from within."

Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., focused on another battlefield: artificial intelligence.

"Trojan horses are things like the announcement that we should slow down on AI," Issa told Fox News Digital, arguing that foreign adversaries can benefit when American political pressure slows U.S. technological development.

"We are in a war in which the other side uses all the clandestine tools," Issa said. "They use their, quite frankly, their social media to our detriment."

Huizenga similarly argued that Americans should view the organizations under examination not individually but as a network.

"It's a network. It's not independent organizations or even people," he said. "You will see some of the same people at different organizations, rallies, or protests."

At the center of much of the hearing were findings from a Fox News Digital investigation into Neville Roy Singham, an American-born communist tech tycoon who lives in Shanghai and has pumped $285 million into six nonprofits including CodePink, the People's Forum and other groups examined during the hearing.

Huizenga alleged in his official opening remarks that Singham uses his wealth and relationships in China to support organizations that promote communist ideology and destabilize American society. He explicitly described Singham, CodePink and a growing network of pro-communist, pro-China groups as "Trojan horses."

‘TROJAN HORSES’ IN AMERICA: CONGRESS PROBES INFLUENCE NETWORKS TIED TO CHINA, IRAN AND CUBA

Singham and CodePink have denied taking direction from the Chinese government. Singham has said his activities reflect his own political beliefs, while Benjamin has said CodePink doesn't receive money from the Chinese Communist Party.

As Fox News Digital reported in June, the Justice Department and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York has convened a grand jury investigation into alleged money laundering, bank fraud and wire fraud by Singham and the organizations he has funded.

No criminal charges have been filed against Singham or CodePink in connection with those allegations.

Huizenga argued that the funding relationships deserve scrutiny.

"Oftentimes it's frankly the origins aren't organic, or if there is a part of it being organic, this is getting fed by outside organizations, oftentimes even outside countries," Huizenga alleged.

Being escorted through the committee-room doors didn't end CodePink's political theater.

Outside the hearing room, Benjamin positioned herself beside the House Foreign Affairs Committee placard and began recording another video, pulling out a comb first to straighten her hair.

When Rep. Fine emerged from the hearing, Benjamin followed him down the hallway firing questions as another member of her team recorded the encounter.

After Fine disappeared into an office, Benjamin returned to the committee entrance, straightened her hair with a comb and resumed recording.

HOUSE COMMITTEE PASSES FOREIGN FUNDING TRANSPARENCY ACT TO EXPOSE FOREIGN DONATIONS TO NONPROFITS

About two hours after Capitol Police escorted the activists from the hearing, CodePink posted a carefully edited video of the day's confrontation on social media, where activists in the broader network began sharing it.

The physical protest was over, but the images it produced were just beginning to travel.

That sequence was precisely why lawmakers said Americans should look beyond the spectacle to who finances and amplifies political messaging.

"This is theater for many of these people," Huizenga said. He said he wanted Americans, through "transparency and disclosure," to understand "not just the what they are doing, but their who is financing them."

The lawmakers gathered to investigate modern "Trojan horses" said the lesson of the ancient story wasn't simply to keep the horse outside the gates but also to understand what — and who — might be inside.

"Transparency, transparency is the watchword," Huizenga said.

Lawmakers say 'transparency and disclosure' are the best defense against influence campaigns exploiting America's democracy

Fox News Digital's Reagan Schroeder and Brooke Curto contributed to this report.

Preston Mizell is a writer with Fox News Digital covering breaking news.

title: What to know about US Federal Reserve’s first interest rate hike in 3 years
excerpt:
For the first time in more than three years, the United States Federal Reserve has raised interest rates amid mounting inflationary pressures and consumer frustration.

The unanimous decision on Wedne...
body_text:
For the first time in more than three years, the United States Federal Reserve has raised interest rates amid mounting inflationary pressures and consumer frustration.

The unanimous decision on Wednesday, supported by all 12 members of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), raised rates by a quarter of a percentage point, underscoring the central bank’s commitment to lowering prices.

The Fed’s benchmark rate is now set between 3.75 percent and 4 percent.

“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters.

The US Fed has a dual mandate of maximising employment and stabilising prices, maintaining a 2 percent inflation target.

After soaring for years during the COVID-19 pandemic, inflation had finally started to taper closer to target. But over the last several years it has been on the upswing once again and hit 3.4 percent last month.

That comes on the back of tariffs unleashed by President Donald Trump on most trading partners, as well as by the US war in Iran and increased spending on artificial intelligence.

The Fed said Wednesday’s rate increase “will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal”.

The rate hike has a litany of possible economic and political ramifications.

The increase will hit any US consumer who is paying interest on credit card debt. It will also make it even more expensive for those who hope to borrow for homes, automobiles and other expensive purchases.

When the Fed raises the cost of borrowing it also reduces demand for items, which could impact US businesses and risk the health of the economy.

The rate increase also comes at an inopportune time for Trump and the Republican Party, less than 50 days before the November midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans or Democrats control the US Congress.

US consumers have faced years of increasingly higher prices, most recently at the gas pump with the average price for a gallon of petrol hitting $4.36 ($1.15 per litre), up 14 cents in the past week and up from $3.18 a year ago, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). Voters could opt to vent their frustrations at the ballot box, offering Democrats a chance to seize one – or even both – chambers.

US banks looking to borrow money from the Fed will immediately start paying the higher lending rate.

Consumers with credit cards, which generally have variable interest rates that closely follow the prime rate that banks charge their customers, could see their minimum payments increase within a month, as could home owners with variable interest rate mortgages.

The decision is a blow for Trump, who has frequently clashed with the Fed over lowering borrowing costs. Trump mounted a pressure campaign against the Fed’s previous chairman, Jerome Powell, over his resistance to doing so.

When Powell’s term ended earlier this year, Trump handpicked his successor, Kevin Warsh, who was placed in the job in May.

At the time, Trump said he would choose someone who supported lower interest rates.

On Sunday during a trip to Ireland, Trump said the US “should be paying the lowest interest rate in the world” after previously threatening to cut off a large section of US trade if rates did not decrease.

On Wednesday, Warsh was asked what his message for Trump was about the rate hike.

“I’ve got nothing for you on a discussion with the president,” he replied.

Nearly three hours after the interest rate decision was announced, Trump lashed out.

“Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform. “We are “carrying” almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!”

Fed members indicated on Wednesday that there would likely be another quarter-point increase this year and those rates would remain unchanged through 2027.

title: Climate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study finds
excerpt:
Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August

Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods a...
body_text:
Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August

Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.

Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3,885 cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning.

“Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, which carried out the study.

“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.”

More than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August.

It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph.

The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off.

“Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.”

The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event.

Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution.

Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the “fingerprints of climate change” were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse.

In the region where the collapse happened, climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since pre-industrial times, and about 1.5C of warming in July and August specifically;

July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse;

The freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, with higher and longer thaw temperatures weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost;

The warming temperature had already driven substantial glacier recession, removing stabilising ice from around the site where the collapse occurred and contributing meltwater;

A 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015 further contributed to slope failure, though its specific contribution to the disaster in August could not be confirmed.

Otto, Clarke and the WWA team said their study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause of the catastrophe. Instead, it was best understood as a destabilising factor on the existing geology.

Clarke said: “We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse.”

Nepal has filed a formal request with the UN loss and damage fund for financial support to address the destruction caused by the flood, a process that requires proof of a link to the climate crisis. The country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has also demanded that top emitting nations such as China and India “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for the disaster.

Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of WWA, said only aggressive cuts to global emissions could begin to address the “losses and damages faced by vulnerable frontline communities”.

He added: “In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that’s done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed.”

title: IMF downgrades Australian economic forecast amid fears of interest rate hike
excerpt:
Global financial institution predicts GDP will grow to just 1.6% in 2027 as Treasury faces rising energy costs and inflation

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking n...
body_text:
Global financial institution predicts GDP will grow to just 1.6% in 2027 as Treasury faces rising energy costs and inflation

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The International Monetary Fund has downgraded its forecast for Australia’s economic growth in 2027, warning that the Reserve Bank may have to hike interest rates further to get price pressures back under control.

The IMF also called on federal and state governments to tighten their belts, with a new report saying more disciplined budgets will rein in rising debt burdens and help solve Australia’s long-running inflation problem.

In a “concluding statement” that followed annual consultations with Treasury, RBA and Australian Prudential Regulation Authority officials, the Washington-based institution predicted that the economy would grow by 1.9% this year.

But it shaved 0.1 percentage points off its forecast for real GDP growth to just 1.6% in 2027, flagging the downgrade was due to the higher likelihood of another RBA interest rate hike.

“Inflation remains a central challenge, while weak productivity growth is weighing on the economy’s potential,” the statement said.

“There is a risk that further large increases in global energy prices lead to stronger second-round effects and lift inflation expectations, warranting further tightening” in monetary policy.

The new assessment will come as a blow to Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, who is already under pressure to present a convincing story of improving living standards and prosperity.

Fuel prices in Australia are rising again after the worsening Middle East conflict pushed the global oil benchmark, Brent crude, above US$108 a barrel on Wednesday, marking a 35% surge since the start of August.

As global energy costs climb and threaten to spill over into domestic inflation, financial markets are pricing in an 80% chance of a RBA rate hike on 29 September.

The IMF largely backed – or at least did not overtly criticise – Labor’s budget changes to investor taxes, although it noted widely publicised concerns around unintended consequences.

“Changes to capital gains taxation and negative gearing can reduce housing-related distortions, but continued efforts to minimise compliance costs and impact on investment are needed during implementation,” the report said.

House price falls had done little to address unaffordable housing, the IMF said. It welcomed the steps taken to boost housing supply, even as it urged states and the federal government to do more.

The report noted that the combined federal and state deficit had widened over the past two years as states spent big on infrastructure projects, along with higher social services costs, especially in healthcare and the national disability insurance scheme.

There was also taxpayer money committed to cushioning the impact of the initial global energy price shock, most notably through cuts to the fuel excise.

New South Wales and Queensland spend more than twice as much on debt interest now than before the pandemic, according to Challenger.

And while “Australia’s overall public debt remains relatively low compared to many other advanced economies”, the IMF officials pointed to rising debts and interest costs, especially in state governments.

“The ongoing efforts to restrain general government spending, amidst strong private demand, would also support disinflation efforts by the RBA.”

In the longer term, poor productivity growth was “Australia’s key structural challenge”, the IMF said.

“Reversing the slowdown in recent years will be crucial to improving living standards” and making our public and private debt obligations sustainable over the long run.

The comments come before Monday’s release of the government’s latest intergenerational report, which will paint a long-term and likely challenging picture of Australia’s economy and budget.

title: Skid Row forgeries, illegal votes and a mayoral candidate: Election fraud cases pile up nationwide
excerpt: The Justice Department says former mayoral candidate Bridget Johnson allegedly registered Jamaican noncitizen Michael Wedderburn to vote before he cast ballots in the 2024 federal election and the may...
body_text:
The Justice Department says former mayoral candidate Bridget Johnson allegedly registered Jamaican noncitizen Michael Wedderburn to vote before he cast ballots in the 2024 federal election and the mayoral race she was running in. (Credit: DOJ)

The Trump administration continues to crack down on voter fraud cases, including a noncitizen allegedly voting in a mayoral race he was fraudulently registered for and a noncitizen arrested for lying about her citizenship to vote in federal elections.

These allegations span a slate of federal election-related cases highlighted by the Justice Department in recent days, adding to a series of prosecutions targeting noncitizen voting, fraudulent voter registrations and other alleged election-related crimes.

DOJ's latest announcements span California, Kansas, Louisiana, Texas and Massachusetts, while federal prosecutors have brought a number of other cases across the country in recent weeks amid the Trump administration's broader efforts to bolster election security ahead of the midterms.

The White House pointed to the new cases that continue to pile up as evidence supporting the administration's crackdown.

DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED

FILE - A woman walks to cast her ballot after filling it in a privacy booth while voting in the gubernatorial election in Newark, New Jersey, Nov. 2, 2021.  (REUTERS/Eduardo Munoz)

"Despite extreme Democrats and the media claiming it never happens, the evidence of non-citizens registering and voting in our elections continues to pile up," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. "Any non-citizens found registering and voting in our elections will be arrested and held accountable. Only Americans should be electing American leaders."

The more than a dozen defendants charged in cases announced this week face allegations ranging from illegal voting and false claims of U.S. citizenship, to fraudulent voter registration and alleged identity fraud. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche warned that individuals "gaming the election system, voting illegally, or committing voter fraud" will face prosecution, while federal prosecutors in Texas said their seven cases "send a clear message" that laws barring noncitizens from voting will be enforced.

Among the defendants were Louisiana mayoral candidate Bridget Johnson, who prosecutors allege fraudulently registered Jamaican noncitizen Michael Wedderburn before he went on to vote in the 2024 federal election and the same mayoral race in which Johnson was a candidate. Johnson allegedly submitted electronically a Louisiana voter-registration application in Wedderburn's name on July 14, 2024, falsely stating that he was a U.S. citizen, according to court documents.

ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT LEARNS FATE AFTER USING STOLEN IDENTITY TO VOTE IN US ELECTIONS FOR DECADES

Johnson was charged with fraudulent voter registration and voting by an alien, while Wedderburn was charged with voting by an alien. If convicted, Johnson faces up to five years in prison, while Wedderburn faces up to one year, along with potential financial penalties, according to federal prosecutors.

Louisiana mayoral candidate Bridget Johnson and Jamaican national Michael Wedderburn are taken into federal custody in connection with an alleged voter-registration and illegal-voting scheme. (Department of Justice)

Other cases announced this week included allegations against three people in California accused in an alleged scheme that used stolen identities of registered voters to manufacture signatures on ballot-initiative petitions. California frequently uses ballot initiatives to put major policy questions directly before voters, with citizen-backed measures capable of changing state law or amending the state constitution. Recent initiatives have included Proposition 36, which increased penalties for certain drug and theft crimes, as well as measures dealing with the minimum wage and rent control.

Prosecutors allege James Brass and Courtney Price went to Los Angeles' Skid Row, where they handed people stolen identities belonging to registered California voters and paid them to copy those voters' personal information onto ballot petitions and forge their signatures. Brass and a third defendant, Jateisha Herron, then allegedly falsely certified that they had personally witnessed the registered voters sign the petitions. Brass allegedly received approximately $41,600 from coordinators working with a petition-management company helping collect signatures, according to prosecutors.

EX-NEW JERSEY MAYOR, HER HUSBAND CHARGED FOR USING FAKE BALLOT SIGNATURES AFTER SHE PLEADED GUILTY TO DUI

The case is the second election-related federal prosecution announced this year involving alleged payments to people on Skid Row.
