In May, federal prosecutors charged a longtime ballot-initiative signature collector with allegedly paying individuals, including homeless people living on Skid Row, to register to vote.

Tents are lined up on the sidewalk in front of the non-profit Midnight Mission's headquarters, while traditional Thanksgiving meals are served to nearly 2000 homeless people in the Skid Row neighborhood of downtown Los Angeles on November 25, 2021. (APU GOMES/AFP via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, in Kansas, prosecutors charged 24-year-old Peruvian national and U.S. permanent resident Mariana Alexandra Dewey with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship, fraudulent election conduct and voting as an alien in a federal election, after arresting her earlier this month. In Massachusetts, federal prosecutors announced a case this week against Nigerian national Gladys Adaeze Okafor, who allegedly claimed to be a U.S. citizen while registering to vote before casting ballots in multiple federal elections.

A handful of cases were announced by federal prosecutors in Texas this week as well, including multiple cases where individuals registered to vote illegally when applying for a Texas driver's license. On the same day those defendants were indicted, a Mexican national was also sentenced to 36 months in federal prison for aggravated identity theft, false statements of citizenship, and illegal voting by an alien, according to federal officials.

INSIDE HOUSE REPUBLICANS' PLAN TO END RUN DEM OPPOSITION AND PASS TRUMP-BACKED VOTER ID

The cases add to the growing list of federal election-related cases brought in the past few weeks, on top of other prosecutions earlier this year involving noncitizens accused of illegally registering or voting in U.S. elections. Less than two weeks ago, the Justice Department charged five people in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Wisconsin in cases involving alleged illegal voting or fraudulent registration tied to the 2022 or 2024 elections. DOJ separately charged an Indian national in Minnesota last week with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship in order to vote in the 2024 general election.

Federal officers knock on the door of an alleged illegal alien who is said to have falsified their citizenship status to vote int he 2024 election. (Homeland Security Investigations (HSI))

But, despite the mounting prosecutions, the Trump administration also faced a setback this week in its efforts to boost election security.

The Supreme Court ruled Monday that the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) could not implement the president's stricter ballot-mail requirements for the 2026 elections, leaving a lower court's nationwide injunction in place. The blocked rules would have required states to use specially designed ballot-mail envelopes with unique voter barcodes, submit envelope designs to USPS for review and provide it with information about intended ballot recipients.

The ruling, however, did not block a separate part of Trump's March executive order directing the federal government to create citizenship lists for states to use in checking their voter rolls.

President Donald Trump next to the US Supreme Court in Washington, D.C. (Fox News)

Conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was appointed by Trump, agreed the rules should not take effect for this year's elections, writing that state and local officials did not have sufficient time to reasonably implement them. Nonetheless, Kavanaugh said there was "at least a fair prospect" that the Postal Service ultimately has the statutory authority to impose the requirements. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented.

Trump blasted the decision Tuesday as another "bad decision" from the Supreme Court and praised Alito and Thomas as "legends," while arguing the ruling would make cheating through mail ballots easier.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: First data center bill clears House as both parties scramble for answers on affordability
excerpt: A growing local backlash against data centers threatens the artificial intelligence boom ahead of the midterm elections. Morgan Stanley highlights five key races where candidates are proposing data ce...
body_text:
A growing local backlash against data centers threatens the artificial intelligence boom ahead of the midterm elections. Morgan Stanley highlights five key races where candidates are proposing data center regulations and moratoriums.

The U.S. House of Representatives passed the Ratepayer Protection Act (RPA) on Wednesday evening, a bill that looks to shield local communities from higher energy electricity and grid infrastructure costs associated with data center development.

The bill, which succeeded with broad bipartisan support in a 417 to 3 vote, is likely one of the last pieces of legislation lawmakers will consider until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. It also puts a spotlight on the data center issue, which has garnered attention as a proxy for affordability, energy and regulatory debates.

It marks the first data-center-related bill passed in the 119th Congress.

WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE

Rep. Gabe Evans speaks during a news conference at Fort St. Vrain Generating Station in Platteville, Colo., on March 9, 2026. (Chet Strange/Bloomberg)

In its current form, the bill does not seek to ban data centers, set limitations on their expansion or really even set regulatory guidelines for them. Instead, it amends existing energy law, the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act (PURPA), so states must consider a federal standard: large data centers that consume 100 megawatts or more would pay the full extra cost of the generation, transmission and distribution upgrades built to serve them.

Companies would also be required to make financial assurances in the event a project is cancelled or moved to prevent local communities from being left holding the bill.

Its sponsor, Rep. Gabe Evans, R-Colo., framed it as a needed step towards keeping data center energy costs from spilling over to local communities.

"As America races to lead the world in AI, we must build the energy infrastructure needed to support this innovation, and stay ahead of competitors like Communist China," Evans said in a statement earlier this year.

"But Colorado families, farmers and small businesses should not be forced to cover the costs of new power generation driven by these developments. The Ratepayer Protection Act is a bipartisan, commonsense solution that protects everyday Americans and ensures our nation can continue to win the AI race," Evans added.

The bill’s Democratic co-sponsor, Rep. Kathy Castor, D-Fla., echoed Evans’ thinking.

AMERICA NEEDS AI TO SURVIVE. WORKING FAMILIES ALSO NEED TO SURVIVE IT

Virginia has long been at the center of America’s data center industry, with Northern Virginia now the largest data center market in the world and home to roughly 13% of global operational capacity. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"My neighbors across Florida are grappling with skyrocketing electric bills. Ratepayers should not have to subsidize wealthy corporations’ growing energy demands, especially from AI data centers," Castor said.

In recent months, candidates across both sides of the aisle have carefully framed their thinking around data centers. Democrats, in particular, have linked the issue to affordability.

Such is the case for Roy Cooper, former governor of North Carolina, who is now waging a bid for the seat of retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C.

Cooper, once having celebrated data center expansion as an avenue for job growth in the Tar Heel State, has since qualified his support.

"Roy believes local communities must have the final say on new projects coming to their area, which includes local moratoriums, and data centers must pay for all of the energy they use without passing on any of their costs to consumers," a spokesperson for Cooper’s campaign said in a statement to Fox News Digital earlier this month.

Republicans have also navigated the political noise around data centers with care.

Cooper’s opponent, former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley, also stressed letting local communities decide for themselves about whether data center expansion is right for them.

MAGA BEGINS TO CRACK AS 2026 GOP ROSTER BACKS AWAY FROM TRUMP'S TECH VISION

Michael Whatley, former chair of the Republican National Committee and Republican U.S. Senate candidate for North Carolina, arrives at the Grace Chapel Fire Department polling location during the North Carolina primary election in Granite Falls, N.C., on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. Senate candidates Roy Cooper and Michael Whatley will look for momentum from the primary vote in what looks to be one of the most expensive races of the 2026 midterms. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Michael Whatley's standard is simple: data centers pay their own way, families pay nothing and communities decide. That means Big Tech builds or buys every megawatt it needs and covers every dime of the grid upgrades to deliver it, with zero costs shifted onto residential ratepayers. It means no special subsidies and no sweetheart deals cut over the heads of taxpayers," Whatley’s campaign said.

Having cleared the House, the data center bill passed on Wednesday heads to the Senate for consideration, where its fate is uncertain.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Dermot Mulroney shares 'Young Guns' reunion photo with Emilio Estevez and original cast members
excerpt:
Actor Charlie Sheen joins the 'Planet Tyrus' podcast to reflect on the turning point that led him to get sober after years of drug and alcohol abuse. Check out more at www.youtube.com/@PlanetTyrus

A ...
body_text:
Actor Charlie Sheen joins the 'Planet Tyrus' podcast to reflect on the turning point that led him to get sober after years of drug and alcohol abuse. Check out more at www.youtube.com/@PlanetTyrus

A number of iconic 80s heartthrobs reunited for a group selfie nearly 40 years after their western film "Young Guns" was released.

Earlier this week, actor Dermot Mulroney made a joint Instagram post with Emilio Estèvez, both having starred in the 1988 movie. "38 years later #youngguns rides again - PALS," the caption of the post read.

Also in the selfie was Charlie Sheen, Estèvez's brother, Kiefer Sutherland, Casey Siemaszko, Lou Diamond Phillips and Terry O'Quinn. The cast of the movie reunited at a fan event in Dallas, Texas on Saturday.

Charlie Sheen, Dermot Mulroney, Kiefer Sutherland, Emilio Estevez, Casey Siemaszko and Lou Diamond Phillips starred in the movie "Young Guns." (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

Fans flooded the comment section of the post, praising the men for never aging.

NOAH WYLE, MATT DAMON, LEONARDO DICAPRIO STILL CAPTIVATING AUDIENCES WELL INTO THEIR 50S

"Does Emilio Estevez ever age? He has the secret to the fountain of youth," one user wrote.

"Emilio looking younger than all of them!" another wrote.

Another Instagram user commented, "If that isn't the most epic reunion I don't know what is!!!!😍"

"Young Guns" included Lou Diamond Phillips, Casey Siemaszko and Dermot Mulroney; bottom: Kiefer Sutherland, Emilio Estevez and Charlie Sheen. (Getty Images)

Mulroney also shared other images from the event on Instagram. "When @kiefersutherland says "never had more fun on a movie" #youngguns you know@you had some fun !" the star captioned his post. He also included a nod to the iconic movie with the hashtag, "#didyouseethesizeofthatchicken."

In the images, the men looked like they were having some fun. The final picture in the carousel of images was the cast of "Young Guns" flipping off the camera and smiling.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Young Guns" is a Western about Billy the Kid (Estèvez) and a group of young outlaws who seek revenge after their mentor is murdered. Their pursuit leads to violence, betrayal, and the famous Lincoln County War.

The stars of the film "Young Guns" pose in 1988. (Getty Images)

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Due to the original film's success, a sequel titled "Young Guns II" was released in 1990, directed by Geoff Murphy. This follow-up picks up later in the timeline as an aging Brushy Bill Roberts claims to be an elderly Billy the Kid, recounting the dramatic final days of the surviving Regulators—primarily Billy, Doc Scurlock, and Chávez y Chávez—while they are hunted down by their former friend-turned-lawman, Pat Garrett.

Emilio Estevez and Charlie Sheen. (Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

The sequel expanded its cast with new stars like Christian Slater and Alan Ruck, and it achieved massive pop culture success largely thanks to its iconic, Academy Award-nominated theme song, "Blaze of Glory," written and performed by Jon Bon Jovi.

Janelle Ash is an entertainment writer for Fox News Digital covering Hollywood, celebrity culture and breaking entertainment news through exclusive reporting, interviews and in-depth storytelling.

title: Australian politics live: Labor to reveal new immigration rules; PM hails narrowing of gender gap
excerpt:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Tanya Plibersek says the new child support legislation (which my colleague Tom McIlroy brought you a moment ago) will enforce travel bans o...
body_text:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Tanya Plibersek says the new child support legislation (which my colleague Tom McIlroy brought you a moment ago) will enforce travel bans of child support dodgers – meaning they won’t be able to fly overseas.

Plibersek says there is more than $2bn of unpaid child support in Australia.

She says the system can be used as an “insidious form of domestic violence where you can continue to harass or intimidate your ex”.

double quotation markWe got 200 cases where the debt is more than $150,000, we got one case where the debt is more than $2m.

The next piece of legislation we introduce will actually have transport or travel bans on people who have, outstanding child support debts of more than $10,000, will be automatically stopped from leaving the country and that is a strong incentive for people to pay.

We also investing more in resources from the tax office to go after people who haven’t been lodging tax returns. We know that one of the ways that minimise their child support or avoid paying is by saying I’ve had no income or have had much less income than they’ve actually had.

‘You don’t know that at all’: Plibersek rejects cabinet division over migration

Tanya Plibersek doesn’t want to say much about migration this morning, other than the broad-brush statement that migration is essential to Australia and the government has already brought net migration down significantly from Covid peaks.

The social services minister also doesn’t want to talk about whether there was any internal cabinet division over Tony Burke’s proposed migration changes.

There’s been plenty of reporting out there in recent weeks over division in the cabinet being part of the reason why it’s taken so long for the policy to be announced – it was initially due to be revealed at the National Press Club more than a month ago.

Plibersek tells ABC News Breakfast: don’t believe everything you hear.

double quotation markYou don’t know that at all. That has been reported and you can’t always believe what you read in the newspapers.

I don’t talk about what happened in cabinet but I can say to you that it is a very constructive discussion that focused on the real issues here. Which is making sure that our immigration system is fit for purpose, that it meets the needs of our country, and that – and by the way, that we continue to celebrate the contributions that migrants to this country make today and have made for many, many years.

Asked again whether she’s saying there were no disagreements, Plibersek replies, “I’m not speaking about what happens in Cabinet, I never do.”

Krishani Dhanji here with you for the final sitting day of the fortnight. Thanks to Martin Farrer for getting us started.

And the sitting fortnight is going out with a bang today with the Labor’s long awaited plan finally being unveiled at the press club today.

We have a fair sense of where some of that will land – including a restriction on international students bringing their family with them, and cracking down on “visa-hopping” – and we’ll bring that speech to you live from 12:30pm.

No doubt the Coalition will want the government to go harder and cut more, the Greens will want more compassion and fewer cuts, and everyone’s going to be comparing the plan with One Nation’s.

It’s going to be a big one – let’s get stuck in.

Tanya Plibersek and Katy Gallagher have announced plans to close gaps that have allowed family and domestic violence perpetrators to continue causing harm through the child support system.

The new laws will scrap legal requirements that mean any information provided by one parent be shared with the other parent, stopping situations where sharing that information could put children or a parent at risk.

Families will also be supported to recover more unpaid child support debts when they move into official arrangements, and new rules will be created to remove the harm that can arise from family tax benefit debts caused by child support payers against their former partners.

In a joint statement, the social services minister and the finance minister said:

double quotation markThere is almost $2 billion of unpaid child support in this country.

There are almost 100,000 parents and carers in the child support system who have experienced or are at risk of experiencing family and domestic violence. Australian children deserve better.

This is the first stage of the most significant reforms to child support in decades, helping create a system that is safer, simpler and more effective for Australian families.

Australia has broken into the top 10 of the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report, ranking eighth out of 148 countries – its highest ranking ever.

The 2026 report marks a significant climb for Australia, moving up 35 places from 43rd since the Albanese government took office.

The government credits this historic high to improved political representation (including a majority-female cabinet), expanded paid parental leave, wage increases in female-dominated sectors and new investments in women’s health.

Anthony Albanese said in a statement that the ranking “slipped to an all-time low of 50th under the previous Coalition government” and acknowledged that the work must continue:

double quotation markThe job is not done and we will continue to focus our efforts on lifting wages, ending gender-based violence, increasing female representation in workplaces, investing in women’s health and more.

The minister for women, Katy Gallagher, said the record ranking was “not by accident”, also recognising areas for improvement:

double quotation markWe know there is more work to do across our priorities of ending violence against women, valuing care, improving women’s economic empowerment, improving women’s health outcomes and strengthening women’s leadership and representation – this is just one measure that shows Australia is moving in the right direction.

International student visa changes expected

International students will see some of the biggest changes in the reform of immigration settings.

Last year Australia issued more than 337,000 international student visas, of which about 45,000 went to dependents or family members of the primary applicant. The vast majority of students will now be expected to be required to come alone.

Burke gave a preview in parliament yesterday.

double quotation markWe do need to get net overseas migration down.

We need to make sure that we deal with the numbers overall, and do so in a sensible, a targeted way that provides the easiest pathway through the Australian economy.

Burke’s speech kicks off at 12.30pm today.

Foreign students will face tough restrictions on the ability to bring family members into Australia under big changes to the country’s immigration system.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, will reveal the changes today at the National Press Club, after plans for a speech more than a month ago were derailed.

Burke’s plan is designed to bring down net overseas migration (Nom) while doing the least damage to the economy.

His speech is titled: “The work of managing the migration program: Who arrives, who stays, who leaves”.

The plan will shift some rules for visa categories away from demand-driven settings, introduced during the Howard government, allowing more control on the numbers of people coming into, and departing, the country.

Labor plans to use legislation to gain more control over arrival numbers but could rely on regulation and directives to departmental officials if it cannot find agreement in parliament.

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

Foreign students will face tough restrictions on the ability to bring family members into Australia under big changes to the country’s immigration system to be announced at the National Press Club this lunchtime by Tony Burke. More details coming up.

title: Hiker in Colorado takes trip to the hospital after being kicked in the back by a moose
excerpt:
NASCAR star Denny Hamlin tells OutKick Outdoors how fishing with professional angler Chris Zaldain has helped accelerate his learning curve and improve his skills on the water.

A man from Westerly, R...
body_text:
NASCAR star Denny Hamlin tells OutKick Outdoors how fishing with professional angler Chris Zaldain has helped accelerate his learning curve and improve his skills on the water.

A man from Westerly, Rhode Island was out on a family hike in Colorado a couple of weeks ago when he, his wife and his son came face-to-face with a momma moose and her baby.

Dean and Rosemary Felicetti were in Colorado visiting their son Gabriel when they decided to go on a hike, reports WJAR. They visited a lake and had their feet in the water before heading back.

View across a shallow alpine lake toward the jagged granite peaks of the Gore Range in Eagle County, Colo., north of Vail. Dense stands of spruce and fir climb the lower slopes while aspen and tall grass line the near shoreline on a cloudy summer day. The high country sits along the edge of the Eagles Nest Wilderness, a popular area for hiking and backcountry access in the Colorado Rockies. (Getty Images)

As they were making their way down the trail so they could go out for Rosemary's birthday dinner, the couple's son alerted them to the moose ahead.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

"He's like, 'Just don't turn your back. Don't run,'" Dean said. "And so we just started backing up, and a baby moose comes off the switchback towards us."

That's when the family hike became the scariest moment of their lives. Right behind the baby moose was momma moose, and she wasn't there to play around with the family. She charged at them immediately.

A mother and baby moose eat close together in Colorado. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

BULL BISON SENDS YELLOWSTONE VISITOR FLIPPING THROUGH THE AIR IN CAMPGROUND ATTACK CAUGHT ON VIDEO

Rosemary scrambled up the hillside while Dean and Gabriel tried to fend off the moose. Dean had his trekking pole and Gabriel was throwing rocks and yelling at it.

While Dean tried to poke at the animal with his trekking pole, it reared up and kicked him in the back. The moose then moved on and left the family with minor injuries.

Bull moose in summer, Quebec, Canada. In spring and summer, antler is covered with skin that gives a velvet texture. This requires intense grazing on a highly nutritious diet. (Getty Images)

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Dean took a trip to the emergency room and had survived the ordeal with only cuts, bruises and a hoof print on his shirt. The couple doesn't blame the moose for kicking their butts.

"We 100% are supportive of the moose's decision as the mom to protect," Dean said. Rosemary added, "She was doing her job."

Who could blame the moose? You're stepping out on its turf and waving around trekking poles. A kick in the back is nothing.

title: Macklemore pledges his $1m Ed Sheeran tour salary to Palestine
excerpt:
Rapper, who was dropped from tour after his speech in support of Palestine, challenges Robert Kraft to do the same

Macklemore has announced that he will donate the $1m salary he was paid as an openin...
body_text:
Rapper, who was dropped from tour after his speech in support of Palestine, challenges Robert Kraft to do the same

Macklemore has announced that he will donate the $1m salary he was paid as an opening act for Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour to organizations working with Palestinian people and relief in Gaza, after being dropped from the tour following backlash to his onstage comments in support of Palestine.

The rapper also challenged Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and prominent donor to Israel who refused to let Macklemore play at his Gillette Stadium outside Boston, to match his donation.

“With everything that has happened over the last 48 hours, I want to bring the conversation back to where it belongs: to the Palestinian people who are still being killed, still living under military occupation, and still fighting for their freedom,” the Grammy-winning artist wrote on Instagram Wednesday. “I will be donating the entire $1 million of my net earnings from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour to six organizations working directly to support the Palestinian people. And I invite Robert Kraft to match my donation. Whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protecting. A Palestinian life is no less valuable than any other life on this earth.”

In a two-minute speech during his set at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on 4 September, Macklemore expressed his desire to see a “free Palestine. I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them.” His remarks prompted a petition from the Israeli American Council demanding his removal from the tour.

Speaking again onstage the following day, he reiterated his support for Palestine and addressed Jewish members of the audience: “Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace, love; for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”

According to Sheeran, who posted his own explanation on Tuesday morning outlining his desire to remain publicly neutral on political causes, Kraft, along with several other venue owners, informed the English singer that his tour could not play at their stadiums if Macklemore continued as an opener, prompting his removal. A day later, all four of Sheeran’s opening acts for the remainder of the Loop tour – Finneas, Aaron Rowe, Boega and Lukas Graham – withdrew from the tour in solidarity with Macklemore and Palestine.

In his post, Macklemore said he hoped to “center the parents carrying their children into hospitals without the basic resources to treat them, and the physicians, paramedics, journalists and aid workers who keep going back in. I want to center the organizers and activists who have paid real costs for standing with Palestine. Their risk is of a far different order than mine.

“Palestinians have lived for decades without basic rights and should not have to wait another day to be free,” he added. “That is where my focus will remain. I will continue to stand with the Palestinian people and their fight for liberation. When the news cycle moves on, which it will, don’t move with it. Free Palestine.”

Earlier Wednesday, Colin Kaepernick, whose NFL career was effectively ended by the NFL’s resistance to his protests against US police violence, joined the chorus of prominent figures criticizing Macklemore’s removal at the behest of NFL stadium owners. “The part that I hope people appreciate and take away in this moment is what [New England Patriots owner] Robert Kraft and what they’re saying by denying Macklemore the opportunity to go out and perform with Ed Sheeran is they are willing to collude,” the former quarterback said on the MeidasTouch podcast. “The [NFL owners] are openly colluding.”

Kaepernick added that he thought NFL owners tried to hound out Macklemore in a similar way to him. “When we filed the grievance, it was like, well, the owners wouldn’t do that,” Kaepernick said. “Everybody just wants to win within the NFL. And the realization is, no. They want to protect their interests. They want to protect their power. They want to protect their money.”

In his own statement Monday, Kraft has said his decision to ban Macklemore from the Patriots’ stadium was due to his “recent actions” and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.

title: Media highlights race of Mississippi hanging victim Tasia Fortune but not the race of suspected killer
excerpt:
Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin and Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley discuss the illegal immigrant arrested for the alleged murder of a Virginia mother on 'The Story.'

The murde...
body_text:
Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin and Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley discuss the illegal immigrant arrested for the alleged murder of a Virginia mother on 'The Story.'

The murder of 29-year-old Mississippi woman Tasia Fortune has shocked the nation as many rushed to claim she was the victim of a hate crime — and even following the arrest of her suspected killer, the media continue to obscure the facts that dispel the narrative.

The mother of four was found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned home in Jackson, Mississippi last month, and was described by Democratic Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, N.Y., and Ayanna Pressley, Mass., as one of several "modern-day lynchings" based on a string of incidents involving Black people being found in a similar manner despite the lack of evidence to support their declaration.

On Friday, 51-year-old Jarques Ratliff, who is also Black, was charged with Fortune's murder. He entered a not guilty plea on Monday.

YET ANOTHER DEM RIPPED ONLINE FOR 'INVENTING RACISM' AS LAWMAKERS PEDDLE DEBUNKED ‘LYNCHING’ CLAIMS

Tasia Fortune is seen in a portrait displayed Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, in Marion, Kentucky. Inset: Jarques Ratliff, who was arrested in connection to Fortune's death. (AP Photo/George Walker IV/Jackson Police Department)

Yet the breaking news coverage of Ratliff's arrest put emphasis on Fortune's race but not his own.

"Police in Jackson, Mississippi, have arrested a man in the case of Tasia Fortune, the 29-year-old Black woman found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned house last month, following the state medical examiner ruling her death a homicide," CNN began its report on Friday and similarly posted on X.

Readers would not know Ratliff's race until they saw his mugshot — placed below the sixth paragraph of the story.

In a separate story from Monday about his not guilty plea, CNN again described Fortune as being Black while not giving the same descriptor as her alleged killer — this time burying his mugshot nearly 20 paragraphs deep.

"A man has been arrested in the killing of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman found hanging from a tree in Mississippi last month," NBC News similarly wrote while omitting Ratliff's race.

Notably, neither NBC News' breaking news report of Ratliff's arrest nor its report on his not guilty plea included his mugshot.

ARREST RIPS APART MEDIA NARRATIVE ON DEATH OF BLACK WOMAN FOUND HANGING FROM MISSISSIPPI TREE

Christy Spivey poses with a portrait of her late daughter Tasia Fortune, Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, in Marion, Ky. (AP Photo/George Walker IV)

ABC News' initial report of Ratliff's arrest failed to even identify his name.

"A man has been arrested and will be charged with homicide in connection with the death of a 29-year-old Black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in Mississippi last month, police announced Friday," ABC News wrote.

However, the Disney-owned network acknowledged Ratliff's name and race in its follow-up report published Monday.

The Associated Press also scrubbed Ratliff's race from its initial reporting, writing, "Mississippi police have arrested a man in the death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman found hanging from a tree last month."

The AP would later acknowledge his race in Monday's report.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Police say Fortune’s body was discovered Aug. 3 in the backyard of a vacant property in the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in Jackson. (Google Maps)

Additionally, USA Today initially refrained from identifying Ratliff's race, beginning its report by telling readers, "A man was arrested Friday, Sept. 11, in connection with the hanging death of a Mississippi Black woman, Jackson police announced," later highlighting how the discovery of her body "was followed by calls for an investigation, including from prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump."

Like other outlets, the paper later acknowledged his race on Monday.

A spokesperson for USA Today told Fox News Digital it stands by its initial report, saying it relied on information disclosed by authorities at the time and that its policy is to only publish mugshots "only when the suspect is particularly notable or poses a risk to the community. Ratliff was already apprehended, so neither condition applied."

Representatives for CNN, ABC, NBC and The Associated Press did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

title: Top Trump military adviser says US must prepare to fight around moon
excerpt:
Gen Dan Caine comments at Washington summit come after US revealed it has deployed weapons in space

American troops need to prepare for combat not only in Earth’s orbit but around the moon, Donald Tr...
body_text:
Gen Dan Caine comments at Washington summit come after US revealed it has deployed weapons in space

American troops need to prepare for combat not only in Earth’s orbit but around the moon, Donald Trump’s top military adviser said on Wednesday, looking ahead to a new frontier in warfare after the US revealed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space.

Gen Dan Caine, chairman of the joint chiefs of staff, told service members and industry figures at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference outside Washington that the US military should adapt now so it “is prepared to fight, endure and win ... from the seabed to cislunar space”.

Cislunar space is a term that describes the region between the earth’s surface and the moon.

The Space Force, the newest military service, which was created by Trump in 2019, is preparing to fight in space and around the moon because “humanity is advancing deeper into space – the Space Force’s job is to help be prepared to defend US interests”, Lt Gen Gregory Gagnon, head of the force’s Combat Forces Command, told reporters separately.

The announcement that the US military is ready to fight in the area between high Earth orbit and the moon itself comes days after air force secretary Troy Meink revealed at the same conference that the US has fielded “on-orbit space control weapons”.

The spate of announcements about space weaponry from military officials over recent days flies in the face of long-standing conventions and international understandings that have held outer space as only to be used for peaceful purposes and remain non-militarized.

The Space Force says potential US foes may look to turn space into a battleground

While multiple nations, including the US, have demonstrated the ability to shoot down satellites in Earth orbit, those demonstrations have taken place from the ground against their own satellites.

However, according to Gagnon, “the intelligence community has been clear that potential adversaries have been seeking to extend warfare into space” and that the US military needs to react.

“Our potential adversaries such as the PRC are actively pursuing activities in the system, in parts of space,” Gagnon said, referring to the People’s Republic of China, the country’s official name.

China established its own military space troops in 2024, charging them with boosting capability to manage space crises.

When asked about the US announcement on deploying weapons in space, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Tuesday that “China always upholds the peaceful use of outer space, maintains outer space security and opposes the weaponization, militarization and an arms race in outer space”.

Guo also urged the US to “stop expanding its military preparations in outer space”.

It is not clear whether deploying weapons in space or possible plans to use them around the moon will run afoul of international treaties that prevent the militarization of space.

The Outer Space treaty of 1967, which the US and China have signed, says celestial objects such as the moon are to be used “exclusively for peaceful purposes,” nuclear weapons cannot be placed in space and countries are “liable for damage caused by their space objects”.

There was a renewed push two years ago to further bolster anti-militarization measures in the United Nations following US reports that Russia was developing a space-based weapon.

Gagnon also says the US aims to double the size of the Space Force over the next five years – to roughly 25,000 service members – and that about two-thirds of that growth would be focused on Combat Forces Command.

title: Reporter for The Athletic fumes over Arch Manning, silent on Josh Jacobs' alleged violence against woman
excerpt: The hyper-sensitive outrage machine immediately went into overdrive, but Dan Dakich is calling out the media crusade for what it really is: completely off the rails. In this episode of Don't @ Me, Dan...
body_text:
The hyper-sensitive outrage machine immediately went into overdrive, but Dan Dakich is calling out the media crusade for what it really is: completely off the rails. In this episode of Don't @ Me, Dan breaks down the ridiculous fake outrage surrounding the Texas quarterback and explains why claiming Arch condones violence against women over a dumb internet video is total nonsense.

On Wednesday, The Athletic posted an op-ed fuming over Arch Manning and Steve Sarkisian.

"Did Arch Manning, Steve Sarkisian and cackling reporters act this way? It can’t be real," Candace Buckner wrote in a headline.

Buckner is referring to Manning citing an AI video earlier this week of Sarkisian slapping ESPN reporter Holly Rowe, which he and the reporters in the room found funny. On Saturday, Sarkisian blew up Rowe during a post-game interview.

Manning has since apologized. Rowe said she accepted the apology.

Arch Manning No. 16 of the Texas Longhorns warms up before a game against the Ohio State Buckeyes at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium on Sept. 12, 2026, in Austin, Texas. (Getty Images)

"I can’t tell which is worse: the phony clip depicting violence against a woman, or the real-life behavior displayed by Sarkisian, then Manning and a room of media members? Before they could edit themselves and add a glossy filter to their apologies, they showed the sordid bits of their individual characters for all to see," she wrote.

For the record, Manning finding the AI-generated clip funny says nothing about his character.

Even if you agree that he should have apologized – if, for nothing else, to mitigate the distraction – his comments are not worth the level of outrage Buckner is exhibiting.

It's also notable that Buckner is showing such fury over Manning, Sarkisian, and reporters over their treatment of women, but not Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs.

From what we can tell, Buckner has not penned a single article about Jacobs, who is facing a felony charge for allegedly strangling his ex-girlfriend.

Josh Jacobs No. 8 of the Green Bay Packers runs off the field during halftime of a preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals at Lambeau Field on Aug. 28, 2026, in Green Bay, Wis. (Getty Images)

Why would a sports reporter for The Athletic show more disgust over a player joking about a meme hitting a woman than a player who was arrested and put on the NFL Commissioner's Exemption list for allegedly hitting women?

We had hoped to find that answer. OutKick contacted The Athletic for comment and to see if we could speak to Candace Buckner for this article. The outlet did not respond.

We will update this story if we hear from either The Athletic or Buckner.

The Athletic's coverage disparity follows a familiar trend in sports media, in which reporters and commentators treat word crimes more seriously than violent crimes.

JAXSON DART FACES MORE BACKLASH FOR INTRODUCING TRUMP THAN NFL PLAYERS FACE FOR VIOLENT CRIMES

Texas Longhorns quarterback Arch Manning answers questions from the media during SEC Media Days at Omni Atlanta Hotel. (Jordan Godfree-Imagn Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

For example, the usual suspects demanded similar accountability as Manning when Jaxon Dart introduced President Trump on stage and when Harrison Butker encouraged women to consider staying at home and raising kids.

Likewise, they were as silent as they were with Jacobs when various players were arrested and charged with serious violent crimes, often against women.

In fact, there was more outrage over Butker's remarks than when his teammate, Rashee Rice, crashed into a car with a young woman and her child, driving 119 mph and fleeing the scene.

These reporters come across as so phony and contrived. How else can you describe a group that is more upset about a joke than abuse?

title: LA homelessness non-profit workers arrested over alleged corruption and bribes
excerpt:
Pair accused of misappropriating millions in taxpayer dollars as Trump officials target alleged fraud in blue states

Federal law enforcement officers have arrested two employees of California-based h...
body_text:
Pair accused of misappropriating millions in taxpayer dollars as Trump officials target alleged fraud in blue states

Federal law enforcement officers have arrested two employees of California-based homelessness non-profits on corruption charges, alleging that they misappropriated millions in taxpayer dollars.

The US justice department has arrested Michael Young, a founder of the Culver City-based nonprofit Home At Last, and Lakiya Malone, an employee of the Los Angeles-based Special Service for Groups. The two are expected to appear in court on Wednesday.

Young is charged with wire fraud in a scheme to embezzle more than $7.5m from contracts with Los Angeles county and other publicly funded agencies, which he used to open a high-end restaurant, nightclub and bingo hall.

Malone is charged with taking more than $180,000 in bribes and kickbacks from the director of another homelessness non-profit, Alexander Soofer, who has agreed to plead guilty in a separate case.

The justice department is also seeking to arrest Donye Mitchell, the CEO of the Los Angeles-based nonprofit The Big Blue Umbrella. Mitchell is charged with wire fraud in a case that alleges he fraudulently obtained $1.2m in public grant funding, which he allegedly used for personal expenses, including his own bail bonds, credit card debt and PlayStation charges

“My message to every fraudster who steals from the vulnerable is clear: we will track you down, bring charges where the evidence leads, and work relentlessly to reclaim every taxpayer dollar you stole,” said assistant attorney general Colin M McDonald of the National Fraud Enforcement Division.

The investigation was led by the homeless fraud and corruption taskforce, which US attorney Bill Essayli formed last year to “investigate fraud, waste, abuse, and corruption involving funds allocated toward the eradication of homelessness within the seven-county jurisdiction of the central district of California”.

The arrests come amid growing Trump administration-backed efforts to root out “fraud” in blue states, such as California.

In April, Donald Trump named JD Vance his “fraud czar”, with a focus on investigating “those blue states where crooked Democrat politicians … have had a ‘free for all’ in the unprecedented theft of taxpayer money”. Months prior, he froze federal childcare funding to Minnesota over accusations of such fraud, and halted more than a quarter-billion dollars in Medicaid funds to the state as part of efforts to ensure it was a “good steward of the American people’s tax money”.

This summer, the Trump administration suspended federal funding to Los Angeles’s homelessness agency, Lahsa, pending an investigation citing allegations of fraud. At the time, about 8% of Lahsa’s budget came from federal funding.

And earlier this week, 12 people in southern California were charged with fraudulently collecting $10m in government childcare payments, despite allegedly caring for few or no children.

“If you fail the taxpayer, if you fail our cities, if you fail our shared mission of ending homelessness, there will be consequences and we will cut you off,” housing and urban development secretary Scott Turner said at a press conference.

title: Popular drugs for bone health linked to significantly lower Alzheimer's risk
excerpt:
Dr. Janet Yoon, a pediatric oncologist and sarcoma specialist at City of Hope in Los Angeles, shares her thoughts on a cluster of rare cancer diagnoses in Ladera Ranch, California.

Commonly used oste...
body_text:
Dr. Janet Yoon, a pediatric oncologist and sarcoma specialist at City of Hope in Los Angeles, shares her thoughts on a cluster of rare cancer diagnoses in Ladera Ranch, California.

Commonly used osteoporosis drugs were linked to a lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other types of dementia in a large study of older adults.

Among a group of 121,492 adults age 60 or older, the use of nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (NBP) was associated with a 16% lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias compared to those who did not take osteoporosis medications.

The risk was 24% less compared to people taking other types of osteoporosis medications.

COMMON CHOLESTEROL DRUG LINKED TO LOWER DEMENTIA RISK WHEN STARTED EARLY

A nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate is a type of medication used to slow bone loss and reduce fracture risk, mainly in people with osteoporosis. Some common types include alendronate, ibandronate, risedronate and zoledronate.

Commonly used osteoporosis drugs were linked to a lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other types of dementia in a large study of older adults. (iStock)

Osteoporosis occurs when the bones become weaker and more likely to break due to a loss of bone mass, according to the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS). The condition is especially common among older adults.

All adults in the Hong Kong study had recently been diagnosed with osteoporosis or suffered a serious fracture in the spine, humerus, wrist or hip. None had previously taken medication for osteoporosis.

3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS

"Emerging evidence points to a bone-brain axis, suggesting a close link between bone and brain health," study author Ching-Lung Cheung, associate professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at the University of Hong Kong’s Li Ka Shing Faculty of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.

"Our previous studies and those of others have found that people with low bone mass or osteoporosis are more likely to develop dementia later in life. This highlights the importance of maintaining good bone health, which may also help reduce the risk of dementia."

Osteoporosis occurs when the bones become weaker and more likely to break due to a loss of bone mass. (iStock)

The study, which was published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia, was observational in design.

"Our findings therefore do not prove that bisphosphonate use reduces dementia risk; this needs confirmation in a clinical trial," Cheung said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Generalizability is another consideration, as our study involved only a Chinese population, and it remains uncertain whether the findings apply to other populations."

Another limitation is that baseline cognitive testing was unavailable, which means patients who already developed cognitive impairment may have been less likely to receive osteoporosis treatment.

The researchers also lacked information about the severity of participants’ osteoporosis and bone fractures, as well as their use of over-the-counter calcium and vitamin D.

Other external factors, such as education level, social isolation, air pollution and vision loss, could also have affected dementia risk. (iStock)

Other external factors, such as education level, social isolation, air pollution and vision loss, could also have affected dementia risk, they acknowledged.

Although the study findings suggest that older patients receiving NBPs for osteoporosis or fragility fractures had lower rates of Alzheimer’s and related dementias, they do not yet justify prescribing bisphosphonates specifically to prevent or treat the disease.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The authors called for more research that will include wider populations, with a focus on whether gender may play a role in the reduced risk.

"The next step is to confirm our observational findings in a clinical trial," Cheung said. "If the benefit is demonstrated, it could have important implications for dementia management."

"We hope these findings encourage patients and healthcare professionals to weigh the overall benefits and risks and use appropriate treatment when indicated."

Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: US interest rates raised for first time in three years
excerpt:
Watch: Federal Reserve chair says rate increase decision was "responsible"

US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to sl...
body_text:
Watch: Federal Reserve chair says rate increase decision was "responsible"

US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices.

Rates were hiked to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% by the Federal Reserve in a unanimous decision despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".

However, Trump said rates "should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World - BY FAR".

Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for people wanting to secure loans, mortgages, and credit cards, but can lead to better returns on savings.

Warsh said during a press conference on Wednesday following the decision that, while there was "an attitude of optimism" within the Fed leadership, inflation remained a problem.

Central banks tend to increase rates when inflation is high to discourage spending and encourage saving in the hope this will reduce the pace of price rises.

But it's a balancing act, as higher rates can also encourage businesses to hold off on investing and hurt economic growth.

Like many central banks, the Fed has a target of keeping inflation at 2% or below. Warsh. Warsh noted that US inflation has been above that target "for more than five years".

Ahead of the midterm elections in November, affordability is one of the top concerns of American voters, who have seen diesel prices hit an all-time high and petrol rise above $4 (£3) a gallon on average.

Global oil prices have surged since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, driving up the price of car fuel as well as the cost of goods and services generally.

Warsh said the decision to raise interest rates that the Fed "cannot affect any individual price whether it be oil prices, whether it be food stuffs at the grocery store", but could ensure price rises do not broaden across the economy.

He added that the strong jobs market and wider economy meant the Fed was focused on stabilising prices, adding that those least well off had most to gain from lower inflation.

Asked about the message the decision sent to Trump, Warsh chuckled before saying "I have got nothing for you on a discussion with the president".

The Federal Reserve is independent of the government, but has faced sharp criticism from Trump over its decisions on rates in recent years.

Trump was heavily critical of Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell for not cutting rates.

The US president appointed Warsh to take over as Fed chair after Powell stepped down at the end of his term earlier this year.

Following Wednesday's announcement, Trump said on social media: "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"

Earlier, White House Press Secretary Kush Desai told Fox News the president and White House had reiterated their "commitment to the independence of the Federal Reserve on numerous occasions" but said that did not prevent Trump being able to voice his opinions.

Warsh said at Wednesday's press conference that "part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane".

The Fed's hike is the first rate move in any direction since they were cut in December 2025. The last time they were raised was in July 2023.

The increase will likely add to increasing mortgage rates for homebuyers, as the rates set by banks and other lenders are heavily influenced by the Fed's policy rate.

Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp, and BNY all raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday to 7% from 6.75%, which will affect rates charged on credit cards and personal loans.

Mortgage costs have climbed over the past year but remain below peaks seen in 2023. A 30-year fixed deal is 6.76% on average, while a 15-year deal is 6.09%, according to figures from Freddie Mac.

Due to many US homeowners having 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, changes to interest rates will not impact many Americans monthly repayments, though they could affect those looking to secure a loan for a home or refinance.

Warsh declined to provide his own view on where he saw interest rates going, but the majority of his fellow policymakers said they believe rates would be hiked again before the end of this year to between 4-4.25%.

A small majority said rates could rise further to the 4.25-4.5% next year, before cuts begin in 2028 and 2029.

The forecast suggested price rises will ease in the coming years, with inflation, the measure used to assess the cost of living, predicted to fall steadily to the Fed's 2% target by 2029.

The US Fed is not alone in facing rising inflation since the Iran war, with the European Central Bank raising rates last week and the Bank of England set to make its own decision on Thursday.

title: Would-be Trump assassin Thomas Crooks had Snapchat, which may hold evidence 'treasure trove': former FBI agent
excerpt: Retired FBI agent Jason Pack tells Fox News Digital that a Snapchat account tied to would-be Trump assassin Thomas Crooks could still hold recoverable evidence, even though the app is known for disapp...
body_text:
Retired FBI agent Jason Pack tells Fox News Digital that a Snapchat account tied to would-be Trump assassin Thomas Crooks could still hold recoverable evidence, even though the app is known for disappearing messages.

Newly released FBI files turned over to the Senate reveal a Snapchat account tied to Thomas Crooks, the man who attempted to assassinate President Donald Trump.

The federal documents turned over to the Senate, first reported by the New York Post, revealed that FBI agents located a Snapchat account belonging to Crooks, with the username "tom_crooks19." Crooks killed one person and seriously injured two others during his attempt to assassinate Trump on July 13, 2024.

According to the FBI documents, an Amazon account was also located. Crooks also had an account with Mailfence, an encrypted email service, which the documents say he logged into multiple times between April 15, 2024 and July 8, 2024. He also used a Gmail account.

TWO YEARS AFTER BUTLER, THREATS AGAINST TRUMP KEEP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT IN SHARP FOCUS

Thomas Matthew Crooks was a 20-year-old from Bethel Park, Pennsylvania, who attempted to assassinate former President Donald Trump during a 2024 campaign rally before being shot and killed by Secret Service agents. (Associated Press | Fox News Digital)

Retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent Jason Pack told Fox News Digital that the Snapchat account may hold a "treasure trove" of evidence.

"When you snap and that picture goes away that everything is gone and that's not true. When I've served search warrants, there's been a treasure trove of information that has come back," Pack said. "It's not like some people think when you've snapped and then it goes away, it's totally gone. That's not entirely the case."

Pack said there are certain elements of Crooks' Snapchat account that may not have been recoverable, but said there's a "good amount of information in there."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Republican presidential candidate former President Donald Trump is rushed offstage by U.S. Secret Service agents after being grazed by a bullet during a rally on July 13, 2024 in Butler, Pennsylvania. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

TRUMP'S DECADE OF ASSASSINATION THREATS RUNS FROM BUTLER SHOOTING TO LATEST GOLF CLUB BREACH

However, Pack said that Crooks was likely very careful when using an app like Snapchat, since it's not fully encrypted.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"What you do see is a pattern of trying to hide things and using aliases and so if he's taking that much care to publicly not be seen picking up deliveries and those types of things you have to assume he's probably taken just as much diligence with his social media and with his digital footprint," he said.

Then-Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump pumps his fist as he is rushed offstage by U.S. Secret Service agents after being grazed by a bullet during a rally on July 13, 2024 in Butler, Pennsylvania. (Anna MoneymakerGetty Images)

FBI Director Kash Patel testified on Tuesday at a Senate Oversight Committee hearing that there's no evidence that Crooks was connected with anyone else.

"We found no evidence that that individual was literally even speaking to any other human being other than his parents, who he resided with," Patel testified.

Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

title: US removes Venezuela from list of drug transit, production countries
excerpt:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has decided to drop Venezuela from its list of major drug transit or production countries, and is considering removing Colombia and Bolivia.

“In ...
body_text:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has decided to drop Venezuela from its list of major drug transit or production countries, and is considering removing Colombia and Bolivia.

“In Venezuela, thanks to my Administration’s arrest and removal of former illegitimate dictator and drug trafficker Nicolas Maduro, we are already seeing the results of growing cooperation with the country’s interim government against cartels,” Trump said in a statement submitted to the US Congress on Tuesday and released Wednesday.

The US abducted Maduro, a leftist and long-time critic of Washington, in January and is trying him in a New York City federal court on drug trafficking charges. Washington has since been working with interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez, securing agreements for US oil companies to access resources in the oil-rich country.

Under US law, the president must inform lawmakers annually about other countries’ efforts at combating narcotics production and trafficking. The US is restricted from giving some types of financial assistance to countries on the list.

Afghanistan, Bolivia, Burma, and Colombia were designated as having “failed demonstrably” by Trump in the recent report, which also criticised Mexico, Canada, Brazil and Nicaragua.

Trump praised Bolivia and Colombia for electing new conservative leaders that broke with previous leftist governments, saying he expects them to ramp up efforts at coca eradication and combating “narcoterrorist” groups but would keep their designations in place for the time being.

“Dramatic political changes in South America over the past year have created historic openings for United States cooperation with governments in the region,” Trump’s statement said, alluding to the wave of right-wing leaders that have replaced leftists who were critical of Washington in the region.

Bolivia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Honduras, Panama, Peru, Venezuela and Colombia are now among those countries led by leaders who have aligned themselves with Trump.

Many have also joined the Shield of the Americas programme, a regional US-led military and security alliance, which members say is aimed at combating narcotics trafficking and other criminal activity in the region.

On Tuesday, the Trump administration announced it was redirecting $52m in foreign military funding towards Latin America, away from partners in Europe and the Middle East.
