And then all eyes are going to be on, do they run out of the tunnel Saturday afternoon in Columbia, South Carolina, or in Baton Rouge, Louisiana? And if that's the case, Dan, the SEC is going to have a decision to make."

OXFORD, Miss. — The upcoming showdown between LSU and Ole Miss already carried plenty of tension. On Tuesday afternoon, however, the rivalry received another jolt outside LSU’s football facility.

In a lawsuit filed this past July, the Ole Miss athletic department is currently suing former players, and current LSU Tigers, Devin Harper and Princewill Umanmielen, on charges of breach of contract tied to their exit from Oxford following the departure of head coach Lane Kiffin.

Both players ended up transferring to LSU this past offseason, which came after participating in the College Football Playoff with Ole Miss.

ELLA LANGLEY, DISTRACTIONS AND LANE KIFFIN: PETE GOLDING CALLS OLE MISS-LSU ‘HIGH SCHOOL HOMECOMING’

Princewill Umanmielen and head coach Lane Kiffin talk during halftime against the Clemson Tigers at Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge, La., on Sept. 5, 2026. (University Images via Getty Images)

The school alleges in their lawsuit against the two players that they were both obligated to pay contract buyouts, which totaled $950,000 between the pair. Ole Miss also alleges in its lawsuit that each player signed a new deal with the school in January, but bolted for the transfer portal once the season ended.

Over the previous months leading up to the lawsuit being filed, Ole Miss officials say that they tried to reach a settlement with both athletes, with both athletes having a buyout clause in their contracts that are sometimes taken care of by the new school where players enroll.

SEC FILES BOMBSHELL LAWSUIT AGAINST LSU, LANE KIFFIN WHILE PRO PLAYERS FIGHT FOR COLLEGE ELIGIBILITY IN COURT

The dispute escalated Tuesday when Umanmielen was served legal papers related to the lawsuit in the parking lot of LSU’s football facility.

LSU officials reportedly declined to engage with Ole Miss’ attorneys, directing them to the athletes, who were responsible for their own contracts.

This led to disagreements as to whether the buyouts would be paid, and who would actually take care of the monetary penalties that came with them allegedly breaking their contracts.

INSIDE A LOUISIANA COURTROOM: SEC-LSU LEGAL CIRCUS PLAYED OUT LIKE A JOHN GRISHAM NOVEL IN STUNNING SHOWDOWN

Princewill Umanmielen No. 1 of the LSU Tigers celebrates during spring practice at the LSU Football Operations Center on April 9, 2026, in Baton Rouge, La. (University Images via Getty Images)

In response to the athlete being served with legal papers, Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry had plenty to say on social media regarding the move made by Ole Miss lawyers.

"The process server found Princewill in the LSU Football Ops parking lot," Landry noted. "Keith Carter (Ole Miss AD) could have saved Ole Miss some money and waited until Saturday. He’ll be easy to find in the Ole Miss backfield often!"

OLE MISS HAD FBI AGENT SWEEP FOOTBALL FACILITY FOR BUGS AFTER LANE KIFFIN LEFT FOR LSU

Head coach Lane Kiffin of the LSU Tigers in action against the Clemson Tigers at Tiger Stadium on September 5, 2026 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. (Photo by Gus Stark/LSU/University Images via Getty Images) (Gus Stark/LSU/University Images via Getty Images)

Any hope that the off-field drama would cool down before Saturday’s matchup has quickly disappeared.

Umanmielen has now been served, while Harper is still awaiting legal papers. The development adds another storyline to an already highly anticipated game.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

In July, when Ole Miss first filed its lawsuit against the players, the school pointed toward the agreements signed and their plans to see the athletes hold up their part of the deal.

"The University of Mississippi values its student-athletes and is committed to honoring all obligations made to them. In return, the university expects that same commitment from its student-athletes and their representatives in upholding their contracts," Ole Miss said in a statement after filing suit.

"Before transferring to another institution, student-athletes Devin Harper and Princewill Umanmielen signed revenue sharing agreements that included a provision requiring them to compensate the university with a predetermined amount if they departed before fulfilling their commitment. The University of Mississippi has a responsibility to enforce its contractual terms, and this position is consistent with the actions of other institutions in the current landscape of college athletics."

The lawsuit and Tuesday’s process-serving incident have only intensified the animosity surrounding the LSU-Ole Miss rivalry.

With legal trouble, transfer drama and a major SEC matchup all colliding, Saturday’s game now has even more fuel behind it.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

title: US Federal Reserve votes to hike rates for the first time since 2023
excerpt:
Move comes after Trump nominated Kevin Warsh as Fed chair and said US should have lowest rates in the world

The US Federal Reserve voted to raise interest rates on Wednesday for the first time since ...
body_text:
Move comes after Trump nominated Kevin Warsh as Fed chair and said US should have lowest rates in the world

The US Federal Reserve voted to raise interest rates on Wednesday for the first time since 2023 as the central bank continues to fight to tamp down inflation.

The Fed’s open market committee voted unanimously to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%. This is the first time the Fed has raised rates since July 2023 and potentially sets Kevin Warsh, the current Fed chair, on a collision course with Donald Trump.

“Inflation remains elevated. Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal,” the committee said in a statement.

The move comes after Trump explicitly said the US should have the “LOWEST RATE of any country in the World” and that he would “stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit” if the central bank doesn’t lower rates. Trump nominated Warsh under the expectation that he would cut rates, though Warsh has said he maintains independence from the White House.

The ongoing US-Israel war with Iran, has driven up inflation, especially energy prices. Gas prices have remained, on average, $1 a gallon more expensive compared with a year ago. Diesel fuel, which is used for buses, trains and trucks, recently reached an all-time high of $6.31.

Concerns about inflation have induced a sell-off in the US bond market, with the yield on the 10-year treasury note hitting a 19-year high earlier this week, despite efforts from the US treasury to calm the market. Typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, trouble in the US bond market can lead to higher interest rates for consumer and business loans.

The Fed uses interest rates as a tool to cool price increases by slowing activity. Higher interest rates impact mortgages, car payments, student debt and other types of loans. After inflation reached a generational high of 9.1% in June 2022, the Fed increased rates 11 times from 2022 and 2023. Rates were brought up to a target range of 5.25% to 5.5% before the Fed eventually started lowering rates in 2024 and 2025.

At the beginning of the year, when the annualized inflation rate was 1% lower than current levels, a Fed rate hike seemed highly unlikely. A majority of Fed officials were actually predicting a rate cut before the end of the year. But inflation in August remained stubbornly high while unemployment was steady, which furthered the chances of a rate hike.

Higher prices have painted a grim economic outlook as voters prepare to head to the polls in November. Recent data and surveys have shown heightened inflation has wiped out wage gains for Americans and dampened consumer outlook. In August, hourly earnings for employees decreased by 0.1% year-over-year after accounting for inflation and fell by 0.3% from the month prior. Consumer sentiment has also rapidly declined, according to a monthly survey from the University of Michigan, while expectations for more inflation have increased.

Candidates on both sides of the political aisle have sought to make cost-of-living concerns and the economy a forefront of their campaigns, but voters are split on which party has the greatest advantage on this issue, according to recent Pew Research Center data.

Meanwhile, Trump has implored Republican voters to pretend as if they are voting for him on their midterm ballot and promised every American a $5000 “Trump dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress. Critics have called the move akin to bribery and warned of the financial implications, especially after the US government debt reached a record-high $40tn last month.

title: Federal Reserve raises interest rates for first time since July 2023 – live
excerpt:
Kevin Warsh, Donald Trump’s pick for Fed chair, raises rates despite intense pressure from president

As expected, the committee said it has “decided to raise the target range for the federal funds ra...
body_text:
Kevin Warsh, Donald Trump’s pick for Fed chair, raises rates despite intense pressure from president

As expected, the committee said it has “decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate. The committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.”

The 12-0 decision will be a blow to Donald Trump who wanted Kevin Warsh to cut rates. The vote means two other Trump Fed appointees - Michelle Bowman and Christopher Waller - agreed that it was time to raise rates, undercutting any potential messaging from the White House that Warsh and co. had been pressured into a rate hike by the other members of the Federal Open Market Committee.

The ongoing US-Israel war against Iran has driven up inflation, especially energy prices. Gas prices have remained, on average, $1 a gallon more expensive compared with a year ago. Diesel fuel, which is used for buses, trains and trucks, recently reached an all-time high of $6.31.

Concerns about inflation have induced a sell-off in the US bond market, with the yield on the 10-year treasury note hitting a 19-year high earlier this week, despite efforts from the US treasury to calm the market. Typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, trouble in the US bond market can lead to higher interest rates for consumer and business loans.

The Fed uses interest rates as a tool to cool price increases by slowing activity. Higher interest rates affect mortgages, car payments, student debt and other types of loans. After inflation reached a generational high of 9.1% in June 2022, the Fed increased rates 11 times from 2022 and 2023. Rates were brought up to a target range of 5.25% to 5.5% before the Fed eventually started lowering them in 2024 and 2025.

At the beginning of the year, when the annualised inflation rate was 1% lower than current levels, a Fed rate hike seemed highly unlikely. A majority of Fed officials were actually predicting a rate cut before the end of the year. But inflation in August remained stubbornly high while unemployment was steady, which furthered the chances of a rate hike.

Higher prices have painted a grim economic outlook as voters prepare to head to the polls in November. Recent data and surveys have shown heightened inflation has wiped out wage gains for Americans and dampened consumer outlook. In August, hourly earnings for employees decreased by 0.1% year-over-year after accounting for inflation and fell by 0.3% from the month prior. Consumer sentiment has also rapidly declined, according to a monthly survey from the University of Michigan, while expectations for more inflation have increased.

Candidates on both sides of the political aisle have sought to make cost-of-living concerns and the economy a forefront of their campaigns, but voters are split on which party has the greatest advantage on this issue, according to recent Pew Research Center data.

Meanwhile, Donald Trump has implored Republican voters to pretend as if they are voting for him on their midterm ballot and promised every American a $5,000 “Trump dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress. Critics have called the move akin to bribery and warned of the financial implications, especially after the US government debt reached a record-high $40tn last month.

We’ve yet to hear from the White House and Donald Trump hasn’t been active on his Truth Social platform so far today, but we’ll no doubt get his reaction to the news soon.

The rate increase is a turnaround for Fed chair Kevin Warsh - who we’ll hear from shortly – and sets him up for a potential showdown with Donald Trump, who nominated him for the job.

Warsh had often suggested last year when under consideration by the US president that the Fed could reduce its key rate, echoing the president’s call for lower borrowing costs.

But Trump’s war on Iran has evidently changed all that, and Warsh has emphasised several times since taking over the role in May that he was committed to the Fed’s independence from political pressures.

The decision was unanimous, with the vote 12 – 0.

In its press release, the committee said:

double quotation markEconomic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

Inflation remains elevated. Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.

As expected, the committee said it has “decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate. The committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.”

According to a Duke University survey of 32 former Fed governors, regional presidents and staffers, 29 endorsed a rate hike, two didn’t respond and one said the Fed should hold rates steady.

“The Fed and new chair’s credibility is on the line,” one former official said.

double quotation markI am no longer confident that PCE inflation will return to 2% in the next year or two without the Fed raising interest rates.

Above all, the upside risks to the inflation outlook have worsened since July: energy prices have not reversed as expected, tariff pass-through continues, and the AI build-out is adding to price pressures.

double quotation markEarlier in the year, it appeared that there was some hope that inflation would decline closer to its 2 percent target within a year or two. That now appears less likely.

While some of the effects of tariffs and war-induced shortages may manifest as price-level effects, with temporary inflation consequences, it’s hard to have much confidence in that. Thus, a more sustained increase in inflation is quite possible.

Clearly, none of those who responded to the poll backed a rate cut, which Donald Trump has been pushing for.

However, they also didn’t think dramatically high rate increases would be necessary to tackle the inflation challenge.

The Fed has two mandates: price stability and supporting the job market. The jobs market has remained robust but spikes in energy prices have put the central bank under pressure to raise rates in order to bring down inflation. Americans have spent over $100bn extra on gasoline and diesel during Trump’s war on Iran than they would have had there been no war, according to estimates by the Climate Solutions Lab at Brown University.

Good afternoon. The US Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023 amid persistently high inflation.

After deciding to hold rates steady at its last meeting in July, the Fed is now anticipated to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point (25 basis points), bringing the benchmark federal funds rate to a new target range of 3.75% to 4%.

The central bank’s last increase effectively bookended its Covid pandemic response, but inflation has remained above its 2% target for more than five years now and has been further exacerbated by Donald Trump’s disastrous and ongoing war against Iran.

The US president has repeatedly demanded that rates be cut, creating intense pressure on his handpicked chair, Kevin Warsh. On Sunday, days before the Fed’s September meeting was due to kick off, Trump said the United States should have “the lowest interest rate in the world” regardless of what the data indicates about inflation or the economy.

If he decides to go ahead with the hike, Warsh will no doubt infuriate the president, who regularly attacked his predecessor Jerome Powell. Trump has so far been more supportive of Warsh since he took charge earlier this year, but he’s become more vocal recently.

“LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT,” the president posted on ​social media two weeks ago.

The Fed’s decision comes just weeks out from November’s crucial US midterm elections, which will determine whether or not Trump’s Republican party retains control of Congress, with affordability and the cost-of-living crisis the major issue for voters.

The Fed is due to release its decision at 2pm ET, and Warsh will hold a press conference at 2.30. We’ll bring you all the latest here, so stay tuned.

title: ESPN re-signs Joe Buck for more than $100 million, highlighting company strategy
excerpt:
Pate wants to capture the "vibe" of college campus before a big game.

ESPN and Joe Buck have agreed to a six-year contract extension worth around $108 million. The deal will raise Buck’s annual salar...
body_text:
Pate wants to capture the "vibe" of college campus before a big game.

ESPN and Joe Buck have agreed to a six-year contract extension worth around $108 million. The deal will raise Buck’s annual salary from $15 million to $18 million, as The Athletic first reported Wednesday.

Buck signed with ESPN in 2022 alongside his longtime broadcast partner, Troy Aikman. In terms of scale, signing Buck and Aikman marked one of ESPN’s most important talent acquisitions in its 40-year history.

The network spent years trying to find a booth that could match the quality of its competitors, from Sean McDonough and Steve Levy to Booger McFarland and Jason Witten. Those pairings did not work.

Joe Buck on the field before the game at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, on Nov. 6, 2023. (Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Buck and Aikman do. In fact, they are often considered the best game duo in all of sports.

Aikman, who signed a five-year, $90 million contract with ESPN, remains unsigned. His contract expires after the Super Bowl in February.

ESPN commentator Troy Aikman walks the field prior to the game between the Kansas City Chiefs and Washington Commanders at Arrowhead Stadium on Oct. 27, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Brooke Sutton/Getty Images)

Buck’s new deal secures him for not only the upcoming Super Bowl but also ESPN’s next one in 2031. At 57, Buck could be in line for another contract after this one.

For context, Al Michaels still calls Thursday Night Football for Amazon Prime at 81.

JOSH PATE DISCUSSES NEW ESPN SHOW, FOUR FACES OF ESPN, PAT MCAFEE AND FUTURE OF MEDIA COMPANY WITH OUTKICK

Joe Buck is now tied with Aikman as ESPN’s third-highest-paid on-air personality, behind Stephen A. Smith and Pat McAfee. Smith makes around $21 million per year, while McAfee makes around $30 million.

Note: McAfee’s deal is not a standard talent contract. He licenses his daily studio show to the network and has a separate agreement that includes roles on "College GameDay," "Monday Night Countdown," and other ESPN appearances.

McAfee is reportedly in contract discussions with ESPN on a renewal worth around $65 million per year.

The deals for Buck, McAfee, Aikman, and Smith highlight ESPN’s strategy under chairman Jimmy Pitaro. The stars get paid. The middle class does not.

ESPN announcers Joe Buck and Troy Aikman stand on the sideline before an NFL wild-card playoff game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Fla., on Jan. 16, 2023. (Getty Images)

Renewals for those four personalities come as ESPN laid off multiple on-air talents in July, following another round of layoffs that affected 20 on-air talents in 2023.

Other ESPN talents in the "star" category include Michael Wilbon, Tony Kornheiser, Kirk Herbstreit, and Mike Breen.

Considering the value of calling a Super Bowl, Buck might be the most valuable of them.

Buck could also return to calling the World Series if ESPN adds the event to its portfolio in 2029. According to The Athletic, Pitaro has told Buck he would like him to call the World Series if ESPN adds it.

The World Series is currently exclusive to FOX, where Buck long called the event, but could be split between multiple broadcast partners in the next rights negotiations.

FOX, ESPN, NBC, and Netflix are among the likely bidders.

title: Lindsay Clancy prosecutors face dilemma: Retrial or plea deal in case involving 3 strangled children
excerpt:
Fox News contributor and constitutional legal scholar Jonathan Turley breaks down recent statements from jurors in Lindsay Clancy's mistrial and predicts where the case is headed next.

Prosecutors pu...
body_text:
Fox News contributor and constitutional legal scholar Jonathan Turley breaks down recent statements from jurors in Lindsay Clancy's mistrial and predicts where the case is headed next.

Prosecutors pursuing a second trial against Lindsay Clancy could face the same obstacle that produced a hung jury the first time: finding 12 Massachusetts jurors willing to unanimously reject her insanity defense.

Jonathan Turley, a Fox News contributor and professor at The George Washington University Law School, said the prosecution must weigh the possibility of another deadlocked trial against the political and emotional consequences of abandoning the case.

"The question is whether they could ever get a jury, particularly in Massachusetts, that would unanimously vote against this defendant," Turley told Fox News Digital. "For prosecutors, they have to weigh that, but they may find the alternative equally unappealing — to simply walk away and say, 'There are three dead children here, but we just don't think we could ever win this case.'"

LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON SIGNALS HE'S OPEN TO A DEAL, HOPES DA WILL 'REVISIT' CASE

Defendant Lindsay Clancy watches jurors enter the courtroom during her murder trial on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)

Neama Rahmani, a former federal prosecutor, said he believes the district attorney's office should try and negotiate a deal — but also that it appears unlikely due to the nature of the crime and the defense's position after deadlocked jurors split 11-1, with only a single holdout in favor of finding Clancy guilty of murder in the strangling deaths of her three young children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months.

"The reason I don't think there's any deal to be made here is Reddington has come out during his media tour and said that he's not going to accept any deal that results in jail time," he told Fox News Digital. "Even if you're talking about first-degree or second-degree murder, in Massachusetts, first-degree, of course, has no possibility of parole. Second-degree has the possibility of a parole. That's not something that Reddington and the defense are going to accept."

Lindsay Clancy's defense lawyer Kevin J. Reddington addresses the media outside of Plymouth Superior Court, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

LINDSAY CLANCY'S LAWYER REVEALS POST-MISTRIAL STRATEGY AS RETRIAL LOOMS

The defense does not dispute that Clancy, a 36-year-old former delivery room nurse, choked her three children to death with exercise bands in January 2023. Then she tried to kill herself.

She survived a fall from a second-story window and is now paralyzed.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Her defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, has argued that she is not criminally responsible for the deaths due to mental illness or defect.

LINDSAY CLANCY'S ATTORNEY ASKS JUDGE TO ACQUIT HER OUTRIGHT, ENDING CASE AND BARRING A RETRIAL

Still, he's said in recent interviews that he is open to talking about a deal, and he told Fox News' Bryan Llenas last week that if prosecutors reduced the top charge to second-degree murder, he would opt for a bench trial — one without jurors — in the hope that she receives probation as punishment.

"I would like to see [Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz] reduce it to a second-degree so we could possibly waive a jury and try the case before a judge," he said. "I would see Tim determine that the case should not go forward and dismiss it, or in the alternative fashion, something where Lindsay gets the mental, physical help that she needs rather than criminal prosecution — because I would not ever, ever in a million years have that woman go to Framingham State Prison."

District Attorney Timothy Cruz leaves Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

As prosecutors weigh a potential retrial, Judge William Sullivan is protecting the names of jurors in her mistrial, ordering their identities to be impounded indefinitely and the confidential juror questionnaires to be impounded for at least the next 10 days.

JUROR ON LINDSAY CLANCY TRIAL SAYS 'WE LET DOWN LINDSAY' FOLLOWING MISTRIAL

Defendant Lindsay Clancy listens during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., on Thursday, July 30, 2026. (CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via AP, Pool)

He cited threats and concerns for their safety.

Clancy, who is charged with murder in the strangling deaths of her three children, is due back in court on Sept. 29.

title: DAVID MARCUS: Big Tech invented AI doomsday to duck real life problems
excerpt: Vice President JD Vance on Monday confirmed the Trump administration is "concerned" about the development of artificial intelligence, but that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic seeking government re...
body_text:
Vice President JD Vance on Monday confirmed the Trump administration is "concerned" about the development of artificial intelligence, but that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic seeking government regulation seems like a "bit of a Trojan horse."

As if Americans didn’t have enough to worry about — making ends meet and planning for the future — the heads of the world’s largest artificial-intelligence companies are now warning that their groundbreaking technology could leave us with no future at all: We may all be dead.

It really is a shame, given that we just survived climate change and COVID-19. Now this? Maybe we can just shut down AI for two weeks to flatten the curve.

This week, Democrats have been jumping all over themselves to hop on board this moribund bandwagon to do what they always do — regulate industry to death and hamper growth.

FILE - Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., conduct a news conference to announce the Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act in the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday, March 25, 2026. ((Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

SANDERS PUSHES 'DEATH PENALTY' FOR CRUCIAL US INDUSTRY THAT COULD GIVE ADVANTAGE TO FOREIGN ADVERSARIES

According to Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., "Congress, under both Democratic and Republican control, has been asleep at the wheel, and we now have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."

Meanwhile, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., warned that "AI technology can be very dangerous when pursued without any guardrails." But given her repeated predictions that the world will end within five years because of climate change, it’s unclear why it matters.

RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION

Look, AI is not going to destroy humanity in the next decade, as Jacob Coxon, a former employee and so-called whistleblower at Anthropic — a leading AI company — warned recently. Frankly, the notion is absurd, which is why nobody can actually explain it.

One must seriously ask oneself, how exactly is AI going to kill me? Is it going to come to my house with a gun, is it going to hack the nuke codes or unleash a deadly virus? Surely, it's not that hard to have human beings as fail-safes in those scenarios.

THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

No, the dangers attendant to AI are not sci-fi fantasies of super intelligence going rogue and plotting the demise of the meat puppets. As exciting as all of that is, the real dangers are much more mundane, and much more implacable.

Across the country, local school boards are struggling with whether and how to use AI in kids’ education. County commissioners are balancing the crime fighting capability of AI-driven cameras against personal freedom. And in Congress, lawmakers are debating outdated laws governing Big Tech’s liability, including Section 230 of the Communications Act, which was written in the technological stone age of 1996.

White House AI proposals highlighted growing concerns over scams, censorship and the future of jobs in an increasingly automated economy. (Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

These practical applications of AI are what Americans are most concerned about, not fabulist movie scenarios meant to scare us all into handing power over the smart set, again.

All the usual suspects, like Bill Gates and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, are out there saying that the threat of AI requires some kind of woke world governing body, but Americans will not accept such trampling of their freedom. Not this time.

TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’

At the end of the day, AI is a product. It's not magic. It's not some unstoppable force of nature. And like any product, from toothpicks to tractors, the government has a role to play in making sure it is safe for the public.

Viewed from this product angle, it is easy to see why Big Tech would rather talk about esoteric threats of Armageddon than what they are doing to fight bias in their algorithms, or take the safety of children online seriously.

Big Tech and retail leaders are promising faster scam detection, stronger verification and better reporting tools for consumers. (Halfpoint/Getty Images)

In fact, what Big Tech is really doing is inventing a problem that isn’t there to avoid addressing the very real ones that are.

Even if we did force AI companies to shut down for two months and put their servers six feet apart with masks on, it would have no impact on the actual issues that people care about regarding so-called artificial intelligence.

Big Tech doomerism is a distraction, because, after all, who has time to worry about teenagers getting addicted to social media or chatbots happily cheering on suicide when the world might end in ten days?

What the American people need and deserve are not grand, fruitless, hand-waiving gestures that seek to halt research that probably can’t be halted anyway — certainly not in China. They need sound policy regarding the practical applications of AI.

People are rightfully suspicious, and even a bit scared of AI technology. But the answers to those fears do not exist in the cloud, so to speak, but on the ground — where the virtual rubber meets the very real road.

The question is not whether AI will kill us, the question is how our society will choose to use it, and human beings remain in charge of that, regardless of predictions of doom.

David Marcus is a columnist living in West Virginia and the author of "Charade: The COVID Lies That Crushed A Nation."

title: Greens just four points behind Labour in urban areas, poll reveals
excerpt:
Exclusive: Party could take 40 seats if result replicated at next election, according to Labour-linked thinktank

The Green party is just four points behind Labour in urban constituencies, putting the...
body_text:
Exclusive: Party could take 40 seats if result replicated at next election, according to Labour-linked thinktank

The Green party is just four points behind Labour in urban constituencies, putting them within touching distance of taking as many as 40 seats if the result was replicated at the next election, according to new polling by a Labour-linked thinktank.

The survey by ThinkLabour, which has extensive links to Andy Burnham’s government, finds that urban voters have moved in large numbers towards Zack Polanski’s party since the 2024 general election. The research highlights the challenge Labour faces holding onto the Holborn and St Pancras seat in the face of a challenge from Polanski himself at next month’s byelection.

The study’s authors warn that evidence from previous electoral battles between the two parties suggests Labour politicians should dial down direct attacks on the Greens for fear of looking like they are “kicking a puppy”.

Christabel Cooper, one of the report’s authors, said: “The previous administration [under Keir Starmer] had always banked on the fact that Labour would be able to say to people who vote Green that they would get Nigel Farage as prime minister.

“But in the 40 seats that we have identified, that is no longer the case – the Greens can claim to be the progressives’ party of choice.”

She added that evidence from other elections where the party has gone head to head with Labour suggests that progressives dislike aggressive attacks on the Greens.

“The sorts of people who would consider voting Labour consider attacking the Greens like kicking a puppy. They think, we are all supposed to be nice and liberal, why are we having a go at the Greens?”

The findings, which have been discussed with strategists in No 10 as they look to solidify separate polling gains made in Burnham’s early weeks as prime minister, show Labour faces a difficult task winning back urban progressives who helped the party win the last election.

ThinkLabour’s former chief executive Alison Phillips is now Burnham’s chief of staff, while other alumni of the organisation have senior roles across government.

The research was carried out as Burnham was about to take office in Downing Street, meaning it will not have captured the full effect of the “Burnham bounce”, which has seen Labour gain ground with progressive voters and pull level with Reform UK.

The poll shows that support for the Greens has increased by 12 points in major cities since the general election, while Labour’s vote share has fallen by 20 points, leaving Labour only 4 points ahead in some of its most reliable strongholds.

It found that the move away from Labour to the Greens has been more pronounced among voters who are financially struggling, undermining the stereotype of Green voters as affluent liberals.

The report warned that urban voters felt they did not know what Labour’s values were, in part because of some of the counterintuitive measures taken by Starmer in his early days as prime minister, such as cutting winter fuel payments.

It also warns that winning these voters back will mean focusing immigration reforms on tackling small boat crossings rather than wider measures to tackle legal migration as well.

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is bringing in measures to make it harder for legal migrants to achieve settled status, which have proved controversial with Labour MPs and activists.

The report said: “On divisive areas such as immigration, where liberals and social conservatives can agree on some outcomes – reducing small boat crossings, for example – it should primarily focus on these.

“Where its policies appear tough or restrictive, Labour must be able to make a convincing progressive case for them, showing how they solve practical problems rather than simply signalling to the right.”

The researchers also found that attacks on the Greens over foreign policy had the most effect with the voters Labour is trying to win back, in part because they found these more credible than other criticisms.

While urban voters did not like Green policies on legalising drugs – which Labour focused on during the failed campaign to win the Gorton and Denton byelection – they did not view them as a particularly credible threat.

Personal attacks on Polanski, meanwhile, went down badly among those considering voting Green, who viewed criticisms of his CV and his past as a hypnotherapist as especially non-credible.

The Green leader has previously come under fire for telling a journalist in 2013 he could enlarge women’s breasts with hypnotherapy – comments he has since said he regrets.

title: Hannah Einbinder's brutal message to Ed Sheeran fuels growing celebrity revolt over Macklemore tour drama
excerpt: 'The Gun Show' host Mike 'Gunz' Gunzelman discusses four opening acts quitting Ed Sheeran's concert tour after Macklemore was dropped. Gunzelman analyzes online pressure on performers to take politica...
body_text:
'The Gun Show' host Mike 'Gunz' Gunzelman discusses four opening acts quitting Ed Sheeran's concert tour after Macklemore was dropped. Gunzelman analyzes online pressure on performers to take political positions and compares the music industry reaction to 2024 college campus demonstrations.

Hannah Einbinder has taken aim at Ed Sheeran amid the growing backlash over Macklemore’s removal from the singer’s U.S. tour.

The "Hacks" star criticized Sheeran on Instagram, joking that she was speaking "as a ginger" before wishing him an especially painful sunburn.

"Ed Sheeran i say this as a ginger. i hope you get a REALLY bad sun burn the kind on the back of your entire body where it hurts to lie down or walk or sit."

MACKLEMORE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER GETTING KICKED OFF ED SHEERAN TOUR AFTER PRO-PALESTINE STANCE

Hannah Einbinder slammed Ed Sheeran over his Palestinian stance. (Getty Images)

Her post came after Macklemore was dropped from Sheeran’s "Loop Tour" following onstage comments supporting Palestine.

Einbinder was among several celebrities to publicly call out Sheeran, who addressed the controversy in a lengthy statement posted Tuesday.

"Macklemore asked to join my tour last year and I agreed, because I respect him as an artist," Sheeran wrote on social media. "As with all my support acts, I agree that they play a setlist of their choosing."

On Monday, Macklemore had claimed that Sheeran told him Robert Kraft, the owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium, had rallied other stadium owners to oppose allowing the rapper to perform. According to his account, the venues allegedly gave Sheeran an ultimatum: "if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues."

Sheeran’s statement offered a different account of the events, saying that after Macklemore’s performances at his New Jersey shows, venues scheduled for upcoming tour dates told organizers they would pull the shows if Macklemore remained on the lineup.

"After Macklemore’s performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting," Sheeran wrote. "I was informed that this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than on everything that was said. I spoke with the venues at length all week to try and build a bridge. One of those people was Robert Kraft. I was also involved in direct talks with promoters along with activists on both sides to try and find a mutual resolution for all, but the venue’s and promoter’s decision was final."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Macklemore was kicked off of Sheeran's tour due to his pro-Palestinian remarks.  (Kevin Mazur/WireImage)

Sheeran said he has deliberately avoided using his professional platform for politics because his audience includes young people and children from diverse backgrounds. Sheeran said concertgoers attend his shows expecting "a place of safety and sanctuary" rather than a political forum.

"There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics – my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds," he wrote. "Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore’s strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes. However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace. I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change."

Sheeran also rejected the suggestion that his decision not to speak publicly about his personal beliefs made him indifferent to the conflict.

"I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care."

MICK JAGGER DOESN'T WANT TO 'LECTURE' FANS, SAYS HIS JOB IS TO MAKE PEOPLE 'HAVE THE BEST TIME'

However, his statement has done little to quiet the criticism.

"Wicked" actor Marissa Bode accused Sheeran of lacking a backbone, writing that although she uses a wheelchair, she still has a "f---ing spine," before adding her support for Palestine on Instagram.

"Ed Sheeran, my legs may not work like they used to before, but at least I have a f---ing spine. Free Palestine, b----," she wrote.

Marissa Bode slammed Sheeran, calling him a "b----." (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images)

Children’s educator and YouTube sensation Ms. Rachel similarly said Sheeran had "caved" to people who opposed Macklemore’s advocacy and argued that silence over Gaza is not neutral.

"Ed Sheeran had an opportunity [to] show that we won’t be bullied into punishing people for supporting Palestine. Instead he caved to people who refuse to accept what the world knows. A genocide is happening in Gaza. We all need to speak out against it."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Ms. Rachel, also known as Rachel Griffin-Accurso, has been open about her stance throughout the years.  (Variety via Getty Images)

PAUL MCCARTNEY SAYS BEATLES CLASSIC UNITES AUDIENCES 'IN TRUMP’S AMERICA' DESPITE POLITICAL DIVIDE

Former Pink Floyd member Roger Waters delivered one of the harshest responses, posting a video in which he contrasted Macklemore’s willingness to speak out with Sheeran’s refusal to take a public position.

"I just have a little message for you," he said in a video he shared on social media. "There are two kinds of people in this world, Ed. There are people who do the right thing. That rapper Macklemore would be one of those people. And there are people, many of them sadly little – excuse me, I nearly used the F-word then, p----s like you who do the wrong thing. Goodbye."

Macklemore has also criticized Sheeran’s stance, though he said their friendship was not necessarily over.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

He argued that Sheeran could not move beyond his public position of "not taking sides," adding that refusing to choose a side in an unequal conflict does not amount to neutrality.

The fallout has also affected Sheeran’s touring lineup.

Responding to Macklemore's claims, Sheeran said he was "not complicit."  (Dia Dipasupil)

Finneas, Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham and Irish folk band Beoga all announced that they would withdraw from upcoming dates in solidarity with Macklemore.

Finneas said artists should not be silenced when speaking for oppressed people, while Rowe condemned the use of wealth and venue power to suppress pro-Palestinian voices.

Lukas Graham wrote that he was grateful for his friendship with Sheeran, but couldn't "carry on with tour as things stand," before withdrawing.

"I'm sorry we won't be there. This is a difficult decision, but it's one I need to stand by," Graham added.

Macklemore has been speaking about Palestine for three years, and said now is not the time to be silenced.  (Fox News Digital)

A week after Macklemore repeatedly called to "Free Palestine" and performed his anti-Israel song "Hind’s Hall" while opening for Sheeran, the rapper was dropped from the remaining U.S. dates he was scheduled to perform on the "Shape of You" singer's tour.

"As the concert promoter for Ed Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour, we have been notified by venues on the upcoming U.S. tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans," Messina Touring Group, the promoter of the U.S. leg of Sheeran’s "Loop Tour," said in a statement to Rolling Stone. "After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates."

While Macklemore said he hopes his relationship with Sheeran won't crumble over this, he stands by his position.

"I didn’t need 10 shows from Ed. I needed 2. Two chances to stand in front of 90,000 people and say the words that somehow became too dangerous to say. Free Palestine. But if those words cost me the stage, while turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I’ve ever been on."

Fox News Digital's Tracy Wright contributed to this post.

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

title: No conspiracy, no mystery, just a gift from a Russian oligarch
excerpt:
A ‘generous wedding gift’ from a ‘dear friend’ raises questions not entirely answered by Bettina and Don Jr’s Instagram caption

This was originally published in This Week in Trumpland. Sign up to rec...
body_text:
A ‘generous wedding gift’ from a ‘dear friend’ raises questions not entirely answered by Bettina and Don Jr’s Instagram caption

This was originally published in This Week in Trumpland. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday

Anyone who has gotten married knows how the costs can rack up. There’s the venue, the photographers, the flowers, the cake, the napkins, the DJ (can you tell I got married earlier this year?), the disco ball that costs a barely believable $700, the outfits for the flower girls, the knives and forks, the tuxedo socks, which you previously didn’t know existed, the gifts for the best man and maid of honour, the events that you decided to throw before and after the day itself (honestly, it’s just a never-ending stream of people with their hands out), the seating chart that despite you making it yourself somehow ended up costing three figures, the chairs that you paid extra for because your now-wife didn’t like the colour of the ones the venue would have provided for free, the tanning moisturiser that you had to buy in two different shades because the first one made you look like a corpse, the teeth whitening, the Uber credit that you have a sneaking suspicion your best friend turned a profit on, the honeymoon and more (for the record, it was a lovely day and worth every penny).

It almost makes one wish they had a recent acquaintance who is a Russian oligarch and a close Putin ally who is willing to spend, for no particular reason, hundreds of thousands of dollars to defray some of the costs.

That’s what Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, managed to wangle for his wedding after-party in May, when Umar Kremlev, president of the International Boxing Association and reported gambling market guru, covered the cost of an entire private island for the newlyweds and their guests and paid for a lavish fireworks show. ProPublica, which broke the story this week, reported that the relationship represents “an extraordinary development: a member of Putin’s circle financially supporting the president’s son and gaining intimate access to the Trump family”.

Well, quite. Do we even need to explain that this matters because Trump Jr is a key player in his dad’s political world? He was a key voice in encouraging Donald Trump Sr’s selection of JD Vance as his running mate two years ago, and has served as a political adviser to Trump, reportedly helping choose members of his cabinet.

That influence makes it extra concerning that Kremlev has managed to develop such a close relationship with Trump Jr. As well as paying for much of Trump Jr’s post-wedding celebration, Kremlev was also among about 50 guests in attendance at what the president called “a small, little private affair” when he explained why he wouldn’t be joining the celebration. The party took place days after, ProPublica reported, Kremlev had accompanied Putin on a trip to China.

double quotation markIn response to detailed questions, a spokesperson for Trump Jr did not dispute the wedding payments from Kremlev. ‘Umar is a personal friend of Don,’ he said. The spokesman said that Kremlev is ‘not someone he has a business relationship with’ and that the men met through a mutual friend in the hunting world and bonded over their love of boxing and the outdoors.

Bettina Trump, Trump Jr’s new wife, attempted some PR damage control on her Instagram on Tuesday, but kind of botched it: she decried “fake news” before going on to confirm that, yep, Kremlev did pay for two nights of celebrations.

“It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift,” she wrote in a caption signed “Don & Bettina”.

In a statement to various outlets the president said he had “never heard” of his son’s close friend.

“Kremlev didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding,” Trump said, somewhat confusingly.

The president, 80, added: “It was an ‘afterparty’ given in their honor. Not a big deal! I was not present at the party.”

Unfortunately for Trump and son, not everyone agrees that the affair is not a big deal.

On Monday House Democrats, who are already investigating ways in which the Trump family has become richer during his presidency, wrote to Trump Jr that the Kremlev affair “may be the most serious allegation against you to date”.

The representative Robert Garcia, the ranking Democrat on the House oversight committee, added: “The secretive and exorbitant gifts you have received as the son of a sitting US president from a member of Putin’s inner circle raises serious national security and public corruption concerns.”

The letter went on: “Given that you reportedly advise your father, the president of the United States, on issues of national security and vetting White House personnel, any possible foreign entanglement deserves close scrutiny.”
 While we wait to see how that goes, there’s an important lesson here for the rest of us: as tempting as it might be to accept a Russian oligarch’s offer to help pay for napkins and forks and knives, people might have some questions – especially if your dad is the president of the United States.

title: Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case found dead at his west London home
excerpt:
HSBC director Nicholas Brandram, 44, was found unresponsive by emergency services on Tuesday evening

A senior city banker suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a moving bus in the “Putney pus...
body_text:
HSBC director Nicholas Brandram, 44, was found unresponsive by emergency services on Tuesday evening

A senior city banker suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a moving bus in the “Putney pusher” case has been found dead.

Nicholas Brandram, 44, was discovered at his home in Chiswick, west London, on Tuesday.

He was arrested in June by the Metropolitan police in connection with a 2017 incident in which a jogger running across Putney Bridge pushed a woman towards an oncoming bus.

She only avoided serious injury after the driver swerved around her at the last moment.

Brandram was a director at HSBC and had previously served in the military, reaching the rank of captain.

He was released on bail by detectives in June after being arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. In September, after answering bail, he was re-bailed with no conditions.

Video footage showed the woman being pushed by a male jogger. She fell into the road, with the jogger running on.

The Met wound down its investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects. The case, which attracted considerable attention, was unsolved.

In a statement on Wednesday, the Met said: “At 19.12 on Tuesday, 15 September officers and the London ambulance service attended an address in Chiswick, Hounslow after a man was found unresponsive inside a property.

“Sadly, a 44-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next-of-kin have been informed.

“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.

“A file will be prepared for the coroner in due course.”

The Daily Telegraph reported in 2013 that Brandram was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, the last female descendant of Queen Victoria, after he was convicted of crashing his Harley-Davidson motorbike into a female cyclist around Hyde Park Corner, before driving off without leaving his details.

In an interview with the Citywealth website in March this year, Brandram said he was a senior relationship manager at HSBC Private Bank.

He said: “I usually bicycle into our office in Mayfair from my home in west London. And then from there, can either stay at my desk, go to Canary Wharf or the City, or get on a train or go to the airport. My first meeting is ideally over breakfast and I’m ideally home for bath time. I’m a co-parenting single father with a three-year-old.”

Brandram said his proudest professional achievement was being invited to a Buckingham Palace garden party after military service in Afghanistan, and that the person he most admired was his mother. “She raised three children as a single parent and is the busiest person I know,” he said. “I’ve never met someone with greater moral integrity and courage, as well as resilience and stamina.”
